0.title: Everyone Did What Was Right in His Own Eyes: The Book of Judges
0.overview:
The message. Judges shows what happens to God’s people when they forget him, and what God does about it. Israel has the land, the law and the promises, and within a generation it is serving the gods of its neighbours. Again and again God hands his people over to their enemies, and again and again, when they groan, he raises up a deliverer to save them. But each time they sink lower, the deliverers grow more flawed, and the book ends in idolatry, rape and civil war under one verdict: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (21:25). Judges is not asking for better leaders. It shows that God’s people need a King who can change their hearts and whose rescue does not end when he dies.

Background: the writer. The book does not name its author; Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, credited Samuel. Its refrain, “In those days there was no king in Israel” (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25), looks back from a time when there was one, and it says the Jebusites were still in Jerusalem “to this day” (1:21), which points to a time before David took the city (2 Samuel 5:6–9), about 1000 BC. One note, that the Danites’ priests served their idol “until the day of the captivity of the land” (18:30), most likely reaches down to the Assyrian deportation of the north in the eighth century BC, though some take it as the loss of the ark in Eli’s day (1 Samuel 4). This commentary takes the book to have been written early in the monarchy, perhaps by Samuel or someone close to him, with that note added later.

When and where. Judges covers the time from the death of Joshua to the rise of Samuel: God “gave them judges until Samuel the prophet” (Acts 13:20). Its dates depend on the date of the exodus, which this commentary, as in Exodus and Joshua, leaves open: on the earlier date (about 1446 BC) the judges span roughly 1380 to 1050 BC; on the later, roughly 1200 to 1050 BC. The years the book gives add up to about 410, but many judges were local leaders whose times overlapped. Israel had no capital, no king and no standing army: twelve tribes loosely bound by the covenant and the tabernacle at Shiloh (18:31). Canaanite towns still held the plains with chariots of iron (1:19). Their gods were Baal, the storm god believed to send rain and harvests, and the fertility goddesses Asherah and Ashtaroth, and to farmers new to the land it seemed only prudent to honour them too.

What a judge was. The Hebrew word means more than a magistrate: a judge was a leader God raised up to rescue his people and then govern them. “The LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them” (2:16). Twelve are named; six are told at length (Othniel, Ehud, Deborah with Barak, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson). The book is narrative history, told with skill and dark humour, and its narrator seldom comments. He records much he does not approve, and expects us to measure it against Deuteronomy, whose warnings the book’s cycle follows step by step.

How the book makes its case. Two introductions show the failure [1:1–3:6]: tribe after tribe “did not drive out” the Canaanites, and then “there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD” (2:10), and the cycle is set out: sin, oppression, crying out, rescue, relapse. The heart of the book [3:7–16:31] runs that cycle six times, each turn lower. Othniel is the model (3:7–11); Ehud strikes down Moab’s king (3:12–30); Deborah and Barak defeat Sisera’s chariots (chapters 4–5). At the centre stands Gideon (chapters 6–8), who tells Israel, “the LORD will rule over you” (8:23), and then makes an ephod that becomes an idol; his son Abimelech murders seventy brothers to become a bramble king (chapter 9). Jephthah, the outcast, makes his terrible vow (chapters 10–12). Samson, set apart from the womb and ruled by his eyes, saves a people who never asked to be saved (chapters 13–16). The close [chapters 17–21] gives two stories, probably from early in the period, placed last to show what the whole age was like: religion made to order (Micah’s idol and the tribe of Dan) and a society coming apart (the outrage at Gibeah and the war against Benjamin). The book opens with Israel asking, “Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites?” (1:1); near its end it asks the same question about its own brothers (20:18).

Heroes or warnings? Hebrews names Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:32), yet Gideon ends in idolatry, Jephthah in the death of his daughter and Samson in a Philistine mill. Some read the judges as models to copy; others see only failures. This commentary’s view is that Hebrews commends particular acts of faith, when they trusted God’s word and “were made strong out of weakness” (Hebrews 11:34), not their whole lives. Judges records their sins without approving them. Its real hero is God, “the LORD, the Judge” (11:27), patient with a people who keep leaving him.

Why such dark stories? Its darkest stories, Jephthah’s daughter, whom he most likely did offer up, and the Levite’s concubine, are among the hardest in Scripture, and some take them as reasons to reject the Bible’s God. But the book tells them to condemn them. Its narrator grieves where its characters do not, and shows where life without God’s rule ends: not in a little private religion but in a woman’s body on a doorstep (19:27). Scripture does not look away from such things, and neither does God.

Where it leads: to Christ. Judges points to Christ chiefly by the need it exposes and by pattern. Each judge is a partial shadow: raised up by God for helpless people, the Spirit of the LORD upon him (3:10), winning by unlikely means. Samson, whose death defeated more enemies than his life (16:30), is a broken picture of the one who conquered by dying, though Samson died for revenge and Christ for his enemies. The angel of the LORD, who calls his own name “wonderful” (13:18), is best read, this commentary holds, as the Son before his incarnation, and Isaiah promised a child called “Wonderful Counselor” who would break the oppressor’s rod “as on the day of Midian” (Isaiah 9:4, 6). Above all, the book cries out for a king. Its two darkest stories begin in Bethlehem (17:7; 19:1), and the book of Ruth, set “in the days when the judges ruled” (Ruth 1:1), ends there with the birth of David’s grandfather. Yet David failed too. So Paul, tracing the story from the judges to David, went on: “Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised” (Acts 13:23). Every judge died and the people slid back; Jesus died and rose, and “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Where everyone did what was right in his own eyes, he did what was right in his Father’s, and gives that righteousness to all who trust him.

For us. Judges warns that God’s people are seldom lost by open revolt. They drift, through comfortable compromises, and they are only one generation from forgetting (2:10), so we must tell our children what the LORD has done. Its refrain, everyone his own judge of right, describes our own age. But the book also comforts. God “was moved to pity by their groaning” (2:18), and “became impatient over the misery of Israel” (10:16). He raises up deliverers no one would have chosen. Our hope is not a better judge but the King who never fails.

1.title: The Incomplete Conquest
1.text: <sup>1</sup>After the death of Joshua, the people of Israel inquired of the LORD, "Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites, to fight against them?"<sup>2</sup>The LORD said, "Judah shall go up; behold, I have given the land into his hand."<sup>3</sup>And Judah said to Simeon his brother, "Come up with me into the territory allotted to me, that we may fight against the Canaanites. And I likewise will go with you into the territory allotted to you." So Simeon went with him.<sup>4</sup>Then Judah went up and the LORD gave the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand, and they defeated 10,000 of them at Bezek.<sup>5</sup>They found Adoni-bezek at Bezek and fought against him and defeated the Canaanites and the Perizzites.<sup>6</sup>Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him and caught him and cut off his thumbs and his big toes.<sup>7</sup>And Adoni-bezek said, "Seventy kings with their thumbs and their big toes cut off used to pick up scraps under my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me." And they brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.<sup>8</sup>And the men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire.<sup>9</sup>And afterward the men of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, in the Negeb, and in the lowland.<sup>10</sup>And Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron (now the name of Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba), and they defeated Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai.<sup>11</sup>From there they went against the inhabitants of Debir. The name of Debir was formerly Kiriath-sepher.<sup>12</sup>And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife."<sup>13</sup>And Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife.<sup>14</sup>When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?"<sup>15</sup>She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.<sup>16</sup>And the descendants of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up with the people of Judah from the city of palms into the wilderness of Judah, which lies in the Negeb near Arad, and they went and settled with the people.<sup>17</sup>And Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they defeated the Canaanites who inhabited Zephath and devoted it to destruction. So the name of the city was called Hormah.<sup>18</sup>Judah also captured Gaza with its territory, and Ashkelon with its territory, and Ekron with its territory.<sup>19</sup>And the LORD was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country, but he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron.<sup>20</sup>And Hebron was given to Caleb, as Moses had said. And he drove out from it the three sons of Anak.<sup>21</sup>But the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.<sup>22</sup>The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and the LORD was with them.<sup>23</sup>And the house of Joseph scouted out Bethel. (Now the name of the city was formerly Luz.)<sup>24</sup>And the spies saw a man coming out of the city, and they said to him, "Please show us the way into the city, and we will deal kindly with you."<sup>25</sup>And he showed them the way into the city. And they struck the city with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and all his family go.<sup>26</sup>And the man went to the land of the Hittites and built a city and called its name Luz. That is its name to this day.<sup>27</sup>Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean and its villages, or Taanach and its villages, or the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, or the inhabitants of Ibleam and its villages, or the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages, for the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land.<sup>28</sup>When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not drive them out completely.<sup>29</sup>And Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites lived in Gezer among them.<sup>30</sup>Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, or the inhabitants of Nahalol, so the Canaanites lived among them, but became subject to forced labor.<sup>31</sup>Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Acco, or the inhabitants of Sidon or of Ahlab or of Achzib or of Helbah or of Aphik or of Rehob,<sup>32</sup>so the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they did not drive them out.<sup>33</sup>Naphtali did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh, or the inhabitants of Beth-anath, so they lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. Nevertheless, the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and of Beth-anath became subject to forced labor for them.<sup>34</sup>The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the plain.<sup>35</sup>The Amorites persisted in dwelling in Mount Heres, in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim, but the hand of the house of Joseph rested heavily on them, and they became subject to forced labor.<sup>36</sup>And the border of the Amorites ran from the ascent of Akrabbim, from Sela and upward.
1.overview:
Where we are. The book opens as Joshua did, at a funeral. Joshua is dead, no one man takes his place, and the tribes must now finish taking the land God has already given them (see the introduction).

The message. God keeps every promise, but his people can stop short of what he gives. Israel begins by asking the LORD and winning, then settles, tribe by tribe, for living alongside the very things it was told to drive out. No one in this chapter rebels against God; they simply stop obeying when it becomes inconvenient, and that quiet drift is how the whole dark story of Judges begins.

Why it was said. The first hearers lived with the results: Canaanite towns in the plains, foreign gods next door, and a nation sliding from its covenant. This chapter shows them how it happened, not by one great revolt but by a thousand small accommodations.

How the chapter makes its case. Israel asks the LORD, and Judah goes up with Simeon and wins (vv. 1–4). A cruel king confesses God’s justice, Jerusalem burns, giants fall at Hebron, and Caleb’s daughter asks for springs and receives more than she asked (vv. 5–16). Then verse 19 sets two facts side by side: the LORD was with Judah, yet Judah “could not” take the plain. Benjamin leaves the Jebusites in Jerusalem (v. 21). Bethel falls through a man who takes Israel’s mercy and leaves to rebuild his old city (vv. 22–26). From there one phrase tolls through the list: “did not drive out” (vv. 27–33). When Israel grew strong it chose forced labour over obedience (v. 28); by verse 32 Asher lives among the Canaanites rather than they among Asher; and Dan is pressed back into the hills (vv. 34–36).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. God names Judah to go up first, the tribe of Jacob’s promised ruler (Genesis 49:10), and from Judah came the King who does not stop short: “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5:5). Israel left enemies in the land because it found them useful; Christ “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25). The unfinished conquest of Judges cries out for the one who finishes.

For us. Most of us do not reject God; we negotiate with sin and call it realism. This chapter asks what we keep because it is useful, and what we have quietly decided God cannot help with. The answer is not grim effort but the conquering Christ, who is with us and does not settle for half.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel begins well and then stops short. After Joshua’s death the people ask the LORD who should go up first, and he names Judah with a promise: “I have given the land into his hand” (vv. 1–2). Judah takes Simeon with him and wins at Bezek, where a captured tyrant confesses that God has repaid him (vv. 3–7). Jerusalem burns, the giants of Hebron fall, Othniel wins a city and a wife, and the Kenites settle with Judah (vv. 8–16). Then comes the turn: the LORD was with Judah, yet Judah could not take the plain (v. 19), and Benjamin leaves the Jebusites in Jerusalem (v. 21), the first of the failures that fill the rest of the chapter.
verseByVerse.theology: The first eighteen verses are the longest stretch of good news in the book. It is downhill from verse 19, and the book never fully recovers.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 10-15 and 20 are lifted almost word for word out of Joshua (Josh. 15:14-19; 14:13). Judges begins by re-running Joshua's best material, and then goes somewhere Joshua never went.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Joshua, the people of Israel inquired of the LORD, "Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites, to fight against them?" The LORD said, "Judah shall go up; behold, I have given the land into his hand." And Judah said to Simeon his brother, "Come up with me into the territory allotted to me, that we may fight against the Canaanites. And I likewise will go with you into the territory allotted to you." So Simeon went with him. Then Judah went up and the LORD gave the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand, and they defeated 10,000 of them at Bezek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel begins well: it asks the LORD what to do, and he answers with a promise, “I have given the land into his hand.” Judah goes first, with Simeon, and wins.

After the death of Joshua. Joshua began “after the death of Moses”; Judges begins after the death of Joshua. Twice now the story has restarted at a funeral. The difference is what happens next. When Moses died, God had already named a successor; here the answer is a tribe, not a man. There is no Joshua to follow Joshua.

The people of Israel inquired of the LORD. What they do is right, and it will not happen like this again: they ask God, the very thing the leaders failed to do at Gibeon, with the priest and the Urim and Thummim (the priest’s sacred lots) available in the camp (Joshua 9:14; Numbers 27:21). The book opens on its highest note. The answer speaks of the gift as already made, as God did all through Joshua: “I have given.” The land is a gift before it is a campaign.

Judah said to Simeon his brother. Judah, the largest tribe, invites Simeon, whose towns lay scattered inside Judah’s own land (Joshua 19:1, 9). The strong tribe does not go alone: come with me, and I will come with you. It is the high-water mark of brotherhood in this book. Near its end Israel will ask the same question and get the same answer, “Judah shall go up first” (20:18), but the enemy will be their brother Benjamin, a tribe nearly wiped out.

The tribe that goes first. Jacob had promised Judah the ruler’s sceptre (Genesis 49:10). From this tribe came David, and from David’s line the King who goes up first for his people and does not stop short: “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5:5).
verseByVerse.note: Judges covers roughly three centuries between Joshua and the monarchy. The “judges” were mostly military deliverers rather than courtroom figures.

verseByVerse.quote: They found Adoni-bezek at Bezek and fought against him and defeated the Canaanites and the Perizzites. Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him and caught him and cut off his thumbs and his big toes. And Adoni-bezek said, "Seventy kings with their thumbs and their big toes cut off used to pick up scraps under my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me." And they brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there. And the men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A cruel king receives exactly what he gave, and confesses that God has repaid him; and Jerusalem, untaken in Joshua’s day, falls.

Cut off his thumbs and his big toes. A man without thumbs cannot grip a sword, and a man without big toes cannot balance or run. He is disabled as a warrior and left alive as an exhibit. The text does not say God commanded it, and nothing in the law of Moses prescribed it; Israel is doing what the kings of Canaan did, and the narrator lets the victim’s own words call it justice on him, not a model for anyone.

As I have done, so God has repaid me. The prisoner’s explanation is better theology than most of what Israel will manage in this book. He does not call his fate bad luck. A Canaanite tyrant, in his humiliation, states the moral law of the universe without being taught it, the principle Jesus put in a sentence, “with the measure you use it will be measured to you” (Matthew 7:2), and Paul made unavoidable: “whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7).

Seventy kings. The number comes back in chapter 9, where an Israelite named Abimelech murders his seventy brothers on one stone to make himself king. By then it will be Israel doing what the Canaanite king did.

Fought against Jerusalem and captured it. The city Judah could not take in Joshua’s day (Joshua 15:63) is captured and burned, and for one verse the unfinished business of the last book is finished. Jerusalem lay on the border between Judah and Benjamin and was counted among Benjamin’s towns (Joshua 18:28), which is why verse 21 blames Benjamin when the victory comes undone.

Was it just? This was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), including child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Leviticus 18:24–28). It was a unique command for one moment in redemptive history, and no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is “not of this world” (John 18:36), and the church’s weapons “are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And afterward the men of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, in the Negeb, and in the lowland. And Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron (now the name of Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba), and they defeated Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai. From there they went against the inhabitants of Debir. The name of Debir was formerly Kiriath-sepher. And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife." And Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife. When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caleb’s household shows faith rewarded: Othniel wins a city, and Achsah asks her father boldly for water and receives more than she asked.

A familiar story. These verses retell Joshua 15:14–19 almost word for word: the same three giants by name, the same challenge from Caleb, the same kinsman, the same daughter.

Othniel the son of Kenaz. When the nation collapses into idolatry two chapters from now, he is the first man God raises up to rescue them (3:9), and the writer records nothing against him.

She dismounted from her donkey. Achsah has been given land in the Negeb, dry country where a field without water is a farm in name only. So she asks for the one thing that makes what she already has worth having, and she asks her father to his face. “Give me a blessing” means “give me a gift.” He gives her the upper springs and the lower springs, both: more than she requested.

Ask your Father. Achsah’s boldness rests on knowing her father’s heart. Jesus invites the same boldness towards a better Father, who gives “good things to those who ask him” (Matthew 7:11). Many of us ask God for too little, as if a dry field were all he meant us to have.

The last unmixed good. It is the last unmixed good thing in the chapter, and it is a woman asking a generous man for water. Everything after verse 19 is about people who settled for less than God had given.

Uncertain wording. “Caleb’s younger brother” could describe Othniel or his father Kenaz, so Othniel was Caleb’s brother or his nephew. “Dismounted” translates a rare verb, used elsewhere only in Joshua 15:18 and of the tent peg going down into the ground (4:21); it most likely means she got down quickly from her donkey to ask.

verseByVerse.quote: And the descendants of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up with the people of Judah from the city of palms into the wilderness of Judah, which lies in the Negeb near Arad, and they went and settled with the people. And Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they defeated the Canaanites who inhabited Zephath and devoted it to destruction. So the name of the city was called Hormah. Judah also captured Gaza with its territory, and Ashkelon with its territory, and Ekron with its territory. And the LORD was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country, but he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron. And Hebron was given to Caleb, as Moses had said. And he drove out from it the three sons of Anak. But the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD was with Judah, yet Judah stopped short at the plain: Israel’s failure was a failure of faith, not of God’s power.

The descendants of the Kenite. The Kenites were the clan of Moses’ father-in-law, a priest of Midian (Exodus 3:1), foreigners with no allotment. They will matter: in three chapters a Kenite woman, Jael, will drive a tent peg through the enemy commander’s skull while every Israelite man in the story is somewhere else (4:17–21). They had been living at “the city of palms”, Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:3), and now move south with Judah into the dry country near Arad.

The LORD was with Judah. The hinge of the chapter is one sentence whose halves do not agree. “The LORD was with Judah”: this book can say nothing higher about anybody. And then: “could not.” Set side by side, “could not” cannot be the whole truth. This is the God who put Pharaoh’s chariots at the bottom of the sea, flattened Jericho’s wall and stopped the sun over Gibeon. Iron is no difficulty to him. What changed was not the odds but how Judah looked at them: they counted the chariots and left God out of the sum. Three chapters later God will rout nine hundred iron chariots in a single battle, as if to settle the question (4:13–15).

In everyday life. So it goes with most of us. We confess the presence of God in general and then draw a map of the places where we assume he cannot help: the entrenched habit, the marriage that has been like this for years, the diagnosis. We give him the hill country and concede the plain.

The book in miniature. Caleb, of the previous generation, drove out the giants. Benjamin, of this one, did not drive out the Jebusites from the city Judah had already burned. The victory of verse 8 was real and was not held, and “to this day” says how long: until David took the citadel (2 Samuel 5:6–9).

Was God not strong enough? No. The LORD had promised victory over chariots: “you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron” (Joshua 17:18). The failure was Judah’s faith, not God’s power, and the angel at Bochim will say so (2:1–3).

Textual note. In verse 18 the Greek Old Testament reads that Judah did not take Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, which fits verse 19 and the later Philistines. The Hebrew says it did, most likely meaning a raid rather than lasting control. Either way, the coast did not stay in Israel’s hands.
verseByVerse.note: “Hormah” means “utter destruction” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–26 — The Man Who Took the Mercy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mercy accepted is not the same as God embraced. The house of Joseph goes up against Bethel, and again “the LORD was with them” (v. 22). Their spies offer a man coming out of the city kindness in return for the way in (vv. 23–24). He shows them, the city falls, and he and his family go free (v. 25). It is Rahab’s story told again, until verse 26: instead of joining Israel, the man goes north to the land of the Hittites, builds a city and names it Luz, after the city he has just betrayed. He was rescued but not changed.
verseByVerse.theology: The episode is written to remind the reader of Rahab, and then to differ from her at every point that matters. She asked for mercy and joined the people who gave it; this man took the mercy and left.
verseByVerse.examples: The land of the Hittites here probably means the country north of Israel, in Syria, well beyond Israel's reach.

verseByVerse.quote: The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and the LORD was with them. And the house of Joseph scouted out Bethel. (Now the name of the city was formerly Luz.) And the spies saw a man coming out of the city, and they said to him, "Please show us the way into the city, and we will deal kindly with you." And he showed them the way into the city. And they struck the city with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and all his family go. And the man went to the land of the Hittites and built a city and called its name Luz. That is its name to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bethel falls through a man who accepts Israel’s mercy but not Israel’s God, and goes off to rebuild his old city somewhere safer.

Please show us the way into the city. Spies, a city, a local who helps them in, and a promise of mercy kept exactly: this is Jericho again. He walks out of a burning city alive with everyone he loves. Up to this point the story is Rahab’s.

Unlike Rahab. Then the difference. Rahab asked for mercy and stayed. She lived in Israel and ended up in the family tree of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), because she wanted the God who was doing this. This man takes the mercy and leaves, goes north out of reach to the land of the Hittites, and names his new town after the pagan town he has just betrayed. He was rescued and not changed: grateful, unharmed, and gone.

Wanting the gift without the Giver. The man of Luz is very modern. Many are glad of what faith seems to offer, peace of mind, a moral compass, a carol service at Christmas, and have no intention of letting God himself rearrange their lives. Augustine diagnosed this in The City of God: the good, he said, use the world in order to enjoy God, while the wicked want to use God in order to enjoy the world. Rahab wanted the God who spared her; the man of Luz wanted only to be spared. The trouble with using God is not that it is too worldly but that it is too small: it settles for his gifts when he is offering himself.

He gave himself. Jesus did not hand out benefits and leave; he gave himself, and he calls us not only to be rescued but to follow. So ask of your own faith the question this story asks: if God gave you everything you prayed for and then stayed away, would you be content? Rahab would not have been.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Disobedience rarely announces itself: it settles in. From here the chapter becomes a list, and one phrase runs through it like a bell: “did not drive out.” Manasseh did not (v. 27), and when Israel grew strong it put the Canaanites to forced labour instead (v. 28). Ephraim did not (v. 29), nor Zebulun (v. 30). With Asher the wording turns round: Asher now lives among the Canaanites (vv. 31–32), and Naphtali the same (v. 33). Dan is not even failing to drive others out; the Amorites drive Dan back into the hills, and the chapter ends with the enemy’s border, not Israel’s (vv. 34–36).
verseByVerse.theology: No region is exempt: the failure runs from Joseph's tribes in the centre of the land to Asher and Naphtali in the far north.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch the small change of wording at verse 32: the Canaanites are now the people of the land, and Asher lives among them.

verseByVerse.quote: Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean and its villages, or Taanach and its villages, or the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, or the inhabitants of Ibleam and its villages, or the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages, for the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land. When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not drive them out completely. And Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites lived in Gezer among them. Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, or the inhabitants of Nahalol, so the Canaanites lived among them, but became subject to forced labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel grew strong enough to obey, it chose profit instead: the Canaanites became a workforce rather than being driven out.

The Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land. The reason given is almost comic in its honesty: of course Canaan objected. These are the towns Joshua listed as Manasseh’s and unconquered (Joshua 17:11–12). Nothing has moved in a generation.

When Israel grew strong. Verse 28 explains the whole chapter. The excuse used to be weakness: Joshua 17 said Manasseh “could not”, stated as fact rather than sin. Then Israel grew strong, the excuse expired, and at the moment obedience became possible they found something better to do. Forced labour is not a defeat; it is a business decision. The command was replaced by a labour policy, and everybody did well.

Forced labor. The law allowed forced labour only for distant cities; the towns of the land were to be destroyed, lest Israel learn their worship (Deuteronomy 20:10–18). The irony seems to have gone unnoticed: a nation redeemed out of forced labour by God’s own hand, within living memory, imposes it on somebody else rather than obey. Ephraim, Joshua’s own tribe, leaves Gezer exactly where Joshua’s book left it (Joshua 16:10).

The sin we keep because it is useful. We seldom keep a sin we hate; we keep the ones that work for us: the anger that gets results, the half-truth that smooths the meeting, the habit that helps us cope. John Owen’s warning holds: be killing sin, or it will be killing you. And we do not fight alone: “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Acco, or the inhabitants of Sidon or of Ahlab or of Achzib or of Helbah or of Aphik or of Rehob, so the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they did not drive them out. Naphtali did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh, or the inhabitants of Beth-anath, so they lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. Nevertheless, the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and of Beth-anath became subject to forced labor for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By now the wording has turned round: the Canaanites are no longer living among Israel; Israel is living among them.

The Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. Everywhere else the formula is that the Canaanites “lived among them”: Israel is the household and the Canaanites the lodgers. In verse 32 the phrase turns round. Asher is the minority in his own allotment, and the Canaanites are called, without comment, “the inhabitants of the land”, the phrase for the people God said to remove, now simply the name for whoever lives there.

How it happened. No day came on which Asher agreed to become a minority. It happened the way it always happens, by not doing something for long enough. Naphtali gets the same wording (v. 33): two northern tribes have become Israelites living in Canaanite country.

Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath. The names in Naphtali’s list say what that costs. Beth-shemesh is the house of the sun; Beth-anath is the house of Anath, the Canaanite war goddess. Naphtali now lives among towns named after other gods, and takes its rent from them in forced labour.

verseByVerse.quote: The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the plain. The Amorites persisted in dwelling in Mount Heres, in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim, but the hand of the house of Joseph rested heavily on them, and they became subject to forced labor. And the border of the Amorites ran from the ascent of Akrabbim, from Sela and upward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conquest runs backwards: Dan, sent to drive out the Amorites, is driven into the hills by them, and the chapter ends with the enemy’s border.

The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back. Every other tribe failed to drive somebody out. Dan is being driven: the Amorites push them up into the hills and “did not allow them to come down to the plain.” In verse 2 God gave the land into Judah’s hand; in verse 34 an Israelite tribe is confined to high ground by the people it was sent to dispossess, and the last verse traces the border of the Amorites, not of Israel.

What happens to Dan next. In chapter 18 the Danites give up on their allotment, march north, steal an idol and a priest on the way, and take a quiet town that had done nothing to anybody. The book’s darkest chapters grow from the pressure recorded here.

The chapter in summary. Across thirty-six verses Israel began by asking God a question and receiving a promise, and ended with a tribe in the hills and a border drawn for the enemy: the people who were given a country are living in somebody else’s.

1.theology:
Nobody rebelled. There is no idol in this chapter, no defiance, no refusal. There is a war that got long, an arrangement that paid, and the words did not drive out repeated eight times. That is the book's diagnosis of how a covenant nation is lost: not by a decision to abandon God but by a series of compromises, each of which seemed reasonable on the day it was made.

Could not. Verse 19 is the hinge, and its two halves do not fit: if the LORD was with Judah, iron was not too much for him. To confess God’s presence in general while marking off areas where we assume he cannot help is not a gap in belief. It is a failure to act on what we already believe.

Profit, not weakness. When Israel grew strong (v. 28), the old excuse expired and the arrangement stayed, because by then it paid.

Who will go up first? The book’s opening question is answered with a tribe, Judah, and a promise, and the tribe goes up and then stops at the plain. The question waits for a better answer. Jacob had said the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and the New Testament names the one in whom that word comes true: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who has conquered (Revelation 5:5). He is the one who goes up first for his people, as a forerunner on our behalf (Hebrews 6:20), and he does not stop short of a single enemy, for he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25).

Mercy without conversion. The man of Bethel takes Rahab's terms and leaves Rahab's God behind. He had no quarrel with Israel's God and no interest in him, and used his rescue to start again on his own terms.
1.examples:
A generation that began by asking God a question ended by keeping the enemy as a workforce, with one tribe a minority in its own allotment and another pushed off its land. There was no moment at which anybody chose it.

The phrase to test yourself against is not “I will not” but “I could not”. Name the plain you have conceded, the habit, the relationship, the fear you have quietly decided will never change, and ask what made you decide that. It is unlikely to have been new evidence about God. Then ask what you have kept because it is useful, that God told you to end. The land was given before a battle was fought, and the Lion of Judah has already gone up first; his Spirit is given to his people for exactly the ground they have conceded. Where you have settled, the way back starts with confession, not with a new resolution.

keyVerse.quote: When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not drive them out completely.
keyVerse.note: This verse explains the whole chapter. Israel’s failure was not finally weakness but choice: when obedience became possible, profit seemed wiser. It is the drift of the whole book in a sentence, and the pattern of every compromise that keeps a useful sin instead of driving it out.

1.reflection:
Israel began by asking the LORD and receiving a promise (vv. 1–2). Where do you most naturally ask God for guidance, and where do you tend to go ahead without asking?

Verse 19 says the LORD was with Judah, yet Judah “could not” take the plain. What “iron chariots” in your life or church have you quietly decided God cannot deal with?

The man of Luz accepted mercy but went off to rebuild his old life (vv. 24–26), while Rahab stayed and joined God’s people. What is the difference between wanting God’s gifts and wanting God himself, and how can you tell which you are seeking?

When Israel grew strong it put the Canaanites to work instead of driving them out (v. 28). Which sins are hardest to fight because they seem useful, and what does it look like to put them to death by the Spirit (Romans 8:13)?

2.title: The Pattern Established
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim. And he said, "I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to give to your fathers. I said, 'I will never break my covenant with you,<sup>2</sup>and you shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land; you shall break down their altars.' But you have not obeyed my voice. What is this you have done?<sup>3</sup>So now I say, I will not drive them out before you, but they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you."<sup>4</sup>As soon as the angel of the LORD spoke these words to all the people of Israel, the people lifted up their voices and wept.<sup>5</sup>And they called the name of that place Bochim. And they sacrificed there to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>When Joshua dismissed the people, the people of Israel went each to his inheritance to take possession of the land.<sup>7</sup>And the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done for Israel.<sup>8</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110 years.<sup>9</sup>And they buried him within the boundaries of his inheritance in Timnath-heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash.<sup>10</sup>And all that generation also were gathered to their fathers. And there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.<sup>11</sup>And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals.<sup>12</sup>And they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They went after other gods, from among the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed down to them. And they provoked the LORD to anger.<sup>13</sup>They abandoned the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth.<sup>14</sup>So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them over to plunderers, who plundered them. And he sold them into the hand of their surrounding enemies, so that they could no longer withstand their enemies.<sup>15</sup>Whenever they marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them for harm, as the LORD had warned, and as the LORD had sworn to them. And they were in terrible distress.<sup>16</sup>Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.<sup>17</sup>Yet they did not listen to their judges, for they whored after other gods and bowed down to them. They soon turned aside from the way in which their fathers had walked, who had obeyed the commandments of the LORD, and they did not do so.<sup>18</sup>Whenever the LORD raised up judges for them, the LORD was with the judge, and he saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge. For the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who afflicted and oppressed them.<sup>19</sup>But whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers, going after other gods, serving them and bowing down to them. They did not drop any of their practices or their stubborn ways.<sup>20</sup>So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he said, "Because this people have transgressed my covenant that I commanded their fathers and have not obeyed my voice,<sup>21</sup>I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died,<sup>22</sup>in order to test Israel by them, whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did, or not."<sup>23</sup>So the LORD left those nations, not driving them out quickly, and he did not give them into the hand of Joshua.
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 gave the symptoms: tribe after tribe settling alongside the Canaanites. Chapter 2 gives the diagnosis, and sets out the pattern that will govern the rest of the book.

The message. Israel’s trouble is not the Canaanites but its own heart: a people who forget what God has done soon forget God himself. Yet the LORD, who disciplines them by handing them over, is moved to pity by their groaning and raises up rescuers they have not deserved. Judges will be a story of human relapse and divine patience, and of a rescue that never lasts because the rescuers die.

Why it was said. The first hearers needed to understand why their history had gone the way it had, under foreign oppressors and foreign gods (see the introduction). This chapter tells them: not because God failed, but because Israel broke the covenant and did not tell its children.

How the chapter makes its case. The angel of the LORD comes up from Gilgal to Bochim and brings a covenant lawsuit: God has kept every promise, Israel has kept none of the terms, so he will no longer drive the Canaanites out (vv. 1–3). The people weep and sacrifice, and nothing changes (vv. 4–5). The narrator steps back to Joshua’s death and adds the sentence Joshua never wrote: another generation arose “who did not know the LORD” (vv. 6–10). Then he sets out the cycle the book will repeat: Israel serves the Baals (vv. 11–13), God sells them to their enemies (vv. 14–15), God raises up judges and saves them, because he is moved to pity (vv. 16–18), and when each judge dies they sink lower than before (v. 19). The nations left in the land become God’s test (vv. 20–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes, and by pattern. Every judge is a small saviour, and the Hebrew word for saving is the root of the name Jesus, “for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). But the judges died, and the rescue died with them. Israel needed a Deliverer who would not stay dead, and a covenant in which God himself would make his people know him (Jeremiah 31:34). Both came in Jesus, who “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:24), and whose Spirit writes the law on the heart.

For us. Faith is never more than one silent generation from being lost, so we must tell our children what the LORD has done. Tears are not the same as repentance. And when we groan under trouble we brought on ourselves, the God who was moved to pity then has given us a Saviour who lives for ever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his covenant; Israel has not kept its side, and tears are not the same as turning. The angel of the LORD comes up from Gilgal to Bochim and speaks as God himself, like a prosecutor stating a case (v. 1). First what God has done and promised: brought them out, brought them in, sworn never to break his covenant. Then the terms: no covenant with the inhabitants, their altars broken down. Then the charge, “you have not obeyed my voice”, and a question (v. 2). The sentence follows: God will not drive the nations out, and they and their gods will be thorns and a snare (v. 3). The people weep, name the place Bochim, “weepers”, and sacrifice, but nothing changes (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: The sentence is not an added punishment but a withdrawal. God simply stops doing the thing Israel had already stopped wanting done. They would not drive the Canaanites out; now neither will he.
verseByVerse.examples: The question at the end of verse 2 has been asked before. What is this you have done? is what God said to the woman in the garden (Gen. 3:13), and what Pharaoh said to Abraham about Sarah (Gen. 12:18). It is the question asked when the thing is already done and cannot be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim. And he said, "I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to give to your fathers. I said, 'I will never break my covenant with you, and you shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land; you shall break down their altars.' But you have not obeyed my voice. What is this you have done? So now I say, I will not drive them out before you, but they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has kept every promise and Israel has broken the covenant’s terms, so he will stop driving out the nations it refused to drive out, and they will become its thorns and snare.

The angel of the LORD. He speaks as God in the first person, without the usual “thus says the LORD”. He does not report God’s words; he uses them as his own.

Up from Gilgal. He comes from Gilgal, where the twelve stones were set up, the nation circumcised, the reproach of Egypt rolled away and the first Passover in the land eaten. The messenger travels from the place where the covenant was celebrated to a place about to be named for weeping.

I will never break my covenant with you. The speech is built like a legal case, and the order matters. First what God has done and promised, all of it kept: brought you up, brought you in, and “I will never break my covenant with you”. Grace comes first, and there is no complaint on that side of the ledger. Then the terms: make no treaties, and pull down the altars. Israel had done neither; chapter 1 is the evidence. Then a question like the one God asked Eve in the garden, the fruit already eaten: “What is this that you have done?” (Genesis 3:13). It is not a request for information.

I will not drive them out. They would not drive the Canaanites out. Very well: neither will he. The consequences are what Moses had warned, almost word for word, thorns in your sides and a snare (Numbers 33:55; Deuteronomy 7:16). What was a warning is now a verdict. Thorns wound; a snare catches. The Canaanites will be an irritation, their gods a trap, and the rest of this book is Israel walking into it. There is a kind of judgment that consists in being allowed to keep what you insisted on having.

What a covenant is. To most of us “covenant” sounds like a contract: each side does its part, and either may walk away when the other fails. We quietly treat God that way. A covenant is a bond sealed by a solemn promise, and here God made the first promise about himself. Timothy Keller often pointed out that wedding vows are not a report of present feelings but a binding promise of future love. God’s covenant is a vow of that kind. The thorns and the snare are its discipline, not its end. The bond holds when Israel’s side fails, and in Christ it holds for good: he kept the terms we broke and sealed the promise with “the blood of the eternal covenant” (Hebrews 13:20). So when you have let him down again, confess it and come back on the strength of his vow, not yours. See also Covenant of Grace in the Theological Dictionary.

For the anxious believer. A believer who fears that God has given him up may take heart from the fear itself. Those who have been given up do not grieve that God is gone, and this same chapter shows God raising up rescuers for people who had earned nothing (v. 18).

Where Christians differ: who is the angel of the LORD? He speaks as God himself and is called “the LORD”. Some take him as a created angel speaking with God’s full authority; some Jewish interpreters took him as a human messenger, perhaps a prophet. Many in the Reformed tradition and before it have seen the LORD appearing in person. This commentary’s view: he is best read as the Son appearing before his incarnation, the same figure who met Joshua as commander of the LORD’s army (Joshua 5:13–15) and who will appear again to Gideon and to Samson’s parents (chapters 6 and 13).
verseByVerse.note: “Bochim” means “weepers” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as the angel of the LORD spoke these words to all the people of Israel, the people lifted up their voices and wept. And they called the name of that place Bochim. And they sacrificed there to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people weep and sacrifice, but nothing changes: real feeling is not the same as repentance.

The people lifted up their voices and wept. The response looks right. They weep, they name the place after the weeping, and they offer sacrifice. A congregation in tears and an altar smoking: on any ordinary reckoning this is a revival meeting.

Nothing changes. Not one Canaanite is driven out the next morning. Not one altar comes down. Within a few verses the same people are bowing to Baal. That is why the scene is in the book: it warns against a particular kind of religious experience, real feeling, genuine tears, an actual sacrifice, and no change of direction whatever.

Godly grief and worldly grief. Paul makes the distinction exactly: “godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). The difference is not in the intensity of the sorrow but in what happens afterwards, and it is often not visible on the day. Weeping at what a sin has cost is not the same as hating the sin. Israel wept at the sentence about thorns and snares. It is possible to leave a church service genuinely moved, having felt something true, and to have changed nothing.

They called the name of that place Bochim. The name stuck, and it is the right name. This place is not called “Repentance”. Its name means “weepers”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — A Generation That Did Not Know
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faithfulness lasted exactly as long as the eyewitnesses. The narrator steps back to the end of Joshua: the people went to their inheritances (v. 6), and served the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders “who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done for Israel” (v. 7). Joshua dies at a hundred and ten and is buried in his own land (vv. 8–9). Then comes the sentence the whole book turns on: when that generation died, another arose “who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel” (v. 10). Nobody rejected God; nobody passed him on.
verseByVerse.theology: Judges repeats the end of the previous book (Josh. 24:28-31) in order to add the one line Joshua never wrote: what happened next.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 is set directly after Joshua's own epitaph, and the contrast is the point.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joshua dismissed the people, the people of Israel went each to his inheritance to take possession of the land. And the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done for Israel. And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110 years. And they buried him within the boundaries of his inheritance in Timnath-heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel stayed faithful only as long as the men who had seen God’s great works were alive.

When Joshua dismissed the people. The narrative jumps backwards: Joshua is alive again, dismissing the assembly at Shechem. The writer is not padding. He is quoting the end of the previous book (Joshua 24:28–31) so that he can add a sentence to it.

Who had seen all the great work. The clause describing the faithful generation contains the whole problem. Faithfulness lasted exactly as long as the eyewitnesses: not as long as the teaching, or the institutions, or the stones at Gilgal, but as long as the men who had watched the Jordan stop flowing. The generation that opened this chapter weeping at Bochim is the generation that buried Joshua.

Uncertain wording. Joshua’s burial place is “Timnath-heres” here and “Timnath-serah” in Joshua 19:50 and 24:30. The two names have the same letters with two reversed. It is not certain which was the original form or whether the town had both; “heres” means “sun”. The place is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: And all that generation also were gathered to their fathers. And there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A generation grew up that did not know the LORD, because nobody had told them what he had done.

There arose another generation. This is the verse the book turns on, and the order of what they did not know is the explanation. They did not know “the work that he had done for Israel”, and so they did not know “the LORD”.

What they lacked. These were not pagans. They were the grandchildren of the men who crossed the Jordan, living in the land and knowing the name of their national God. What they had not been given was the account: the Jordan standing in a heap, the walls of Jericho going down, the hail at Beth-horon, the day the sun stood still. They had the country and not the story.

Telling the next generation. Everything in Joshua was built to prevent this. Twelve stones were set up at Gilgal to provoke a child’s question: “When your children ask in time to come, ‘What do those stones mean to you?’” (Joshua 4:6). The whole law was read aloud with the women, the little ones and the foreigners present. A stone was set up at Shechem as a witness (Joshua 24:27). The stones did not fail; they were still standing. What failed was that somebody’s father, walking past them for the fortieth time, did not say anything.

Who did not know the LORD. It does not say they rejected the LORD or argued with him. They did not know him. There was no controversy, only an absence, and the Baals moved into it. The church is never more than one silent generation away from this. Faith is not carried in the blood and does not pass on by nearness to a building.

They shall all know me. The Bible’s final answer to verse 10 is more than better telling. Through Jeremiah God promised a new covenant in which he would write his law on hearts, “for they shall all know me” (Jeremiah 31:34). Hebrews says that covenant has come in Jesus (Hebrews 8:6–12). Parents and churches must still tell the story, but the knowing of God that no generation could hand on by itself is the gift of the Son and his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–15 — The Baals, and the Selling
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel abandoned the God who rescued it, he handed it over to the enemies it had chosen to live beside. The first turns of the cycle are stated in formula. Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals (v. 11); they abandoned the God who brought them out of Egypt and bowed to the gods of the peoples around them (vv. 12–13). So the LORD’s anger was kindled: he gave them over to plunderers and sold them to their enemies (v. 14). Whenever they marched out his hand was against them, exactly as he had warned, and they were in terrible distress (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Notice the order in verse 12: they abandoned the LORD first, and then went after the gods around them. The emptiness came before the replacement.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel's defeats in this book are not the failure of their God to protect them. They are his discipline, and verse 15 says they had been warned of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals. And they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They went after other gods, from among the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed down to them. And they provoked the LORD to anger. They abandoned the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel abandoned the God who had rescued it for the gods its neighbours said controlled the rain.

Evil in the sight of the LORD. The formula that runs through the rest of the book appears here for the first time. Everything in Judges is measured by it, not by what worked or what the neighbours thought.

Served the Baals. Serving the Baals was not a philosophical decision. Baal was the storm god, believed to control the rain, and therefore the barley, and therefore whether a family ate in the spring; the Ashtaroth were goddesses of fertility (see the introduction). Israel had come out of forty years of manna into farming a country it did not understand, and the locals had settled expertise about this soil. The Baals came with the agricultural advice.

They abandoned the LORD. Israel might have called this sensible farming. The narrator calls it what it was, twice: “they abandoned the LORD”, with the identifying clause attached, “the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt”. That clause is the charge: they exchanged the God who had plainly rescued them for gods who were merely said to send the weather. Jeremiah puts the trade in a single picture: “my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

The gods that come with the job. Nobody in Israel thought of it as apostasy; they thought of it as learning how things work here. That is how idols still arrive: not as rival religions but as the settled wisdom of whatever world we move in. The firm has its Baal, and so do the university, the hospital ward, the start-up and the school gate: an unspoken account of what really makes the rain fall, whether it is the right network, the hours, the image or the numbers. The Baals were never mainly about ritual. They were about control, a way of making an uncertain future answer to your effort, and that is why they were so hard to give up and why they asked for more every year.

A Father who knows. The LORD offered Israel what the Baals could not: not a technique for securing the rain but a Father who knew they needed it. Jesus says the same to anxious people with jobs and mortgages: “your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32). And he proved it by giving not good weather but his Son.
verseByVerse.note: Baal was the Canaanite storm and fertility god; the Ashtaroth were images of the goddess Astarte.

verseByVerse.quote: So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them over to plunderers, who plundered them. And he sold them into the hand of their surrounding enemies, so that they could no longer withstand their enemies. Whenever they marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them for harm, as the LORD had warned, and as the LORD had sworn to them. And they were in terrible distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself handed his unfaithful people over to their enemies, exactly as he had warned, and their distress was real.

He gave them over to plunderers. The writer will not let God stand at a distance from the disaster. God gave them over; God sold them. The raiders did not come by chance. “Sold” is the harder word: what a man does with a slave he no longer wants, used of a nation God had bought out of slavery himself.

As the LORD had warned. The clause that keeps this from being cruelty is “as the LORD had warned”. Deuteronomy had set it out in advance, in public, read aloud to the whole nation with the children present (Deuteronomy 28:25). This is a Father’s discipline of a people already his, not the end of the covenant.

They were in terrible distress. The narrator does not gloat. The misery is deserved, announced and self-inflicted, and he still records that it was terrible. That matters, because the God who sold them is about to be described as moved to pity by their groaning (v. 18).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rescues a people who have not repented, but the rescue lasts only as long as the rescuer. The LORD raised up judges who saved Israel from its plunderers (v. 16), yet Israel did not listen even to them and kept whoring after other gods (v. 17). Verse 18 gives the reason for every rescue in the book: the LORD was with the judge, and he “was moved to pity by their groaning”. Verse 19 closes the loop: whenever the judge died they turned back and became more corrupt than their fathers. The cycle spirals downwards, and the book is already asking for a Deliverer who does not die.
verseByVerse.theology: The word for what the judges did is yasha, to save, the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 18 is among the tenderest sentences in the book, and the reason the cycle does not simply end.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them. Yet they did not listen to their judges, for they whored after other gods and bowed down to them. They soon turned aside from the way in which their fathers had walked, who had obeyed the commandments of the LORD, and they did not do so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without waiting for Israel to repent, God raised up deliverers to save them, yet even while being rescued they kept chasing other gods.

Then the LORD raised up judges. One word turns the chapter: “then”. Israel has not repented, has not asked, has not changed. The previous verse ended in distress and this one begins with rescue, and the only thing between them is God. The LORD raised up; the judges saved; Israel does nothing but is rescued.

Judges. The word does not mean chiefly a man in a courtroom. The Hebrew shophet is one who puts things right for God’s people, and in this book that usually means a leader raised up in a crisis to rescue a region from its oppressor and then to govern it (see the introduction). Deborah, settling disputes under her palm (4:5), is the one shown judging in the courtroom sense.

Who saved them. The Hebrew verb for saving is the root of the name Jesus, and Matthew explains the name when it is given: “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Every judge is a small, borrowed, temporary version of that, raised up for one crisis in one region and then buried.

They whored after other gods. The word is deliberately offensive. It is the vocabulary of a betrayed marriage, the Bible’s regular way of saying that idolatry is not a mistake of the mind but adultery against the God to whom they belong. And the timing is the worst part: they did not listen to their judges, so this was happening while the rescue was going on.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever the LORD raised up judges for them, the LORD was with the judge, and he saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge. For the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who afflicted and oppressed them. But whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers, going after other gods, serving them and bowing down to them. They did not drop any of their practices or their stubborn ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God rescued Israel because he was moved to pity by their suffering, but every rescue ended when the judge died, and each relapse went deeper.

The LORD was with the judge. Here is the sentence that keeps this book from being unbearable. The secret of every deliverance is the phrase that explained Judah’s victory in chapter 1: the LORD was with him. Never the man’s ability; the book will make that unmistakable by choosing the least likely men it can find.

Moved to pity by their groaning. Then the reason God does it at all. Not because they repented, nor because they prayed, but because “the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning”. Groaning is not repentance. It is the noise a person makes under a weight picked up voluntarily and warned about in advance. God is moved by the sound of people suffering the exact consequences he told them would come. It is the same movement recorded when he heard a different groaning from a different slavery: “God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant” (Exodus 2:24).

Does God change? The verb for “moved to pity” is the one elsewhere translated “relent”, and here it describes real compassion, not a change of plan. God “is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind” (Numbers 23:19); what never changes is that he is the kind of God who is moved by his people’s misery.

More corrupt than their fathers. Then the loop closes, and two words give the book its shape. “Died”: the trigger for every relapse is a funeral, and the deliverance lasted exactly as long as the deliverer. “More”: each turn ends lower than the last.

A Deliverer who would not stay dead. The arrangement fails not because the judges were bad, but because they were mortal and the people were not changed by being rescued. Hebrews puts its finger on the same weakness in Israel’s priests: they “were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office”, but Jesus “holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:23–24). Israel did not need a better judge; every improvement on Othniel would still be buried. It needed a Deliverer who would not stay dead, and who could change the people he saved.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nations Israel would not drive out become the nations God leaves in order to test them. Because Israel has broken his covenant and not obeyed his voice (v. 20), God will no longer drive out the nations Joshua left when he died (v. 21). They remain “in order to test Israel by them, whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did, or not” (v. 22). So the nations stayed, not driven out quickly, and God had not given them into Joshua’s hand either (v. 23). What Israel brought on itself, God turns to his own purpose.
verseByVerse.theology: The same nations are two things at once: the consequence of Israel's disobedience (v. 3) and the instrument of God's testing (v. 22).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 23 looks back as far as Joshua's day: the business was unfinished before anybody now living was born.

verseByVerse.quote: So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he said, "Because this people have transgressed my covenant that I commanded their fathers and have not obeyed my voice, I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died, in order to test Israel by them, whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did, or not." So the LORD left those nations, not driving them out quickly, and he did not give them into the hand of Joshua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations Israel failed to drive out are both the result of its disobedience and God’s chosen means of testing whether it will walk in his way.

In order to test Israel. The decision of verse 3 is restated as settled policy, and then a purpose clause changes how the whole book must be read. The same Canaanites are two things at once: the natural result of a job left unfinished, and an instrument deliberately left in place “in order to test”. Scripture says both, nineteen verses apart, and shows no anxiety about it. The thing Israel brought on itself is the thing God is using. A reader who drops either will misread what follows, and most of his own life.

Whether they will take care to walk. What is tested is not their theology but their walking. The exam is conducted over a lifetime and marked by ordinary behaviour.

He did not give them into the hand of Joshua. The last clause should not be walked past. The man who left nothing undone of all that the LORD commanded Moses (Joshua 11:15) still died with nations standing, and the writer says this was God’s doing, not Joshua’s failure.

A strange comfort. That is a strange comfort, and a real one. There was never a moment in Israel’s story when the ground was entirely held, and there is not one in ours. The struggle that remains in a believer’s life, a temptation or a weakness, is not always evidence of a battle lost; sometimes it is a test, left there on purpose by a God who has already made the believer his own and means to see how he walks.

2.theology:
Judgment as withdrawal. God's sentence at Bochim is to stop doing what Israel had already stopped wanting done (v. 3). It is the judgment Paul names three times in one chapter, God gave them up (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28), and its most frightening feature is that it required God to do nothing at all.

One generation. Verse 10 does not say the next generation rejected God; it says they did not know him, because they did not know his work. Faith arrives by somebody telling somebody, and it stops when they stop.

Moved by groaning, not by repentance. Verse 18 gives the reason God keeps raising up deliverers, and it is not Israel's contrition or their prayers. He was moved to pity by their groaning, and that is the only reason this book has more than three chapters.

The flaw is mortality. The trigger for every relapse is a funeral (v. 19). The system fails not because the judges were poor, several were remarkable, but because they died, and because being rescued did not change anybody. Israel needed a deliverer who would not stay dead, and a covenant that changes the heart.
2.examples:
Then: A nation wept at a place they named after the weeping, offered sacrifices, and drove out nobody. A generation later their children knew the name of their God and nothing he had done, and took farming advice from the neighbours about which god sent rain.

Now: Two tests come out of this chapter. The first is Bochim: genuine tears, a real sacrifice, and no Canaanite driven out the next morning. Ask what actually changed after the last time you were deeply moved. Godly grief is not produced by trying to feel worse; it is the Spirit's work, turning us towards the Christ whose sacrifice did what Bochim's could not, and he gives the strength to deal tomorrow with the sin that has to go. The second is verse 10, aimed at parents and churches. The stones at Gilgal were still standing; what had stopped was somebody answering the question, telling children what the LORD has done before telling them what to do.

keyVerse.quote: Whenever the LORD raised up judges for them, the LORD was with the judge, and he saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge. For the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who afflicted and oppressed them.
keyVerse.note: This verse is why the book is bearable. Every rescue in Judges comes from God’s pity, not Israel’s repentance, and every rescue lasts only “all the days of the judge”. Both halves point beyond the book: to the compassion of God, and to the need for a Saviour whose days never end.

2.reflection:
At Bochim the people wept and sacrificed, yet nothing changed (vv. 4–5). What is the difference between being moved and repenting? How can you tell which is happening in you?

Verse 10 describes a generation that “did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.” What are you doing, as a family or a church, to tell the next generation what God has done? Where has that telling gone quiet?

The Baals promised rain and harvests in return for service (vv. 11–13). What are the “Baals” of your workplace or community, the unspoken beliefs about what really makes life work, and how does trusting a heavenly Father free you from them?

God rescued Israel because he “was moved to pity by their groaning” (v. 18), and every rescue ended when the judge died. How does this chapter make you more thankful for a Saviour who lives for ever?

3.title: Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the nations that the LORD left, to test Israel by them, that is, all in Israel who had not experienced all the wars in Canaan.<sup>2</sup>It was only in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before.<sup>3</sup>These are the nations: the five lords of the Philistines and all the Canaanites and the Sidonians and the Hivites who lived on Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon as far as Lebo-hamath.<sup>4</sup>They were for the testing of Israel, to know whether Israel would obey the commandments of the LORD, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.<sup>5</sup>So the people of Israel lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.<sup>6</sup>And their daughters they took to themselves for wives, and their own daughters they gave to their sons, and they served their gods.<sup>7</sup>And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth.<sup>8</sup>Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia. And the people of Israel served Cushan-rishathaim eight years.<sup>9</sup>But when the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer for the people of Israel, who saved them, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.<sup>10</sup>The Spirit of the LORD was upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand. And his hand prevailed over Cushan-rishathaim.<sup>11</sup>So the land had rest for forty years. Then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.<sup>12</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>He gathered to himself the Ammonites and the Amalekites, and went and defeated Israel. And they took possession of the city of palms.<sup>14</sup>And the people of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.<sup>15</sup>Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, and the LORD raised up for them a deliverer, Ehud, the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a left-handed man. The people of Israel sent tribute by him to Eglon the king of Moab.<sup>16</sup>And Ehud made for himself a sword with two edges, a cubit in length, and he bound it on his right thigh under his clothes.<sup>17</sup>And he presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.<sup>18</sup>And when Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who carried the tribute.<sup>19</sup>But he himself turned back at the idols near Gilgal and said, "I have a secret message for you, O king." And he commanded, "Silence." And all his attendants went out from his presence.<sup>20</sup>And Ehud came to him as he was sitting alone in his cool roof chamber. And Ehud said, "I have a message from God for you."
