And he arose from his seat.<sup>21</sup>And Ehud reached with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly.<sup>22</sup>And the hilt also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly; and the dung came out.<sup>23</sup>Then Ehud went out into the porch and closed the doors of the roof chamber behind him and locked them.<sup>24</sup>When he had gone, the servants came, and when they saw that the doors of the roof chamber were locked, they thought, "Surely he is relieving himself in the closet of the cool chamber."<sup>25</sup>And they waited till they were embarrassed. But when he still did not open the doors of the roof chamber, they took the key and opened them, and there lay their lord dead on the floor.<sup>26</sup>Ehud escaped while they delayed, and he passed beyond the idols and escaped to Seirah.<sup>27</sup>When he arrived, he sounded the trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. Then the people of Israel went down with him from the hill country, and he was their leader.<sup>28</sup>And he said to them, "Follow after me, for the LORD has given your enemies the Moabites into your hand." So they went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan against the Moabites and did not allow anyone to pass over.<sup>29</sup>And they killed at that time about 10,000 of the Moabites, all strong, able-bodied men; not a man escaped.<sup>30</sup>So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest for eighty years.<sup>31</sup>After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel.
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 set out the cycle: sin, oppression, crying out, rescue, relapse. Chapter 3 names the nations God left in the land, shows Israel failing the test, and then runs the cycle for real, three times.

The message. Israel forgets God, but God does not forget Israel. When his people cry out under the oppression they brought on themselves, he raises up deliverers, and he chooses the least likely: a younger brother, a left-handed man from the smallest tribe, a farmer with a cattle prod. The power is never in the man but in the Spirit of the LORD, and the victory is always the LORD’s gift.

Why it was said. The first hearers, surrounded by stronger neighbours and their gods (see the introduction), needed to know that compromise with those gods leads to slavery, and that the God of the exodus still saves the helpless who cry to him.

How the chapter makes its case. The nations left in the land are a test of obedience and a school of war for a generation that had never fought (vv. 1–4). Israel fails at once: it intermarries and serves their gods (vv. 5–6). Then the cycle runs in model form: Israel forgets the LORD, is sold to Cushan-rishathaim, cries out, and the Spirit of the LORD comes on Othniel, who wins forty years of rest and dies (vv. 7–11). Again Israel sins, and God strengthens Eglon of Moab for eighteen years (vv. 12–14). Ehud, a left-handed Benjaminite, kills the king in his roof chamber, escapes while the courtiers wait outside, and leads Israel to eighty years of rest (vv. 15–30). Shamgar, with an oxgoad, also saves Israel (v. 31).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. Othniel is the model judge because “the Spirit of the LORD was upon him”, and Isaiah promised a Son of David on whom the Spirit would rest (Isaiah 11:2); at Nazareth Jesus read, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me”, and said that this was fulfilled (Luke 4:18–21). Each deliverer is weak in the world’s eyes, as Christ was in his crucifixion. But the contrast matters as much as the likeness: Othniel died and the rest he won died with him; Ehud freed Israel by a hidden blade and a pretext, but Christ freed his people from the tyrant behind every tyrant by dying himself (Hebrews 2:14–15), and the rest he gives does not end (Hebrews 4:8–10).

For us. Most people do not argue their way out of faith; they forget their way out, one comfortable compromise at a time. The remedy is to keep God’s works in front of us, as the Lord’s Supper does. And when we cry out under the results of our own drift, God still rescues, through means no one would choose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Left to Teach Them War
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The enemies left in the land are both a test and a school, and Israel fails the test at once. The nations are left “to test Israel” (v. 1), and stranger still, to teach war to a generation that had never fought, so that they would learn to depend on God for themselves (v. 2). They are named: the Philistines, the Canaanites, the Sidonians and the Hivites (v. 3). The test is whether Israel will obey what God commanded through Moses (v. 4). The result follows in two verses: Israel lived among the peoples of the land, married their sons and daughters, and served their gods (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: A generation that had never fought is given an enemy, and the writer calls it an education.
verseByVerse.examples: The peoples named in verse 5 are almost the same list Israel was told to devote to destruction (Deut. 7:1). Now Israel lives among them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the nations that the LORD left, to test Israel by them, that is, all in Israel who had not experienced all the wars in Canaan. It was only in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before. These are the nations: the five lords of the Philistines and all the Canaanites and the Sidonians and the Hivites who lived on Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon as far as Lebo-hamath. They were for the testing of Israel, to know whether Israel would obey the commandments of the LORD, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God left enemies in the land to test Israel’s obedience and to teach a generation that had never fought to depend on him in battle.

To teach war. The first purpose is the testing announced at the end of chapter 2. The second is put as though it were the whole point: “only in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before.”

The generation after the fighting. This generation was born after the fighting stopped. They grew up in houses their parents had taken, ate from vineyards somebody else had planted, and had never faced an enemy across a field. They had inherited the results of faith without ever exercising any. So God leaves the Philistines and the Canaanites in place, and the writer calls it a school: not a mistake, but a course of instruction for people who had grown up soft in a country won by other men’s obedience.

To know whether Israel would obey. The test is not of their doctrine but of their obedience, and what they must obey is already written down in the law of Moses (v. 4). Nothing new will be asked of them.

In everyday life. Remember this before reading every remaining difficulty as a failure. A settled Christian who has never had to depend on God for anything is not in a stronger position than one who has; he is in a more dangerous one, and has no way of knowing it until something is left standing in his way.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people of Israel lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. And their daughters they took to themselves for wives, and their own daughters they gave to their sons, and they served their gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel failed the test: it married into the Canaanite peoples and ended up worshipping their gods.

The people of Israel lived among the Canaanites. The result of the test uses the wording chapter 1 introduced at Asher: Israel lived among them, as if Israel were the incomers in someone else’s country.

Their daughters they took to themselves for wives. Then the sequence, in one direction with no pause: they took wives, they gave daughters, they served their gods. Nobody married a Canaanite in order to worship Baal. The worship arrived at the end of a chain that began with an ordinary decision about a wedding.

Why God forbade these marriages. That is exactly why God had forbidden them. It was never about ancestry: Rahab married into Judah, Ruth the Moabite is in the same family tree, and a Kenite clan is settled among them in chapter 1. Moses stated the ground plainly: “they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:4). Paul reasons the same way when he tells believers, “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14): the heart does not stay independent of what it has bound itself to. Israel married the families and ended up at the family altars.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a believer already married to an unbeliever should leave. Paul says plainly that such a believer should stay if the spouse is willing (1 Corinthians 7:12–14). The warning is for those still choosing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first full turn of the cycle shows how God saves: by his Spirit, through a deliverer he raises up. Israel did evil, forgot the LORD and served the Baals and the Asheroth, images of the goddess Asherah (v. 7). So God sold them to Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, for eight years (v. 8). They cried out, and the LORD raised up Othniel, Caleb’s younger brother, who saved them (v. 9). “The Spirit of the LORD was upon him”, and God gave the king into his hand (v. 10). The land had rest forty years, and then Othniel died (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Othniel is the model, and the writer gives him no faults. He is from Caleb's family, the Spirit rests on him, he wins, and the land is quiet for a generation. Every judge after this is measured against him, and every one falls short.
verseByVerse.examples: Mesopotamia here is, in Hebrew, Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers", far to the north-east: the oppressor comes from a long way off.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth. Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia. And the people of Israel served Cushan-rishathaim eight years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel did not reject God; it forgot him, and so God sold it to a foreign king.

They forgot the LORD their God. One verb explains the whole book, and it is not a dramatic one. Not rejected, not renounced: forgot. There is no record anywhere in Judges of Israel deciding that the God of the exodus was untrue; the writer keeps describing a nation mislaying him. Chapter 2 said the generation did not know him. This one says they forgot him.

How forgetting happens. Forgetting takes no effort at all. It is what happens to anything not deliberately kept in front of the mind, and Moses spent a whole book warning about it: “Take care lest you forget the LORD your God”, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them (Deuteronomy 8:11–12).

How a culture loses God without an argument. We assume people stop believing because they have been argued out of it. Some have. But most drift from faith in prosperous places looks like this verse. Nobody refuted the God of the exodus; there was simply less and less occasion to think about him. Full barns, busy lives and a culture that no longer mentions him will do what no sceptic could. C. S. Lewis, in The Screwtape Letters, has his senior devil advise that the safest road to hell is the gradual one, a gentle slope with no signposts. Forgetting is that road.

God remembers. The answer is not first to try harder to remember, because memory left to itself fails. It is that God remembers us: in this same book he hears their groaning and acts (2:18). And on the night he was betrayed Jesus gave forgetful people a meal, “do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19), so that what he did would be set in front of them again and again, by his own hand.

Cushan-rishathaim. Say the oppressor’s name aloud. It reads in Hebrew as something like “Cushan of double wickedness”, and it is hard to imagine a king calling himself that. Eight years under a tyrant, and the narrator will not grant him much dignity.

Uncertain wording. Who Cushan-rishathaim was is unknown. “Mesopotamia” is literally Aram of the two rivers, far to the north-east, yet his opponent comes from the far south of Judah; some suggest “Aram” was confused with the similar-looking “Edom”, but that is a guess.
verseByVerse.note: Attempts to identify Cushan with a ruler known from outside the Bible remain uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer for the people of Israel, who saved them, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother. The Spirit of the LORD was upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand. And his hand prevailed over Cushan-rishathaim. So the land had rest for forty years. Then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel cried out, God gave them a deliverer and put his Spirit on him, and the land had forty years of rest until Othniel died.

When the people of Israel cried out to the LORD. It is not called repentance; they are simply in pain and make a noise about it, the groaning that moved God to pity in 2:18.

Othniel the son of Kenaz. The man raised up is already known. Othniel took Kiriath-sepher and married Achsah in chapter 1, and belongs to the one family chapter 1 had nothing against: Caleb’s.

The Spirit of the LORD was upon him. Here is the sentence that will explain every deliverance in this book. Not his lineage, though it was good, nor his record. The book will prove the point by putting the Spirit of the LORD on men with far worse credentials: a frightened farmer hiding in a winepress, a rejected son of a prostitute, a man who could not keep away from Philistine women. The one qualification is the Spirit, and it is given rather than earned.

The Spirit without measure. The prophets carry that line forward to the Deliverer who would not die and leave his people leaderless. Of the coming son of David, Isaiah wrote, “the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him” (Isaiah 11:2). In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me”, and said that the Scripture was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:18–21). Othniel had the Spirit for a campaign. Christ has him without measure, and gives him to his people.

So the land had rest for forty years. Forty years is a full generation of peace, and it is real. Then the word on which everything turns: “died”. Othniel is the model judge, without a single criticism anywhere in Scripture, and he was mortal, and the rest he won was buried with him. The best available deliverer, doing everything right, could not give Israel anything that outlasted his own funeral.

What the rest was. Rest meant the raiders gone and the harvest eaten by those who sowed it, as God had promised: “when he gives you rest from all your enemies around, so that you live in safety” (Deuteronomy 12:10). Yet the quiet years are when Israel forgot, and each new oppression grew up inside the rest before it. We do the same with a calm season, the job secure, the scan clear: the quiet becomes the thing we lean on, rather than the God who gave it. Hebrews reads these rests as signposts: “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). That rest is found in Christ, and it does not come and go with the seasons. So when a quiet stretch comes, use it as Israel did not: to tell again what God has done.
verseByVerse.note: Othniel was Caleb’s younger brother (some read it as his nephew).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rescues his people through the most unlikely man and the most unlikely means, and makes their oppressor ridiculous. Again Israel does evil, and this time God strengthens the oppressor: Eglon of Moab, with Ammon and Amalek, takes Jericho and rules Israel eighteen years (vv. 12–14). Israel cries out and God raises up Ehud, a left-handed Benjaminite, who straps a short sword to his right thigh (vv. 15–16). He delivers the tribute, returns with a secret message and kills the king alone in his roof chamber (vv. 17–22). He locks the doors and walks out while the servants wait outside, embarrassed (vv. 23–26). Ehud sounds the trumpet, Israel seizes the fords of the Jordan, ten thousand Moabites fall, and the land has rest eighty years (vv. 27–30).
verseByVerse.theology: God's deliverer is a man from the smallest tribe with a disqualified sword arm, carrying a homemade blade to a tribute ceremony. The whole plan depends on the thing about him a guard would have written off.
verseByVerse.examples: Eighty years is the longest rest recorded in the book. It is also, like every other rest here, measured in the lifetime of one man.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He gathered to himself the Ammonites and the Amalekites, and went and defeated Israel. And they took possession of the city of palms. And the people of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel sinned again, God himself strengthened its enemy, and Israel served Moab for eighteen years.

The LORD strengthened Eglon. “Again”: Othniel is barely in the ground and the wheel has come round. Then a hard verb. God does not merely allow the oppressor; he equips him. That is uncomfortable and it is consistent. Israel’s troubles in this book come not from God’s absence but from his attention, the discipline of a Father who has not let go.

The city of palms. The city of palms is Jericho. The first city God gave them, whose walls fell at a shout, is now a Moabite forward base. Cushan held them eight years; Eglon holds them eighteen. The oppressions are getting longer, as chapter 2 said the spiral would run.

Distant cousins. Moab was family, descended from Lot, and Israel had been forbidden to attack them in the wilderness because of it (Deuteronomy 2:9). The people God brought out of the greatest empire on earth are paying tribute to their distant cousins.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, and the LORD raised up for them a deliverer, Ehud, the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a left-handed man. The people of Israel sent tribute by him to Eglon the king of Moab. And Ehud made for himself a sword with two edges, a cubit in length, and he bound it on his right thigh under his clothes. And he presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God raised up a left-handed man as deliverer, and his very difference became the way past the king’s guard.

A left-handed man. The narrator gives one physical detail about this man, the one the whole story turns on. In a world where every soldier drew from the left hip with his right hand, the enemy did not expect a left-handed one.

Ehud, the son of Gera, the Benjaminite. He is also a Benjaminite, and Benjamin means “son of the right hand” (so the ESV note at Genesis 35:18). The trait ran in that tribe: later in this book Benjamin fields seven hundred left-handed men who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss (20:16).

A sword with two edges. He makes the weapon himself, two-edged and short enough to hide under a cloak, and straps it to his right thigh. If he was searched at all, a guard would look on the left, and so the blade passes the guards on a man they believe to be unarmed. The tribute itself was his way in. A subject people paid its overlord a yearly levy in goods, carried by porters and presented to the king in person, so the man leading the delegation had a reason to stand in Eglon’s presence that no guard would question.

Now Eglon was a very fat man. The last sentence of verse 17 prepares for what is coming. His name is probably part of the joke, close to the Hebrew for a calf. A king grown heavy on eighteen years of another nation’s tribute is about to be dealt with like livestock.

Uncertain wording. “Left-handed” is literally “bound” or “restricted as to his right hand”. It may describe a defect, a sword arm that did not work as it should, or a skill: a man trained to fight left-handed, perhaps with the right arm bound in boyhood (compare 1 Chronicles 12:2, where Benjaminites use either hand). Either way, the enemy did not expect it. The measure of the sword, “a cubit”, translates a word found only here; most take it as a short cubit, perhaps about eighteen inches.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word for this measure occurs only here in the Old Testament; most take it as a short cubit.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who carried the tribute. But he himself turned back at the idols near Gilgal and said, "I have a secret message for you, O king." And he commanded, "Silence." And all his attendants went out from his presence. And Ehud came to him as he was sitting alone in his cool roof chamber. And Ehud said, "I have a message from God for you." And he arose from his seat. And Ehud reached with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly. And the hilt also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly; and the dung came out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ehud gets the tyrant alone with a “message from God”, and kills him in a scene Scripture tells with open scorn for oppressors.

He himself turned back at the idols near Gilgal. He sends the delegation home first, so that no other Israelite is near the palace when it happens, and turns back at the idols near Gilgal. The ground where the twelve stones were set up now has idols standing near it.

I have a secret message for you, O king. Ehud says he has a secret, and Eglon empties the room: the one thing an oppressor cannot resist is secret information, and he dismisses his own bodyguard to get it. Then: “I have a message from God for you.” Eglon stands up to receive it. Whatever he believed about the God of Israel, he stood.

The dung came out. The message from God is a short blade, described with a bluntness that has embarrassed readers for centuries. Scripture can write an oppressor’s death with dignity and declines to do it here. A strand runs through the Bible that laughs at tyrants, “He who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:4), and this is the crudest page of it.

Is Ehud’s deception approved? Ehud was raised up by the LORD (v. 15) to free Israel from an occupier in a war of liberation. Scripture records his method without holding it up as a pattern. It gives no Christian licence to deceive or to kill; private persons may not take vengeance (Romans 12:19). Hebrews does not name Ehud, and where it names his fellow judges it commends their faith, not every act (Hebrews 11:32).

A better Deliverer. The deliverers of this book are flawed pointers to a better one. Ehud carried a hidden blade and a false pretext into a tyrant’s room. Christ said he had spoken nothing in secret (John 18:20), and he freed his people from the tyrant behind every tyrant by dying himself (Hebrews 2:14–15).

Uncertain wording. “Idols” (v. 19) can also mean carved stones or a quarry; some wonder whether the memorial stones at Gilgal were meant, but the text does not say. The last clause of verse 22 uses a word found nowhere else; it may mean the blade came out at the back, but the ESV’s reading is likely and fits the servants’ assumption (v. 24).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ehud went out into the porch and closed the doors of the roof chamber behind him and locked them. When he had gone, the servants came, and when they saw that the doors of the roof chamber were locked, they thought, "Surely he is relieving himself in the closet of the cool chamber." And they waited till they were embarrassed. But when he still did not open the doors of the roof chamber, they took the key and opened them, and there lay their lord dead on the floor. Ehud escaped while they delayed, and he passed beyond the idols and escaped to Seirah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ehud locks the doors and walks away, and the courtiers’ embarrassed waiting outside becomes his escape.

Closed the doors of the roof chamber. He locks up. A man who has just killed a head of state in his own palace stops, pulls the doors to, turns the key, and walks out through the household.

Surely he is relieving himself. The servants arrive, find the doors locked, and reach the obvious conclusion: their king is using the lavatory.

They waited till they were embarrassed. The writer, who could have moved straight to the discovery, stops to record their state of mind. The courtiers stand outside a locked door, too well-bred to knock, while the assassin gets further away by the minute.

The delay is the escape route. What saves the deliverer is not his speed but the manners of his enemies, and the writer’s point is not subtle: when God moves against an oppressor, the oppressor’s own household serves God’s plan. Eighteen years of domination ends with a locked door and a group of embarrassed men who cannot bring themselves to interrupt.

Uncertain wording. “Porch” (v. 23) translates a rare word of uncertain meaning (so the ESV note); it may have been a vestibule or some other way out.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of the Hebrew for “porch” is uncertain (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: When he arrived, he sounded the trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. Then the people of Israel went down with him from the hill country, and he was their leader. And he said to them, "Follow after me, for the LORD has given your enemies the Moabites into your hand." So they went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan against the Moabites and did not allow anyone to pass over. And they killed at that time about 10,000 of the Moabites, all strong, able-bodied men; not a man escaped. So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest for eighty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ehud turns the assassination into Israel’s deliverance: the LORD has given the enemy into their hand, and the land has rest for eighty years.

He sounded the trumpet. The assassination was not the deliverance; it was the opening. Ehud blows a trumpet in the hills and the same Israelites who have paid tribute for eighteen years come down after him. The oppression was never as solid as it looked; what was missing was somebody to move first.

The LORD has given your enemies. His speech is two clauses, and the second is the whole theology of the book: “the LORD has given”, spoken as already done, as at Jericho and in 1:2. The killing of Eglon did not create the victory; it acted on one already granted.

The fords of the Jordan. The tactics are sound too. The fords of the Jordan are the only way home for a Moabite army on the wrong side of the river, and Israel takes them first.

Eighty years. Eighty years, twice what Othniel achieved and the longest peace in the book, came out of one day in a locked room. The Moabites had let him in armed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God needs no better equipment than what is already in a man’s hand. In a single verse Shamgar the son of Anath kills six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad, a farmer’s cattle prod, “and he also saved Israel” (v. 31). There is no account of Israel’s sin or cry, no years of rest, and his very name is a puzzle; he may not even have been an Israelite. Yet he is given the same verb as Othniel and Ehud. Set beside them, he completes a list of deliverers no nation would have chosen: a younger brother, a left-handed man and a farmer. The Philistines named here will become the great enemy of Samson’s day.
verseByVerse.theology: No cycle, no years, no oppression narrated and no rest recorded: a name, a farm implement, a number, and the same verb used of Othniel.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the first time the Philistines appear as an enemy in this book. The whole Samson cycle is against them, and they are still there when Saul dies.

verseByVerse.quote: After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man with a farm tool saves Israel from the Philistines: God needs no better equipment than what is already in a person’s hand.

Shamgar the son of Anath. There is no cycle here: no apostasy, no crying out, no years of rest. Even the name is a puzzle: Anath was a Canaanite war goddess, and some think Shamgar was not an Israelite at all. God’s rescues are not limited to the people one would expect.

With an oxgoad. The weapon is the point. An oxgoad is a wooden pole eight feet long or so, with an iron spike for driving cattle and a flat blade for scraping a ploughshare. It is what a man has in his hand when he is working, and it is not a sword.

Three unlikely deliverers. Set the three deliverers side by side, as the writer has arranged them: a younger brother, a left-handed man from the smallest tribe, and a farmer with an oxgoad. Nothing in that list is what a nation would choose. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, and what is low and despised, so that no human being might boast in his presence (1 Corinthians 1:27–29).

And he also saved Israel. Shamgar is given the same verb as Othniel and Ehud, the word behind the names of Joshua and Jesus. A man with a stick is entered in the record with the same word as everybody else, and God did not need better equipment than what was already in his hand.

Uncertain wording. “Son of Anath” may name his father, his home town (such as Beth-anath, 1:33), or mark him out as a warrior, after the war goddess; the text does not say which.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Anath” may name his father, his home town, or even mark him out as a warrior; the text does not say which.

3.theology:
The enemy as a school. Verse 2 says the nations were left to teach war to a generation that had never fought. The difficulty still standing in a Christian life is not automatically evidence of a battle lost; it may be the very place where a believer learns to depend on God.

They forgot. The verb in verse 7 is the ordinary one, and it takes no effort at all. Judges never once records Israel deciding that the God of the exodus was untrue, and Moses warned that the danger comes with plenty, not with persecution.

The one qualification. What explains Othniel is not his family, though it was the best in the book, but one clause: the Spirit of the LORD was upon him (v. 10). The book will put the Spirit of the LORD on a frightened farmer hiding in a winepress, the rejected son of a prostitute, and a man who could not keep away from Philistine women. The qualification is given, not earned.

Improbable instruments. Ehud's deliverance turns on the trait a recruiting officer would have written off, and Shamgar's weapon is what happened to be in his hand at work. It is the pattern Paul states outright: God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, so that no human being might boast (1 Cor. 1:27-29).
3.examples:
A generation that had never fought a battle married into the neighbours and ended up at their altars. Then God raised up a model judge who died, an assassin whose disability was the plan, and a farmer with a stick, and every deliverance was real and every one wore off.

Two things carry over to us. Verse 6 is the sequence to watch, because nobody in it chose to change gods; they chose relationships, and the worship followed. And verse 7 is the honest description of most spiritual decline: not rejection but forgetting, which requires no decision. The remedy is not a stronger grip but remembering what God has done, which is why he gives his word, the Lord's Supper and his people, and his Spirit, who brings to remembrance what Christ has said (John 14:26). And when you find you have forgotten, the God of this chapter still answers the cry of people who had forgotten him.

keyVerse.quote: But when the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer for the people of Israel, who saved them, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother.
keyVerse.note: Here is the gospel shape of the whole book. Israel brought its slavery on itself, yet when it cried out, the LORD raised up a deliverer who saved them. The rescue starts with God, not with Israel’s worthiness, and it points to the greater Deliverer on whom the Spirit rests for ever.

3.reflection:
God left enemies in the land to teach a generation that had never fought to depend on him (vv. 1–2). What difficulties in your life might God be using in this way? How does that change the way you face them?

Israel’s slide into idolatry began with ordinary decisions about marriage (vv. 5–6) and ended in forgetting the LORD (v. 7). Where are you most in danger of forgetting God, not by rejecting him but by being too busy or too comfortable to think of him?

Othniel, Ehud and Shamgar were a younger brother, a left-handed man and a farmer with a cattle prod. Why do you think God so often works through unlikely people? How does that encourage you?

Othniel won forty years of rest, and then he died (v. 11). How does the rest Christ gives (Hebrews 4:8–10) differ from the rest the judges won, and how can you enjoy it this week?

4.title: Deborah and Barak
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD after Ehud died.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim.<sup>3</sup>Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD for help, for he had 900 chariots of iron and he oppressed the people of Israel cruelly for twenty years.<sup>4</sup>Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time.<sup>5</sup>She used to sit under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the people of Israel came up to her for judgment.<sup>6</sup>She sent and summoned Barak the son of Abinoam from Kedesh-naphtali and said to him, "Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you, 'Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor, taking 10,000 from the people of Naphtali and the people of Zebulun.<sup>7</sup>And I will draw out Sisera, the general of Jabin's army, to meet you by the river Kishon with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand'?"<sup>8</sup>Barak said to her, "If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go."<sup>9</sup>And she said, "I will surely go with you. Nevertheless, the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." Then Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh.<sup>10</sup>And Barak called out Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh. And 10,000 men went up at his heels, and Deborah went up with him.<sup>11</sup>Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent as far away as the oak in Zaanannim, which is near Kedesh.<sup>12</sup>When Sisera was told that Barak the son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor,<sup>13</sup>Sisera called out all his chariots, 900 chariots of iron, and all the men who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the river Kishon.<sup>14</sup>And Deborah said to Barak, "Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?" So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with 10,000 men following him.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak by the edge of the sword. And Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot.<sup>16</sup>And Barak pursued the chariots and the army to Harosheth-hagoyim, and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword; not a man was left.<sup>17</sup>But Sisera fled away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.<sup>18</sup>And Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid." So he turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug.<sup>19</sup>And he said to her, "Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty." So she opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink and covered him.<sup>20</sup>And he said to her, "Stand at the opening of the tent, and if any man comes and asks you, 'Is anyone here?' say, 'No.'"<sup>21</sup>But Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand. Then she went softly to him and drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground while he was lying fast asleep from weariness. So he died.<sup>22</sup>And behold, as Barak was pursuing Sisera, Jael went out to meet him and said to him, "Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking." So he went in to her tent, and there lay Sisera dead, with the tent peg in his temple.<sup>23</sup>So on that day God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the people of Israel.<sup>24</sup>And the hand of the people of Israel pressed harder and harder against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
4.overview:
Where we are. Ehud dies, and the cycle turns a third time. The oppressor is Jabin king of Canaan, reigning in Hazor, the city Joshua had burned (Joshua 11:10–11), and his commander Sisera has nine hundred chariots of iron, the very thing Judah would not face in 1:19.

The message. The LORD fights for his people and keeps his word, even when they are slow to obey. He has already given his command and his promise; he draws the enemy to the place he chose, turns the strength of the chariots into their ruin, and finishes the work through the people no one expected: a prophetess under a palm tree, a hesitant general and a woman in a tent. “Does not the LORD go out before you?” (v. 14).

Why it was said. Israel lived under the threat of better-armed neighbours (see the introduction). This chapter tells them that iron chariots are no obstacle to the God who commands them, and that the honour belongs to him, not to the bravest man in the story.

How the chapter makes its case. Israel sins again and is sold to Jabin, whose chariots oppress them cruelly for twenty years (vv. 1–3). God has already put Deborah in place, a prophetess judging Israel under her palm (vv. 4–5). She reminds Barak of God’s command and promise: Sisera will be drawn to the Kishon and given into his hand (vv. 6–7). Barak will go only if she goes; she agrees, and tells him the honour will go to a woman (vv. 8–10). A Kenite moves his tent near Kedesh (v. 11). At the river the LORD routs Sisera’s chariots, and Sisera flees on foot (vv. 12–16). He hides in Jael’s tent, and she kills him with a tent peg as he sleeps (vv. 17–22). God subdues Jabin, and Israel presses on until he is destroyed (vv. 23–24).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and promise. The LORD who “goes out before” his people is seen fully in Jesus, “the founder of their salvation” and their forerunner (Hebrews 2:10; 6:20), who went ahead of them into death and out of it. And many readers have heard, in the woman who “crushed his head” (5:26), an echo of the first promise, that the woman’s offspring would bruise the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). Jael was not that offspring. The promise was kept by Christ, who destroyed the enemy of his people not by deceiving a guest but by giving his own life for them (Hebrews 2:14).

For us. God has already spoken; the question is whether we will go. Weak faith that clings to visible props is not rejected, but it misses the joy of honour. And no enemy’s strength, iron or otherwise, is an obstacle to the God who goes ahead of us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Nine Hundred Chariots, and a Woman Under a Palm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel forgets God again, he hands it to its strongest oppressor yet, but he has already placed the person through whom he will speak. Israel does evil after Ehud’s death (v. 1), and the LORD sells them to Jabin king of Canaan, ruling from Hazor, with Sisera commanding his army (v. 2). Sisera’s nine hundred chariots of iron let him oppress Israel cruelly for twenty years, the longest oppression so far, and Israel cries out (v. 3). Then the narrator introduces Deborah, a prophetess and the wife of Lappidoth, already judging Israel. She sits under a palm in the hill country of Ephraim, and the people come to her for judgment (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: A danger that one generation refuses to face grows larger for the next.
verseByVerse.examples: Twenty years is the longest oppression yet, and it is called cruel: each turn of the cycle runs lower than the last.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD after Ehud died. And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim. Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD for help, for he had 900 chariots of iron and he oppressed the people of Israel cruelly for twenty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Ehud died Israel sinned again, and God sold it to a Canaanite king whose iron chariots crushed it for twenty years.

After Ehud died. The trigger is named without comment. Eighty years of rest ended at a funeral, exactly as chapter 2 said.

Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. There is a king in Hazor. Joshua took it, killed its king and burned the city, the only town in the northern campaign he burned, because it had been “the head of all those kingdoms” (Joshua 11:10–11). A century or so later a Jabin reigns there with a standing army. Nothing had to be conquered for that to happen; the site was left empty and somebody moved back in. What God’s people do not occupy does not stay unoccupied.

900 chariots of iron. In 1:19 the LORD was with Judah, yet Judah “could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron.” That excuse sounded practical at the time. It has now multiplied into a twenty-year occupation described as cruel, the longest oppression yet: eight years under Cushan, eighteen under Eglon, twenty now.

Two kings named Jabin? Readers sometimes ask how a Jabin can reign in Hazor when Joshua killed a king of that name (Joshua 11:10). The likeliest answer is that Jabin was a dynastic name, used by more than one king of Hazor, much as Pharaoh was used in Egypt.
verseByVerse.note: Hazor lay north of the Sea of Galilee and was one of the largest cities in Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. She used to sit under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the people of Israel came up to her for judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the rescue begins, God already has a prophetess in place, applying his word to his people’s disputes while the men who should lead do nothing.

Deborah, a prophetess. Three things said about Deborah are unusual. She is a prophetess, the only judge in the book also called that: the others are given the Spirit for a campaign; she is given words. She is the wife of Lappidoth, in an ordinary household. And she “was judging Israel” in the plain sense: people brought disputes and she settled them. Elsewhere in this book “judge” usually means rescuer; Deborah is the one who actually judges, and she is doing it before any of this starts.

Under the palm of Deborah. Israel is under occupation, with no army worth the name and no king, and there is one fixed point in the country where the word of God is applied to ordinary disputes, day after day, by a woman under a palm tree. The nation has a court.

A mother in Israel. The song in the next chapter tells us how she saw it herself: the villagers ceased in Israel “until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel” (5:7). When the men who should have led did not, God did not stop governing his people. He put somebody else under the tree.

What the chapter plainly honours. God gave his people a woman who knew his word and applied it faithfully when the men had failed, and he still gives his church such women.

Where Christians differ: does Deborah’s leadership settle church office? Some hold that she is a precedent for women in every office, including elder and pastor. Others note that she was a prophetess raised up in an extraordinary time, and that her role exposes the failure of the men: Barak will not go without her, and the honour goes to a woman (v. 9). She never served as a priest, and she gave God’s word to a man to lead the army. Many faithful Christians read Deborah differently, out of real love for Scripture, and the question deserves patience rather than suspicion. This commentary’s view: the complementarian view. Deborah’s office was a prophet’s, given by God in a crisis, while the New Testament governs church office directly and gives standing rules for the elders who teach and govern the church, who are to be qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). Women served God with great honour in Israel, as they do in the church, but Deborah does not overturn that order.

Uncertain wording. “Lappidoth” means “torches”, and some have taken “wife of Lappidoth” as “a woman of fire” rather than as her husband’s name. Most read it as a name.
verseByVerse.note: Lappidoth means “torches”, and some have taken the phrase as “a woman of fire” rather than as her husband’s name; most read it as a name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — Has Not the LORD Commanded You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s command and promise are already given, and the question is whether his servant will go. Deborah summons Barak and asks whether the LORD has not commanded him to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor (v. 6). God promises to draw Sisera out to the Kishon with his chariots and give him into Barak’s hand (v. 7). Barak sets a condition: he will go only if Deborah goes with him (v. 8). She agrees at once, but tells him the road will not lead to his glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman (v. 9). Ten thousand men go up behind Barak, and Deborah goes with him (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Barak's home, Kedesh-naphtali, lay in the occupied north, within reach of Hazor.
verseByVerse.examples: God sold Israel into Jabin's hand (v. 2); now God will sell Sisera into a woman's hand. The transaction is reversed, by the same seller.

verseByVerse.quote: She sent and summoned Barak the son of Abinoam from Kedesh-naphtali and said to him, "Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you, 'Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor, taking 10,000 from the people of Naphtali and the people of Zebulun. And I will draw out Sisera, the general of Jabin's army, to meet you by the river Kishon with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Barak already has God’s command and God’s promise: God will bring the enemy to the chosen place and give him into Barak’s hand.

Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you? This is not Deborah handing Barak a new commission. She is asking a man who already has one why nothing has happened. The muster point was chosen, the tribes named, the numbers given, and Barak was at home in Kedesh-naphtali with his orders in his pocket. The problem in the north is not that God has been silent. It is that a man has heard him and stayed where he was.

I will draw out Sisera. The command comes wrapped in a promise, and the promise does the harder half of the work. Israel does not have to find Sisera; the enemy will be brought to the chosen ground. And “I will give him into your hand”, the promise of this whole history, is said before anybody has marched.

By the river Kishon. The ground God names is the last place a sensible commander would pick. The plain of Jezreel is flat and open, exactly the country chariots were built for. God proposes to fight nine hundred iron chariots on their own terrain, and says he will personally arrange the enemy’s attendance.
verseByVerse.note: Mount Tabor rises from the Jezreel valley; the Kishon river runs through it.

verseByVerse.quote: Barak said to her, "If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go." And she said, "I will surely go with you. Nevertheless, the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." Then Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh. And Barak called out Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh. And 10,000 men went up at his heels, and Deborah went up with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Barak will obey only if Deborah comes too; God graciously grants it, but the honour of the victory will go to a woman.

If you will go with me, I will go. Barak’s answer is not a refusal, and it is not obedience either. It is a condition. Be fair to him. He does not deny the word or dispute the odds, and Hebrews lists him among those who by faith conquered kingdoms (Hebrews 11:32–33). But he has the command of God through a prophetess the whole country trusts, and what he wants in addition is a person he can see standing next to him.

I will surely go with you. She agrees at once, without a lecture, and tells him the cost. The cost is not the victory, which is certain, but the honour of it: “the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.” Barak, and the reader, will assume she means herself. She goes; a man who needed her presence in order to obey is given it, and the ten thousand assemble.

Weak faith and a kind God. God does not withdraw the commission from a man who asked for a crutch. He gives him the crutch and the commission, and quietly moves the honour somewhere else. It is the kindness of a God who works with weak faith rather than waiting for strong faith, and the reason Barak’s name stands in Hebrews is not the quality of his obedience but the faithfulness of the one he finally trusted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD wins the battle on the very ground where the enemy seemed strongest. An aside notes that Heber the Kenite had moved his tent near Kedesh (v. 11), a detail that will matter soon. Sisera hears that Barak is on Mount Tabor and brings all nine hundred chariots to the river Kishon, exactly where God said he would draw him (vv. 12–13). Deborah gives the word: today the LORD has given Sisera into your hand, for the LORD goes out before you (v. 14). Barak comes down, the LORD routs the chariots, and Sisera abandons his chariot and flees on foot. Not one of his army is left (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The verb in verse 15 belongs to God: the LORD routed Sisera, infantry from a hill against armour on the plain where chariots are supposed to win.
verseByVerse.examples: Nine hundred iron chariots had made a nation afraid for twenty years, and the man who commanded them finishes the day running across country on foot like anybody else.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent as far away as the oak in Zaanannim, which is near Kedesh. When Sisera was told that Barak the son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor, Sisera called out all his chariots, 900 chariots of iron, and all the men who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the river Kishon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A small note about a tent prepares the end of the story, while Sisera, acting on good information, marches exactly where God said he would.

Heber the Kenite. An aside about a man moving house. The Kenites entered this book in 1:16, settling with Judah in the south. Heber has left them and pitched his tent near Kedesh, precisely where Barak is mustering. Six verses later it is the most important sentence in the chapter (v. 17).

Sisera called out all his chariots. Sisera does exactly what God said he would: “I will draw out Sisera… to meet you by the river Kishon.” He comes of his own initiative, with everything he has, to the spot named in advance, responding to intelligence about an outnumbered enemy on a hill. Everything he concludes is correct, and it takes him to the place God chose.

Uncertain wording. Moses’ father-in-law is called Jethro and Reuel elsewhere (Exodus 3:1; 2:18). The Hebrew word here can also mean brother-in-law, and Numbers 10:29 makes Hobab the son of Reuel, so Hobab may have been Moses’ brother-in-law.

verseByVerse.quote: And Deborah said to Barak, "Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?" So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with 10,000 men following him. And the LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak by the edge of the sword. And Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot. And Barak pursued the chariots and the army to Harosheth-hagoyim, and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword; not a man was left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has gone ahead of his people, and he destroys the chariots on the ground where they seemed strongest.

Up! The order treats the battle as already decided: “this is the day in which the LORD has given”, not will give. And then the whole argument as a question: “Does not the LORD go out before you?” Barak is told that somebody has already gone ahead of him into the battle.

He went ahead into death. That is the shape of the greatest rescue too. Christians are not sent to win a battle nobody has fought. Jesus went ahead of them into death and out of it, and Hebrews calls him the founder of their salvation and their forerunner (Hebrews 2:10; 6:20).

So Barak went down from Mount Tabor. Ten thousand men walk off a defensible hill onto flat ground towards massed chariots, because a woman told them the LORD had gone in front.

The LORD routed Sisera. The swords in Israelite hands are mentioned, and they are not the explanation. The next chapter gives it in one line of poetry: “The torrent Kishon swept them away” (5:21). The river came down, the plain turned to mud, and nine hundred iron chariots became nine hundred heavy objects stuck in a floodplain. Their weight, which made them unstoppable on dry ground, held them fast in the mud.

Fled away on foot. Then the detail the writer enjoys. The chariot was the reason a nation had lain down for twenty years, and Sisera abandons it in a field. Barak, whatever was wrong with his faith in verse 8, pursues properly, all the way back to their base.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God finishes the victory through an unexpected hand, and Israel for once completes the work. Sisera runs to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber, because Heber is at peace with Jabin (v. 17). She welcomes him, covers him, gives him milk instead of water, and he tells her to say no one is there (vv. 18–20). As he sleeps from weariness she drives a tent peg through his temple (v. 21). When Barak arrives she shows him the man he is seeking, dead (v. 22). Deborah’s word has come true. God subdues Jabin, and Israel presses harder and harder until he is destroyed (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Heber's household had peace with Jabin (v. 17); Jael breaks with her husband's treaty to side with Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: The last two verses record something that has not happened anywhere else in this book: a job finished. Israel pressed harder and harder until they destroyed Jabin. Chapter 1 is a list of things left standing; this is the one enemy who is not left standing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: But Sisera fled away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite. And Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid." So he turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug. And he said to her, "Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty." So she opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink and covered him. And he said to her, "Stand at the opening of the tent, and if any man comes and asks you, 'Is anyone here?' say, 'No.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sisera runs to the one tent where he expects safety, and the hospitality he trusts becomes his trap.

To the tent of Jael. Now the aside about Heber’s tent shows its purpose. Sisera runs for the one place in the district where he has a treaty. His reasoning is sound and his information correct.

Turn aside, my lord. Everything Jael says is what an exhausted fugitive most wants to hear, “my lord”, twice “turn aside”, and “do not be afraid”, and the first thing she does is cover him up. He asks for water; she gives him milk, heavier and likelier to send a worn-out man to sleep, and covers him again. Every detail is more hospitable than what was asked, and the hospitality is the trap. A guest under a tent roof was under the host’s protection absolutely; that is what Sisera is counting on, and why he does not watch her.

His last words. His last recorded words are an order to lie for him. He posts as his sentry the woman who is about to kill him, and goes to sleep.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “rug” occurs only here; it was some kind of covering, a blanket or rug, but its exact form is unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand. Then she went softly to him and drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground while he was lying fast asleep from weariness. So he died. And behold, as Barak was pursuing Sisera, Jael went out to meet him and said to him, "Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking." So he went in to her tent, and there lay Sisera dead, with the tent peg in his temple. So on that day God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the people of Israel. And the hand of the people of Israel pressed harder and harder against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jael kills the enemy commander with the tools of her own trade, Deborah’s word comes true, and God subdues Jabin until Israel destroys him.

A tent peg and a hammer. These are not improvised weapons; they are the tools of her trade. Among tent-dwellers pitching the tent was often women’s work, and Jael had driven pegs into hard ground more times than she could count. The commander of nine hundred chariots dies in his sleep by domestic equipment, and the writer does not soften a syllable of it.

As Barak was pursuing Sisera. Barak arrives at a run, and a woman steps out of a tent and offers to show him what he is looking for. Deborah’s word in verse 9 comes true, and not as Barak had supposed. He will get the victory in the record and the credit in Hebrews, but the honour of killing Sisera has gone to a woman, and not even to Deborah.

So on that day God subdued Jabin. The chapter signs off by naming the author of the whole thing, and it is not Barak, Deborah or Jael. Then a sentence unlike anything else in this book: Israel pressed “harder and harder” until they destroyed Jabin. Set that against the eightfold “did not drive out” of chapter 1, and every other victory in Judges ending in a rest that wears off. Here, once, the work is carried through. Hazor is not mentioned again in this book.

What God used. It took a woman under a palm tree already doing her job, a man who would not move until she came, ten thousand men who walked onto chariot ground, a river that came down at the right hour, and a housewife with a mallet. God arranged every piece, including the tent near Kedesh, and took the credit in a single sentence.

Is Jael praised for treachery? She took Israel’s side against a tyrant who had oppressed God’s people for twenty years, when many of Israel’s own men held back, and Deborah’s song blesses her for that (5:24). The blessing honours where she stood, as Rahab’s faith is honoured (Hebrews 11:31); it is not a pattern for breaking faith with a guest in ordinary life. This was war, and Sisera was God’s judged enemy. Hebrews does not name Jael.

A better Deliverer. The deliverers of this period are flawed pointers to a better one. Jael crushed the enemy’s head by a deception; Christ defeated the enemy of his people, the one who had the power of death, not by deceiving a guest but by giving his own life for them (Hebrews 2:14–15).

4.theology:
What is not faced grows. The iron chariots of 1:19 were an excuse that sounded practical at the time; now there are nine hundred of them, and the burned-out capital Israel did not occupy has a king in it again. Neither required a new decision by anybody. They are what happens to ground that is left unoccupied.

A question, not a call. Barak is not being commissioned in verse 6 but asked why nothing has happened since he was. The problem in the north was never that God had been silent.

The transaction reversed. In verse 2 the LORD sold Israel into Jabin's hand; in verse 9 the LORD will sell Sisera into a woman's hand. The same verb and the same seller. Israel’s oppression and Israel’s deliverance both come from the same hand.

Ordinary equipment. The chapter's deliverance is carried by a woman already doing her job under a tree, a river doing what rivers do, and a tent peg. Nothing in it was fetched in specially.
4.examples:
A general sat at home with his orders while a woman held court under a palm tree and a foreign army ran the north. When he finally moved, he moved on condition, walked ten thousand men off a hill onto chariot ground, and arrived at the end of the chase to find the war already finished by somebody with a tent peg.

Two questions come out of it. The first is Deborah's, aimed at people who have already been told what to do: has not the LORD commanded you? Many Christians who seem to be waiting for guidance already have it and are not acting on it. But hear the second half of her sentence too: does not the LORD go out before you? The command comes with the promise, and the Spirit who gives the courage to go down the hill is given before the battle, not after it. The second question is about the iron chariots, the thing you decided years ago was beyond reach. It has not stayed the size it was when you decided. And if, like Barak, you have obeyed late and on conditions, the God of this chapter still used him, and has a Deliverer whose obedience was neither late nor conditional, offered in your place.

keyVerse.quote: And Deborah said to Barak, “Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?” So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with 10,000 men following him.
keyVerse.note: The battle is decided before it is fought: the LORD “has given” Sisera, and he goes out ahead of his people. Barak’s part is simply to go down the mountain on the strength of that word. Christians face every enemy in the same way, following a Saviour who has already gone ahead of them into death and out of it.

4.reflection:
Deborah asks Barak, “Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you?” (v. 6). Is there something God has already made clear to you in his word that you have not yet acted on? What is holding you back?

Barak would go only if Deborah went with him (v. 8), and God graciously agreed. What does this show about how God deals with weak faith? Where do you lean on visible props rather than on God’s promise?

Nine hundred iron chariots were swept away on the very ground where they seemed strongest (vv. 13–15). What seems unbeatable in your life or your world, and how does “Does not the LORD go out before you?” (v. 14) change how you face it?

God used a prophetess, a hesitant general, a flooded river and a woman with a tent peg. How does this chapter encourage you about the ordinary, unnoticed work God gives you to do?

5.title: The Song of Deborah
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day:<sup>2</sup>"That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the LORD!<sup>3</sup>"Hear, O kings; give ear, O princes; to the LORD I will sing; I will make melody to the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>4</sup>"LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom, the earth trembled and the heavens dropped, yes, the clouds dropped water.<sup>5</sup>The mountains quaked before the LORD, even Sinai before the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>6</sup>"In the days of Shamgar, son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were abandoned, and travelers kept to the byways.<sup>7</sup>The villagers ceased in Israel; they ceased to be until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel.<sup>8</sup>When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates. Was shield or spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel?<sup>9</sup>My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"Tell of it, you who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets and you who walk by the way.<sup>11</sup>To the sound of musicians at the watering places, there they repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD, the righteous triumphs of his villagers in Israel. "Then down to the gates marched the people of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, break out in a song! Arise, Barak, lead away your captives, O son of Abinoam.<sup>13</sup>Then down marched the remnant of the noble; the people of the LORD marched down for me against the mighty.<sup>14</sup>From Ephraim their root they marched down into the valley, following you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen; from Machir marched down the commanders, and from Zebulun those who bear the lieutenant's staff;<sup>15</sup>the princes of Issachar came with Deborah, and Issachar faithful to Barak; into the valley they rushed at his heels. Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.<sup>16</sup>Why did you sit still among the sheepfolds, to hear the whistling for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.<sup>17</sup>Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why did he stay with the ships? Asher sat still at the coast of the sea, staying by his landings.<sup>18</sup>Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the field.<sup>19</sup>"The kings came, they fought; then fought the kings of Canaan, at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo; they got no spoils of silver.<sup>20</sup>From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera.<sup>21</sup>The torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon. March on, my soul, with might!<sup>22</sup>"Then loud beat the horses' hoofs with the galloping, galloping of his steeds.<sup>23</sup>"Curse Meroz, says the angel of the LORD, curse its inhabitants thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.<sup>24</sup>"Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, of tent-dwelling women most blessed.<sup>25</sup>He asked for water and she gave him milk; she brought him curds in a noble's bowl.<sup>26</sup>She sent her hand to the tent peg and her right hand to the workmen's mallet; she struck Sisera; she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple.<sup>27</sup>Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell—dead.<sup>28</sup>"Out of the window she peered, the mother of Sisera wailed through the lattice: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the hoofbeats of his chariots?'<sup>29</sup>Her wisest princesses answer, indeed, she answers herself,<sup>30</sup>'Have they not found and divided the spoil?— A womb or two for every man; spoil of dyed materials for Sisera, spoil of dyed materials embroidered, two pieces of dyed work embroidered for the neck as spoil?'<sup>31</sup>"So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might." And the land had rest for forty years.
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 told in prose how the LORD routed Sisera’s chariots through Deborah, Barak and Jael. Chapter 5 tells the same victory again as a song, sung “on that day” (v. 1), one of the oldest poems in the Bible.

The message. The victory belongs to the LORD, who still marches out for his people as he did at Sinai and turns heaven and the weather against those who crush them. The right response is praise, and willing, costly commitment: the song blesses those who offered themselves, shames those who stayed at home, and ends praying that all God’s enemies perish and his friends shine like the rising sun.

Why it was said. Israel had chosen new gods and paid for it with twenty years of occupation (v. 8; see the introduction). A people whose next generation could forget the LORD (2:10) needed a song to carry the memory, and this song asks to be retold at every watering place (v. 11).

How the chapter makes its case. The song blesses the LORD for volunteers and summons kings to listen (vv. 1–3), then remembers the LORD marching from Seir with the earth shaking (vv. 4–5). It recalls the misery of the occupation and its cause, new gods, until Deborah arose (vv. 6–8), and calls everyone to retell the LORD’s triumphs (vv. 9–11). The roll call names the tribes who came and those who stayed with their sheep and ships (vv. 12–18). Heaven fights, the Kishon sweeps the chariots away, and Meroz is cursed for not coming (vv. 19–23). Jael is blessed and Sisera falls, while his mother waits at a window for plunder that will never come (vv. 24–30). The song closes in prayer, and the land has rest (v. 31).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by the character of God it reveals, and by pattern. The LORD who marches out to fight for helpless people came in person in his Son, and won the decisive battle at the cross. The willing volunteers anticipate the Messiah’s people: “Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power” (Psalm 110:3). The crushed head of the oppressor echoes the first promise (Genesis 3:15), and the friends who shine like the sunrise will “shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43), where the redeemed sing of a victory they did not win, “the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3).

For us. Salvation is God’s work, and our first response is praise that tells it again. But the song also asks where we were when the call came. Christ went out onto the exposed field for us; those he has won need not sit among the sheepfolds deliberating while his cause needs them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The God Who Marched from Seir
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song begins with praise and with memory: the victory just won is one more step in the LORD’s march from Sinai. Deborah and Barak bless the LORD that leaders led and the people volunteered, and summon foreign kings to hear (vv. 1–3). The LORD comes from Seir and Edom, the earth trembling and the clouds pouring rain, as at Sinai (vv. 4–5). Then the occupation, seen from the ground: empty roads, deserted villages, a disarmed nation, all because new gods were chosen, until Deborah arose “as a mother in Israel” (vv. 6–8). The section ends by blessing the willing commanders and calling rich and poor alike to retell the LORD’s righteous triumphs at the wells (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's first response to its rescue is a song, as it was at the Red Sea (Exod. 15). Worship comes before analysis, and the song does its thinking in the form of praise.
verseByVerse.examples: When ordinary life shrinks, when the roads empty and people stop going out, the song invites us to ask not only what has gone wrong around us but what has been chosen in place of God (v. 8).

verseByVerse.quote: Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day: "That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the LORD! "Hear, O kings; give ear, O princes; to the LORD I will sing; I will make melody to the LORD, the God of Israel. "LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom, the earth trembled and the heavens dropped, yes, the clouds dropped water. The mountains quaked before the LORD, even Sinai before the LORD, the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song begins by blessing the LORD that his people volunteered, and reaches back to Sinai: the God who won this battle is the God who came marching from the south with the earth shaking.

On that day. Deborah and Barak sing on the day itself. And the first thing the song blesses God for is not the victory but the volunteering: “the people offered themselves willingly”. After a chapter in which the general had to be sent for, gratitude starts with the fact that people came. The theme returns in verse 9, and the roll call (vv. 12–18) lists who came and who did not.

Hear, O kings. The audience is not Israel but kings and princes, the kind just beaten. Deborah tells the rulers of the region what happens to armies that come against her God.

When you marched from the region of Edom. Before a word about Sisera, the song goes back to Sinai. Seir and Edom lie south of the Dead Sea, on the road up from Sinai, and the picture is the LORD marching north out of the desert with the ground shaking under him, as at the mountain that smoked and quaked (Exodus 19:16–18; Deuteronomy 33:2).

Why Sinai matters here. This is the song’s whole argument. The battle in Galilee is one more stage of a march that began at Sinai, with the same weather in both: “the clouds dropped water”. A storm is about to destroy Sisera’s chariots, and the song has already told us who walks in it. Canaan credited the storm to Baal; the song gives it to the LORD.

The willing people of a greater Captain. A psalm uses the same word for the Messiah’s people: “Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power” (Psalm 110:3). Deborah’s volunteers came because the LORD had marched out ahead of them. Christ went out first and alone, and his people offer themselves gladly, not to earn a place in his army but because the battle is already his.

Uncertain wording. The opening phrase of verse 2, “that the leaders took the lead”, is rare Hebrew. Its words can also mean “when locks hung loose”, perhaps warriors with unbound hair as a sign of dedication for battle; ESV takes it of leaders taking the lead. Either way it praises wholehearted commitment, and its partner line is clear.
verseByVerse.note: “Even Sinai” may be rendered “the One of Sinai” (ESV note). The Hebrew of this song is very old and in places hard, so translations differ more here than in the prose of chapter 4.

verseByVerse.quote: "In the days of Shamgar, son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were abandoned, and travelers kept to the byways. The villagers ceased in Israel; they ceased to be until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel. When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates. Was shield or spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel? My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD. "Tell of it, you who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets and you who walk by the way. To the sound of musicians at the watering places, there they repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD, the righteous triumphs of his villagers in Israel. "Then down to the gates marched the people of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The occupation had emptied Israel’s roads and villages and left it defenceless, because Israel had chosen new gods; then God raised up Deborah, and now everyone, rich and poor, is to retell what the LORD has done.

The highways were abandoned. Twenty years of occupation, seen from ground level, are described in terms of roads. The main routes were where you were robbed, so travellers kept to back lanes and trade moved at the pace of frightened people. The days of Shamgar (3:31) and of Jael mark the time.

The villagers ceased in Israel. Worse, the unwalled settlements emptied. Farming families gave up the open country for towns with gates, the fields went out of cultivation, and the nation began quietly starving in its own land. Tyranny does not usually announce itself in massacres; it shrinks ordinary life until people stop going out.

I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel. The turn comes in one line, and the title she gives herself is not judge, prophetess or commander, but “a mother in Israel”. It fits. She did not lead the army herself: she sent for the man who should have gone already, went with him when he would not go alone, and told him when to move. The country was rescued by someone who cared for it like a mother.

When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates. Verse 8 states the cause chapter 4 never spelled out: the idolatry was not a religious matter alongside a political one but the reason the roads emptied. The second half asks a question with a terrible answer: forty thousand men in Israel and not a shield or spear among them, a nation disarmed by its occupiers, as the Philistines would later keep Israel without a blacksmith (1 Samuel 13:19–22).

Tell of it. Then a summons to remember, aimed at everybody. Those who ride on white donkeys and sit on rich carpets are the wealthy; those who walk by the way are everyone else. Both are to talk about this at the watering places, where villagers meet every day. In chapter 2 a generation grew up that did not know what the LORD had done (2:10); here his “righteous triumphs” (literally “righteous acts”) are to be told at every well. His victories are not raw power but justice, putting right what the oppressor had done.

Our watering places. Faith is kept alive the same way now, by ordinary people telling what God has done where they meet. At the Lord’s Supper “you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26): a greater deliverance than Deborah’s, told at a table.

Uncertain wording. Several words here are rare. “Villagers” (vv. 7, 11) may mean the people of the open villages, as ESV takes it, or warriors or leaders. Verse 8 can also be read “God chose new leaders”, though “new gods were chosen” fits the book’s pattern (2:11–14). The “rich carpets” and the “musicians” (perhaps singers, or archers in older versions) are also uncertain. The sense is clear even where single words are not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the LORD calls, his people are measured by whether they come. Deborah is roused to sing and Barak to lead away his captives (v. 12). Then the roll: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun and Issachar march down into the valley (vv. 13–15a). Reuben has great searchings of heart and stays among the sheepfolds; Gilead stays beyond the Jordan, Dan with his ships, Asher by his landings (vv. 15b–17). None of their reasons is wicked, and all of them kept them at home. Zebulun and Naphtali, who bore the brunt of it, “risked their lives to the death” on the heights (v. 18).
