verseByVerse.theology: A muster roll is an unusual thing to set to music. The song makes the record of who came part of Israel's worship, so that faithfulness and its absence are both remembered before God.
verseByVerse.examples: Most of us will never be Deborah or Jael. The roll call is where ordinary believers find themselves, among the tribes who came or among those who stayed at home.

verseByVerse.quote: "Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, break out in a song! Arise, Barak, lead away your captives, O son of Abinoam. Then down marched the remnant of the noble; the people of the LORD marched down for me against the mighty. From Ephraim their root they marched down into the valley, following you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen; from Machir marched down the commanders, and from Zebulun those who bear the lieutenant's staff; the princes of Issachar came with Deborah, and Issachar faithful to Barak; into the valley they rushed at his heels. Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart. Why did you sit still among the sheepfolds, to hear the whistling for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart. Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why did he stay with the ships? Asher sat still at the coast of the sea, staying by his landings. Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the call came, some tribes risked everything and others stayed at home for good reasons, and the song records both so that every hearer asks which he would have been.

Awake, awake, Deborah! The song rouses its own singer and its general: Deborah to sing, Barak to lead his captives away (v. 12).

Then down marched the remnant. Five names come first, and the verbs are all of movement: marched down, came, rushed at his heels, Issachar running downhill towards nine hundred chariots. Machir (v. 14) is the leading clan of Manasseh (Numbers 26:29), here probably the half of the tribe west of the Jordan, since Gilead across the river is named among those who stayed at home (v. 17).

Great searchings of heart. The song’s treatment of Reuben is the sharpest thing in it. He is not accused of cowardice or treachery. He is charged with “great searchings of heart”, and the phrase comes twice, before and after the question, so that no one can miss it. Reuben thought about it seriously and with real feeling. Between the repetitions is a picture devastating in its ordinariness: sitting among the sheepfolds, listening to the whistling for the flocks, within earshot of his livelihood while the deliberating went on.

Gilead, Dan and Asher. The other three are given no motive but their occupations: Gilead has a river in the way, Dan has shipping, Asher his landings. None is a wicked excuse. They are the reasons anyone would give: distance, business, responsibilities that do not pause because someone else is in trouble.

Zebulun and Naphtali. The two tribes Barak mustered (4:6) get the highest line in the song: they “risked their lives to the death” on the exposed heights. Set the two halves of the roll call side by side, because that is what the poem is for: Reuben, deliberating within earshot of the sheep; Zebulun, on the heights of the field.

The age of great searchings of heart. Reuben would fit in well today. We prize reflection, and rightly distrust people who rush into things. But endless options can make deliberating a place to live rather than a road to a decision. Kierkegaard, writing in the 1840s, described his own as an age of reflection that weighs every cause seriously and commits itself to none, and thought it more dangerous than an age of rash passion. Keeping our options open feels like freedom; often it is a way of making sure a commitment never costs us the flocks. The song does not mock Reuben’s thinking. It notices that the thinking took the whole battle, and that careful thought was never meant to replace coming.

The one who did not stay at home. The gospel meets us here, because it is not first a call for our commitment but news of Christ’s. He did not consider our trouble from a safe distance. He “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), and did not merely risk his life to the death but gave it. People loved like that can stop deliberating and come.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verses 13–15 is compressed, and translations differ (“From Ephraim their root” is one example); the “lieutenant’s staff” is literally the staff of a scribe or marshal, an officer who mustered troops. The two phrases translated “great searchings of heart” differ by one letter in Hebrew: the first (v. 15) may mean “great resolves”. If so, the irony sharpens: great resolutions, great deliberations, and nobody came. Dan “with the ships” is puzzling too, since Dan’s first allotment reached towards Joppa (Joshua 19:40–46); it may mean Danites working on coastal shipping.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–23 — From Heaven the Stars Fought
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The battle was won from heaven, and the only curse in the song falls on Israelites who would not come. The kings of Canaan fight at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo and carry off no silver (v. 19). The stars fight from their courses, and the Kishon, swollen by the storm, sweeps the army away while the horses gallop in flight (vv. 20–22). Then the angel of the LORD curses Meroz, a town that stayed at home, “because they did not come to the help of the LORD” (v. 23). Standing aside while God rescues his people is not neutrality.
verseByVerse.theology: The song credits the victory to heaven and to the creation together: the stars fought, and the river swept the enemy away. Israel's part was real, but it was not what decided the day.
verseByVerse.examples: Meroz is cursed for staying away from what God was doing. It is worth asking where he is at work around us, and whether we have kept our distance.

verseByVerse.quote: "The kings came, they fought; then fought the kings of Canaan, at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo; they got no spoils of silver. From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera. The torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon. March on, my soul, with might! "Then loud beat the horses' hoofs with the galloping, galloping of his steeds. "Curse Meroz, says the angel of the LORD, curse its inhabitants thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kings of Canaan were beaten from heaven, as a storm swelled the Kishon and swept their chariots away; and the song’s only curse falls on an Israelite town that would not come.

They got no spoils of silver. The kings came for plunder and went home with nothing, if they went home at all.

From heaven the stars fought. Chapter 4 said only that the LORD routed Sisera; the song tells how. The Kishon is a trickle for most of the year and a torrent when rain falls on the hills, and the plain turns to a bog in an afternoon. Nine hundred iron chariots on flat ground in mud: the weight that made them irresistible on a dry plain fixed them where they stood. The galloping hoofs of verse 22 are horses in flight. Whatever “the stars fought” means precisely, the claim is that creation itself was ranged against Sisera. He worshipped gods who were supposed to run the weather. The weather killed him.

Even winds and sea obey him. The weather the song gives to the LORD later obeyed a man in a boat on the lake of Galilee, and his disciples asked, “What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?” (Matthew 8:27). The song has already answered: the God who marched from Seir.

Curse Meroz. Then the harshest sentence in the song, aimed not at Canaan but at an Israelite settlement near enough to have come. Reuben was chided and Dan asked a question; Meroz is cursed, thoroughly, by the angel of the LORD, who brought God’s charge against Israel at Bochim (2:1–3). The charge is not that Meroz fought on the wrong side, but that they did not come “to the help of the LORD against the mighty”, though God plainly needed no reinforcements. They are held responsible for not turning up to a battle he had already won.

Why the curse is just. The God who curses Meroz had come up from Sinai for these people before any of them lifted a spear. To stand aside when he is rescuing his people is not neutrality but taking a side. The warning is meant to send his people back to him, not to make them earn the rescue. And every believer who has stayed at home when he called may hear the better word: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

Uncertain wording. “From heaven the stars fought” may describe the rain that fell from the sky, the heavenly host fighting for Israel, or simply the whole created order taking the LORD’s side; the song does not explain it. “March on, my soul, with might!” (v. 21) is difficult Hebrew, and some translate it differently. Meroz is mentioned nowhere else, and its site is unknown.
verseByVerse.note: The Kishon drains the Jezreel valley and runs north-west to the sea below Mount Carmel; in the dry season it is little more than a stream.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two women close the battle, and the song sets them side by side. Jael, the Kenite’s wife, is “most blessed of women”: she gives Sisera milk in a noble’s bowl and kills him with a tent peg and mallet, and the lines fall like hammer blows (vv. 24–27). Then the song crosses into enemy country, to a window where Sisera’s mother waits for his chariot. Her wise ladies, and she herself, explain the delay: the men are dividing the spoil, women and embroidered cloth (vv. 28–30). We pity her, then see what she was ready to celebrate, and we know what she does not: her son is dead.
verseByVerse.theology: The song blesses a deed that most readers find hard, and the comment below takes up directly the question of Jael and her guest.
verseByVerse.examples: Even in a victory song, Israel's poet sees the grief on the other side. That is worth learning for the way God's people speak about those they oppose, without pretending that evil was not evil.

verseByVerse.quote: "Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, of tent-dwelling women most blessed. He asked for water and she gave him milk; she brought him curds in a noble's bowl. She sent her hand to the tent peg and her right hand to the workmen's mallet; she struck Sisera; she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple. Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell—dead. "Out of the window she peered, the mother of Sisera wailed through the lattice: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the hoofbeats of his chariots?' Her wisest princesses answer, indeed, she answers herself, 'Have they not found and divided the spoil?— A womb or two for every man; spoil of dyed materials for Sisera, spoil of dyed materials embroidered, two pieces of dyed work embroidered for the neck as spoil?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jael is blessed for striking down the oppressor when whole tribes stayed at home, and the song then shows Sisera’s mother waiting for plunder that will never come, so that we feel both pity and the evil she took for granted.

Most blessed of women be Jael. The song answers the curse of Meroz with a blessing in the strongest terms it can find. Only one other person in Scripture is greeted in words like these: when Mary comes to Elizabeth’s house, Elizabeth cries out, “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:42). The mother of the Lord and a Kenite housewife with a mallet: both blessings are spoken over a woman through whom God did what nobody expected.

The workmen’s mallet. The poem tells the deed more slowly than the prose did and names the tools twice: the tent peg and the “workmen’s mallet”. It was not a weapon that happened to be lying about but the equipment of a trade, in a hand that used it every day.

He sank, he fell. Then the hammering. Read verse 27 aloud and the sound is the point: “he sank, he fell, he lay still… where he sank, there he fell”. The lines beat like a mallet on a peg, and the last word of the stanza, “dead”, is the last word about Sisera.

The mother of Sisera. Then the song leaves the battlefield, crosses into enemy country and stops at a window, where a woman watches the road for her son and has begun asking aloud why his chariot is so long in coming. We know why; she does not. It is one of the most humane moments in the Old Testament, written by the winning side on the day of victory.

A womb or two for every man. Then comes the reassurance she settles on, the ugliest line in the song: the delay must be the dividing of plunder, and the first item is women, “a womb or two for every man”, in the crudest of terms. It shows what such an army did in the villages, and why the highways of verse 6 were empty. In three verses the song makes us pity her and then shows us what she was comfortable with.

She crushed his head. One line has long made Christians think further back: “she crushed his head” (v. 26). Many hear in it an echo of the first promise, that the woman’s offspring would bruise the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). The song does not say so, and Jael is no saviour. But each time God breaks an oppressor through the weak he keeps that promise in a small way, until “the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20), because Christ was “crushed for our iniquities” first (Isaiah 53:5).

Does the song bless betrayal? It blesses her for taking the LORD’s side against a tyrant who had oppressed his people for twenty years, at the hour when whole tribes stayed at home (v. 24). Rahab is honoured in the same way for where she stood (Hebrews 11:31). The song is no pattern for breaking faith with a guest in ordinary life: this was war, and Sisera was an enemy God had already judged. Hebrews does not name Jael, and even the judges it does name are commended for their faith, not for everything they did (Hebrews 11:32; see the introduction).

verseByVerse.ref: v. 31 — Like the Sun as He Rises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song ends in prayer: may all the LORD’s enemies perish like Sisera, and may those who love him be like the sun rising in its strength. The two halves are one wish, that evil should end and goodness shine. It is not private revenge but the longing of a people who have seen what oppression does, and it reaches forward to the day when the righteous will shine in their Father’s kingdom. Then the narrator adds a single sentence: the land had rest for forty years, the gift of the God the whole song has praised.
verseByVerse.theology: The closing prayer looks beyond this one battle to the end of all evil and the shining of all who love God, a hope the rest of Scripture takes up.
verseByVerse.examples: The rest is real, it is dated, and it lasts one generation; the reader of Judges knows what the next sentence of the book will be. Peace in this world, however hard won, is always for a time.

verseByVerse.quote: "So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might." And the land had rest for forty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song ends praying that every enemy of the LORD will perish like Sisera and that those who love him will shine like the rising sun; and God gave the land forty years of rest.

So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! The first half is hard, and should not be tidied up. It is prayed straight after the scene of a bereaved mother, by people who have seen what these enemies did to their villages. Prayers like this run all through the Psalms, and they ask one thing: that evil should not be managed or balanced, but end. The last book of the Bible contains the same prayer, from souls under the altar, and it is answered rather than rebuked (Revelation 6:10).

Praying it as Christians. Christians pray it in the light of the cross. Jesus taught his people to pray for their enemies (Matthew 5:44), and the prayer that evil should end is answered in two ways: some enemies of God are made his friends, as Paul was, and the rest will meet the justice he has promised. Every friend of God was once his enemy, reconciled by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10).

But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might. The second half is the one to take away. (In Hebrew “your friends” is literally “those who love him”.) The picture is the first minute of full light after a night, when the sky goes from grey to too bright to look at. That is what the poem asks for those who love God: not safety, not comfort, not even victory, but that they should be like that sunrise. The New Testament finishes the thought: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43). Their light will be borrowed, for Christ is the true dawn, “the sunrise” that visits us “from on high” (Luke 1:78).

And the land had rest for forty years. Then one flat sentence, and the singing stops. Forty years of quiet, bought by a woman under a palm tree, a man who had to be fetched, two tribes on the heights, a river in spate and a housewife with a mallet, and every bit of it credited in the song to the God who came up out of the south with the mountains shaking and the clouds dropping water.

5.theology:
One march, from Sinai to the Kishon. Before a word about Sisera, the song describes God coming up out of Edom with the clouds dropping water (vv. 4-5), and the same weather returns in verse 21 when the river takes the chariots. What happened in that valley was not a lucky storm but God arriving. The same God would one day arrive in person, and at the cross Jesus disarmed the powers behind every Sisera (Colossians 2:15).

What the absent tribes were doing. The song never calls Reuben, Gilead, Dan or Asher cowards. It records their occupations and sets them beside Zebulun, who came. Reuben's charge is the most searching in the book because it is not indifference: he took the matter seriously and stayed within earshot of his flocks.

Meroz. The one community cursed in this song is cursed for doing nothing, by the angel of the LORD who brought God’s charge against Israel at Bochim. The only thing the Bible ever says about Meroz is this sentence cursing it for staying home.

Two women at the end. Jael is called most blessed of women, echoed only in Elizabeth's greeting to Mary (Luke 1:42). Then the song stops at the enemy's window, where another woman's comfort tells the reader what had been happening on those empty highways for twenty years.
5.examples:
Then: A nation that had kept off the main roads for twenty years sang, on the day of its rescue, a song that named the tribes who came and those who did not, cursed a village for staying home, blessed a housewife with a mallet, and paused at the window of the enemy commander's mother.

Now: Reuben is the one to think about longest, because he is the most respectable figure in the poem. He did not refuse; he deliberated, in earnest, within hearing of his own business, and the moment passed. The song's question to him is one to put to yourself about whatever you are weighing: what are you sitting among while the searching of heart goes on? The God who calls is the one who has already marched out for his people and won; he does not ask us to save him, but to come where he is working. Every reader has been Reuben more than once, and Christ never was: he went all the way into the battle that mattered, and his obedience covers our staying home. So the answer to a Reuben moment is not self-reproach but confession, and the Spirit who stirred Zebulun gives the willingness that verse 2 blesses God for.

keyVerse.quote: So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might.
keyVerse.note: The song’s last prayer gathers up everything before it: the LORD fights for his people, and evil will not have the last word. Its two halves are one wish, that God’s enemies should end and those who love him should shine, and the New Testament promises both, when “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43).

5.reflection:
The song’s first thanks is not for the victory but for people who “offered themselves willingly” (vv. 2, 9). What has the LORD done that makes a willing response possible, and where is he asking you to offer yourself now?

Israel was told to retell the LORD’s triumphs at the watering places (v. 11). Where are the ordinary places in your week where you could speak of what God has done, and what keeps you from it?

Reuben had “great searchings of heart” and stayed among the sheepfolds (vv. 15–16). Which of the reasons in verses 15–17 most often keeps you at home when God’s people need you, and how does Christ setting his face towards Jerusalem change that?

The song both pities Sisera’s mother and shows the evil she took for granted (vv. 28–30), and then prays that God’s enemies perish (v. 31). How can Christians long for evil to end while praying for their enemies?

6.title: The Call of Gideon
6.text: <sup>1</sup>The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the hand of Midian seven years.<sup>2</sup>And the hand of Midian overpowered Israel, and because of Midian the people of Israel made for themselves the dens that are in the mountains and the caves and the strongholds.<sup>3</sup>For whenever the Israelites planted crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East would come up against them.<sup>4</sup>They would encamp against them and devour the produce of the land, as far as Gaza, and leave no sustenance in Israel and no sheep or ox or donkey.<sup>5</sup>For they would come up with their livestock and their tents; they would come like locusts in number—both they and their camels could not be counted—so that they laid waste the land as they came in.<sup>6</sup>And Israel was brought very low because of Midian. And the people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>When the people of Israel cried out to the LORD on account of the Midianites,<sup>8</sup>the LORD sent a prophet to the people of Israel. And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I led you up from Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery.<sup>9</sup>And I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you, and drove them out before you and gave you their land.<sup>10</sup>And I said to you, 'I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell.' But you have not obeyed my voice."<sup>11</sup>Now the angel of the LORD came and sat under the terebinth at Ophrah, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, while his son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from the Midianites.<sup>12</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to him and said to him, "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor."<sup>13</sup>And Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? And where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us, saying, 'Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?' But now the LORD has forsaken us and given us into the hand of Midian."<sup>14</sup>And the LORD turned to him and said, "Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?"<sup>15</sup>And he said to him, "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house."<sup>16</sup>And the LORD said to him, "But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man."<sup>17</sup>And he said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, then show me a sign that it is you who speak with me.<sup>18</sup>Please do not depart from here until I come to you and bring out my present and set it before you." And he said, "I will stay till you return."<sup>19</sup>So Gideon went into his house and prepared a young goat and unleavened cakes from an ephah of flour. The meat he put in a basket, and the broth he put in a pot, and brought them to him under the terebinth and presented them.<sup>20</sup>And the angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and put them on this rock, and pour the broth over them." And he did so.<sup>21</sup>Then the angel of the LORD reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. And fire sprang up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. And the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.<sup>22</sup>Then Gideon perceived that he was the angel of the LORD. And Gideon said, "Alas, O Lord GOD! For now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face."<sup>23</sup>But the LORD said to him, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die."<sup>24</sup>Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it, The LORD Is Peace. To this day it still stands at Ophrah, which belongs to the Abiezrites.<sup>25</sup>That night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull, and the second bull seven years old, and pull down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is beside it<sup>26</sup>and build an altar to the LORD your God on the top of the stronghold here, with stones laid in due order. Then take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you shall cut down."<sup>27</sup>So Gideon took ten men of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.<sup>28</sup>When the men of the town rose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down, and the Asherah beside it was cut down, and the second bull was offered on the altar that had been built.<sup>29</sup>And they said to one another, "Who has done this thing?" And after they had searched and inquired, they said, "Gideon the son of Joash has done this thing."<sup>30</sup>Then the men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son, that he may die, for he has broken down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah beside it."<sup>31</sup>But Joash said to all who stood against him, "Will you contend for Baal? Or will you save him? Whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because his altar has been broken down."<sup>32</sup>Therefore on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is to say, "Let Baal contend against him," because he broke down his altar.<sup>33</sup>Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East came together, and they crossed the Jordan and encamped in the Valley of Jezreel.<sup>34</sup>But the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him.<sup>35</sup>And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.<sup>36</sup>Then Gideon said to God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said,<sup>37</sup>behold, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said."<sup>38</sup>And it was so. When he rose early next morning and squeezed the fleece, he wrung enough dew from the fleece to fill a bowl with water.<sup>39</sup>Then Gideon said to God, "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece. Please let it be dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground let there be dew."<sup>40</sup>And God did so that night; and it was dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground there was dew.
6.overview:
Where we are. After Deborah’s victory the land had rest for forty years (5:31). Now the cycle turns again: Israel does evil, and the LORD gives it into the hand of Midian. This is the start of the story of Gideon, the central judge of the book (chapters 6–8).

The message. God comes to the weak and frightened and makes them his instruments, not by first making them strong but by being with them. He answers Israel’s cry by naming its real problem, idolatry; he calls a man hiding in a winepress a “mighty man of valor”; he speaks peace to him; he starts the deliverance in his father’s back yard; and he bears with his fears with astonishing patience.

Why it was said. Israel had gone back to Baal and was being stripped bare by raiders every harvest (see the introduction). The first hearers needed to see that God’s silence was discipline, not desertion, and that he could still raise up a deliverer from the least of the least.

How the chapter makes its case. Seven years of Midianite raids drive Israel into caves, and Israel cries out (vv. 1–6). God sends a prophet first, to name the sin behind the suffering (vv. 7–10). The angel of the LORD finds Gideon threshing in a winepress and calls him (vv. 11–14). Gideon pleads his weakness and is told, “I will be with you” (vv. 15–16). Fire from the rock gives the sign, and the LORD speaks peace to a terrified man (vv. 17–24). Gideon’s first task is to pull down his father’s altar of Baal, which he does by night, and his father defends him (vv. 25–32). Midian gathers, the Spirit clothes Gideon and four tribes answer his trumpet (vv. 33–35). Then he asks for the fleece to be wet, then dry, and God patiently does both (vv. 36–40).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him, and, this commentary holds, by his own appearing. The angel of the LORD, who speaks as the LORD and whose face Gideon fears to have seen, is best read as the Son before his incarnation. The altar called “The LORD Is Peace” anticipates the one of whom Paul says, “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). And the God who does not break a bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3) is seen fully in Jesus, who came back for doubting Thomas and offered him his hands.

For us. God’s call never rests on our strength, and our true assessment of our weakness does not cancel it. Obedience may begin at home and may be done with shaking hands, and it is still obedience. And when our faith is weak, the God who answered Gideon twice is the Father of Jesus Christ, who is patient with those who are slow to believe.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Locusts, Caves, and a Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s suffering has a cause, and God names it before he removes it. For seven years Midian and its allies sweep in at every harvest like locusts, with camels beyond counting, and strip the land of crops and livestock, so that Israel hides in caves and strongholds (vv. 1–6). When Israel cries out, the LORD does not at once send a deliverer. He sends an unnamed prophet who recites what God has done, from Egypt to the gift of the land, and repeats the one command they broke: do not fear the gods of the Amorites (vv. 7–10). The rescue to come will deal with the real problem, not just the stated one.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter opens with the LORD giving his people into Midian's hand (v. 1). The raids are discipline, and discipline has a purpose: to bring a people back to the God they have left.
verseByVerse.examples: When we ask God to take away a pain, he sometimes deals first with something we did not mention. That is not indifference to the pain; it is care for the whole person.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the hand of Midian seven years. And the hand of Midian overpowered Israel, and because of Midian the people of Israel made for themselves the dens that are in the mountains and the caves and the strongholds. For whenever the Israelites planted crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East would come up against them. They would encamp against them and devour the produce of the land, as far as Gaza, and leave no sustenance in Israel and no sheep or ox or donkey. For they would come up with their livestock and their tents; they would come like locusts in number—both they and their camels could not be counted—so that they laid waste the land as they came in. And Israel was brought very low because of Midian. And the people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Israel did evil, God gave it into Midian’s hand, and for seven years raiders stripped the land bare at every harvest until Israel, living in caves, cried out to the LORD.

Dens, caves and strongholds. Picture verse 2: God’s people, in the land he swore to give them, living not in towns or on farms but in dens, caves and strongholds up in the hills. A generation earlier the complaint was about towns not taken; now Israelites are digging holes to sleep in on ground that is legally theirs.

Whenever the Israelites planted crops. The oppression is agricultural, and the timing is the cruelty: not a single invasion but a raid every harvest. Israel is left alone to plough, sow, weed and watch the crop come up; when it is ready to cut, the raiders arrive and camp on it. They take the grain, and then the sheep, oxen and donkeys, which means next year’s ploughing as well. It is not the terror of a battle but the slow exhaustion of working hard, year after year, at something you know you will not keep.

Like locusts in number. Two details explain how it was possible. The first is the comparison with locusts: not an army but a swarm, arriving in season, eating everything green and moving on. The second is the camels, among the earliest records of camels used in war on this scale. A camel raid could cross desert horses could not, appear where nobody was watching and be gone before a defence could form. Israel had no answer to it.

The people of Israel cried out for help. As always in this book, it is not called repentance. They are hungry and frightened, and they make a noise. Even so, the LORD hears it.
verseByVerse.note: Midian's homeland lay in the desert south-east of Israel, east of the Gulf of Aqaba; the Amalekites and the people of the East (v. 3) were other desert tribes who rode with them.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people of Israel cried out to the LORD on account of the Midianites, the LORD sent a prophet to the people of Israel. And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I led you up from Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery. And I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you, and drove them out before you and gave you their land. And I said to you, 'I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell.' But you have not obeyed my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Israel’s cry first with a prophet, who reminds them of all God has done and names the sin behind their suffering: they have not obeyed his voice.

The LORD sent a prophet. This is the surprise of the chapter. In every earlier cycle Israel cried out and the LORD raised up a deliverer. Here God sends a preacher, and he is never named.

I led you up from Egypt. The sermon recites what God has done, in the first person, as at Bochim (2:1). Four verbs, all his: I led you up, I brought you out, I delivered, I drove them out; and one gift, I gave you their land. Only then the command, “I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites”, and the charge, in the angel’s words from 2:2. The order matters: the command was never the price of the rescue. It was given to people already brought out, to show them how to live with the God who had rescued them.

But you have not obeyed my voice. The prophet states the case and stops, with no promise and no comfort. That withholding is a kindness, not a cruelty. Israel’s cry so far says nothing about Baal, and a rescue that left the Baal worship in place would only lead to another seven years like these. God takes the crying out seriously enough to answer the real problem rather than the stated one.

Conviction is help. We bring God our troubles and want them removed. He often answers first by showing us what lies beneath them, because he means to rescue us properly. Conviction is not the opposite of his help but often its first part.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–24 — The LORD Is with You, Mighty Man of Valour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls the least likely man and makes him his deliverer by being with him. The angel of the LORD sits under the terebinth at Ophrah while Gideon threshes wheat in a winepress, and greets him, “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor” (vv. 11–12). Gideon answers with honest complaint (v. 13), and the LORD sends him (v. 14). Gideon pleads his weakness and hears the answer given to Moses, “I will be with you” (vv. 15–16). He asks for a sign; fire springs from the rock and consumes his offering (vv. 17–21). Terrified that he has seen the angel of the LORD face to face, he is given peace, and builds an altar, “The LORD Is Peace” (vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Gideon's call follows the pattern of Moses' call closely: an appearance, an objection, a promise of God's presence and a sign. God is not inventing a new way of saving; he is doing again what he did at the exodus.
verseByVerse.examples: Gideon's complaint in verse 13 is not punished. God lets a frightened man say what he thinks and answers him with a calling rather than a rebuke. Honest prayer, even bitter prayer, is not shut out.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the angel of the LORD came and sat under the terebinth at Ophrah, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, while his son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from the Midianites. And the angel of the LORD appeared to him and said to him, "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel of the LORD comes to a frightened man hiding his harvest in a winepress and calls him what God will make him: a mighty man of valour, because the LORD is with him.

Under the terebinth at Ophrah. Neither figure is where a reader would expect. The angel of the LORD is sitting under a tree; Gideon is threshing wheat in a hole in the ground.

Beating out wheat in the winepress. Wheat was threshed on a threshing floor: a flat, open place, usually on a rise, because the process depends on wind. You beat the grain out and throw it up so the breeze carries the chaff away. A winepress is the opposite: a pit cut down into rock, out of the wind, where grapes were trodden. Nothing about it works for threshing, and the writer tells us why Gideon is there anyway: “to hide it from the Midianites”. The picture is a man crouched in a stone pit, doing a job badly in the one place it cannot be done well, because the alternative is being seen.

The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor. Both halves of the greeting look wrong: “The LORD is with you”, said to a man in a hole in an occupied country, and “mighty man of valor”, said to someone hiding his breakfast. The Hebrew phrase is a real title, used of soldiers of proven courage and of men of substance. It is the last description anybody in Ophrah would have given Gideon that day, Gideon included. God is not flattering him and is not being ironic. He is naming what this man is going to be before there is any evidence for it, and by naming him so, he begins to make him so.

The God who names us before we are it. The pattern runs through Scripture. An angel greets a young woman in Nazareth, “the Lord is with you!” (Luke 1:28), and Jesus names a wavering fisherman “Peter”, the rock (John 1:42). In Christ God still calls people what they are not yet, “holy and beloved” (Colossians 3:12), and then makes them so.

Seeing God and living. How could Gideon see him face to face and live (v. 22; Exodus 33:20)? God showed himself in a veiled form, and the word “Peace be to you. Do not fear” (v. 23) kept him.

Where Christians differ: who is the angel of the LORD? In verse 14 the text simply says “the LORD turned to him”, and in verse 22 Gideon fears for his life because he has seen this messenger face to face. Some take him as a created angel carrying God’s full authority. Many in the Reformed tradition, and before it, see the LORD himself appearing in person. This commentary’s view: he is best read as the Son before his incarnation, the one through whom God has always made himself known (John 1:18; see the note on 2:1–3).
verseByVerse.note: Ophrah, Gideon's home town, belonged to the clan of Abiezer in western Manasseh; its exact site is not known.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? And where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us, saying, 'Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?' But now the LORD has forsaken us and given us into the hand of Midian." And the LORD turned to him and said, "Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gideon answers the greeting with an honest complaint that God has forsaken Israel, and God answers not with an explanation but with a commission: go, for I am sending you.

Why then has all this happened to us? Gideon does not thank the messenger for the compliment. He argues with its first half, and the argument is the honest complaint of a man who has been reading his circumstances.

Where are all his wonderful deeds? Set this beside 2:10, because Gideon has the opposite problem. There the tragedy was a generation that “did not know the LORD or the work that he had done”. Gideon knows the work. He can quote it, “his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us”, with the sentence that goes with them: “Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?” Somebody had answered the child’s question about the stones at Gilgal after all (Joshua 4:6). And he has looked at the stories, looked at the winepress, and concluded that they belong to different worlds.

A common kind of unbelief. It is not ignorance or denial. It is a man who believes every word of what God did, has quietly stopped expecting anything like it now, and treats his own circumstances as the more recent and reliable evidence.

But now the LORD has forsaken us. It is a serious charge, and in this book precisely wrong. What has happened to Israel is not abandonment: chapter 2 said God gave them over, sold them, was against them for harm (2:14–15). Gideon has mistaken discipline for desertion.

And the LORD turned to him. The reply answers none of his questions. God does not defend himself, explain the seven years or give a theology of suffering. He gives the man a job. And the phrase is deliberately puzzling: “Go in this might of yours.” What might? All Gideon has shown is the ability to hide grain and complain accurately. The sentence is either mockery or a promise about what is now in him, and the question that follows settles which: “do not I send you?” The whole commission rests on the sending: not on the strength, which is not there, but on the one who sends.

Why do the old stories feel like another world? Gideon’s problem is very modern. He does not doubt that the sea parted; he cannot imagine it happening in a world of raiders and hiding. Many feel the same about the Bible: lovely, perhaps true once, but from another universe. The German scholar Rudolf Bultmann argued that people who use electric light and the radio cannot also believe in the New Testament’s world of spirits and miracles. Notice the move, because it is Gideon’s: the present is treated as the reliable witness and the past as the suspect one, simply because it is past. But the winepress was never the whole of reality, only the part Gideon could see. And the reply he got was not a lecture but a visitor and a sending. In Jesus the God of the exodus came and sat under our tree, and his resurrection is not an old story about somebody else’s world but the first morning of a new one, which is why it can reach a man in a hole in the ground.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house." And the LORD said to him, "But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gideon’s list of his weaknesses is accurate, and God does not dispute it; he answers with himself: “I will be with you.”

My clan is the weakest in Manasseh. His objection is not false modesty but an accurate report, and each fact is a step down. Manasseh is a middling tribe; within it his clan is the weakest; within the clan he is the least in his father’s house. He is at the bottom of a small heap.

How can I save Israel? What is wrong is the question itself. It assumes the saving depends on his resources, and if that were so, his list would settle the matter. God does not argue with the list. He does not tell Gideon he has hidden potential or that Manasseh is stronger than he thinks. Every fact is allowed to stand.

But I will be with you. This exchange has happened before, almost word for word, at a burning bush. Moses said, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?” and God answered, “But I will be with you” (Exodus 3:11–12). The question was about the man; the answer was about God. That is the shape of every genuine call in Scripture. The objection is usually correct and always beside the point. Neither man is told he is capable. Both are told who is coming with them.

Christ with us. The promise runs from Moses and Gideon to its fullness in Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), who sent his weak disciples into the world with the same assurance: “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). God still chooses “what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27), so that no one may boast in his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, then show me a sign that it is you who speak with me. Please do not depart from here until I come to you and bring out my present and set it before you." And he said, "I will stay till you return." So Gideon went into his house and prepared a young goat and unleavened cakes from an ephah of flour. The meat he put in a basket, and the broth he put in a pot, and brought them to him under the terebinth and presented them. And the angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and put them on this rock, and pour the broth over them." And he did so. Then the angel of the LORD reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. And fire sprang up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. And the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gideon asks for a sign and brings a generous offering; the angel touches it with his staff, fire springs from the rock to consume it, and he vanishes.

Show me a sign. He asks for proof that it is really God speaking, and then asks the visitor to wait while he fetches something.

A young goat and unleavened cakes. Take in what he brings out, in the seventh year of raiders who leave “no sustenance in Israel”: a whole young goat, and an ephah of flour, about the amount Abraham had Sarah bake for the three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18:6). Gideon has been threshing in a pit to save a little grain, and he takes a large part of what his household has and cooks it for a stranger under a tree. Whatever is wrong with his faith, his hospitality is not calculating.

Pour the broth over them. The instruction turns a meal into an offering. Meat and bread on a rock, with the broth poured over it all, soaking everything and making it much harder to burn.

Fire sprang up from the rock. The staff touches it and fire comes up out of the rock, not down from the sky but up through the stone beneath the food. It burns a soaked meal to nothing, and the visitor is gone. Gideon asked for proof of identity, and he gets fire out of the ground and an empty space under the tree.

An offering accepted. Fire from the LORD consuming an offering was the sign that he accepted it (Leviticus 9:24). Gideon’s gift is received, which means Gideon is received. Every such offering waited for the one sacrifice God accepted once for all, Christ’s offering of himself (Hebrews 10:10).
verseByVerse.note: An ephah was about 3/5 bushel (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon perceived that he was the angel of the LORD. And Gideon said, "Alas, O Lord GOD! For now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face." But the LORD said to him, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die." Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it, The LORD Is Peace. To this day it still stands at Ophrah, which belongs to the Abiezrites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Realising that he has seen the angel of the LORD face to face, Gideon fears he will die; the LORD speaks peace to him, and he builds an altar called “The LORD Is Peace.”

Alas, O Lord GOD! The proof he asked for arrives, and the first thing it produces is terror. He has been talking face to face with someone he now recognises, and Israel knew that this kills a man. God told Moses, “man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20), and Jacob said in astonishment at Peniel, “I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered” (Genesis 32:30). Gideon’s terror is the right instinct of a man who has just realised who was sitting under the tree while he complained.

Peace be to you. The LORD answers in three short sentences, “Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die”, and they are the gospel in the order it always comes: peace first, then the command not to fear, then the reason. Nothing in Gideon has changed between his terror and this answer. He has not offered, promised or improved. The word is simply spoken over him.

The LORD Is Peace. He names the altar after the sentence that saved his life: in Hebrew, YHWH Shalom. It is a strange name for a man about to fight a war, and the right one. Gideon has discovered not that God is on his side against Midian but that God is at peace with him, a frightened man who had just accused God of desertion. The stone was still standing when the book was written (“to this day”).

Christ our peace. Centuries later Paul put the same word at the centre of everything, and made it a person rather than an altar: “For he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). And the risen Jesus greeted his frightened disciples with the very words spoken to Gideon: “Peace be with you” (John 20:19). God is at peace with sinners not because they have stopped being afraid of him, but because his Son has made peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–32 — The Altar in His Father's Yard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deliverance from Midian begins with the idol in the deliverer’s own family. The same night, the LORD commands Gideon to pull down his father’s altar of Baal, cut down the Asherah beside it and offer a bull on a new altar to the LORD (vv. 25–26). Gideon obeys with ten servants, but by night, because he is afraid (v. 27). In the morning the men of the town demand his death for insulting Baal (vv. 28–30). His father Joash answers that a god who needs defending is no god: “If he is a god, let him contend for himself” (v. 31). Gideon is nicknamed Jerubbaal, “Let Baal contend”, a standing dare that Baal never takes up (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: In a nation that cries to the LORD in trouble and lives by Baal the rest of the year, reform has to begin somewhere, and God begins it in one household.
verseByVerse.examples: Most of us have something in our own back garden that we have learned to live with. The chapter suggests that is where God's work in us is likely to start, and that it may be done with trembling hands.

verseByVerse.quote: That night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull, and the second bull seven years old, and pull down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is beside it and build an altar to the LORD your God on the top of the stronghold here, with stones laid in due order. Then take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you shall cut down." So Gideon took ten men of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gideon’s first task is to pull down his own father’s altar to Baal and offer a sacrifice to the LORD in its place, and he obeys fully, but by night, because he is afraid.

The altar of Baal that your father has. The first assignment is not Midian but his father’s back yard. Joash, who owns the field where the angel sat, maintains a shrine to Baal with an Asherah beside it. An Asherah was a wooden pole or carved tree set up beside an altar as the sign of Asherah, the Canaanite mother goddess worshipped with Baal, and the law had told Israel to cut such poles down (Deuteronomy 7:5). Israel cried out to the LORD in distress; this is where the family went the rest of the year. There is no delivering Israel from Midian while the deliverer’s own father runs a Baal altar, and God begins where Gideon actually lives.

That night. The command comes the same night as “Peace be to you”, from the God who has just made peace with him. It is not the condition of that peace but the first thing a man at peace with the LORD does.

The second bull seven years old. The bull is seven years old, as old as the oppression (v. 1), and it is burned on the wood of the idol that brought it. The idol becomes firewood for the offering that replaces it.

He did it by night. The narrator will not tidy him up. He did every instruction, in the dark, because he was afraid of his own family and neighbours. Both halves are recorded, and neither cancels the other. This is obedience with shaking hands, and Scripture calls it obedience; there is no rebuke anywhere in the chapter. A great deal of Christian courage looks like this from the inside: the command obeyed and the fear real at the same time, and the fear does not disqualify the obedience.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 25 is unclear about the animals. ESV has two bulls, “your father’s bull, and the second bull seven years old”; other translations read one bull, the second in his father’s herd. Only “the second bull” is sacrificed (vv. 26, 28), so the meaning is little affected. The site of the new altar, “the top of the stronghold”, and the phrase “stones laid in due order” are also not wholly certain.

verseByVerse.quote: When the men of the town rose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down, and the Asherah beside it was cut down, and the second bull was offered on the altar that had been built. And they said to one another, "Who has done this thing?" And after they had searched and inquired, they said, "Gideon the son of Joash has done this thing." Then the men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son, that he may die, for he has broken down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah beside it." But Joash said to all who stood against him, "Will you contend for Baal? Or will you save him? Whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because his altar has been broken down." Therefore on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is to say, "Let Baal contend against him," because he broke down his altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town demands Gideon’s death for pulling down Baal’s altar, but his father answers that a god who must be defended is no god, and Gideon is named Jerubbaal, “Let Baal contend.”

Bring out your son, that he may die. The town wakes to find its shrine demolished and a sacrifice burning on a new altar built from the wreckage. They investigate, find him, and come for a death sentence. Look at who these men are: Israelites, the same people who cried out to the LORD in verse 6 because the Midianites were eating their harvest, now demanding death for a man who pulled down a Canaanite altar. That is how far it has gone. The nation prays to the God of the exodus when the raiders come, and lynches anyone who interferes with Baal.

If he is a god, let him contend for himself. The defence comes from the last man anyone would expect: Joash, who owned the altar. His argument takes one sentence, and it demolishes a great deal. A god who needs a mob to defend his honour has already lost the argument. If Baal is what the town says, he can deal with one man overnight; if he needs the men of Ophrah to do it for him, he is not worth the altar they are avenging. Elijah will make the same case on Carmel with heavier irony, and Isaiah about men who burn half a tree and pray to the other half (1 Kings 18:27; Isaiah 44:15–17). A god you have to protect is not a god.

The mob that defends a god. We like to think only religious societies hunt blasphemers. But watch a thoroughly secular office or online crowd when someone pulls down one of its altars, questioning a cherished cause or doubting the agreed line. The response is often Ophrah’s, “Bring out your son, that he may die”, socially if not literally. Every culture has its sacred things, and you can tell what they are by what people feel they must avenge. Joash’s question cuts through all of it. Whatever has to be protected by a crowd is not ultimate; it depends on us, and so it cannot save us.

The God who needs no defenders. The true God never needed a mob to defend his honour. When the crowd finally came for him, it was to put him to death, and he let them, praying for their forgiveness (Luke 23:34). A God like that does not make his people anxious defenders but free ones, who can tell the truth without needing to destroy anyone who disagrees.

Gideon was called Jerubbaal. He gets a nickname out of it, and it is a standing dare: “Let Baal contend.” Every time someone says the name, the challenge is repeated and Baal’s silence is noted again. Gideon carries it for the rest of his life, and his sons after him.
verseByVerse.note: “Jerubbaal” means “let Baal contend.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit clothes a weak man, and God is patient with his remaining fear. Midian and its allies cross the Jordan and camp in the Valley of Jezreel (v. 33). The Spirit of the LORD clothes Gideon; he blows the trumpet and his clan, his tribe and three more tribes answer (vv. 34–35). Then, with all this already given, Gideon asks God for a sign with a fleece: wet fleece on dry ground, and then, since wool holds dew anyway, dry fleece on wet ground (vv. 36–40). God gives both without a word of rebuke. The point is not the method but the God who bears with his servant.
verseByVerse.theology: This section holds together the two sides of Gideon: clothed with the Spirit, and still afraid. Both can be true of a believer at the same time.
verseByVerse.examples: If you are asking God for one more sign about something he has already made plain, this passage does not shame you. Nor does it recommend fleeces. It points you to the God who is patient with the fearful, and to his word, which is clearer than any sign.

verseByVerse.quote: Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East came together, and they crossed the Jordan and encamped in the Valley of Jezreel. But the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Midian gathers for war, the Spirit of the LORD clothes Gideon, and the man who hid in a winepress blows the trumpet and four tribes answer.

Encamped in the Valley of Jezreel. The whole confederation crosses the Jordan and camps in the great plain, the same valley where the Kishon took Sisera’s chariots (5:21). They are not raiding this time; they have come to stay.

The Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon. This is the sentence that changes him, and the Hebrew is unusual. It does not say the Spirit came upon Gideon, as with Othniel (3:10). It says the Spirit of the LORD clothed himself with Gideon: put him on, as a man puts on a coat. Gideon is not handed a power to use as he chooses; he is worn, and the Spirit acts through him. The same phrase is used twice more in the Old Testament, both times of the Spirit taking hold of a man so that he speaks or acts beyond himself (1 Chronicles 12:18; 2 Chronicles 24:20). It is the only explanation offered for what happens next.

He sounded the trumpet. The man who was hiding grain in a pit blows a trumpet and summons his clan, his tribe and three more tribes, and they come. Nothing about his circumstances has altered. His clan is still the weakest in Manasseh and he is still the least in his father’s house; his account of himself in verse 15 remains accurate. What has changed is who is wearing him.

The Spirit and the Son. The Spirit came on the judges for a task and a time. On Jesus he came to remain (John 1:32–33), and he anointed him to “proclaim liberty to the captives” (Luke 4:18). The risen Christ now pours out that Spirit on all his people, the weak and the least among them, “clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49) for the work he gives them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon said to God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, behold, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said." And it was so. When he rose early next morning and squeezed the fleece, he wrung enough dew from the fleece to fill a bowl with water. Then Gideon said to God, "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece. Please let it be dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground let there be dew." And God did so that night; and it was dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground there was dew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though God has already given him every assurance, Gideon asks for a sign with a fleece, twice, and God patiently grants both, showing not a method of guidance to copy but a God who bears with weak faith.

What he has already been given. Take stock first. The angel of the LORD has commissioned him in person and promised, “I will be with you.” He has seen fire come out of a rock, heard “Peace be to you” when he expected to die, carried out a night raid and survived it, and the Spirit of the LORD is wrapped round him like clothing. Then he lays out a fleece.

As you have said. He says it twice. He is not asking whether God said it but whether God meant it. The request is not for information; it is for reassurance. And God does it, without comment: a bowlful of water wrung from the wool, and dry ground all round it.

Let not your anger burn against me. He asks again, and the way he asks shows he knows what he is doing. This is a man apologising in advance, and it closely echoes Abraham as he kept lowering the number for Sodom (Genesis 18:30, 32).

The second test. Before mocking him, notice that his second test is the intelligent one. Wool left out overnight draws and holds dew while the ground dries in the first sun, so the first result could have happened by itself; dry wool on wet ground cannot. Gideon spotted the flaw in his own experiment. He is not being lazily superstitious. He is being careful, and his carefulness shows how much he still needs.

And God did so that night. God does that too, in one sentence, with no rebuke, no lecture about the signs already given, no weary sigh in the text at all.

What the passage recommends. The chapter is not recommending fleeces. Gideon was not seeking guidance he lacked but confidence in guidance he already had, and anyone who has asked God for one more confirmation of something perfectly clear knows which of the two he was doing. What the passage recommends is its God. He does not break a bruised reed or quench a faintly burning wick (Isaiah 42:3), and here is what that looks like: a frightened man asking for the same assurance twice in two nights, and getting it twice, from the one who had called him a mighty man of valour while he was hiding in a hole.

He offered Thomas his hands. Matthew says that sentence from Isaiah describes Jesus (Matthew 12:18–21), and the Gospels show him doing exactly this. Thomas asked for one more proof after the others had seen the risen Lord, and Jesus came back a week later and offered him his hands and his side (John 20:26–27). He also said, “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29). The weak are borne with; they are also invited to grow.

Where Christians differ: should Christians “put out a fleece” to find God’s will? Many believers ask God for a sign, an outward circumstance, to confirm a decision, and point to Gideon. Others note that Gideon already knew God’s will and was asking for reassurance, not guidance. This commentary’s view: God guides his people chiefly through his word, prayer, wisdom and godly counsel, and believers should not demand signs or treat circumstances as a code. Gideon is not a pattern for decision-making, but he is a comfort: God is patient with those whose faith is weak, and he gives in Christ an assurance that no fleece could give.

6.theology:
Named for what he will be. God calls a man hiding grain in a pit a mighty man of valor, naming what he will become before there is any evidence for it (v. 12).

The objection is correct and irrelevant. God does not dispute a word of Gideon's account of his own weakness. He answers it, as he answered Moses, with his presence: but I will be with you (v. 16).

Knowing the stories is not enough. Gideon can quote the wonderful deeds his fathers recounted, yet he has weighed them against the winepress and concluded that God has forsaken Israel (v. 13). He believes the history and has stopped expecting anything like it now.

Obedience with the hands shaking. Gideon pulls down his father's altar exactly as commanded, and does it at night because he was too afraid to do it by day (v. 27). Both halves are recorded, and there is no rebuke, either for that or for the fleece, asked for twice after everything he had already been given. The God of this chapter does not break a bruised reed or quench a smouldering wick (Isa. 42:3), the words Matthew applies to Jesus (Matt. 12:20), and verse 40 is what that looks like in practice.
6.examples:
Then: A man from the least family of the weakest clan was crouched in a winepress saving a few bushels of wheat from raiders when somebody sat down under the tree above him and called him a mighty man of valour. Before he was sent against an army he was sent against his own father's shrine, and he did it after dark because he was frightened.

Now: Two things. The first is verse 13: it is possible to know exactly what God has done, to be able to recite it, and to have quietly concluded from your own circumstances that he has stopped. Gideon had the stories; what he had lost was the expectation. The second is verse 27. If you are waiting to stop being afraid before you obey, this chapter records a man who obeyed at night instead, and God did not mention it again. The courage did not come from Gideon, and it does not come from us: the same Spirit who clothed him lives in every believer now, and where our obedience is half-hearted or frightened or late, Christ's was whole, and it is his that stands for us before God.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD said to him, “But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man.”
keyVerse.note: Gideon’s list of his weaknesses is true, and God does not dispute it. He answers with himself, as he answered Moses at the burning bush. The whole Gideon story, and every true call, rests on this promise, which reaches its fullness in Christ: “behold, I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

6.reflection:
Israel cried out about Midian, but God first sent a prophet to name their idolatry (vv. 7–10). Why might God answer our troubles by first exposing what lies beneath them? Has he done that with you?

Gideon believed the old stories but could not imagine God acting in his own day (v. 13). Where do you find it hard to believe that the God of the Bible is at work in your world now?

God did not argue with Gideon’s list of weaknesses but answered, “I will be with you” (vv. 15–16). What is on your own list, and how does the presence of Christ change what you are willing to attempt?

Gideon obeyed by night because he was afraid (v. 27), and asked twice for a sign (vv. 36–40), yet God was patient. How does God’s patience with Gideon, and Christ’s with Thomas, encourage you where your faith feels weak?

7.title: Gideon's 300
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the people who were with him rose early and encamped beside the spring of Harod. And the camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.<sup>2</sup>The LORD said to Gideon, "The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.'<sup>3</sup>Now therefore proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, 'Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return home and hurry away from Mount Gilead.'" Then 22,000 of the people returned, and 10,000 remained.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to Gideon, "The people are still too many. Take them down to the water, and I will test them for you there, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall go with you,' shall go with you, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall not go with you,' shall not go."<sup>5</sup>So he brought the people down to the water. And the LORD said to Gideon, "Every one who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself. Likewise, every one who kneels down to drink."<sup>6</sup>And the number of those who lapped, putting their hands to their mouths, was 300 men, but all the rest of the people knelt down to drink water.<sup>7</sup>And the LORD said to Gideon, "With the 300 men who lapped I will save you and give the Midianites into your hand, and let all the others go every man to his home."<sup>8</sup>So the people took provisions in their hands, and their trumpets. And he sent all the rest of Israel every man to his tent, but retained the 300 men. And the camp of Midian was below him in the valley.<sup>9</sup>That same night the LORD said to him, "Arise, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand.<sup>10</sup>But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant.<sup>11</sup>And you shall hear what they say, and afterward your hands shall be strengthened to go down against the camp." Then he went down with Purah his servant to the outposts of the armed men who were in the camp.<sup>12</sup>And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the people of the East lay along the valley like locusts in abundance, and their camels were without number, as the sand that is on the seashore in abundance.<sup>13</sup>When Gideon came, behold, a man was telling a dream to his comrade. And he said, "Behold, I dreamed a dream, and behold, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian and came to the tent and struck it so that it fell and turned it upside down, so that the tent lay flat."<sup>14</sup>And his comrade answered, "This is no other than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel; God has given into his hand Midian and all the camp."<sup>15</sup>As soon as Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped. And he returned to the camp of Israel and said, "Arise, for the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand."<sup>16</sup>And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars.<sup>17</sup>And he said to them, "Look at me, and do likewise. When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do as I do.<sup>18</sup>When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"<sup>19</sup>So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when they had just set the watch. And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands.<sup>20</sup>Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"<sup>21</sup>Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled.<sup>22</sup>When they blew the 300 trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army. And the army fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.<sup>23</sup>And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian.<sup>24</sup>Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and capture the waters against them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan." So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan.<sup>25</sup>And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb. Then they pursued Midian, and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
7.overview:
Where we are. Gideon has been called, has heard “Peace be to you”, has pulled down his father’s altar, has been clothed by the Spirit and has been given his two signs (chapter 6). Now Midian and its allies lie in the Valley of Jezreel, and the battle comes.

The message. The LORD saves his people in a way that leaves them no room to boast. He cuts Gideon’s army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred, “lest Israel boast over me” (v. 2), meets his servant’s fear with kindness, and wins the battle while his people stand still holding lights and trumpets. Salvation belongs to the LORD, and he arranges it so that nobody can misread who won.

Why it was said. Israel had already credited its harvests to Baal (chapter 6; see the introduction). A people so ready to give the glory elsewhere needed a victory that could only be God’s, and later generations needed the memory of it: “the day of Midian” became Israel’s shorthand for God breaking an oppressor (Isaiah 9:4).

How the chapter makes its case. God declares the army too many, and the fearful go home, twenty-two thousand of them (vv. 1–3). A test at the water leaves three hundred (vv. 4–8). God meets Gideon’s fear by sending him to overhear an enemy soldier’s dream of a barley loaf flattening a tent, and Gideon worships (vv. 9–15). The three hundred surround the camp with trumpets and torches in jars, and at the signal they blow, smash and shout (vv. 16–20). They stand still, and the LORD turns the enemy’s swords on one another (vv. 21–22). The tribes join the pursuit, Ephraim seizes the fords, and the princes Oreb and Zeeb are killed (vv. 23–25).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by promise. The chapter’s principle, strength made unmistakably God’s through weakness, is the shape of the gospel: “we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). Isaiah took the day of Midian as the pattern for the greater deliverance brought by the child who is born, on whom the light dawns in Galilee (Isaiah 9:1–6; Matthew 4:15–16). And the decisive victory was won by one man, apparently helpless, on a cross, so that salvation is “not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:9).

For us. God still works through the few and the weak, so that the glory goes to him. We are saved not by our strength but by Christ’s, and we serve by standing where he puts us and holding out his light. And when we are afraid, the God who sent Gideon to the edge of the camp knows our fear and gives what our faith needs.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God makes the army small so that no one can mistake whose victory it is. Gideon camps at the spring of Harod with thirty-two thousand men, Midian to the north (v. 1). The LORD says they are too many, “lest Israel boast over me” (v. 2). By the law of war the fearful are sent home, and twenty-two thousand go (v. 3). Ten thousand are still too many, so God tests them at the water and separates the three hundred who lap (vv. 4–6). With these, God promises, “I will save you” (v. 7). The rest go home, leaving their provisions and trumpets, and the camp of Midian lies below in the valley (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's danger was not only Midian but the story Israel would tell afterwards. Pride in a victory can do as much harm as a defeat.
verseByVerse.examples: It is humbling to be made smaller on purpose. When God strips away what we were relying on, it may be so that, when help comes, there is no doubt where it came from.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the people who were with him rose early and encamped beside the spring of Harod. And the camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley. The LORD said to Gideon, "The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.' Now therefore proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, 'Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return home and hurry away from Mount Gilead.'" Then 22,000 of the people returned, and 10,000 remained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Gideon his army is too big, because a large army would let Israel claim the victory for itself, and twenty-two thousand fearful men go home.

Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon). He is called Jerubbaal first, “Let Baal contend”, and the dare has now been ignored by Baal for some time.

Beside the spring of Harod. The army camps at a spring at the foot of Mount Gilboa, on the southern edge of the Jezreel valley, with Midian spread to the north by the hill of Moreh. Harod sounds like the Hebrew for “trembling”, the word used of the fearful in verse 3: the camp is pitched at Trembling Spring, and before the day is out two thirds of the army will prove the name true.

Too many for me. Then the sentence the whole chapter serves, and it has nothing to do with tactics. God’s objection to thirty-two thousand men facing a swarm like locusts is that they are too many, because a large army would seem to explain the victory by itself. Read the reason again: “lest Israel boast over me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” God is arranging not only a victory but an account of it that nobody can misread. The shrinking of the army is a lesson about God, taught with numbers.

Whoever is fearful and trembling. The first cut is not Gideon’s idea.
