Moses had written it into Israel’s law of war: before battle the officers shall say, “Is there any man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own” (Deuteronomy 20:8). Gideon reads out the standing law, and two thirds of his army go home. Twenty-two thousand men admit in public that they are afraid and walk away, which shows what seven years had done to the country.

The story we most like to tell. There is no story the modern West loves more than the one God refuses to let Israel tell: “My own hand has saved me.” It is the plot of the self-made founder and the graduate thanking her own hard work. Some of it is true; effort is real. But the story quietly makes the winners proud, since they deserve it, and the losers ashamed, since they must deserve that too, and it leaves no room for gratitude, which is where worship begins. God thins Gideon’s army not because he objects to Israelites fighting, but because he will not let them misread their own rescue, and he is just as careful with ours.

Nothing to boast of. The gospel is the one story in which the only thing we contribute is the need: “not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:9). That sounds humiliating, and it is the most freeing thing in the world, because people who did not save themselves have nothing left to prove and no one left to despise.

Uncertain wording. “Hurry away from Mount Gilead” is puzzling. Gilead usually names the hill country east of the Jordan, the wrong side of the river for this camp, so this is probably a local name for a height near Gilboa, or the text has suffered in copying. The Hebrew verb rendered “hurry away” is also rare. The sense is plain either way: anyone who wants to leave may go home now, quickly, before the fear spreads.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Gideon, "The people are still too many. Take them down to the water, and I will test them for you there, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall go with you,' shall go with you, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall not go with you,' shall not go." So he brought the people down to the water. And the LORD said to Gideon, "Every one who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself. Likewise, every one who kneels down to drink." And the number of those who lapped, putting their hands to their mouths, was 300 men, but all the rest of the people knelt down to drink water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten thousand are still too many, so God himself sorts them at the water and leaves the smallest possible number, three hundred.

The people are still too many. Ten thousand remain against a valley full of camels, and God says it again: still too many.

I will test them for you. The verb is a metalworker’s word, to refine metal so that the dross is separated out (as in Malachi 3:3). And notice who does the sorting. Gideon does not pick his men; God says, “This one shall go with you,” and Gideon only carries out the verdict. The army that wins this battle will be one God chose, man by man.

Lapping and kneeling. Much has been written about the alertness of men who scoop water to the mouth and keep their eyes up, as against those who put their faces down to drink. It may be right, but the text does not say so, and it does not say the three hundred were chosen for any quality at all. What it says is that God sorted them by something arbitrary and kept the smaller group. The point is the smallness of the number. If the lappers had been chosen as the best soldiers, we would be back at a victory that could be credited to good selection, and verse 2 has ruled that out.

What it does not mean. Not that God prefers incompetence or that planning is unspiritual; Gideon’s generalship later is sound (vv. 16–24). It means that the means God uses, however capable, must never take the credit.

Uncertain wording. It is not clear exactly how the two groups drank. The phrase “putting their hands to their mouths” stands awkwardly in the Hebrew, and interpreters differ on whether the three hundred lapped from their hands or put their faces to the water like a dog, and the rest knelt. The number, three hundred, is the point, and that is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Gideon, "With the 300 men who lapped I will save you and give the Midianites into your hand, and let all the others go every man to his home." So the people took provisions in their hands, and their trumpets. And he sent all the rest of Israel every man to his tent, but retained the 300 men. And the camp of Midian was below him in the valley.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises that he will save Israel with the three hundred, and sends everyone else home.

With the 300 men who lapped I will save you. The subject of the verb is the LORD: “I will save you and give the Midianites into your hand.” The three hundred are not told they are good enough for the task. They are told who will do it. Everyone else is sent home, not in disgrace but simply because they are not needed.

Provisions and trumpets. The men who leave hand over their supplies and their trumpets, and the detail matters: three hundred men are about to be issued with an army’s worth of trumpets, and the plan in verse 16 depends on it. Ninety-nine in every hundred have gone home, and Gideon stands on a hillside above a valley full of Midianites with a small company, a great many horns and a promise.

My power is made perfect in weakness. Paul learned the same lesson: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). The church is often tempted to think it must be large and well resourced before God can use it. Gideon’s three hundred say otherwise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God meets his servant’s fear with kindness and gives him the assurance he needs. That night the LORD orders the attack, adding, “if you are afraid to go down”, take Purah and listen (vv. 9–11). Gideon creeps to the outposts of a camp spread like locusts, with camels as the sand of the seashore (v. 12). He overhears a soldier telling a dream: a barley loaf rolls into the camp and flattens a tent. His comrade interprets it: this is the sword of Gideon, and God has given Midian into his hand (vv. 13–14). Gideon worships, and returns to rouse his men: “the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand” (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God knows what we are made of and remembers that we are dust (Ps. 103:14). He provides for his servants as they really are, not as they ought to be.
verseByVerse.examples: The word Gideon needed came from the last place he would have looked. It is worth listening for God's encouragement in unexpected voices, while testing every voice by his word.

verseByVerse.quote: That same night the LORD said to him, "Arise, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand. But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant. And you shall hear what they say, and afterward your hands shall be strengthened to go down against the camp." Then he went down with Purah his servant to the outposts of the armed men who were in the camp. And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the people of the East lay along the valley like locusts in abundance, and their camels were without number, as the sand that is on the seashore in abundance. When Gideon came, behold, a man was telling a dream to his comrade. And he said, "Behold, I dreamed a dream, and behold, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian and came to the tent and struck it so that it fell and turned it upside down, so that the tent lay flat." And his comrade answered, "This is no other than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel; God has given into his hand Midian and all the camp." As soon as Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped. And he returned to the camp of Israel and said, "Arise, for the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God knows Gideon is still afraid and, instead of rebuking him, sends him to the enemy camp to overhear a dream that tells him the victory is already given, and Gideon worships.

For I have given it into your hand. That same night God says two things. The first is the order and the promise in the usual form: go down, “for I have given it into your hand”. The second is the tenderest line in the Gideon story.

But if you are afraid to go down. Notice what does not follow. There is no “Do not be afraid”, and no rebuke for still being frightened after the angel, the fire, the Spirit and two nights of fleeces. God simply accepts that he is afraid and works with it: take Purah your servant, go and listen, and “afterward your hands shall be strengthened”. God is not embarrassed by his servant’s nerves and does not require him to pretend; he gives him a companion and a plan. Gideon takes the servant, and the narrator lets it stand without comment.

Like locusts in abundance. What he sees is not reassuring. The valley is full, locusts again, and camels beyond counting, “as the sand that is on the seashore”, the phrase God used to Abraham about his descendants (Genesis 22:17). Midian looks like the people of promise; Israel looks like three hundred men.

A cake of barley bread. He arrives just as a man is describing a dream about a cake of barley bread. Barley was the cheaper grain, the bread of the poor, and harvests like it are what these men had been stealing off Israelite fields for seven years. In the dream a loaf of the stuff they have been robbing rolls into the camp and knocks a tent flat. The second man interprets it exactly, down to the name. Two enemy soldiers, in the dark, in their own camp, tell each other that God has handed them over to a farmer from Ophrah. The one sentence Gideon needed to hear is spoken by the enemy, about the enemy’s own destruction.

He worshiped. Standing in the dark at the edge of a hostile camp with one servant beside him, the first thing he does is bow. See what it took: not the angel, the fire, the Spirit or the fleece, but a frightened man overhearing a stranger’s nightmare. God knew what would reach Gideon and had it waiting for him. Then he goes back and speaks as God had spoken to him: “Arise, for the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand.”

A High Priest who sympathises. The God who said, “if you are afraid”, is the God revealed in Jesus, who said to his frightened friends, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid” (Matthew 14:27). “We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). He does not wait for us to stop being afraid before he helps us. He comes to us in our fear and gives what our faith needs.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “cake” is found only here, and its meaning is uncertain; it may describe something round or rolling, which fits a loaf tumbling into the camp. The general sense, a loaf of barley bread, is clear.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The battle is won by the LORD while his people stand still. Gideon gives each of the three hundred a trumpet and an empty jar with a torch inside, divides them into three companies, and tells them to watch him and do the same (vv. 16–18). At the beginning of the middle watch they blow the trumpets, smash the jars, hold up the torches and cry, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” (vv. 19–20). Every man stands in his place; the enemy panics and flees, for the LORD sets every man’s sword against his comrade (vv. 21–22). No Israelite sword is drawn in the camp.
verseByVerse.theology: The battle cry names the LORD first and Gideon second (v. 20). God uses human instruments, but the credit is never shared equally.
verseByVerse.examples: The weapons of the three hundred were a light and a sound, carried in clay jars. Paul's picture of the gospel as treasure in jars of clay, so that the power plainly belongs to God and not to us (2 Cor. 4:7), fits this night well, though he does not mention it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars. And he said to them, "Look at me, and do likewise. When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do as I do. When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gideon arms his three hundred with nothing that can kill, trumpets and torches hidden in jars, and gives one order: watch me and do as I do.

Trumpets and empty jars. Count the hands it takes. Each man gets a trumpet and an empty jar with a lit torch inside, which is what the jar is for: a clay pot over a flame hides it completely until the pot is broken. That is two hands, and nothing in either can hurt anybody. No sword is issued. The men are going into a night attack on a valley full of raiders carrying a musical instrument and a pot.

Look at me, and do likewise. The whole battle order is just that: watch me and copy me. There is no strategy to memorise and no contingency plan. Three companies take up positions on three sides of a sleeping army in the dark, and every man watches one man and does what he does.

For the LORD and for Gideon. The shout names the arrangement exactly: not for Israel, the tribes or freedom, but for a God and a farmer, in that order.

verseByVerse.quote: So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when they had just set the watch. And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands. Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!" Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled. When they blew the 300 trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army. And the army fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the signal the three hundred blow trumpets, smash jars and shout, and while they stand still in their places, the LORD turns the enemy’s swords on one another and the whole army flees.

At the beginning of the middle watch. The timing is professional. The middle watch probably began around ten at night, and Gideon moves at the changeover, when the new sentries are settling in with eyes not yet used to the dark and the men coming off duty are heading for their blankets.

They blew the trumpets and smashed the jars. Consider it from inside the camp. A man wakes in the dark to trumpets on three sides at once. A trumpet probably belonged to the leader of a unit, so three hundred horns would sound like three hundred companies. At the same instant three hundred flames appear in a ring where a moment ago there was nothing, and a war cry announces a sword. Nobody in that valley sees three hundred men; everybody hears an army that has already surrounded them.

Every man stood in his place. Verse 21 is the sentence to hold on to. The three hundred do not charge, advance or engage. They stand still, holding a light and making a noise, and the enemy disintegrates in front of them. It is what Moses told Israel at the sea: “Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today” (Exodus 14:13).

The LORD set every man’s sword against his comrade. What actually killed the Midianites was each other, in the dark and in panic, unable to tell friend from enemy. Yet the text says it was God. Verse 2 said the army had to be too small for Israel to claim the credit, and the final arrangement removes even the sword.

Light in jars of clay. Christians have long heard this night in Paul’s words: “we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). The light was hidden in pots until the pots were broken. The supreme case is Christ himself, whose body was broken so that the light of life might shine out to the world. And our weakness, which we spend so much effort hiding, may be the very place his light is seen.

Uncertain wording. The places named in verse 22, Beth-shittah, Zererah, Abel-meholah and Tabbath, cannot all be located with confidence, though the flight evidently ran down the Jordan valley towards the crossings.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hands the follow-up of his victory to ordinary people doing ordinary work. Men from Naphtali, Asher and Manasseh join the pursuit (v. 23). Gideon sends to Ephraim to seize the waters and the fords of the Jordan ahead of the fleeing army, and they do (v. 24). They capture the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, and kill them at places that keep their names, the rock of Oreb and the winepress of Zeeb, and bring their heads to Gideon (v. 25). The man once hiding in a winepress sees Midian’s prince die in one.
verseByVerse.theology: Ephraim's part here sets up the quarrel at the start of the next chapter, when the tribe complains that it was not called sooner (8:1).
verseByVerse.examples: Places named after a battle keep its story alive. Christians have their own memorial of rescue, the Lord's Supper, kept in remembrance of Christ (1 Cor. 11:24).

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian. Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and capture the waters against them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan." So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan. And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb. Then they pursued Midian, and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once God has won the battle, the tribes join in the pursuit, Ephraim seizes the fords, and the princes of Midian are killed at places that keep their names.

The men of Israel were called out. Now the rest of Israel is recalled, presumably including many who went home afraid, and there is something generous in it. The part of the work that could only be credited to God was done by three hundred men holding crockery; the pursuit, ordinary soldiering that takes days, is given back to the tribes. God worked an unmistakable miracle and then handed the follow-up to ordinary people doing ordinary work, and the telling does not despise it.

Capture the waters. Gideon’s generalship is sound. He sends to Ephraim to seize the fords before the fleeing army reaches them, as Ehud had done at the same river (3:28), and the retreat is closed.

Oreb and Zeeb. The names mean “raven” and “wolf”. Two princes are taken and killed, and the places keep their names, which is how a country remembers such a night. And Zeeb dies at a winepress. The last winepress in this story had a man crouched in it, threshing wheat out of the wind, hiding a few bushels from the very people this prince commanded. Now the Midianites are dying in one.

What God did. The book does not comment, and does not need to. God took a man out of a pit, let him be nicknamed with a dare to a dead god, reduced his army by ninety-nine in every hundred so that nobody could get the story wrong, sent him to overhear a stranger’s dream about a barley loaf, and had him stand still in the dark holding a jar while the valley emptied.

As on the day of Midian. Isaiah, some four or five centuries later, still used this night as shorthand for what God does to an oppressor: “the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as on the day of Midian” (Isaiah 9:4). The verses around it speak of a light shining on people who walked in darkness, and a child who is born, whose government has no end (Isaiah 9:2, 6–7). Matthew quotes the opening of that passage, the light dawning on Galilee, when Jesus begins to preach there (Matthew 4:15–16). The day of Midian was a small rescue in the northern country where the great one would begin.

7.theology:
An explanation, not just a victory. Verse 2 gives the reason for every reduction that follows, and it concerns God’s honour, not tactics. God will not win this in a way that leaves room for my own hand has saved me. The arithmetic runs from thirty-two thousand to three hundred to a battle in which nobody on Israel's side draws a sword at all. The gospel is built the same way: God saves in Christ so that no one may boast in his presence, and the one who boasts must boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:29-31; Ephesians 2:8-9).

God works with the fear rather than against it. The offer in verse 10 is unprompted, and there is no rebuke in it. God gives Gideon what he needs to go, and he goes.

Standing still. The three hundred do not charge; they stand in their places (v. 21), and the LORD does the fighting.

The day of Midian. Centuries later Isaiah uses this night as the standard picture of God breaking an oppressor (Isa. 9:4), in a passage about a child who is born to us (see vv. 23-25).
7.examples:
Then: An army of thirty-two thousand was cut to three hundred on purpose, and the three hundred were sent into a night attack carrying a pot and a horn. They stood still in a ring around a sleeping valley, broke the pots, and watched an army kill itself in the dark.

Now: Verse 10 is the one to keep. Here is what God does with a frightened man who has already been given more assurance than most people get in a lifetime: he does not shame him, does not withdraw the commission, and does not tell him to feel differently. He offers him a companion for the walk down, and the command comes wrapped in a promise already kept, I have given it into your hand. If you are waiting to stop being afraid before you go, this is a chapter about a man who went with somebody else beside him. Christians do not walk down alone either: the Spirit is given to them, and the brothers and sisters God puts beside them are his Purahs.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD said to Gideon, “The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’”
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter serves this sentence. God shrinks the army so that the victory can only be his, and so that Israel cannot tell the story of its rescue as a story about itself. The gospel works the same way: salvation is “not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:9).

7.reflection:
God cut the army “lest Israel boast over me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me’” (v. 2). Where are you most tempted to tell your story as one of your own achievement, and what would it look like to give God the credit?

God did not rebuke Gideon’s fear but said, “if you are afraid”, and gave him what he needed (vv. 10–11). How does this change the way you bring your fears to God, and the way you treat fearful people in your church?

The three hundred won by standing still and holding out a light (vv. 19–21). How does 2 Corinthians 4:7 help you see your own weakness and ordinariness as places where Christ’s light can shine?

After the miracle, the ordinary work of the pursuit was given back to the tribes (vv. 23–25). What ordinary, unglamorous work has God given you, and how does knowing that the victory is his change the way you do it?

8.title: Gideon's Failure

And they accused him fiercely.<sup>2</sup>And he said to them, "What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?<sup>3</sup>God has given into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. What have I been able to do in comparison with you?" Then their anger against him subsided when he said this.<sup>4</sup>And Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the 300 men who were with him, exhausted yet pursuing.<sup>5</sup>So he said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian."<sup>6</sup>And the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?"<sup>7</sup>So Gideon said, "Well then, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will flail your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers."<sup>8</sup>And from there he went up to Penuel, and spoke to them in the same way, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered.<sup>9</sup>And he said to the men of Penuel, "When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower."<sup>10</sup>Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army, about 15,000 men, all who were left of all the army of the people of the East, for there had fallen 120,000 men who drew the sword.<sup>11</sup>And Gideon went up by the way of the tent dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and attacked the army, for the army felt secure.<sup>12</sup>And Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he threw all the army into a panic.<sup>13</sup>Then Gideon the son of Joash returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres.<sup>14</sup>And he captured a young man of Succoth and questioned him. They answered, "As you are, so were they. Every one of them resembled the son of a king."<sup>19</sup>And he said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you."<sup>20</sup>So he said to Jether his firstborn, "Rise and kill them!" And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.<sup>28</sup>So Midian was subdued before the people of Israel, and they raised their heads no more. 8.overview:
Where we are. Three hundred men with jars and torches have routed Midian in the Jezreel valley, and Ephraim has killed the two princes at the fords (chapter 7). Gideon is still chasing the two kings across the Jordan.

The message. Success tests a servant of God more searchingly than danger. Gideon, who trembled before the battle, is hardened by winning it, and in the same breath as the finest thing he ever says, “the LORD will rule over you” (v. 23), he asks for the gold that becomes Israel’s snare. God’s gifts, held as if they were ours, become idols, and a people who lean on a deliverer rather than on God forget both when he is buried.

Why it was said. Israel kept looking for security in a strong man and in religion of its own making (see the introduction). This chapter shows that even a true deliverer cannot keep a nation faithful, and that the pull towards a king and a shrine of our own begins in the hour of victory.

How the chapter makes its case. A soft answer calms Ephraim’s anger about credit (vv. 1–3). Succoth and Penuel refuse the exhausted three hundred bread, and Gideon threatens them (vv. 4–9), then captures the kings at Karkor (vv. 10–12). On the way back he flails the elders of Succoth and kills the men of Penuel (vv. 13–17), and executes the kings to avenge his own brothers (vv. 18–21). He refuses the crown for God’s sake (vv. 22–23), asks for the earrings, and makes an ephod that all Israel whores after (vv. 24–27). Forty years of rest follow, with seventy sons and a son called “my father is king” (vv. 28–32), and at his death Israel forgets the LORD and Gideon’s family alike (vv. 33–35).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by the need it exposes. Gideon was right that Israel needed the LORD himself to rule over them, and wrong in everything he did next: no human deliverer can be trusted with the gold and the throne. God’s answer was to come and rule in the person of his Son. Jesus refused the crown a crowd tried to force on him (John 6:15), took nothing that was not his, and, where Gideon broke an oppressor and then began to act like one, was himself broken for the people who had failed him.

For us. The hour of blessing is the dangerous hour. Hold God’s gifts with open hands, and let no good thing, even a souvenir of answered prayer, become the place we go instead of to him. Where we have already made an ephod, the way back is confession to the God who keeps steadfast love with those who fail him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A soft answer turns away wrath, and Gideon gives one. Ephraim arrives after the battle, angry not about Midian but about being left out of the glory (v. 1). Gideon answers with generous, calculated flattery: Ephraim’s gleanings outweigh his clan’s whole vintage, and God gave the two princes into their hands, not his (vv. 2–3). Their anger subsides. It is the last time in the chapter that Gideon puts someone else’s honour before his own, and the contrast with what follows, and with the slaughter of Ephraimites in Jephthah’s day (12:1–6), shows what one man’s willingness to yield the credit can save.
verseByVerse.theology: The quarrel is about credit, arriving after the danger has passed. Nobody from Ephraim was at the spring of Harod when there were thirty-two thousand men and God said there were too many.
verseByVerse.examples: Keep this scene. The same tribe will bring the identical complaint to Jephthah in chapter 12, almost word for word, and that time nobody answers softly, and forty-two thousand Ephraimites die at the fords of the Jordan (12:1-6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Ephraim said to him, "What is this that you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they accused him fiercely. And he said to them, "What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer? God has given into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. What have I been able to do in comparison with you?" Then their anger against him subsided when he said this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim picks a fight over who gets the credit, and Gideon defuses it by giving it to them: a soft answer turns away wrath.

What is this that you have done to us? The grievance is not what it pretends to be. Ephraim is not angry that Midian ate the harvest for seven years; they are angry that they were left out of the glory, and they say so after the battle, after the rout, after the two princes are dead. The strongest tribe of the central hills had reasons to expect the lead: Joshua had been an Ephraimite, the tabernacle stood at Shiloh in its territory, and Jacob had set Ephraim ahead of his elder brother Manasseh (Genesis 48:19–20). Now a man from the weakest clan of Manasseh had saved Israel without them.

The gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim. Gideon’s answer is skilled flattery, and it works. What Ephraim gleaned, the leftovers picked after the grape harvest, is worth more than his whole clan’s vintage: their share of the mopping up outweighs his share of the victory. It is not true, and it is exactly what they want to hear. He also points them to God: “God has given into your hands the princes of Midian” (v. 3).

Their anger against him subsided. “A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). Here is the soft answer, doing its work on men who came looking for a fight over nothing. The difference between this quarrel and the slaughter of Ephraimites in Jephthah’s day (12:1–6) was one man’s willingness to let somebody else have the credit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The three hundred press on after the beaten enemy, and two Israelite towns will not risk feeding them. Exhausted yet pursuing, Gideon’s men cross the Jordan after Zebah and Zalmunna (v. 4). Succoth and then Penuel refuse bread, waiting to see who wins before they commit (vv. 5–6, 8), and Gideon answers with threats of torture and destruction (vv. 7, 9). Then the narrative turns to the battle: fifteen thousand men remain of the eastern army, secure in the desert, and Gideon comes on them from the caravan route, captures both kings and routs the rest (vv. 10–12). The victory is real; so is the change in the man.
verseByVerse.theology: Succoth and Penuel are Israelite towns, not Midianite ones. The threat in this section comes from inside Israel, and before long so does the cruelty.
verseByVerse.examples: If you are tired in the Christian life, you are in good company here. The three hundred were not chasing in hope of a victory still to be won; they were following up one God had already given, and that is the believer's position too.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the 300 men who were with him, exhausted yet pursuing. So he said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian." And the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?" So Gideon said, "Well then, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will flail your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers." And from there he went up to Penuel, and spoke to them in the same way, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered. And he said to the men of Penuel, "When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worn out but still chasing the enemy, Gideon’s men are refused bread by two Israelite towns that will not commit until the outcome is safe, and Gideon answers them with threats of torture.

Exhausted yet pursuing. Carry those three words about with you. The three hundred have been awake since before the middle watch, have run down a valley and crossed a river, and are following two kings into the desert on empty stomachs. Few phrases in Scripture describe ordinary Christian perseverance better: not fresh, not visibly winning, worn out, and not stopping.

Please give loaves of bread. The request is modest: loaves, from his own countrymen, for men chasing the enemy of the whole nation.

The officials of Succoth. The refusal is a sneer over a rational calculation. Succoth sits east of the Jordan, exposed. If Gideon succeeds, they have lost a few loaves; if he fails, Midian is back next harvest and will know which towns fed the raiding party. The word that gives them away is already: “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand?” It is a very old form of practical unbelief: not denying that God can do it, but refusing to commit until the outcome is safe, and everyone who practises it calls it prudence. Penuel answers the same way (v. 8).

I will flail your flesh. Here the chapter turns, in Gideon. His faith is intact: “when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand.” What has entered is something else: a promise of torture, made to fellow Israelites, over bread. The man who would not tear down an altar by daylight because he feared the town (6:27) now threatens to flail the elders of one town and pull down the tower of another for insulting him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army, about 15,000 men, all who were left of all the army of the people of the East, for there had fallen 120,000 men who drew the sword. And Gideon went up by the way of the tent dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and attacked the army, for the army felt secure. And Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he threw all the army into a panic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gideon’s tiny force falls on the remnant of the eastern army where it feels safe, and captures both kings: the victory is still God’s doing.

About 15,000 men. The arithmetic of the night in the valley is given here for the first time: 120,000 dead, 15,000 left. That remnant is still fifty times the size of Gideon’s force, and it could have destroyed the three hundred without difficulty if it had turned round and looked.

For the army felt secure. He takes the caravan route round to the east, the route of the tent dwellers, and comes at them from the desert side, the direction nobody watches. The narrator gives the reason it worked in four words: “the army felt secure.” They had put enough distance between themselves and the Jezreel valley to relax; nobody chases a beaten army that far on foot.

Captured the two kings of Midian. Both kings are taken alive, and it will turn out in a few verses that Gideon had his own reasons for wanting them alive (vv. 18–19).

Are the numbers realistic? Either the host was as large as stated and God destroyed it, setting its men against one another (7:22), or “thousand” here means a military unit, much smaller than a thousand men. Either way the point stands: three hundred men won because God fought.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — What He Did on the Way Back
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon’s return from the battle reveals what winning has done to him, and a private motive for the whole pursuit. He seizes a young man of Succoth, gets a written list of seventy-seven officials and elders, and carries out his threat with desert thorns (vv. 13–16). At Penuel he breaks down the tower and kills the men of the city (v. 17), Israelites killed by Israel’s judge. Then he questions the captured kings about men killed at Tabor, learns that they were his own brothers, and kills Zebah and Zalmunna himself after his young son is too afraid to do it, taking the gold off their camels (vv. 18–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Justice and revenge can look alike from the outside. This section shows a judge punishing real wrongs and, at the same time, settling his own scores.
verseByVerse.examples: Parents who have been shown patience by God are called to show it to their children. And anyone who was shamed as a child for being afraid may know that God does not treat his children so: as a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Ps. 103:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon the son of Joash returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres. And he captured a young man of Succoth and questioned him. And he wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men. And he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your men who are exhausted?'" And he took the elders of the city, and he took thorns of the wilderness and briers and with them taught the men of Succoth a lesson. And he broke down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gideon comes back and carries out his threats, torturing the elders of Succoth and killing the men of Penuel: Israel’s deliverer has begun to treat Israel as an enemy.

Seventy-seven men. The first thing he does on his return is compile a list. He seizes a young man of Succoth, questions him, and the young man writes out seventy-seven names, every official and elder in the town: a literate youth doing clerical work under duress, producing a list of men to be punished.

Taught the men of Succoth a lesson. He quotes their own sentence back at them with the kings standing there, and both promises are kept. Desert thorns are not a figure of speech: this is torture, applied methodically to seventy-seven named men who had refused a meal. At Penuel the tower comes down and the men of the city are killed: Israelites, killed by Israel’s judge, for declining to feed his soldiers.

Silence is not approval. The book records it without comment, but this is the narrator who will shortly tell us the ephod became a snare: he is showing us a man coming apart. Set the two halves of Gideon side by side. In chapter 6 he says, “my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house” (6:15). In chapter 8 he tortures seventy-seven elders and destroys a town for wounding his dignity. What changed between the two chapters was not his theology. It was that he won.

A deliverer who became an oppressor. Every judge is a flawed pointer to the true Deliverer. Gideon broke an oppressor and then began to act like one; Christ broke the oppressor and was himself broken for the people who had failed him.

Why then does Hebrews praise Gideon? Hebrews lists Gideon among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:32) because it commends what he did by faith: he believed God against impossible odds and went down to the camp with three hundred men. It does not commend Succoth’s thorns, the blood feud or the ephod, and this chapter makes sure no reader could think so (see the introduction).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 16 says that he “taught” or “made known to” the men of Succoth. A Hebrew word differing by one letter means “threshed”, the verb behind “flail” in Gideon’s threat (v. 7), and many scholars think that was the sense intended here. Either way the sense is plain: the threat was carried out.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?" They answered, "As you are, so were they. Every one of them resembled the son of a king." And he said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you." So he said to Jether his firstborn, "Rise and kill them!" But the young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a young man. Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Rise yourself and fall upon us, for as the man is, so is his strength." And Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments that were on the necks of their camels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The execution of the Midianite kings turns out to be a private blood feud for Gideon’s own brothers, carried out with a cruelty that reaches even his son.

Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor? A question comes out of nowhere, about an incident the book has never mentioned, and the answer is flattery from two men in chains: they looked like you, like the sons of a king.

They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. This sentence puts the whole pursuit in a new light. Gideon’s full brothers had been killed by these two men at Tabor, and he has said nothing about it until now. Then the admission: “if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you.” In this moment the execution is not an act of national deliverance but a blood feud, and he says so out loud. Somewhere under the trumpets and the torches and “a sword for the LORD and for Gideon” (7:20), a private account has been running, and it is being settled now.

The deliverance was still real. None of that makes the deliverance false. God did give Midian into his hand, and the barley loaf did flatten the tent (7:13). But the man God used had reasons of his own, and the book is honest enough to let us hear one of them. God uses people whose motives are mixed, and does not thereby approve the mixture.

Rise and kill them! He tells his eldest boy to do it. To be executed by a youth was a deliberate humiliation for a warrior, and a father is arranging it for his son to carry out. The boy cannot, and the text says why, plainly and without contempt: “he was afraid, because he was still a young man.” There is a terrible echo in that line. The last person in this story who held back because he was afraid was Gideon himself, who dared to pull down the altar only at night. God met that fear with patience, a companion and a plan (7:10–11). Gideon meets his son’s fear by doing the job himself in front of everybody.

He took the crescent ornaments. The kings ask him to do it himself, and he does. Then the narrator adds the last clause on purpose: he took the crescent-shaped gold ornaments from the necks of their camels. Keep that detail. It is about to matter a great deal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Crown Refused and the Gold Requested
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon speaks the truth about Israel’s King and then takes the gold that ruins Israel. The men of Israel offer him a dynasty (v. 22), and he refuses it in words that could hardly be better: “the LORD will rule over you” (v. 23). In the next breath he asks for the golden earrings from the spoil (v. 24), and the army gladly fills a cloak with forty pounds of gold, besides royal ornaments and purple (vv. 25–26). Gideon makes an ephod, a priestly object, and sets it up in Ophrah, and it becomes what the Canaanite gods were meant to be: something all Israel whores after, and a snare to Gideon and his family (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Refusing a title is easier than refusing what comes with it. Gideon's words are right; his request shows where his heart had drifted.
verseByVerse.examples: Some of the most dangerous moments in a life with God come after a success, not after a failure. The gifts God gives can quietly become objects of trust in their own right.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel offers Gideon a dynasty, and he refuses it with the truest words he ever speaks: Israel already has a King, the LORD.

Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also. This is not only gratitude; it is a proposal to change how Israel is governed. They want a dynasty, for the reason nations always want one: somebody delivered them and they would like the arrangement made permanent. It is also the very error the whole book has been diagnosing. Every rest in Judges ends when the judge dies, and Israel’s solution is not to hold on to God but to make the deliverer hereditary.

The LORD will rule over you. This is the finest sentence Gideon ever speaks. He refuses all three generations and gives the reason without softening: Israel has a King already, and the offer, however well meant, would put a man in his place. He has it exactly right. Generations later, when the nation demands a king to be like the other nations, God tells Samuel what is really happening: “they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them” (1 Samuel 8:7). Whatever comes next, Gideon said this, and he meant it.

He took his throne another way. The sentence waits for its fulfilment. God’s answer in the end was that he himself would rule his people in the person of a son of David. When a crowd tried to make Jesus king by force after he fed them, he withdrew (John 6:15); he took his throne another way, by the cross and the empty tomb. In him, “the LORD will rule over you” and a man on the throne are at last the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon said to them, "Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil." (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.) And they answered, "We will willingly give them." And they spread a cloak, and every man threw in it the earrings of his spoil. And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was 1,700 shekels of gold, besides the crescent ornaments and the pendants and the purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and besides the collars that were around the necks of their camels. And Gideon made an ephod of it and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the very next breath Gideon asks for the gold, and the ephod he makes from it becomes the idol that ensnares Israel and his own family: he refused the crown and took the treasury.

Let me make a request of you. Read verses 23 and 24 together, because nothing separates them: “the LORD will rule over you … Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil.” He declines the crown and asks for the treasury, and there is no sign that he noticed any distance between the two.

1,700 shekels of gold. Seventeen hundred shekels is something over forty pounds of gold, and that is only the earrings. The list goes on: the crescents, the pendants, the purple (royal cloth, coloured with the most expensive dye in the ancient world) and the collars off the camels. The man who would not be king now owns the wardrobe of two kings.

Because they were Ishmaelites. The narrator explains the earrings by calling the Midianites Ishmaelites. The name seems to have been used loosely for the camel-riding traders and nomads of the desert, descendants of Ishmael and others: in Joseph’s story the same caravan is called both Ishmaelite and Midianite (Genesis 37:25–28). Such peoples carried much of their wealth on their bodies, in gold.

Gideon made an ephod of it. An ephod was a priest’s garment. The high priest wore one, and attached to it was the breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, by which Israel enquired of God (Exodus 28:4–30). The tabernacle was at Shiloh, and the appointed way of enquiring of God was through the priesthood; now Ophrah has a golden object made from the spoils of the deliverance, standing in the town of the man God used. He refused to be king and made himself a shrine.

All Israel whored after it there. The two key words are the ones the book has used all along. “Whored after” is what Israel does with other gods (2:17). “Snare” is the word God used at Bochim about the gods of the nations: “their gods shall be a snare to you” (2:3). Both are now attached to a thing an Israelite judge made, out of the plunder of a victory God gave him, in the town where he had torn down an altar to Baal. He began by demolishing a false shrine at night because he was afraid, and ended by building one in daylight, with gold he had asked for himself. He was never tempted by the crown; the snare came in through the one door he had left open.

When the gift becomes the shrine. Gideon did not abandon God. He made something golden to remember God by, and then everyone worshipped the souvenir. That is the subtlest idolatry there is, and it is very much ours: the good gift turned into the thing we live for. Augustine drew a distinction that helps: some things are to be enjoyed for their own sake and others used on the way to that enjoyment, and our disorder, he argued, is that we try to enjoy what we should use and use what we should enjoy. We use God to get his gifts. The answered prayer becomes the career, the family, the ministry, the platform, and slowly the gift holds the heart while God is consulted about how to keep it. The cure is not to despise the gift, any more than the victory over Midian was a bad thing, but to see the Giver more clearly than the gold.

No ephod, but a Person. That is why the New Testament gives us no ephod at all, only a Person. We draw near to God “by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:20).

Uncertain wording. What Gideon’s ephod was is not certain. Elsewhere an ephod is a garment worn by a priest, but forty pounds of gold is far too much to wear, so many think this was a gold-covered image or an oracle object set up for consulting God, perhaps draped with or shaped like a priestly ephod (compare 17:5; 18:14). Either way it was a rival place of worship, and it drew Israel away from the LORD.
verseByVerse.note: Gideon's ephod is the first of several unauthorised shrines in Judges; Micah's household shrine in chapter 17 also has an ephod (17:5).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Forty years of rest end in a royal household, a forgotten God and a betrayed family. Midian is broken for good and the land has rest (v. 28). Gideon goes home and lives like the king he refused to be: many wives, seventy sons, and a son by a concubine in Shechem whom he names Abimelech, “my father is king” (vv. 29–31). He dies in a good old age (v. 32), and at once Israel turns to Baal-berith, forgets the LORD who rescued them, and shows no steadfast love to Gideon’s family (vv. 33–35). Every piece of the next chapter’s disaster was assembled during the rest.
verseByVerse.theology: Faithfulness that rests on a man rather than on God ends when the man dies. Israel's loyalty lasted exactly as long as Gideon did (v. 33).
verseByVerse.examples: Gideon's public words refused a crown; the name he let his son carry claimed one. Children usually learn from what is said at home.

verseByVerse.quote: So Midian was subdued before the people of Israel, and they raised their heads no more. And the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon. Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and lived in his own house. Now Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring, for he had many wives. And his concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he called his name Abimelech. And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Midian is broken and the land has forty years of rest, but Gideon lives like the king he refused to be, and names a son “my father is king”.

So Midian was subdued. The formula closes the cycle properly, and it should be said before the rest: by the standard of this book it is a real success. The raids stopped for good. A generation grew up who could plant a crop and eat it.

Seventy sons, for he had many wives. Then the writer tells us, without a word of comment, what living in his own house looked like. Seventy sons and many wives are not a large family but a royal household. Keeping wives on that scale required a king’s income, and seventy sons are exactly what a dynasty is built from: heirs, alliances, a name that cannot be extinguished. He refused the crown in verse 23 and then lived exactly like the thing he had refused to be called. The title was declined and the life adopted, a distinction that satisfies nobody but the man making it.

He called his name Abimelech. Abimelech is Hebrew for “my father is king”. Whatever Gideon said in public at the assembly, that is the sentence a boy carried round Shechem for the rest of his childhood: the son of a concubine in a town away from home, walking about with a name that announced a claim his father had formally refused. He will spend the next chapter acting on that claim, and one of the first things he does is kill the seventy sons of verse 30.

In a good old age. Gideon dies old and is buried in his father’s tomb, the same father whose altar he pulled down in the dark and who defended him the next morning (6:28–31).

Was Gideon’s polygamy acceptable to God? The narrator records it without approving it. It went against God’s design for marriage (Genesis 2:24) and the law for kings (Deuteronomy 17:17), and its fruit was Abimelech, who murdered seventy brothers (chapter 9).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals and made Baal-berith their god. And the people of Israel did not remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them from the hand of all their enemies on every side, and they did not show steadfast love to the family of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) in return for all the good that he had done to Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as Gideon is buried, Israel forgets the LORD who saved it and shows no loyalty to the family of the man he used: forgetting God and betraying one another go together.

As soon as Gideon died. The trigger is a funeral, exactly as 2:19 said it always would be, and this time the narrator does not even leave a decent interval.

Baal-berith. The name means “lord of the covenant”, or “Baal of the treaty”, a god honoured at Shechem (9:4, 46). Israel is in a covenant already, with the God who brought them out of Egypt; they have gone and found a Baal who offers the same service.

Did not remember the LORD their God. By now this is the book’s diagnosis. They did not reject him or argue with him; they forgot him, a nation that had watched three hundred men break jars in the dark.

They did not show steadfast love. The last verse adds the human failure. The word is hesed, the loyal covenant kindness God shows his people and expects them to show each other, and they did not show it to Gideon’s family. The two failures stand in one sentence for a reason: a people who stop remembering what God has done soon stop keeping faith with each other.

The stage is set. Seventy sons are living in Ophrah, a man named “my father is king” is living in Shechem, the town has adopted a god called lord of the covenant, and nobody in Israel feels any obligation to the family of the man who saved them. Everything needed for the next chapter is in place, and every piece of it was assembled during forty years of rest. The God whom Israel forgot did not forget them: he keeps hesed with those who fail him, and in Christ he kept it to the end.

8.theology:
What winning did to him. The man who called himself the least in his father's house now tortures elders for wounding his dignity. His theology has not changed (v. 7); what changed is that he won.

The crown and the treasury. Verse 23 is exactly right: Israel already had a King. Verse 24 is the next sentence from the same mouth, and the gold became the snare that the crown never was.

The title refused, the life adopted. Gideon declined to be called king and lived like one. The speed with which Israel forgot both the LORD and Gideon's family when he died (vv. 33-35) shows how little of its faith had rested on God himself.
8.examples:
Then: A man who would not move until he had asked for signs twice, and then pulled down an idol after dark because he was frightened, finished his career torturing the elders of an Israelite town over bread, executing two kings for the death of his brothers, refusing a crown in one sentence and asking for forty pounds of gold in the next.

Now: The chapter's question is what happened to him after the success. The snare came not from the enemy, nor from the crown he knew God well enough to refuse, but from the spoils of a genuine victory everybody agreed was God's. Blessing received is the moment to hold it with open hands, remembering whose it was, and it is the Spirit, not our own vigilance, who keeps the heart from turning gifts into ephods. Where we have already made one, the way back is the one Gideon never took: confession, to the God who, unlike Israel in verse 35, keeps hesed with those who fail him, because the true Judge and King never took what was not his, and his faithfulness is counted to us.

keyVerse.quote: Gideon said to them, “I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you.”
keyVerse.note: This is the truest thing Gideon ever said: Israel already had a King, and no deliverer should take his place. The tragedy of the chapter is that the next verse asks for the gold, and Gideon lives like the king he refused to be. The sentence waits for Jesus, in whom the LORD ruling and a man on the throne are at last the same thing.

8.reflection:
Ephraim’s anger was about credit (vv. 1–3). Where do you notice the desire for recognition in yourself or your church, and what does Gideon’s soft answer teach about ending such quarrels?

“Exhausted yet pursuing” (v. 4). Where are you weary in following Christ, and what keeps a tired believer going?

Gideon spoke rightly about God (v. 23) and then asked for the gold (v. 24). Why is success often more dangerous to faith than hardship? What gift of God are you tempted to turn into an “ephod”?

Israel forgot the LORD and showed no steadfast love to Gideon’s family (vv. 33–35). How are remembering God and keeping faith with one another connected, and how can we help each other remember?

9.title: Abimelech the Bramble King
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family,<sup>2</sup>"Say in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, 'Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you?' Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh."<sup>3</sup>And his mother's relatives spoke all these words on his behalf in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother."<sup>4</sup>And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him.<sup>5</sup>And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.<sup>6</sup>And all the leaders of Shechem came together, and all Beth-millo, and they went and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.<sup>7</sup>When it was told to Jotham, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim and cried aloud and said to them, "Listen to me, you leaders of Shechem, that God may listen to you.<sup>8</sup>The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.'<sup>9</sup>But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which gods and men are honored, and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>10</sup>And the trees said to the fig tree, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>11</sup>But the fig tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my sweetness and my good fruit and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>12</sup>And the trees said to the vine, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>13</sup>But the vine said to them, 'Shall I leave my wine that cheers God and men and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>14</sup>Then all the trees said to the bramble, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>15</sup>And the bramble said to the trees, 'If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.'<sup>16</sup>"Now therefore, if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house and have done to him as his deeds deserved—<sup>17</sup>for my father fought for you and risked his life and delivered you from the hand of Midian,<sup>18</sup>and you have risen up against my father's house this day and have killed his sons, seventy men on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he is your relative—<sup>19</sup>if you then have acted in good faith and integrity with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you.<sup>20</sup>But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo; and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem and from Beth-millo and devour Abimelech."<sup>21</sup>And Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer and lived there, because of Abimelech his brother.<sup>22</sup>Abimelech ruled over Israel three years.<sup>23</sup>And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech,<sup>24</sup>that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.<sup>25</sup>And the leaders of Shechem put men in ambush against him on the mountaintops, and they robbed all who passed by them along that way. And it was told to Abimelech.<sup>26</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him.<sup>27</sup>And they went out into the field and gathered the grapes from their vineyards and trod them and held a festival; and they went into the house of their god and ate and drank and reviled Abimelech.<sup>28</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem; but why should we serve him?<sup>29</sup>Would that this people were under my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech. I would say to Abimelech, 'Increase your army, and come out.'"<sup>30</sup>When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled.<sup>31</sup>And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly, saying, "Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his relatives have come to Shechem, and they are stirring up the city against you.<sup>32</sup>Now therefore, go by night, you and the people who are with you, and set an ambush in the field.<sup>33</sup>Then in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, rise early and rush upon the city. And when he and the people who are with him come out against you, you may do to them as your hand finds to do."<sup>34</sup>So Abimelech and all the men who were with him rose up by night and set an ambush against Shechem in four companies.<sup>35</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed went out and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city, and Abimelech and the people who were with him rose from the ambush.<sup>36</sup>And when Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!" And Zebul said to him, "You mistake the shadow of the mountains for men."<sup>37</sup>Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming from the direction of the Diviners' Oak."<sup>38</sup>Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are not these the people whom you despised? Go out now and fight with them."<sup>39</sup>And Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought with Abimelech.<sup>40</sup>And Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him. And many fell wounded, up to the entrance of the gate.<sup>41</sup>And Abimelech lived at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his relatives, so that they could not dwell at Shechem.<sup>42</sup>On the following day, the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told.<sup>43</sup>He took his people and divided them into three companies and set an ambush in the fields. And he looked and saw the people coming out of the city. So he rose against them and killed them.<sup>44</sup>Abimelech and the company that was with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city, while the two companies rushed upon all who were in the field and killed them.<sup>45</sup>And Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt.<sup>46</sup>When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith.<sup>47</sup>Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem were gathered together.<sup>48</sup>And Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon, he and all the people who were with him. And Abimelech took an axe in his hand and cut down a bundle of brushwood and took it up and laid it on his shoulder. And he said to the men who were with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done."<sup>49</sup>So every one of the people cut down his bundle and following Abimelech put it against the stronghold, and they set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.<sup>50</sup>Then Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against Thebez and captured it.<sup>51</sup>But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled to it and shut themselves in, and they went up to the roof of the tower.<sup>52</sup>And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it and drew near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire.<sup>53</sup>And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.<sup>54</sup>Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" And his young man thrust him through, and he died.<sup>55</sup>And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, everyone departed to his home.<sup>56</sup>Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers.<sup>57</sup>And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
9.overview:
Where we are. Gideon refused a crown and then lived like a king, and as soon as he died Israel turned to Baal-berith and forgot his family (8:22–35). Now his son Abimelech, born to a concubine in Shechem, reaches for the crown his father declined.

The message. God sees the blood of the innocent and repays it, even when he seems absent. A man who murders his way to a throne, and the men who pay for it, destroy each other exactly as a wronged son foretold, and the narrator insists that this was God’s doing (vv. 23–24, 56–57). The chapter also exposes the kind of ruler people choose when they do not want God to rule them: a bramble that offers shade it cannot give and fire it can.

Why it was said. Israel would ask again and again for a king like the nations (see the introduction). This chapter is the book’s first answer: a king chosen because “he is our brother”, ruling by fear, and ending at a tower door.

How the chapter makes its case. Abimelech wins Shechem with an appeal to blood, murders seventy brothers with hired men and is crowned by the oak (vv. 1–6). Jotham, the one survivor, shouts a fable from Mount Gerizim: olive, fig and vine refuse to reign, and the bramble accepts; then he curses both king and city with fire (vv. 7–21). After three years God sends an evil spirit between them to repay the murders (vv. 22–24). Shechem turns to banditry and to Gaal (vv. 25–29), Zebul betrays Gaal (vv. 30–41), and Abimelech razes Shechem and burns a thousand people in their temple (vv. 42–49). At Thebez a woman drops a millstone on his head (vv. 50–55), and the narrator states the meaning: God returned the evil on both (vv. 56–57).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by contrast. Abimelech killed his brothers to take a throne. Jesus is the King who reverses the fable: like the olive, he had glory to leave, and left it, not to hold sway but to serve and give his life (Philippians 2:6–8; Mark 10:45). He “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11), and the shade he offers is real. And where the blood of seventy cried out for judgment, his blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24).

For us. God is not mocked: those who do evil and those who fund or enable it will answer to him, though his hand is often hidden. Be wary of leaders who want power most and have least to give, and of loyalties built only on being “one of us”. And bring every guilty hand to the blood that speaks mercy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abimelech takes a throne by appealing to kinship and paying for murder. He asks Shechem’s leaders a rigged question, seventy rulers or one, and clinches it with blood: “I am your bone and your flesh” (vv. 1–2). They agree because “he is our brother” and give him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith to hire worthless men (vv. 3–4). He kills his seventy brothers on one stone at Ophrah, and only Jotham, the youngest, escapes by hiding (v. 5). Then Shechem crowns him beside the oak and the pillar, the place where Joshua had set up a stone as a witness against Israel (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: This is Israel's first attempt at a king, and it is a warning. When the nation later asks Samuel for a king (1 Sam. 8), this chapter stands behind the request.
verseByVerse.examples: Jotham survives by hiding, and God preserves him to speak. Even in the worst of times God keeps a witness alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family, "Say in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, 'Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you?' Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." And his mother's relatives spoke all these words on his behalf in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother." And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him. And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself. And all the leaders of Shechem came together, and all Beth-millo, and they went and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech wins Shechem by appealing to blood, pays for the murder of his seventy brothers with temple silver, and is crowned at the very place where Israel had sworn to serve the LORD.

Which is better for you? The campaign opens with a question written so that only one answer is possible, and it takes for granted something untrue. Nobody has offered Shechem seventy rulers. Gideon refused the crown for himself and his sons in as many words (8:23), and nothing suggests his sons had designs on anything.

I am your bone and your flesh. The clinching argument is not policy but blood: vote for me because I am one of you. And it works, for exactly that reason: “He is our brother.” Not he is competent, not he is godly, not he has any claim, but he is ours.

Out of the house of Baal-berith. The money comes out of the temple of Baal-berith, the god Israel adopted as soon as Gideon died (8:33). The shrine Israel set up in place of the LORD funds the murder of the deliverer’s family. Count the coins against the corpses: seventy pieces of silver, seventy brothers, one coin each. That was the going rate for a son of the man who saved the country, and it bought men the narrator calls worthless and reckless: idle, unattached and available.

On one stone. The detail turns an atrocity into a ceremony. This is no raid that got out of hand but an execution conducted at a single place, one man after another, at the house in Ophrah where the angel once sat under the tree (6:11).

For he hid himself. One escapes, and the writer says how. Jotham survives by doing what his father did in chapter 6: getting out of sight of the people looking for him.

By the oak of the pillar at Shechem. They crown him at the worst possible place. At Shechem Joshua gathered all Israel, made them promise three times to serve the LORD, and set up a great stone under the terebinth as a witness: “it has heard all the words of the LORD … lest you deal falsely with your God” (Joshua 24:26–27). They make a man who murdered his brothers king at the foot of the stone placed there to stop them dealing falsely with God.

Why does “one of us” beat “good for us”? Shechem’s choice is not ancient history. Across the world, and not only in politics, people increasingly ask first whether a leader, an argument or a news story is ours, and only afterwards whether it is true. George Orwell noticed, in his essay on nationalism, that the partisan judges an action not by what it is but by who did it: the same atrocity is an outrage or a regrettable necessity depending on the side. It feels like loyalty. It is really a way of being saved by belonging: if I am with my people, I am in the right. But a people bound by blood alone comes apart the moment someone redraws the line of who counts as “us”, as this chapter will show (v. 28).

A family made by his blood. Jesus redrew the line the other way. When his family came looking for him, he looked at the crowd around him and said, “whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Mark 3:35). He made brothers out of strangers and enemies at the cost of his own blood, and in a family made like that nobody has to be the brother left out.

Uncertain wording. “Beth-millo” means “house of the fill” or “house of the earthwork”. It was probably a fortified part of Shechem built on a raised platform of packed earth, and its people may be the same as the “leaders of the Tower of Shechem” in verse 46, but this is not certain. Either way, the city’s whole leadership shares in the coronation.
verseByVerse.note: Abimelech means “my father is king”, a name at odds with Gideon’s refusal of kingship (8:23).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one surviving son tells a fable that exposes the king Shechem has chosen and calls down a curse on both parties. From Mount Gerizim Jotham calls on the leaders of Shechem to listen (v. 7). The trees seek a king: the olive, the fig and the vine all refuse to leave their fruitfulness to sway over others, and only the bramble accepts, offering shade it cannot give and threatening fire (vv. 8–15). Jotham then applies it: if Shechem has dealt in good faith with Gideon’s house, let them rejoice in Abimelech; if not, let fire come from each to devour the other (vv. 16–20). Then he flees and lives at Beer (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Jotham does not argue with Shechem; he tells them a story and lets them recognise themselves in it, as the prophet Nathan later does with David (2 Sam. 12:1-7).
verseByVerse.examples: Satire can be a faithful weapon. Jotham's fable has kept its force for three thousand years because it tells the truth about power in a form people remember.

verseByVerse.quote: When it was told to Jotham, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim and cried aloud and said to them, "Listen to me, you leaders of Shechem, that God may listen to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the mountain of blessing above the city, the last of Gideon’s sons calls Shechem to hear him, warning that God will hear them as they hear the wronged.

On top of Mount Gerizim. Gerizim is the mountain of blessing, where half the tribes stood when the law was read (Joshua 8:33; Deuteronomy 27:12). It stands directly above Shechem, and it is often said that a voice from its slopes carries down to the town. Jotham chooses the place where blessings were pronounced to pronounce a curse.

That God may listen to you. His opening words are a warning folded into a plea. The leaders of Shechem will one day cry to God, as Israel always does when trouble comes (6:6), and how God hears them then is tied to how they hear the wronged man now. A city that will not listen to the last survivor of a massacre has no claim to be heard by heaven (compare Proverbs 21:13).

The first fable. What follows is the first fable in the Bible, a story in which trees talk, and it is very funny in a bleak way.

verseByVerse.quote: The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.' But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which gods and men are honored, and go hold sway over the trees?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
