The trees go looking for a king, and the olive, the most valuable tree in the land, refuses: it will not leave a life of real usefulness to God and people to stand above the rest.

The trees once went out to anoint a king. The fable opens with the trees wanting a king, exactly as Israel wanted when they asked Gideon to rule over them (8:22). The first tree they ask is the olive, whose oil anointed kings, lit the lamps of the tabernacle and consecrated the priests.

By which gods and men are honored. Olive oil was poured on the grain offering (Leviticus 2:1) and on the heads of honoured guests (Psalm 23:5): oil “to make his face shine” (Psalm 104:15). That is a life of real use to God and to people, and the olive will not leave its abundance for a throne.

Hold sway over the trees. The verb means to sway or wave to and fro, as a tree does in the wind. Seen from the olive’s side, kingship is standing above the rest and swaying, with no fruit in it at all.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word behind “gods” can mean either God or gods, so the olive may mean the honour its oil gives to God and to people; since oil and wine were offered to the LORD, that is quite possible. The same is true of the vine in verse 13.

verseByVerse.quote: And the trees said to the fig tree, 'You come and reign over us.' But the fig tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my sweetness and my good fruit and go hold sway over the trees?' And the trees said to the vine, 'You come and reign over us.' But the vine said to them, 'Shall I leave my wine that cheers God and men and go hold sway over the trees?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fig and the vine refuse as well: the trees that are actually producing something will not stop doing it in order to rule.

The fig tree and the vine. Three times over the productive trees ask why they would stop bearing fruit in order to wave about above everybody else. Each refusal has the same shape: they have work to do, and the work is better than the position.

My sweetness and my good fruit … my wine. Olive, fig and vine are the great crops of the promised land, “a land of wheat and barley, of vines and fig trees and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey” (Deuteronomy 8:8), and every man “under his vine and under his fig tree” became Israel’s picture of peace (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4). The wine that “cheers God and men” is the drink offering poured out as “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (Numbers 15:7) and the wine that gladdens a feast. These trees give the land its food, its worship and its joy, and that is what they would have to leave behind to rule.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the trees said to the bramble, 'You come and reign over us.' And the bramble said to the trees, 'If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only the bramble wants the throne: it promises shelter it cannot give and threatens fire it can, and that is the kind of king Shechem has chosen.

Then all the trees said to the bramble. The bramble says yes at once, and a hill-country audience would have laughed at both halves of its answer.

Take refuge in my shade. A bramble is a thorn scrub that grows a foot or two off the ground. There is no shade under it, and anyone who tried to take refuge there would be cut to pieces. The one thing it promises is the one thing it cannot give.

Let fire come out of the bramble. A dry bramble on a hillside is the most flammable thing in the country, what starts the fires that burn out whole slopes. It cannot shelter anybody and it can burn everybody, and the cedars of Lebanon, the tallest and most magnificent trees there are, are precisely what it threatens.

If in good faith. The offer comes with a condition and a threat: loyalty, or fire. That is the shape of every reign built on fear, and the exact shape Abimelech’s rule will take. Jotham will pick up the bramble’s words, “if in good faith”, when he applies the story to Shechem (see the note on vv. 16–21).

The point of the fable. Its argument is not that kingship is wrong. It is that the people most fit to lead will not usually want the job, and the one who wants it most is often the one with nothing to give up. The fable also waits for a King who reverses it. The Son of God had glory to leave, and left it, not to hold sway but to serve, and his shade is real: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).
verseByVerse.note: The bramble of the fable is probably a kind of buckthorn or boxthorn, a low thorny shrub common in the hill country.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore, if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house and have done to him as his deeds deserved— for my father fought for you and risked his life and delivered you from the hand of Midian, and you have risen up against my father's house this day and have killed his sons, seventy men on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he is your relative— if you then have acted in good faith and integrity with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you. But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo; and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem and from Beth-millo and devour Abimelech." And Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer and lived there, because of Abimelech his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jotham drops the story and states the case: Shechem repaid Gideon’s self-sacrifice with the murder of his sons, so let king and city destroy each other with fire.

My father fought for you. The case is about debt. Gideon fought for Shechem, risked his life (the Hebrew is stronger, something like “threw his life out in front of him”) and delivered them from Midian. That is what they owed; the killing of his sons is what they paid. Jotham states the two facts side by side, lets the arithmetic stand, and names their reason: “because he is your relative”. He also calls Abimelech “the son of his female servant”, a pointed reminder of the claim to royal blood.

If you acted in good faith. His “if” is heavy with sarcasm, and it is also a real offer: if this was honourable, then enjoy each other and live with what you have chosen.

Let fire come out from Abimelech. The curse is precise and runs both ways: fire out of Abimelech to consume Shechem, and fire out of Shechem to consume Abimelech. He asks for no army and no judgment from outside, only that the two parties destroy each other, which is what partners in an alliance like this one generally do. The bramble threatened fire in the fable; here it is applied, and everything Jotham asks for happens before the chapter ends. Verse 57 will name him when it does.

And Jotham ran away. Then he runs. He does not stay to see it or raise a faction, and he never appears again. The last surviving son of the man who saved Israel spends the rest of his life at Beer, out of his brother’s reach.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–29 — God Sent an Evil Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself begins the unravelling, so that the murder of the seventy is repaid on both the killer and his backers. After three years God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem, and the men who betrayed Gideon’s house betray their king, so that the blood of the seventy comes on Abimelech and on those who strengthened his hands (vv. 22–24). Shechem sets ambushes on the mountain roads and robs travellers (v. 25). A newcomer, Gaal son of Ebed, wins the city’s confidence, and at a harvest festival in their god’s temple he mocks Abimelech as an outsider and boasts what he would do if Shechem were under his hand (vv. 26–29).
verseByVerse.theology: God's justice in this chapter works slowly. Three years pass between the murders and the first sign of judgment, and the guilty may have thought they had got away with it. God's silence is not his indifference.
verseByVerse.examples: Alliances built on shared guilt rarely hold. What united Shechem and Abimelech was a crime, and a crime makes a poor foundation for trust.

verseByVerse.quote: Abimelech ruled over Israel three years. And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech, that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three years God himself sends discord between Abimelech and Shechem, so that the blood of the seventy is repaid on the man who killed them and on the men who paid for it.

Abimelech ruled over Israel three years. The verb is not the usual word for reigning as king (the word used when Shechem made him king in v. 6) but a more general one, to act as ruler or prince, and “Israel” probably means only the towns round Shechem that accepted him. The narrator will not dignify the reign with a full royal title.

God sent an evil spirit. Whatever exactly the phrase means, and it is meant to unsettle, the writer’s point is who was behind it. The suspicion that grows between the two parties is not accidental, nor merely the natural fate of a conspiracy. It was sent. The men who betrayed Gideon’s house now betray their own partner: Jotham had asked whether they acted “in good faith” (v. 16), and the answer arrives as treachery returned for treachery.

The reason for everything. Verse 24 gives the reason for all that follows, so that no reader will mistake the quarrels and ambushes for the real cause: God is repaying the murder of the seventy.

Who strengthened his hands. Two parties are named, and the second is the one that usually escapes. Abimelech killed them; the men of Shechem “strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.” They swung nothing. They paid out of a temple treasury and let a hired gang do the work. The book holds both accountable in one sentence: those who fund, vote for, excuse or quietly enable what they would never do themselves are not bystanders. Anyone who sees himself there need not wait for a millstone; the blood of Jesus speaks mercy over those who confess (see the note on vv. 56–57).

Does God send evil? Here he sends a spirit of discord as judgment on men already guilty of murder (v. 24), working through their own free and guilty choices, as with Saul (1 Samuel 16:14) and Ahab (1 Kings 22:22). God is never the author of sin (James 1:13), but he rules even the evil of the wicked and turns it to justice.

verseByVerse.quote: And the leaders of Shechem put men in ambush against him on the mountaintops, and they robbed all who passed by them along that way. And it was told to Abimelech.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shechem begins to undermine its king by organised banditry on the roads he was supposed to keep safe.

In ambush against him on the mountaintops. The ambush is “against him”. The roads through the pass at Shechem were trade routes; a ruler was expected to keep them safe and probably took a share of the traffic. Robbing the caravans shamed Abimelech and cut off his income without open revolt. “And it was told to Abimelech”: he knows, and for the moment he waits. The mountaintops will come back in verse 36.

They robbed all who passed by. Banditry on the highways was the very mark of oppression in Deborah’s song (5:6), and now it is organised by Israelites against anybody who passes.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him. And they went out into the field and gathered the grapes from their vineyards and trod them and held a festival; and they went into the house of their god and ate and drank and reviled Abimelech. And Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem; but why should we serve him? Would that this people were under my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech. I would say to Abimelech, 'Increase your army, and come out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A newcomer wins the city by turning its own argument against Abimelech: he is not one of us after all.

Gaal the son of Ebed. The city takes to the newcomer at once, which is what a city does when it has already stopped trusting the man it crowned.

In the house of their god. The scene is a harvest festival: the grapes are gathered and trodden in the winepress, and in the temple of their god the wine flows and the talk turns against the king. The god is the one whose treasury paid for his coronation.

Is he not the son of Jerubbaal? Listen to the argument that finishes Abimelech, because it is the argument that made him. Shechem crowned him as their own bone and flesh. Gaal’s case is that he is not: he is Jerubbaal’s son, an outsider from Ophrah, and Shechem should serve its own ancient line. Hamor had ruled Shechem in Jacob’s day (Genesis 33:19; 34:2), so Gaal appeals to the city’s old Canaanite ruling family; Shechem was evidently a mixed town, and its Canaanite citizens remembered who had been there first. Nothing about Abimelech has changed. The city has simply applied its own principle in the other direction, which is what happens to every arrangement built on being “one of us”.

Would that this people were under my hand! Gaal’s answer to the man who wanted power is to want it himself. His challenge, “Increase your army, and come out”, is wine courage at a festival, and he will be held to it within days. It is overheard by the one man who should not have heard it: Zebul, named in the same speech as Abimelech’s officer (see the note on vv. 30–33).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first half of Jotham’s curse comes true: fire goes out from Abimelech and devours Shechem. Zebul, Abimelech’s governor, sends word and plans a dawn ambush (vv. 30–33). Gaal sees men coming down the mountains, Zebul mocks him, and Gaal is beaten back to the gate and driven out (vv. 34–41). The next day Abimelech kills the people in the fields, takes the city, razes it and sows it with salt (vv. 42–45). The leaders of the Tower of Shechem take refuge in the stronghold of El-berith, and Abimelech and his men pile brushwood against it and burn about a thousand men and women inside (vv. 46–49).
verseByVerse.theology: The violence grows: from seventy brothers on one stone to a whole city razed and a thousand people burned. Evil that is not repented of rarely stays the same size.
verseByVerse.examples: Abimelech's men do whatever he does, as Gideon's once did. Following a leader is only as good as the leader followed, and Christians are called to imitate others only as they imitate Christ (1 Cor. 11:1).

verseByVerse.quote: When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly, saying, "Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his relatives have come to Shechem, and they are stirring up the city against you. Now therefore, go by night, you and the people who are with you, and set an ambush in the field. Then in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, rise early and rush upon the city. And when he and the people who are with him come out against you, you may do to them as your hand finds to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech’s man inside the city betrays Gaal and plans a dawn ambush, supplying the plan and leaving the killing to someone else.

Zebul the ruler of the city. Zebul governs Shechem for Abimelech and keeps his position through the whole festival of insults. Gaal had named him in the speech (v. 28), so the insult was personal, and his anger is kindled. He sends a message out unseen.

Go by night. The plan is a night march and a dawn rush on the city, the kind of plan Gideon used, without anything that made Gideon’s victory God’s work.

As your hand finds to do. That is, deal with them as the occasion allows (compare 1 Samuel 10:7). Zebul supplies the plan, the timing and the excuse, and leaves the killing to someone else, much as Shechem once did (v. 24).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “secretly” (v. 31) is uncertain in Hebrew. It may instead be a place name, “at Tormah”, perhaps the Arumah of verse 41 where Abimelech was living. Either way the message leaves the city unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abimelech and all the men who were with him rose up by night and set an ambush against Shechem in four companies. And Gaal the son of Ebed went out and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city, and Abimelech and the people who were with him rose from the ambush. And when Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!" And Zebul said to him, "You mistake the shadow of the mountains for men." Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming from the direction of the Diviners' Oak." Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are not these the people whom you despised? Go out now and fight with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the ambush closes in, Zebul mocks Gaal with false reassurance until it is too late to escape, then throws his boast back at him.

In four companies. Abimelech does as Zebul proposed, dividing his men as Gideon divided his three hundred (7:16), and they lie hidden on the slopes round the city through the night. At dawn Gaal stands in the gate, where a town’s leaders sat and its business was done, as if he already ruled there.

You mistake the shadow of the mountains for men. A small scene of pure malice: Gaal sees movement on the hills and says so, and Zebul, who arranged the ambush and is standing beside him, tells him he is seeing shadows. He keeps him talking until the companies are too close to escape.

The center of the land … the Diviners’ Oak. Gaal names the landmarks one by one as the companies close in. The Diviners’ Oak was a sacred tree where soothsayers gave oracles, possibly the ancient tree near Shechem mentioned in Genesis 12:6, the oak of Moreh.

Where is your mouth now? Then Zebul drops the pretence and quotes Gaal’s festival speech back at him: “Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?” Boasting is cheap until the enemy is at the gate.

Uncertain wording. “The center of the land” is literally “the navel of the land”. It probably names the high ground beside Shechem, which sits between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal at the heart of the country, but the exact place is not known.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought with Abimelech. And Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him. And many fell wounded, up to the entrance of the gate. And Abimelech lived at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his relatives, so that they could not dwell at Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gaal is forced to make good his boast, is beaten back to the gate and driven out, and Abimelech waits outside the city he has not yet punished.

Go out now and fight with them. Gaal must fight in front of the city, on ground he has not chosen, with the men he talked into it the night before. He is beaten to the gate, many fall, and Zebul drives him out. That is the whole career of Gaal son of Ebed: he arrives, is trusted, makes a speech at a party, and is gone within two verses of the fighting starting.

Abimelech lived at Arumah. Abimelech does not ride into Shechem in triumph. He stays at Arumah, probably a few miles south-east, and leaves Zebul to expel Gaal’s clan. The revolt is crushed, but the city that hosted it has not been dealt with, and the next morning will show that he has not forgotten it (see the note on vv. 42–49).

verseByVerse.quote: On the following day, the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told. He took his people and divided them into three companies and set an ambush in the fields. And he looked and saw the people coming out of the city. So he rose against them and killed them. Abimelech and the company that was with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city, while the two companies rushed upon all who were in the field and killed them. And Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt. When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith. Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem were gathered together. And Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon, he and all the people who were with him. And Abimelech took an axe in his hand and cut down a bundle of brushwood and took it up and laid it on his shoulder. And he said to the men who were with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done." So every one of the people cut down his bundle and following Abimelech put it against the stronghold, and they set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech destroys the city that crowned him and burns a thousand people inside their own temple: the first half of Jotham’s curse, fire out of Abimelech, comes true.

He rose against them and killed them. The next morning the townspeople go out to work, and Abimelech is waiting. He takes the gate first so that nobody can get back inside, and kills the people in the open: farmers, in the fields, in the morning.

Sowed it with salt. A day of street fighting follows, the population is killed, and the town is pulled down and sown with salt. This was not meant to ruin the soil, since the amounts involved could never sterilise a field; it was a curse performed in public, declaring that nothing would grow and no one would live there again. The man is destroying the city that made him king, in the language reserved for places under a curse, three years after they crowned him at the oak.

The stronghold of the house of El-berith. The last of them shut themselves into the temple stronghold, the strongest building in the city and the house of their god, El-berith, “God of the covenant”, almost certainly the Baal-berith whose treasury paid the seventy pieces of silver (v. 4).

What you have seen me do. This sentence ought to stop any reader who has just come through chapter 7. It echoes Gideon’s words to the three hundred at the edge of the Midianite camp: “Look at me, and do likewise” (7:17). The same idea and posture, one generation later. Gideon’s men copied him and an enemy army destroyed itself in the dark. Abimelech’s men copy him and carry firewood up to a temple full of their own countrymen.

About 1,000 men and women. A thousand people burn inside the house of their god, and the first half of Jotham’s curse is complete, as he said it: “let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem” (v. 20). The bramble has burned what asked it to reign. The god they trusted could not shelter them, any more than the bramble could.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of the curse comes true, and the narrator names the hand behind it all. At Thebez Abimelech takes the city, but its people shelter in a strong tower (vv. 50–51). As he approaches the door to burn it, a woman drops an upper millstone on his head, and he has his armour-bearer kill him so that no one can say a woman did it (vv. 52–54). His army goes home (v. 55). Then the narrator speaks for the first time since verse 24: God returned Abimelech’s evil against his father, and made all the evil of Shechem return on their heads, and Jotham’s curse came upon them (vv. 56–57).
verseByVerse.theology: Abimelech dies doing the thing that killed Shechem, at a door with fire in his hand, and the second half of Jotham's curse arrives from the one direction he was not watching: from above, and from a woman he never saw.
verseByVerse.examples: Abimelech spent his dying breath on his reputation. It is worth asking what we are spending our lives to have said about us, and whether it matters more to us to be known by God (1 Cor. 8:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against Thebez and captured it. But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled to it and shut themselves in, and they went up to the roof of the tower. And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it and drew near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire. And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull. Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" And his young man thrust him through, and he died. And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, everyone departed to his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Thebez, as Abimelech comes to burn another tower, an unnamed woman drops a millstone on his head, and his last act is a vain attempt to protect his reputation.

Then Abimelech went to Thebez. Thebez is probably modern Tubas, about ten miles north-east of Shechem; most likely it had joined the revolt. It goes the same way: the city taken, the people shut in the tower, up on its roof. He has done this before, and it worked. So he walks up to the door with fire in his hand, personally, because there is no reason to think it will fail twice.

An upper millstone. The upper millstone of a hand mill was the stone a woman turned every morning to grind the day’s flour: round, heavy, yet a woman could lift it, and from the roof of a tower it is a perfectly adequate weapon. She is not named and is not a soldier. She is somebody on a roof with the household equipment, and she ends the career of the first man in Israel to call himself king.

Lest they say of me. His last recorded thought is about his reputation. He has minutes to live with a crushed skull, and what occupies him is what people will say afterwards. So he has his armour-bearer stab him to secure another version, a fair summary of the whole life: everything he did was about what would be said of him.

It did not work. The story is told here in full, millstone and all, and it was still being told generations later. When Joab briefs a messenger on how to report a death at a wall, he expects the king to ask, “Who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall?” (2 Samuel 11:21). The one thing he spent his dying breath preventing is the one detail that survived.

Everyone departed to his home. There is no succession, no mourning, no burial recorded, and no rest for the land at the end of this cycle, because this was never a deliverance. Abimelech is the one man in the book who is said to have ruled Israel and never said to have saved anybody. His army is called “the men of Israel”, and that is the sorrow of the chapter: an Israelite army, led by a son of Gideon, has spent three years burning Israelite towns, and when he falls there is nothing left to fight for.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers. And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator names what has been happening all along: God returned the evil on Abimelech and on Shechem, both of them, and Jotham’s curse came true.

Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech. After fifty-five verses of politics and ambushes without a word of comment, the narrator states the meaning in two sentences. God returned it, both halves, to both parties: to the man who killed his brothers and to the men who paid for it out of a temple. And it came about through the curse of a youngest son who shouted from a mountainside and then went to live quietly at Beer.

Against his father. The murder of the seventy is called an evil done against his father. Abimelech had traded on Gideon’s name and then destroyed Gideon’s house; the wrong was against the dead man’s family and memory as well as his sons, and God, who is “father of the fatherless” (Psalm 68:5), took it up.

Hidden providence. Nothing in the chapter looks like the hand of God while it is happening. It looks like a squalid provincial coup coming apart in the usual way: a rigged question, hired men, a conspiracy, a drunken speech, an ambush, a betrayal, a siege, a woman on a roof. The blood of seventy brothers cried out from one stone in Ophrah for three years, and it was answered by a bramble, a piece of bad advice at a city gate and a millstone. God is named in verse 23 and again in verse 56, and those two verses hold everything in between. When God seems absent and the wicked prosper, he is still at work, and evil still comes home.

Blood that speaks a better word. Abel’s blood cried from the ground in the same way (Genesis 4:10), and Scripture’s last answer to such blood is not judgment alone. The blood of Jesus “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24): mercy for the guilty, bought by the one brother who let himself be killed for the rest.

9.theology:
Those who paid are not bystanders. Verse 24 repays both the man who killed and the men who paid for the killing, and puts them in the same sentence.

The bramble. The fable's warning is that the one with nothing to give is often the one who wants to rule. It also waits for a king who reverses it. The olive would not leave its abundance to reign; the Son of God left the glory he shared with the Father, not to hold sway but to serve and to give his life (Philippians 2:6-8; Mark 10:45). Abimelech killed seventy brothers to take a throne. Jesus is not ashamed to call his people brothers, and he died to bring them to share his glory (Hebrews 2:10-11).

The argument that makes you can unmake you. Shechem crowned Abimelech because he is our brother, and Gaal turned the city against him by claiming he was not one of them after all (v. 28). Any loyalty built on being “one of us” can be undone by the same argument.

Providence that looks like nothing. Most of the chapter reads as an ordinary coup coming apart, and that is how it looked to everybody in it. The narrator frames it with two sentences about God, who sent the spirit (v. 23) and returned the evil (vv. 56-57).
9.examples:
Then: A man bought a crown with temple money at a rate of one silver piece per brother, ruled three years, burned a thousand of his own supporters inside their sanctuary, and died at a tower door because a woman dropped the top half of her kitchen mill on his head. His last request was that nobody should be able to say a woman killed him.

Now: Two things carry straight across. The first is verse 24 and the men who strengthened his hands: the people who fund, vote for, excuse or quietly enable what they would never do themselves, and who are named in the same sentence as the man who did it. Anyone who sees himself there need not wait for the millstone; the blood of Jesus speaks a better word than the blood of the seventy, and it is spoken over those who confess. The second is the fable: the person campaigning hardest for the position is very often the one with no fruit to leave behind, and the olive, the fig and the vine are usually busy.

keyVerse.quote: Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers.
keyVerse.note: After a long story in which God seems absent, this verse names him as the one who was acting all along. Evil done in the dark, and the help given to it, comes home under his hand. It prepares us for the cross, where God dealt with evil in full and opened mercy to the guilty.

9.reflection:
Shechem chose Abimelech because “he is our brother” (v. 3). Where are we tempted to judge leaders, causes or claims by whether they are “ours” rather than whether they are good and true?

In Jotham’s fable the fruitful trees would not leave their work to rule, and the bramble jumped at the chance (vv. 8–15). What does this teach about the kind of leaders we should look for, and about our own desire for position? How does Jesus reverse the fable?

The men of Shechem “strengthened his hands” (v. 24) without striking a blow. In what ways can we share in wrongs we do not commit ourselves?

God is named only at the start and end of the conflict (vv. 23, 56–57). How does this chapter help you trust God when he seems absent and wrongdoers seem to prosper?

10.title: Tola, Jair, and Renewed Apostasy
10.text: <sup>1</sup>After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.<sup>2</sup>And he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir.<sup>3</sup>After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years.<sup>4</sup>And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities, called Havvoth-jair to this day, which are in the land of Gilead.<sup>5</sup>And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.<sup>6</sup>The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him.<sup>7</sup>So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the Ammonites,<sup>8</sup>and they crushed and oppressed the people of Israel that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the people of Israel who were beyond the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead.<sup>9</sup>And the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was severely distressed.<sup>10</sup>And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to the people of Israel, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians and from the Amorites, from the Ammonites and from the Philistines?<sup>12</sup>The Sidonians also, and the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you out of their hand.<sup>13</sup>Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more.<sup>14</sup>Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."<sup>15</sup>And the people of Israel said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day."<sup>16</sup>So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and he became impatient over the misery of Israel.<sup>17</sup>Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they encamped in Gilead. And the people of Israel came together, and they encamped at Mizpah.<sup>18</sup>And the people, the leaders of Gilead, said one to another, "Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
10.overview:
Where we are. Abimelech’s bloody reign has ended under a millstone (chapter 9). Two quiet judges follow, and then the cycle turns again, lower than before, and leads into the story of Jephthah (chapters 11–12).

The message. God is not to be used, yet he cannot bear his people’s misery. When Israel collects the gods of every neighbour and then cries for help, God refuses: “I will save you no more” (v. 13), and sends them to the gods they chose. The refusal exposes whether they want God or only relief. When they confess, accept his verdict, and put away their idols with nothing promised, his compassion breaks through: “he became impatient over the misery of Israel” (v. 16).

Why it was said. Israel treated the LORD as one helper among many, to be called on in emergencies (see the introduction). This chapter shows that he will not be one god on a shelf, and that real repentance turns from idols to him without bargaining.

How the chapter makes its case. Tola and Jair judge for forty-five quiet years (vv. 1–5). Then Israel serves the gods of every surrounding nation and forsakes the LORD, and he sells them to the Philistines and the Ammonites at once; Gilead is crushed for eighteen years and the Ammonites cross into Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim (vv. 6–9). Israel confesses, and God answers with a list of past rescues and a refusal: go and cry to your gods (vv. 10–14). Israel accepts the verdict, asks anyway, and puts the gods away, and God’s soul can bear their misery no longer (vv. 15–16). The chapter ends with two armies facing each other and Gilead’s leaders advertising for anyone to lead them (vv. 17–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him and by the need exposed. The God whose patience gave way over Israel’s misery came near in his Son, who saw the crowds “harassed and helpless” and had compassion on them (Matthew 9:36). And the elders’ question, “Who is the man who will begin to fight?” (v. 18), finds no worthy answer in Judges; God’s answer is the Man who fought for his people when no one else could, and gave his life for them.

For us. We may not keep the gods of the nations, but we keep other masters, and none of them can save us in the time of distress. True repentance says “we have sinned” and means it, and puts the idols away without first demanding a promise. And it does not find God reluctant: whoever comes to Christ he will never cast out (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After Abimelech’s horrors God gives Israel forty-five years of quiet under two judges, and the book has almost nothing to say about them because nothing went wrong. Tola of Issachar arises “to save Israel”, lives at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim, judges twenty-three years, and is buried there (vv. 1–2). Jair the Gileadite judges twenty-two years; his thirty sons ride thirty donkeys and hold thirty towns in Gilead, the Havvoth-jair (vv. 3–4). He dies and is buried at Kamon (v. 5). The quiet is a mercy, though the donkeys and towns hint that the office is becoming a family business.
verseByVerse.theology: Quiet years are a gift, even when nothing in them seems worth writing down. Faithfulness that makes no headlines is still faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: Jair's thirty sons on thirty donkeys is a display of rank, since a donkey was what a man of standing rode, and it is Gideon's seventy sons in miniature. The judges have begun to look like dynasties, and Ibzan and Abdon will do the same thing again (12:9, 14).

verseByVerse.quote: After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim. And he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir. After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years. And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities, called Havvoth-jair to this day, which are in the land of Gilead. And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Abimelech, God gives Israel forty-five years of quiet under two judges, a mercy so uneventful that there is almost nothing to report.

After Abimelech there arose to save Israel. After the fire and the millstone come two verses about a man who did nothing worth reporting. Tola is given a father, a grandfather, a tribe, an address, a length of service and a grave. No oppression is named, no battle, no crisis, no failure. He arose “to save Israel”, from what we are not told, and judged for twenty-three years and was buried where he lived.

Jair the Gileadite. Jair gets one detail, and it is about status: thirty sons, thirty donkeys, thirty towns. A donkey was what a man of rank rode, and thirty sons each with his own mount and his own town is a display, a family that has arranged the map to suit itself. The office is quietly becoming a family business, and nobody says a word against it. The towns were already called Havvoth-jair, “the villages of Jair”, in Numbers 32:41, after an earlier Jair of Manasseh; this judge was perhaps his descendant, or the old name was renewed in his day.

Thirty donkeys … thirty cities. The Hebrew plays on the words: the word used here for the cities sounds just like the word for the donkeys, as if every son had a donkey and a town to match.

Forty-five quiet years. Before the criticism, notice what these five verses contain: forty-five years in which no apostasy is recorded, no raiders come, and nobody has to be rescued. Coming straight after a chapter in which a thousand people burned inside a temple, that is not a dull passage. It is a mercy, and the reason there is nothing to tell is that nothing was wrong. Faithful, unspectacular years are God’s gift.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s idolatry is now complete, and God hands them to two oppressors at once. They serve the Baals and the Ashtaroth and the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon and the Philistines, every neighbour in every direction, and they forsake the LORD altogether (v. 6). In anger God sells them to the Philistines and the Ammonites (v. 7). For eighteen years the Ammonites crush Israel east of the Jordan in Gilead (v. 8), and then they cross the river to fight Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim, and Israel is in great distress (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry is rarely content with one god. Once the LORD is no longer enough for a people, nothing else is either.
verseByVerse.examples: This is also the first oppression that comes from two directions at once. Ammon holds Gilead in the east and the Philistines press from the west, and the two threats will run on into the next six chapters: Jephthah against Ammon, Samson against the Philistines.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him. So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the Ammonites, and they crushed and oppressed the people of Israel that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the people of Israel who were beyond the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead. And the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was severely distressed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel takes up the gods of every surrounding nation and abandons the LORD entirely, and God hands them to two oppressors at once, whose grip spreads from Gilead into the heartland.

The Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon. Count the entries. First come the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the usual charge in this book; then the gods of Syria to the north, Sidon on the coast, Moab and Ammon across the Jordan, and the Philistines to the south-west. Seven in all, and between them every neighbour Israel has, in every direction. This is not a nation drifting into one local cult because the rain matters. It is a nation that has collected the full set, taking up the religion of every people on every border, and kept them all.

They forsook the LORD and did not serve him. This is the flattest sentence in the book. There is no qualification and no partial credit: not that they served him badly or now and then, but that they did not serve him.

The Philistines and the Ammonites. Seven gods bring two oppressors at once. Every earlier cycle had one main enemy: Cushan, Eglon, Jabin, Midian. Now Israel is pressed from two sides, Ammon east of the Jordan and the Philistines on the western plain. The Ammonite story follows in chapters 11–12, the Philistine one with Samson.

The Ammonites crossed the Jordan. Gilead had been taking it for eighteen years on the east bank; now the Ammonites cross the river and go for the heartland: Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim. That is a fair picture of what tolerated evil eventually does. The trouble that could be lived with while it stayed on the far side of the water does not stay there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — I Will Save You No More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel confesses its sin, and for the only time in the book God refuses to save them. Their cry this time is a real confession: they have forsaken their God and served the Baals (v. 10). God answers with a list of seven peoples from whom he has rescued them whenever they cried out (vv. 11–12). Yet they have forsaken him, so he will save them no more (v. 13). Let them cry to the gods they have chosen, and let those gods save them in their distress (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: A confession can be honest and still be only the first word. God's refusal tests whether Israel wants him, or only his help (see vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.examples: If you have ever felt that God has said no to you, notice that this chapter does not end at verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals." And the LORD said to the people of Israel, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians and from the Amorites, from the Ammonites and from the Philistines? The Sidonians also, and the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you out of their hand. Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel at last confesses, God refuses to save them, reminding them of every past rescue and sending them to the gods they have chosen: he will not be used as one helper among many.

We have sinned against you. This is the best prayer Israel has prayed in the book so far. Every earlier cycle records only that they cried out; this time the cry is a confession. They name the offence, the one offended, and what they did.

Did I not save you? By any ordinary reckoning this is what God has been waiting for. Yet his answer begins with a list, and the list is the point: Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, Sidonians, Amalekites, Maonites. Seven oppressors, seven rescues, set against the seven sets of gods in verse 6. In effect God says: here is the list of everyone you have worshipped; here is the list of everyone I have saved you from. They are the same length, and some names appear on both. Israel is serving “the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines” (v. 6), peoples God delivered them from. They have adopted the religion of their oppressors. And the words that keep returning describe what they have just done once more: “you cried out to me, and I saved you.”

I will save you no more. Nowhere else in this book is a cry for help answered with a refusal. There is no precedent for it and no softening after it, and it answers the most honest confession Israel has managed in ten chapters. The refusal tests what the confession is worth: do they want God, or only relief from Ammon?

Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen. The force of this is that it is not a threat. He is sending them elsewhere: you have served seven other sets of gods for years; take the request to them. “Let them save you in the time of your distress”, the very thing those gods are supposed to do. This is the judgment of Bochim (2:3) said outright. There God said he would no longer drive out the nations Israel had declined to remove. Here he says he will not answer prayers a people have not really addressed to him. In both cases the sentence is that they may keep what they chose, and the horror of it is that God does not have to do anything at all.

The full set, in modern form. We do not keep seven shrines, but we may keep seven gods. Max Weber observed a century ago that the old gods had risen from their graves, no longer as persons but as impersonal powers, and resumed their struggle for control of our lives. He was thinking of rival values, success, beauty, the nation, pleasure, knowledge, each demanding to be served absolutely. Most of us serve several at once and never notice, because none of them asks to be called god. Verse 14 is a fair test of them all: “let them save you in the time of your distress.” A career cannot sit with you in a cancer ward. A reputation cannot forgive you. A body you have perfected will age anyway. The gods we choose can demand; they cannot rescue (see the note on Isaiah 44:9–20).

I will carry and will save. Isaiah drew the difference in a picture: the idols have to be carried on the backs of weary animals, but the LORD says, “I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save” (Isaiah 46:4). Two verses later in this chapter he does it, for people who had nothing to offer (v. 16).

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, reads “Midianites” for “Maonites” (v. 12), which would recall Gideon’s victory. The Hebrew has Maonites, probably a people of the south.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–16 — They Put Away the Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel accepts God’s verdict, asks for mercy anyway, and acts without any promise, and God’s compassion breaks through. They say again, “We have sinned”, and submit to whatever seems good to him, asking only that he deliver them this day (v. 15). Then, for the first time in the book, they actually put away the foreign gods and serve the LORD, and he can no longer bear the misery of Israel (v. 16). Repentance with nothing promised meets a God whose heart is moved.
verseByVerse.theology: The last clause of verse 16 is hard to translate and worth the effort: literally, his soul was shortened over the misery of Israel. It is the idiom used of a man at the end of his endurance, and it is used again of Samson when nagging "shortened his soul to death" (16:16; ESV "his soul was vexed to death").
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone who fears they have used up God's patience: in this book his patience runs out only once, and when it does, it runs out in the direction of mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day." So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and he became impatient over the misery of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel accepts God’s verdict, asks for mercy anyway, and puts away its idols with nothing promised, and God, moved by their misery, cannot hold back his compassion.

Do to us whatever seems good to you. Israel does not argue. God has said he will not save them, and they do not protest, bargain, or point out how long they once served him. They agree with the sentence and ask anyway: “Only please deliver us this day.” It is a prayer with no claim in it. They have conceded that they deserve nothing and asked for everything.

They put away the foreign gods. Here is a clause that has not appeared once in ten chapters. They went home, got rid of all seven sets, and served the LORD instead. Every earlier cry in this book is only words; this time something is thrown out. And the order matters. Nothing has been promised; God has said no; they have accepted it and asked anyway; and with no assurance of any kind they clear out the shrines. That is not repentance bought by a guarantee. It is repentance performed in the dark. Nor did it earn his help: the honesty to say “we have sinned” and mean it is itself the work of God’s Spirit.

He became impatient over the misery of Israel. The last clause says that God could not stand it any longer. Not that he changed his mind about their guilt or that they had earned anything since he refused them: he looked at the misery of a people who deserved every bit of it, and his patience gave way. Everything the book has said about him since 2:18 is in that clause. He was moved by their groaning then; here, having formally declined to save them, he cannot watch.

The God who came near. The God whose soul was shortened over Israel came near in his Son, who saw the crowds “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” and had compassion on them (Matthew 9:36). At the cross he bore their misery and ours himself.

Did God go back on his word? No. The refusal was real, and it exposed whether Israel wanted God or only relief. When they put the idols away with nothing promised, they were no longer the people he had refused, and God’s warnings are spoken so that sinners will turn (Jeremiah 18:7–8). If you fear that God has said to you, “I will save you no more”, read verse 16 again: a people who came with nothing but “we have sinned” were not finally turned away, and Jesus promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

Uncertain wording. Literally God’s “soul was short” over Israel’s misery, an idiom for being unable to bear something any longer. Most take it, as here, to mean he could not bear to see them suffer. A few read it as weariness with Israel’s pleas, as if their repentance were only another attempt to use him; but 2:18, where he is “moved to pity by their groaning”, favours the first reading.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The armies gather, and Israel has no leader. The Ammonites muster and camp in Gilead, and the Israelites camp at Mizpah (v. 17). The leaders of Gilead ask one another who will begin the fight, and offer to make him head over all Gilead (v. 18). No one steps forward, and no word from God is recorded. The question hangs over the end of the chapter, and the next chapter’s answer will be a man they had driven out.
verseByVerse.theology: The leaders' question, who will lead us, is one Israel keeps asking through Judges and Samuel. The Bible's final answer is a King whom God himself provides.
verseByVerse.examples: When nobody will step forward, God is not short of servants. He often finds them where respectable people were not looking.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they encamped in Gilead. And the people of Israel came together, and they encamped at Mizpah. And the people, the leaders of Gilead, said one to another, "Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the enemy camped against them, Israel has no leader and no word from God, and Gilead’s elders can only advertise the post to anyone willing to fight.

Who is the man who will begin to fight? Two armies face each other, and Israel has no leader. The elders of Gilead stand in a camp in front of an enemy, asking each other not “what is the plan?” but “who is the man?” Nobody steps forward. They are reduced to advertising the post, and the reward offered is the highest office in the region: whoever begins the fight becomes head over all Gilead.

No commission recorded. In chapter 4 God had already commissioned Barak, and he had to be sent for. In chapter 6 God went and found a man threshing in a winepress. Here no commission is recorded at all, and a committee offers promotion to anybody who will volunteer. Gideon was offered the crown after he won; this man is offered headship before he starts, by men out of alternatives.

What comes next. The answer to their advertisement, in the next chapter, will be a man they had already thrown out of town (11:1–3). The leaders of Gilead are about to discover that the only person willing to take the job is somebody they had personally disqualified.

The Man who came. “Who is the man?” is never truly answered in Judges. Isaiah heard the LORD say, “I looked, but there was no one to help … so my own arm brought me salvation” (Isaiah 63:5). God answered it himself in Christ, who was offered no reward but came of his own will to fight for a people who had rejected him.

10.theology:
Seven and seven. The list of gods in verse 6 and the list of rescues in verses 11-12 are the same length, and the argument runs on the comparison. Israel has adopted the religion of the people God saved them from.

The refusal. Therefore I will save you no more (v. 13) is the one refusal in the book, and like the sentence at Bochim (2:3) it lets Israel keep what it chose.

Repentance performed in the dark. Every earlier cycle records a cry; this one records a clear-out (v. 16), after God has said no and nothing has been promised.

His soul was shortened. Israel had earned nothing since the refusal, yet God's patience gave way in the direction of mercy, as 2:18 said of him and as the cross would show again.
10.examples:
Then: A nation that had collected the gods of all seven of its neighbours finally said so out loud, was told to go and ask them for help, agreed that it deserved the answer, asked anyway, and then went home and threw the idols out before anyone had promised it a thing.

Now: Verse 16 is the model and verse 15 is the hard part. They made no claim, do to us whatever seems good to you, and cleared the house without any assurance that it would make a difference. Most repentance waits until something has been promised. Their clear-out was not a way of earning his help: it came after a lifetime of rescues they had done nothing to deserve, and the honesty to say we have sinned and mean it is itself the Spirit's work. And verse 14 is the warning underneath it all: the worst thing God can say to a person is not “no”. It is "go and ask the thing you have actually been serving, and see what it can do for you". If that sentence frightens you, read verse 16 again: a people who came with nothing but we have sinned were not finally turned away, and Jesus has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

keyVerse.quote: So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and he became impatient over the misery of Israel.
keyVerse.note: For the first time in Judges, Israel does more than cry out: it puts away its idols, with no promise that God will help. And the verse ends not with Israel’s merit but with God’s heart, unable to bear his people’s misery. It shows what true repentance looks like and the compassion that meets it, seen fully in Christ.

10.reflection:
Tola and Jair gave Israel forty-five quiet years (vv. 1–5). How should we value the ordinary, unspectacular seasons of faithfulness in our lives and churches?

Israel served the gods of every neighbour (v. 6). What rival “gods” compete for our trust today, and what would it mean to hear God say, “let them save you in the time of your distress” (v. 14)?

Israel confessed, accepted God’s verdict and put away their idols before any promise was given (vv. 15–16). How does this differ from repentance that is really a bargain? What might you need to put away?

“He became impatient over the misery of Israel” (v. 16). How does this picture of God’s heart, seen fully in Jesus, encourage you to come back to him when you have failed?

11.title: Jephthah
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead was the father of Jephthah.<sup>2</sup>And Gilead's wife also bore him sons. And when his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You shall not have an inheritance in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman."<sup>3</sup>Then Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob, and worthless fellows collected around Jephthah and went out with him.<sup>4</sup>After a time the Ammonites made war against Israel.<sup>5</sup>And when the Ammonites made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob.<sup>6</sup>And they said to Jephthah, "Come and be our leader, that we may fight against the Ammonites."<sup>7</sup>But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?"<sup>8</sup>And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have turned to you now, that you may go with us and fight against the Ammonites and be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."<sup>9</sup>Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me home again to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them over to me, I will be your head."<sup>10</sup>And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD will be witness between us, if we do not do as you say."<sup>11</sup>So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and leader over them. And Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.<sup>12</sup>Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said, "What do you have against me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?"<sup>13</sup>And the king of the Ammonites answered the messengers of Jephthah, "Because Israel on coming up from Egypt took away my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan; now therefore restore it peaceably."<sup>14</sup>Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites<sup>15</sup>and said to him, "Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites,<sup>16</sup>but when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.<sup>17</sup>Israel then sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let us pass through your land,' but the king of Edom would not listen. And they sent also to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel remained at Kadesh.<sup>18</sup>"Then they journeyed through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab and arrived on the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the boundary of Moab.<sup>19</sup>Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our country,'<sup>20</sup>but Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory, so Sihon gathered all his people together and encamped at Jahaz and fought with Israel.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites, who inhabited that country.<sup>22</sup>And they took possession of all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.<sup>23</sup>So then the LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel; and are you to take possession of them?<sup>24</sup>Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? And all that the LORD our God has dispossessed before us, we will possess.<sup>25</sup>Now are you any better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend against Israel, or did he ever go to war with them?<sup>26</sup>While Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, and in Aroer and its villages, and in all the cities that are on the banks of the Arnon, 300 years, why did you not deliver them within that time?<sup>27</sup>I therefore have not sinned against you, and you do me wrong by making war on me. The LORD, the Judge, decide this day between the people of Israel and the people of Ammon."<sup>28</sup>But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words of Jephthah that he sent to him.<sup>29</sup>Then the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh and passed on to Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed on to the Ammonites.<sup>30</sup>And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will give the Ammonites into my hand,<sup>31</sup>then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering."<sup>32</sup>So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD gave them into his hand.<sup>33</sup>And he struck them from Aroer to the neighborhood of Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a great blow. So the Ammonites were subdued before the people of Israel.<sup>34</sup>Then Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah. And behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances. She was his only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter.<sup>35</sup>And as soon as he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you have become the cause of great trouble to me. For I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow."<sup>36</sup>And she said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD; do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, now that the LORD has avenged you on your enemies, on the Ammonites."<sup>37</sup>So she said to her father, "Let this thing be done for me: leave me alone two months, that I may go up and down on the mountains and weep for my virginity, I and my companions."<sup>38</sup>So he said, "Go." Then he sent her away for two months, and she departed, she and her companions, and wept for her virginity on the mountains.<sup>39</sup>And at the end of two months, she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow that he had made. She had never known a man, and it became a custom in Israel<sup>40</sup>that the daughters of Israel went year by year to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year.
11.overview:
Where we are. Israel has served the gods of every neighbour, and the LORD has sold them to the Philistines and the Ammonites (10:6–7). He “became impatient over the misery of Israel” (10:16), and Gilead’s leaders, with Ammon camped against them, promised to make head whoever would begin the fight (10:18).

The message. God saves his people by grace, through a deliverer they had thrown out, and his help is never for sale. Jephthah, the rejected son, hands Israel’s case to “the LORD, the Judge”, and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him; yet in the next breath he tries to buy the victory with a vow, and it costs him his only child. The chapter shows how far a sincere man can go wrong when he does not know what God is like or what his word says.

Why it was said. Israel had absorbed the religion of the nations around it (see the introduction), in which gods had to be paid for their favours and children could be the price. This chapter shows that religion surviving even in a man the Spirit used, and the grief it brings.

How the chapter makes its case. Jephthah, son of a prostitute, is driven out by his brothers (vv. 1–3), then hired by the same elders in their distress, on oath before the LORD (vv. 4–11). Before he fights, he answers Ammon’s claim with history: Israel took the land from Sihon, who attacked them, and has held it three hundred years; let the LORD, the Judge, decide (vv. 12–28). God’s Spirit comes upon him, at once he vows to offer whatever comes out of his house, and the LORD gives the victory (vv. 29–33). Then his only daughter comes out dancing, and he does with her according to his vow (vv. 34–40).

Where it leads. To Christ by contrast and by the need it exposes. Jephthah tries to pay God for a victory, and an only child dies for nothing. On Moriah God stopped Abraham’s hand and provided a ram (Genesis 22:13–14); at the cross he gave his own only Son, and that death paid for everything. And the outcast whom his brothers welcomed back only when they needed him points, faintly, to the one who “was despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3) and who saves those who rejected him, not for a price but freely.

For us. We cannot buy what God gives, and trying to pay him back on our own terms can do real damage at home. Know his word, so that sincerity does not lead us astray. And if you have only ever been valued for what you could deliver, God loved you in Christ while you had nothing to give.
11.theology:
Grace that cannot be bought. The Spirit came first, and the victory in v. 32 answers the Spirit in v. 29, not the bargain in v. 30 (see vv. 29-31). Trading a life for a battle is how the neighbouring nations prayed, and of such offerings God says they never came into his mind (Jer. 7:31).

Knowing God's word. Jephthah knows Israel's history well enough to lecture a king from it, yet he does not know what his own God's law says about vows. The law offered a way to redeem a person vowed to the LORD, and it forbade burning children outright, so I cannot take back my vow was sincere and it was wrong (see vv. 39-40).

Did he kill her? The old reading that he dedicated her to lifelong virginity rests on a possible or in v. 31 and the triple stress on her virginity. It is not foolish, but it is the weaker case: olah, the Hebrew for “burnt offering”, never means anything but a sacrifice wholly burned, v. 35 makes no sense if the outcome is religious service, Israel had no order of celibate women, and the daughters go out to lament her. Either way the vow was faithless, unnecessary and pagan in shape when he made it.

Hebrews 11:32. Jephthah is named for faith alongside Gideon, Barak and Samson. Hebrews commends what these men did by faith (Heb. 11:33-34), not everything they did.
11.examples:
Then: A man his family had written off argued Israel's case better than any leader in the book, referred the verdict to God, went out with the Spirit of the LORD upon him, and then offered to pay for a victory he had already been given.

Now: Look at the promises you have made to God in a crisis. If a vow was made to secure something, ask whether God had not already promised it, and whether what you call devotion is really a payment plan for grace. Nothing is owed for what Christ has already bought; what is left is thanks, which the Spirit works in us freely. Notice too what destroyed Jephthah's house: not unbelief, but sincerity without knowledge of God’s law. God has given his word so that his people need not grope in the dark, and his Spirit opens it to those who ask. And if you have already spoken a rash word or made a vow God never asked for, the way back is not to pay it at any cost but to bring it to him, confess it, and be released by the one whose vow was kept perfectly for us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Son of a Prostitute
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man God will use to deliver Gilead begins as its outcast. Jephthah is a mighty warrior, but his mother was a prostitute, and when his father’s other sons grow up they drive him out with a legal ruling: no inheritance in our father’s house (vv. 1–2). He goes beyond Israel’s border to the land of Tob, and worthless men gather round him and go out raiding with him (v. 3). On paper he looks much like Abimelech in chapter 9: a son by another woman, at odds with his brothers, leading empty men. What will set him apart is not his background but the Spirit of the LORD (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: God's choice of deliverers keeps passing over the respectable: left-handed Ehud, Deborah judging under a palm tree, Gideon the least man of the weakest clan, and now a prostitute's son.
verseByVerse.examples: The book is about to make a great deal turn on a man his own family had written off. Scripture repeats that shape, from Joseph to David, and it reaches its height in the stone the builders rejected that became the cornerstone, words Jesus took for himself (Ps. 118:22; Matt. 21:42). Jephthah is a dim and flawed instance of it, but it is the same God at work.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead was the father of Jephthah. And Gilead's wife also bore him sons. And when his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You shall not have an inheritance in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman." Then Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob, and worthless fellows collected around Jephthah and went out with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The deliverer God will use begins as an outcast, thrown out of his father’s house because of his mother and leading a band of drifters beyond Israel’s border.

A mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Two facts in one sentence, and the second had already decided his life. Jephthah is a mighty warrior, the phrase the angel used of Gideon in the winepress (6:12), and in his case plainly true. But his mother was a prostitute, which in that society settled where he could live, what he could inherit and who would speak to him.

You shall not have an inheritance. What his brothers say is a ruling on the estate, not merely an insult (see inheritance). He is evicted from his father’s house for something that happened before he was born, by the respectable half of the family, protecting an inheritance they had done nothing to earn.

Worthless fellows. Tob lay outside Israel, up towards Syria, and the men who gather round him there are worthless fellows, literally empty men, the same word used of the crew Abimelech hired with temple silver (9:4). On paper, the man Gilead is about to make its head looks very like Abimelech: a son by another woman, at odds with his brothers, leading a band of worthless men. The difference will not be their backgrounds. It will be that in verse 29 the Spirit of the LORD comes on this one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — Hiring the Man They Threw Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The community that threw Jephthah out now needs him, and he makes them admit it before he agrees. When Ammon attacks, Gilead’s elders go to Tob and ask him to be their commander (vv. 4–6). He asks why the men who hated him have come now, in their distress, and they answer by raising the offer: head over all Gilead (vv. 7–8). He accepts on condition that the LORD gives the victory, the elders swear with the LORD as witness, and Jephthah repeats the agreement before the LORD at Mizpah (vv. 9–11). He is the first in the scene to speak of God, but the bargain is struck before God is asked.
verseByVerse.theology: This is a negotiation, not a call. Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon: God raised them up or spoke to them. Here a committee that has run out of options hires a man on terms, and the terms are settled before the fighting starts.
verseByVerse.examples: There is something here for anyone who has been valued only for what they could do. Jephthah's bitterness is understandable, and he is right about the elders. But God does not love his people for their usefulness: the son who came home hoping to be taken on as a hired servant was given a robe and a ring instead (Luke 15:19-22).

verseByVerse.quote: After a time the Ammonites made war against Israel. And when the Ammonites made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob. And they said to Jephthah, "Come and be our leader, that we may fight against the Ammonites." But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?" And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have turned to you now, that you may go with us and fight against the Ammonites and be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In their distress the men who drove Jephthah out come to hire him, and he makes them admit what they did: they need him, but they have never valued him.

The elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah. At the end of chapter 10 the leaders of Gilead promised to make head whoever would begin the fight against Ammon (10:18). No respectable candidate has come forward, and the man they come for is the one their own community legally expelled.

Did you not hate me? He does not make it easy for them, and he is not wrong. A formal disinheritance is a public act, and the elders signed off on it. Why have you come to me now when you are in distress: we both know you would not be in Tob if Ammon were quiet. There is bitterness in it, and complete accuracy. He is being valued for his usefulness by people who never valued him for anything else.

That is why we have turned to you now. They concede the whole charge. They neither deny driving him out nor apologise; they say, in effect, yes, and that is exactly why we are here. And they raise the offer: verse 6 asked for a battlefield leader; verse 8 offers head over all the inhabitants of Gilead, the permanent office they had advertised. The price has gone up in two verses because they can see he might say no.

Valued for what you can deliver. Jephthah’s story is uncomfortably familiar. Many people are welcome exactly as long as they are useful: the employee kept while the numbers are good, the friend rung when there is a favour to ask, the child praised for grades and quietness. Immanuel Kant argued that a person must never be treated merely as a means, and most of us know the particular hurt of being treated that way. The deeper damage is what it teaches us to expect. A man who has only ever been valued for what he could deliver will assume that God works the same way, and that is exactly what Jephthah does at Mizpah: he bargains (v. 30).

Loved with nothing to deliver. God’s choosing runs the other way. He set his love on Israel not because they were many (Deuteronomy 7:7), and in Christ he loved us when we had nothing to deliver at all: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). People loved like that can stop auditioning, for God or for anyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me home again to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them over to me, I will be your head." And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD will be witness between us, if we do not do as you say." So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and leader over them. And Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jephthah accepts and credits any victory to the LORD, yet he fixes his terms in advance and only then brings the bargain before God.

And the LORD gives them over to me. He has the terms sworn in advance, but the middle clause is the best thing in the sentence. Jephthah is not promising to win; if there is a victory it will be God’s doing. The outcast raider is the first in this scene to mention the LORD; the elders had not. Yet he is still bargaining, for the headship, in advance, on terms.

Before the LORD at Mizpah. Then he repeats the whole agreement aloud before the LORD at Mizpah. This is a man who believes that words spoken to God are binding. Hold that thought. When he says in his doorway, “I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow” (v. 35), it will not be a sudden scruple but the same conviction, right in itself, running all the way through the chapter.
