Notice the order. The arrangement is brought before the LORD only after it has been agreed. God will honour Jephthah’s leadership anyway (v. 29), but nobody in the chapter asked him first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–28 — A History Lesson to a King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before he fights, the raider argues his case and hands the verdict to God. Jephthah asks Ammon’s king what his grievance is, and the king claims the land between the Arnon and the Jabbok, taken by Israel on its way up from Egypt (vv. 12–13). Jephthah answers from history: Israel asked Edom and Moab for passage and took no for an answer, and it took this land from Sihon the Amorite, who attacked them (vv. 14–22). The LORD gave it, just as Ammon keeps what its own god gives (vv. 23–24). Balak never disputed it, and in three hundred years no one tried to recover it (vv. 25–26). So let the LORD, the Judge, decide; but the king will not listen (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: It is the longest speech by any judge in the book, and its instinct is right: settle the facts, establish the claim, and put the verdict in God's hands rather than seize it.
verseByVerse.examples: Sixteen verses of careful history, three arguments and a formal appeal to God changed nothing (v. 28). Jephthah did everything right here, and the war happened anyway. A good case, well made, does not always end a quarrel; sometimes it only shows who was in the right when the quarrel turned violent. That is worth remembering when patient, honest reasoning seems to have been wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said, "What do you have against me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?" And the king of the Ammonites answered the messengers of Jephthah, "Because Israel on coming up from Egypt took away my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan; now therefore restore it peaceably." Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said to him, "Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jephthah’s first act as head of Gilead is not to attack but to ask Ammon’s king what his grievance is, and to answer it with argument.

What do you have against me? Everything in the raider’s background predicts a fight; instead he sends messengers to ask what the actual grievance is. Deuteronomy 20:10 requires exactly this, offering terms of peace before a siege, and whether Jephthah knows the statute or is simply being sensible, he does what the law asks and what no one else in this half of the book bothers with.

Took away my land. The answer is a territorial claim with a date on it, and it deserves to be heard properly. The king is not saying that Israel is offensive or that the borders are inconvenient. He is saying: that land was ours, you took it on the way up from Egypt, give it back. It is the kind of claim made in every century, and he evidently believes it.

Thus says Jephthah. The reply is not a threat but an argument. Thus says Jephthah borrows the formula a prophet uses, and there is some swagger in a border chieftain adopting it, but what follows is a serious piece of work.

verseByVerse.quote: but when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh. Israel then sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let us pass through your land,' but the king of Edom would not listen. And they sent also to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel remained at Kadesh. "Then they journeyed through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab and arrived on the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the boundary of Moab. Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our country,' but Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory, so Sihon gathered all his people together and encamped at Jahaz and fought with Israel. And the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites, who inhabited that country. And they took possession of all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel did not take the disputed land from Ammon at all: it asked permission at every border and took this land from Sihon the Amorite, who attacked them.

So Israel remained at Kadesh. The defence opens with what Israel asked for and did not get. Twice Israel requested passage, from Edom and from Moab; twice it was refused, and twice Israel accepted the refusal. A nation that took land by force whenever it was told no would not have waited. They went the long way round rather than cross a border they had no right to cross, and camped beyond the Arnon, the river that marked Moab’s boundary. Jephthah argues from named places and exact borders.

Sihon king of the Amorites. A third request went to Sihon, and this time the refusal came with an army: Sihon mobilised and marched out to Jahaz to attack. Everything turns on that, and the answer to Ammon’s claim is one word: Amorites.

From the Arnon to the Jabbok. Compare the two descriptions. Ammon claimed the land “from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan” (v. 13). Jephthah says Israel took from the Amorites the territory “from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan” (v. 22). The boundaries match, but the previous owner is different. The land was not Ammonite when Israel arrived. It was Sihon’s, and Sihon had taken it from Moab not long before (Numbers 21:26). Israel took it from the man who attacked them, in a war they did not start, having asked first. Ammon is claiming compensation for a loss somebody else suffered.

verseByVerse.quote: So then the LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel; and are you to take possession of them? Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? And all that the LORD our God has dispossessed before us, we will possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What settles the question is that the LORD gave Israel the land; Jephthah presses the point in the Ammonite king’s own terms, though he blurs whose god is whose.

The LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed the Amorites. So far the argument has been legal and historical, the kind that would stand in a human court. Now Jephthah says what actually settles it: the Amorites were not evicted by Israelite arms. The LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed them, and what God has granted, a king of Ammon cannot reassign.

What Chemosh your god gives you. This verse has long troubled readers, because it sounds as though Jephthah thinks Chemosh is real. Take the difficulty at full strength: your god gives you land, our God gives us land, and each nation keeps what its own deity provides. That is the belief that each people has its own god, and it falls short of what Israel was taught: “the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other” (Deuteronomy 4:39).

Diplomacy. Two things can be said. The first is that this is diplomacy. Jephthah writes to a foreign king in that king’s own terms, arguing from a premise his correspondent already holds: by your principles, you keep what Chemosh gives; by the same principle, leave alone what the LORD has given. It is a form of argument, not necessarily the writer’s creed.

A more uncomfortable possibility. The second is more uncomfortable and may also be true. Chemosh was the god of Moab; Ammon’s god was Milcom. Perhaps the king of Ammon was claiming old Moabite land as overlord of both peoples, so that Jephthah answers him in Moab’s terms, and Moab runs through the whole letter (vv. 15, 17–18, 25). But if Jephthah has simply run the two peoples together, his theology is roughly right and careless in its details. A man who can lecture a king from Israel’s history, yet blur which god he is talking about, is just the kind of man who will make the vow that follows.
verseByVerse.note: Ammon's god appears in Kings both as Milcom and as Molech (1 Kings 11:5, 7), the god to whom the law forbids Israel to give its children (Lev. 18:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Now are you any better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend against Israel, or did he ever go to war with them? While Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, and in Aroer and its villages, and in all the cities that are on the banks of the Arnon, 300 years, why did you not deliver them within that time? I therefore have not sinned against you, and you do me wrong by making war on me. The LORD, the Judge, decide this day between the people of Israel and the people of Ammon." But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words of Jephthah that he sent to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jephthah closes with precedent and three centuries of undisputed possession, then refuses to judge his own case and hands it to the LORD, the Judge.

Balak the son of Zippor. A last argument from precedent, and a good one. Balak, king of Moab, had every reason to fight for that land and never did. He was frightened enough of Israel to hire Balaam to curse them from a hilltop (Numbers 22), which tells you what he thought of his chances in the field, yet he never disputed the title. If the rightful owner did not press the claim, why is Ammon pressing it now?

300 years. Then comes the length of settled possession: three hundred years without one attempt to recover the land. Any lawyer would reach for this: if it was yours, you have had three centuries to say so. Jephthah even names the towns, Heshbon, Aroer and the cities along the Arnon, so the king can check the roll himself.

The LORD, the Judge, decide this day. He ends by refusing to judge his own case. He has made his argument, but he does not declare himself the winner; he hands the file upward. In a book where every strong man has so far settled his quarrels with his own hands, a leader who submits a dispute to God for a verdict is doing something the others never thought of.

Entrusting the case to God. The same instinct, perfected, is seen in Jesus: “when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). Make your case honestly when you are wronged, and then leave the verdict with God.

Where Christians differ: what do the three hundred years say about the date of the exodus? Taken exactly, the figure fits the earlier date (about 1446 BC) and the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1, once we allow that some judges ruled at the same time in different regions, and it puts Jephthah around 1100 BC. Christians who date the exodus later, in the thirteenth century BC, take three hundred as a round number or a diplomat’s generous claim. This commentary’s view: faithful scholars differ here, and the date is left open (see the introduction); Jephthah’s argument stands either way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–33 — The Spirit, and Then the Vow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah, and in the very next verse he makes his vow; those two verses side by side are the heart of the chapter. God has already equipped him and sent him through Gilead and Manasseh against Ammon (v. 29). But Jephthah tries to secure the victory by promising that whatever comes out of his house to meet him when he returns in peace will be the LORD’s, offered as a burnt offering (vv. 30–31). The LORD gives Ammon into his hand, twenty cities, and the oppression is broken (vv. 32–33). The victory answers the Spirit, not the bargain.
verseByVerse.theology: Vows as such were lawful in Israel, and many were freely and rightly made (Num. 30; Ps. 116:14). What is wrong here is not that Jephthah vowed, but what he vowed and why.
verseByVerse.examples: The shape of the bargain is not Israelite. Offering a life in exchange for a victory is what the neighbours did: the king of Moab offers his eldest son on his own city wall when a battle turns against him (2 Kings 3:27).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh and passed on to Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed on to the Ammonites. And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will give the Ammonites into my hand, then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah, and at once he tries to buy with a vow the victory God is already giving him, promising as a burnt offering whatever comes out of his house to meet him.

The Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah. Read verse 29, then verse 30, and let nothing soften what stands between them. The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah, the same words the book used of Othniel (3:10): God taking hold of a man and equipping him for the work. Whatever the elders negotiated, God has now put his own hand on the appointment.

If you will give the Ammonites into my hand. Then, with the Spirit of God already upon him, he tries to buy what he has just been given. Verse 29 is grace: unasked, unpriced, already granted. Verse 30 is a bargain for the same thing. A man who has survived by fixing the terms of every deal beforehand has brought that habit into the presence of God, and God does not do business on those terms.

Whatever comes out from the doors of my house. Consider what he offers. What comes out of a man’s house to meet him when he comes home in triumph is, most naturally, his household: women came out to meet returning victors (1 Samuel 18:6), and “to meet” is the language of people coming out to greet someone. People have tried hard to make this a promise about a goat, but the words do not fit that well (see the note below).

Never in God’s mind. Of offerings like this, Israel’s God says that he did not command them, “nor did it come into my mind” (Jeremiah 7:31). Jephthah has learned the history, but he prays like a man who picked up his religion in Tob, outside Israel.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew is literally “the one coming out”, which can refer to a person or an animal; some translations have “whoever”. Many Israelite houses of the period seem to have kept animals in ground-floor rooms, so some think he had an animal in mind. But “to meet me” suits a person, and one animal would be a strange price for a whole war. Most likely he expected a person, or at least knowingly accepted that it might be one.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV note gives “whoever” as a possible rendering of “whatever comes out” in v. 31.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD gave them into his hand. And he struck them from Aroer to the neighborhood of Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a great blow. So the Ammonites were subdued before the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD gave Ammon into Jephthah’s hand, and the victory answers the Spirit God had given, not the bargain Jephthah offered.

The LORD gave them into his hand. Twenty cities fell, and the oppression of chapter 10 was broken. The narrator never says what God thought of the vow, and that silence is the hardest thing in the chapter. But the order of the verses points one way: the victory in verse 32 answers the Spirit in verse 29, not the bargain in verse 30. It was not a payment God had agreed to.

Paying for grace. Jephthah does not see that, and he rides home from the greatest day of his life convinced that he owes for it. The mistake is not confined to his day. A man can receive something entirely by grace and spend the rest of his life paying for it. He will call that gratitude, and it will look like devotion, and it will do damage in his house, because underneath it is the settled belief that God gave on terms, and the terms are now due.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The victory march ends at Jephthah’s own door, in the darkest scene in the book so far, told with great restraint. His only child comes out to meet him with tambourines and dancing, and he tears his clothes, blames her, and says he cannot take back his vow (vv. 34–35). She tells him to keep his word to the LORD and asks only for two months on the mountains with her friends, to weep for the marriage and children she will never have (vv. 36–38). Then he does with her according to his vow, and the daughters of Israel lament her four days every year (vv. 39–40).
verseByVerse.theology: There is no word from God in these verses, neither rebuke nor approval. The reader is left to weigh the father's words against the daughter's, and to see what the text grieves over.
verseByVerse.examples: Read these verses with the daughter as well as the father. If you are reading them alongside someone who has been hurt by another person's religion, the comment at vv. 39-40 speaks to them directly.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah. And behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances. She was his only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter. And as soon as he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you have become the cause of great trouble to me. For I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first out of the door is his only child, dancing to welcome him, and Jephthah grieves, yet blames her, and believes he cannot take back his word.

His daughter came out to meet him. The behold makes us stand in the road with him. What comes out of the house is exactly what should come out of a house on such a day: a girl with a tambourine, doing what Miriam did at the sea (Exodus 15:20) and what the women would later do for Saul and David (1 Samuel 18:6). Israel’s victories were met with dancing daughters. She has no idea. She is first out of the door because she is the gladdest person in Gilead.

She was his only child. The narrator stops the story to tell us, and says it twice over: he had no other son or daughter. Jephthah was thrown out of his father’s house with the words “You shall not have an inheritance” (v. 2). He has fought his way to the headship of all Gilead, and this girl is everything he has to leave it to.

You have brought me very low. The grief is real, and the sentence is monstrous. Look at the pronouns. You have brought me very low. You have become the cause of great trouble to me. She has done nothing but come home to meet her father, and in his first words she is the one who has done it, he is the one who suffers, and the trouble is his, not hers. Not once does he say, What have I done?

I cannot take back my vow. Here is the terrible part, because he is half right. Vows to God are not disposable: “It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay” (Ecclesiastes 5:5). Jephthah’s reverence is real, and that is why it kills. What he is wrong about is I cannot (see vv. 39–40).

verseByVerse.quote: And she said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD; do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, now that the LORD has avenged you on your enemies, on the Ammonites." So she said to her father, "Let this thing be done for me: leave me alone two months, that I may go up and down on the mountains and weep for my virginity, I and my companions." So he said, "Go." Then he sent her away for two months, and she departed, she and her companions, and wept for her virginity on the mountains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His daughter, with the least to gain, speaks better than anyone in the chapter: she tells her father to keep his word to the LORD and asks only for time to mourn the family she will never have.

My father. She does not argue or run, and she does not point out that the vow was his, not hers. She takes her father’s premise more seriously than he does, that a word given to God must be kept, and she gives God’s victory over Ammon as the reason. The LORD has done his part, she says; do yours.

Nobody taught her badly. That is the awful thing. She has been raised to believe that God is to be taken at his word and honoured at cost, and she is about to be destroyed by a man who believes the same and does not know God’s law.

Weep for my virginity. She asks for two months, not for a reprieve. Notice exactly what she grieves: not, in the first place, her life, but her virginity, that she will never marry, never bear a child, never carry her father’s name into another generation. In that world a woman’s future was her children, and the loss is total: the family ends, and she ends with it. She spends those two months on the hills with her friends, weeping, and then she walks back down. In all of this her father says only one word to her: Go.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of two months, she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow that he had made. She had never known a man, and it became a custom in Israel that the daughters of Israel went year by year to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jephthah did with his daughter as he had vowed, most likely offering her as a burnt offering: a sacrifice God never asked for and his law forbade, and Israel’s daughters mourned her every year.

According to his vow. The narrator will not describe it. One clause for the thing itself, and then a sentence about her, not him: she had never known a man. The writer who gave us the tent peg through Sisera’s temple and the fat closing over Ehud’s blade turns his face away here.

The book gives her no name. Her father has a name, a family line, a tribe, a hometown, an office and a long speech. She has four days a year and a description: the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite. The girls of Israel kept her memory when the record did not.

There was a way out. Leviticus 27:1–8 lets a person vowed to the LORD be redeemed for a fixed sum of silver paid to the sanctuary. That law may not have been written with a burnt-offering vow in mind, but another settles the matter: the LORD had forbidden his people to burn their sons and daughters (Deuteronomy 12:31; 18:10), and a vow to do what God forbids binds no one, as the Westminster Confession, a classic Reformed statement of faith, also says (22.7). This is not a loophole; it is God’s law making room for exactly the situation Jephthah was standing in. He could quote three hundred years of history to a foreign king, and he did not know what his own God’s book said about vows. That is what ignorance of Scripture costs when a sincere man is the one who is ignorant.

Moriah. Set this chapter beside the one other place in Scripture where a father takes his only child up a mountain for a burnt offering. On Moriah God commanded it, then stopped it with a shout, and provided a ram caught in a thicket, and Abraham named the place “The LORD will provide” (Genesis 22:12–14). At Mizpah God commanded nothing, no voice came from heaven, and no substitute was found, because nobody had asked God for any of this. It was a man’s own idea from beginning to end, and man’s own religion has never yet produced a ram.

He was the substitute. So God, in the end, brought his own only Son up a hill and did not stop it. There was no substitute that day either, for the opposite reason: he was the substitute. Jephthah’s daughter died for nothing, because of a word her father should never have spoken and could have redeemed for a few shekels. The Son of God’s death won everything for his people, because of a word the Father had spoken before the world began. No unnamed girl need ever again walk down off a mountain to pay for a victory. It has been paid for.

For those harmed by a parent’s religion. If you were harmed by a parent’s religion, by vows, rules or fears laid on you that God never asked for, see whose side the text takes. It offers no word in the father’s defence; it grieves with the daughter, and it set the whole nation grieving with her every year. God does not want children offered up to anyone’s piety. If such harm is still going on, seek safety and tell someone you trust, such as a pastor or a biblical counsellor.

Doesn’t this prove that religion is dangerous? Christopher Hitchens subtitled one of his books How Religion Poisons Everything, and a reader of this chapter can feel the force of it. Here are sincerity, reverence and a vow kept at terrible cost, and the result is a dead girl. The Bible does not dodge the charge. It makes it first: the narrator plainly grieves with the daughter, and the prophets condemn this kind of piety in God’s own name. But notice what actually killed her. Not too much of the God of Israel, but a god imagined on the pattern of the nations around, one who must be paid for his favours. Irreligion has its own altars of that kind: the twentieth century sacrificed millions to secular visions of race and class, and quieter cultures offer their children to parental ambition. The deepest problem is not whether we believe but what we believe God is like. The cure for poisonous religion is not no God, but the true one, who gives before he asks.

Why is Jephthah in Hebrews 11? He is named among those commended for faith (Hebrews 11:32), with Gideon, Barak and Samson. Hebrews is not approving everything in those lives; it names men who, at particular moments, believed God and acted on it, and who “conquered kingdoms … were made strong out of weakness … put foreign armies to flight” (Hebrews 11:33–34). Jephthah went out against Ammon trusting the LORD, the Judge, to decide the case, and God honoured that. Hebrews commends a man for the faith he had. It has never said that everything the man did was faith.

Where Christians differ: did Jephthah kill her? A long-standing view holds that he did not, but dedicated her to lifelong service at the sanctuary, so that what she and Israel mourned was her perpetual virginity. Two things are urged for it: the Hebrew word translated “and” in verse 31 can sometimes mean “or” (whatever comes out shall be the LORD’s, or I will offer it up), and the passage stresses her virginity three times in four verses, an odd thing to stress if the point were her death. It is not a foolish reading, and serious interpreters have held it. This commentary’s view: it is the less likely reading, and honesty requires saying so. A burnt offering (Hebrew olah) is something killed and wholly burned on an altar; the word never means dedicated service anywhere in the Old Testament. A man does not tear his clothes and cry that he has been brought very low because his daughter is going to serve at the tabernacle; there was no order of celibate women in Israel for her to join; and the daughters of Israel do not visit her, they go out to lament her. The plain reading, that he offered her up, is almost certainly right. Either way, the vow was faithless, unnecessary and pagan in shape, for the victory had already been given.
verseByVerse.note: Leviticus 27:4-5 sets the redemption price at thirty shekels for a woman aged twenty to sixty and ten shekels for a girl aged five to twenty.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD, the Judge, decide this day between the people of Israel and the people of Ammon.
keyVerse.note: Here, at his best, Jephthah refuses to judge his own case and hands it to God, and the title he uses names the real hero of the whole book. The tragedy of the chapter is that the same man then tries to pay the Judge for a verdict he was already giving freely. The Judge of all the earth would one day give his verdict for his people at the cross, at his own cost, not theirs.

11.reflection:
Gilead’s elders wanted Jephthah only when they needed him (vv. 7–8), and he learned to bargain for everything, even with God (v. 30). Where have you been valued only for what you could deliver, and how has that shaped the way you approach God?

Verse 29 is grace and verse 30 is a bargain. In what ways are Christians tempted to try to pay God back for what he has freely given, and what damage can that do to us and to those around us?

Jephthah knew Israel’s history well enough to argue with a king, yet did not know what God’s law said about vows like his (Leviticus 27; Deuteronomy 12:31). Why does sincerity need to be joined to knowledge of Scripture? What practical step would help you know God’s word better?

Compare Jephthah’s daughter with Isaac on Moriah (Genesis 22) and with Jesus on the cross. What do the three scenes together teach about what God is like and what he asks of us?

12.title: Jephthah's Conflict and the Minor Judges
12.text: <sup>1</sup>The men of Ephraim were called to arms, and they crossed to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us to go with you? We will burn your house over you with fire."<sup>2</sup>And Jephthah said to them, "I and my people had a great dispute with the Ammonites, and when I called you, you did not save me from their hand.<sup>3</sup>And when I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hand and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into my hand. Why then have you come up to me this day to fight against me?"<sup>4</sup>Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought with Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because they said, "You are fugitives of Ephraim, you Gileadites, in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh."<sup>5</sup>And the Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. And when any of the fugitives of Ephraim said, "Let me go over," the men of Gilead said to him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" When he said, "No,"<sup>6</sup>they said to him, "Then say Shibboleth," and he said, "Sibboleth," for he could not pronounce it right. Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time 42,000 of the Ephraimites fell.<sup>7</sup>Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city in Gilead.<sup>8</sup>After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.<sup>9</sup>He had thirty sons, and thirty daughters he gave in marriage outside his clan, and thirty daughters he brought in from outside for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years.<sup>10</sup>Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.<sup>11</sup>After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel, and he judged Israel ten years.<sup>12</sup>Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.<sup>13</sup>After him Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.<sup>14</sup>He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel eight years.<sup>15</sup>Then Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
12.overview:
Where we are. Jephthah has broken Ammon’s power, but at the cost of his only daughter (11:32–40). Now the proudest tribe in the north crosses the Jordan to quarrel with him, as it once quarrelled with Gideon (8:1–3), and after his death three more judges pass in eight verses.

The message. A deliverer who is right but not gentle can do more harm to God’s people than their enemies did, and leaders who serve themselves give no rest. Jephthah wins the argument with Ephraim and kills forty-two thousand of his own people at the fords; then for the first time one of the great deliverers dies and the land has no rest, and the judges who follow are remembered for their sons, marriages and donkeys. Israel needs a peace and a rest that none of its judges can give.

Why it was said. Israel was a loose union of tribes, bound together only by the covenant (see the introduction). This chapter shows the bond fraying: tribal pride, insults across the river, and a judgeship that has become a family business.

How the chapter makes its case. Ephraim threatens to burn Jephthah’s house for not calling them to the battle, and he answers with the record, every word true and none of it soft (vv. 1–3). The quarrel becomes a war: Gilead seizes the fords of the Jordan, and every fugitive who cannot say “Shibboleth” is killed (vv. 4–6). Jephthah dies after six years, with no rest for the land (v. 7). Ibzan, Elon and Abdon follow, with sixty marriages, a blank decade and seventy donkeys, but no enemy named and no deliverance recorded, and the chapter ends with a judge buried “in the hill country of the Amalekites” (vv. 8–15).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes. Jephthah could argue with a foreign king for peace and would not answer his own brothers gently; Jesus “himself is our peace”, who broke down “the dividing wall of hostility” by his own death (Ephesians 2:14). The land has no rest under its judges, and the book will never again say that it did; “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). Christ gives the rest no judge could, and asks for no password at the river: “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13).

For us. Being right is not the same as being wise, and those justified by grace need not win every argument to know who they are. Beware of the tests by which Christians shut out other Christians for an accent. And ask whether the compromises we no longer notice have become part of the map.
12.theology:
Right, and wrong. Every sentence Jephthah speaks in vv. 2-3 is true, and forty-two thousand men die for it, where Gideon's gentler answer to the same complaint ended the quarrel (8:2-3).

Shibboleth. Christ sets no test of accent for those who come to him: everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, because there is no distinction (Rom. 10:12-13).

The missing rest. The land had rest closed the accounts of Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Gideon, and is never said again in the book. Hebrews says even Joshua did not give the true rest, which remains for the people of God (Heb. 4:8-10). Christ gives it (Matt. 11:28), and he won it by laying down his own life, not by taking his brothers'.

Amalek on the map. A district in Israel's heartland bears the name of the people God swore to blot out (Ex. 17:14), and nobody thinks it needs explaining (see vv. 11-15).
12.examples:
Then: A tribe too proud to fight the war showed up in force to argue about the credit, was answered with the plain facts, and lost forty-two thousand men at a river crossing to a test that examined nothing but their accent.

Now: Two things to take away. First, in the next disagreement where you are demonstrably in the right, ask what it would cost to give away credit you had actually earned, because Gideon did that and the quarrel ended, and Jephthah proved his case and buried the dead. Jephthah's own best sentence makes it possible: the LORD gave them into my hand. Credit that was a gift to begin with can be given away, and the Spirit who produces gentleness (Gal. 5:22-23) makes the soft answer more than a technique. Where we have already been Jephthah, harsh and right, Christ was the one who did not insist on his rights, and the way back is to confess it and go to the brother. Second, name your own shibboleths. Every congregation has a word, a translation, a position on a secondary matter that quietly decides who is one of us. Test it honestly: is this the gospel, or is it an accent? The Lord asks nobody who comes to him to prove himself by pronunciation.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim picks a quarrel about credit, and Jephthah answers with the truth but without gentleness. The men of Ephraim cross the Jordan and threaten to burn his house over him for fighting Ammon without them (v. 1), the complaint they once made to Gideon, now with arson added. Jephthah replies that he did call them and they did not come, that he took his life in his hand, and that the LORD gave the victory (vv. 2–3). Every word is accurate, and the centre of it, that the LORD won the battle, is the best thing he says. But he does not do what Gideon did and turn away their anger, and the next verse is war.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the second time Ephraim has made this complaint (8:1), and the two answers it receives carry the chapter's lesson: how a true thing is said can decide what follows.
verseByVerse.examples: Many quarrels, in churches and in families, are not about what they claim to be about. Ephraim's complaint about procedure was really a complaint about credit.

verseByVerse.quote: The men of Ephraim were called to arms, and they crossed to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us to go with you? We will burn your house over you with fire." And Jephthah said to them, "I and my people had a great dispute with the Ammonites, and when I called you, you did not save me from their hand. And when I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hand and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into my hand. Why then have you come up to me this day to fight against me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim threatens Jephthah for winning without them, and he answers with the truth, including that the LORD gave the victory, but without the gentleness that might have stopped a war.

Why did you not call us? Ephraim has said this before, almost word for word, to Gideon (8:1): a complaint about credit dressed as a complaint about procedure, from the proudest tribe in the north. But to Gideon they only “accused him fiercely”. To Jephthah they promise arson with the family inside. Ammon had been pressing Gilead since 10:8 without Ephraim crossing the river to help. They cross it now, in force, because somebody else won.

When I called you, you did not save me. His answer is accurate. Ephraim says he did not call; he says he did, and they did not come, and nothing suggests he is the one lying. I took my life in my hand is the phrase of a man who went out without support and knew it. And the centre of the reply is right: the LORD gave them into my hand. The argument about credit is beside the point, because neither side won the battle: the LORD did.

Right, but not wise. So why is it the wrong answer? Because Gideon had the same complaint from the same tribe and gave away credit he had earned, with generous words that were not strictly true, and their anger subsided (8:2–3). “A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). Jephthah stands on the record, right about the facts and right about the theology, and in the next three verses forty-two thousand Israelites are killed. The man who insists on his accuracy in a quarrel may win the argument and do great harm by winning it.

The idol of being right. Few things feel more virtuous than being right. Much of our public life now runs on it: the comment that wins the thread, the clip that destroys the opponent, the family argument replayed for years because we know we had the facts. Jephthah had the facts. What he did not have was any reason to give them up, and that is where the idol shows itself. When being right is what makes me acceptable, every disagreement becomes a trial of my worth, and I cannot afford to lose even when losing would save lives. Gideon, for all his faults, could let Ephraim have the credit, because that day the credit did not hold his heart.

Justified, and free to be gentle. The gospel loosens the grip at the root. A Christian is someone who has admitted, before the only Judge who matters, that he was wrong, and has been declared righteous anyway, “not having a righteousness of my own” (Philippians 3:9). Someone justified like that does not need to win the argument to know who he is, and so, perhaps for the first time, he is free to be gentle.

Uncertain wording. “Crossed to Zaphon” may name a town in the Jordan valley belonging to Gad (Joshua 13:27), or the same Hebrew word may simply mean “crossed northward”. Either way, Ephraim crosses the Jordan to Jephthah’s side in force.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israelites kill Israelites at the river, one at a time, sorted by an accent. The men of Ephraim taunt the Gileadites as runaways, and Jephthah’s men defeat them (v. 4). Then Gilead seizes the fords of the Jordan, the manoeuvre the book praised when Ehud and Gideon used it against foreign enemies, and turns it on fellow Israelites (v. 5). Each fugitive is told to say “Shibboleth”; the Ephraimites cannot make the sound, and every one who says “Sibboleth” is killed. Forty-two thousand of Ephraim fall (v. 6). No foreign enemy in the book has done this much harm to a single tribe.
verseByVerse.theology: Civil war is the darkest kind of war in Judges, and here it grows out of a quarrel over honour between tribes who should have stood together as brothers.
verseByVerse.examples: Divisions among God's people rarely begin with doctrine. They often begin with wounded pride and an insult, as this one did (v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought with Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because they said, "You are fugitives of Ephraim, you Gileadites, in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh." And the Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. And when any of the fugitives of Ephraim said, "Let me go over," the men of Gilead said to him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" When he said, "No," they said to him, "Then say Shibboleth," and he said, "Sibboleth," for he could not pronounce it right. Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time 42,000 of the Ephraimites fell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Insulted as runaways, Jephthah’s men defeat Ephraim and hold the fords of the Jordan against their own countrymen, killing every man who cannot say “Shibboleth”.

You are fugitives of Ephraim. The insult that starts the killing is about status. The taunt is that the Gileadites are nobodies: runaways and leftovers of Ephraim and Manasseh, living out east on land nobody wanted, with no proper standing among the tribes. Of all the men in Israel to say that to, they say it to Jephthah, who was thrown out of his father’s house as the wrong sort of son and has spent his life as the outsider respectable people call in when they are desperate.

The fords of the Jordan. Seizing the fords is a manoeuvre this book has praised twice. Ehud took the fords against Moab and not a man escaped (3:28–29). Gideon sent to Ephraim to take the waters against Midian, and they did it and killed Oreb and Zeeb (7:24–25). It is the standard way of finishing a beaten enemy in this country: hold the crossings and let the retreat come to you. Here it is Israelites holding the river against Israelites, and the tribe now trying to get through once held these same waters against Midian.

Then say Shibboleth. Shibboleth means an ear of grain, or a flowing stream, and it is not a password: there is nothing to guess and no secret to betray. It is a dialect trap. The Ephraimites pronounced the first sound differently, and a man from the western hills could not make it, however hard he tried and however loudly he swore he was not an Ephraimite. He was condemned by an accent he had never chosen and could not hear.

Killed by other Israelites. Set the figure beside the rest of the book. Not one of these men was killed by Ammon, Moab, Midian, Canaan or Philistia. They were killed by other Israelites, one at a time, at a river crossing, after a hearing that lasted one word. And it is not even the worst the book has to show: the civil war of chapters 20–21 will cost more than sixty thousand lives, fought by mustered armies over three days. This was a queue at a ford.

No letter to his own. The man who ran that checkpoint had written sixteen verses of patient history to a foreign king to prevent a war (11:12–27). To his own countrymen he sent nothing at all.

No dialect that disqualifies. The Lord, the true Judge, sets no such test for those who come to him. “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved”, and Paul’s whole point in writing it is that “there is no distinction between Jew and Greek” (Romans 10:12–13): no dialect disqualifies. Christ knows his own (John 10:14), and he has never once asked anyone to prove it by pronunciation.

Shibboleths in the church. The church has its own versions of this test, and the word is still in the language. A shibboleth is a test of belonging that has nothing to do with the truth of the gospel: the phrase you must use, the translation you must carry, the position on a secondary question that marks you as one of us. It sorts people efficiently. It also puts on the far side of the river a great many who love the Lord Jesus and merely say it with a different accent.

Uncertain wording. Three things here are uncertain. The taunt in verse 4 is compressed in Hebrew, and its exact sense is unclear, though the ESV’s reading, a sneer at the Gileadites as Ephraim’s runaways, is the usual one. No one knows precisely how the Ephraimites said the word; the text says only that they could not pronounce it right. And the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a clan unit, so some think “42,000” counts units rather than men; large numbers in these books are a known puzzle. On any reading, a great many Israelites died at that river.
verseByVerse.note: The fords were the few shallow crossing places of the Jordan, and whoever held them controlled all movement between the east and west banks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Six Years, No Rest, and Seventy Donkeys
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jephthah’s judgeship ends without rest, and the three judges who follow are remembered for their households, not their deeds. Jephthah judges six years and is buried in Gilead, and for the first time a great deliverer’s story ends with no rest recorded (v. 7). Ibzan of Bethlehem arranges sixty marriages for his children and judges seven years (vv. 8–10). Elon of Zebulun judges ten years, and nothing else is told (vv. 11–12). Abdon has forty sons and thirty grandsons on seventy donkeys, judges eight years, and is buried in Ephraim “in the hill country of the Amalekites” (vv. 13–15). No enemy is named, no deliverance is told, and no one cries to the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: Not every period of a nation's life is dramatic. These brief notices ask whether we can see God's people drifting even when nothing seems to be happening.
verseByVerse.examples: It is worth asking what in our own lives has stopped looking like an enemy simply because we have lived with it for a long time.

verseByVerse.quote: Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city in Gilead. After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. He had thirty sons, and thirty daughters he gave in marriage outside his clan, and thirty daughters he brought in from outside for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years. Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jephthah dies after six years without bringing the land rest, and his successor Ibzan uses his office to build a network of family alliances.

Jephthah judged Israel six years. Six years is the shortest term of any major judge in the book (Othniel had forty, Ehud eighty, Deborah forty, Gideon forty), and the sentence that closed all four of those accounts is missing here: the land had rest. It is not said of Jephthah, and it will not be said again. He broke Ammon, but the reason for the missing rest is in the verses just above: the peace was spent on a civil war. A deliverer who kills forty-two thousand of the people he delivered has not given anybody rest.

Buried in his city in Gilead. He is buried in his own city, in the country he was driven out of, as its head. He got everything he negotiated for and lost the only person he had.

Ibzan of Bethlehem. His Bethlehem is probably the town in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15) rather than David’s town in Judah, though some take it as the southern one. The whole record of the man describes a political operation. Thirty daughters sent out to other clans and thirty brought in for his sons is a network of sixty families tied to his house by marriage. It is how dynasties were built.

He judged Israel seven years. No oppressor is named: no enemy, no battle, no deliverance, no cry to God. Here is what the office has become. Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Gideon were raised up against an enemy. Ibzan is raised up against nobody, and spends his term arranging weddings.

verseByVerse.quote: After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel, and he judged Israel ten years. Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun. After him Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel. He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel eight years. Then Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two more judges pass with nothing to report but a grave and a family on seventy donkeys, and the chapter ends with a judge of Israel buried in hills that still bear the name of Israel’s oldest enemy.

Elon the Zebulunite. Elon judged ten years, and the writer has nothing whatever to report: not one act, word or enemy, only his name, tribe, term and grave.

Seventy donkeys. The count has been rising all through this section. Jair had thirty sons on thirty donkeys (10:4). Ibzan had thirty sons and sixty marriage alliances. Abdon has forty sons and thirty grandsons, and seventy mounts for them. A donkey was a mark of rank, so this is a family that rides out in a body, seventy strong, and everybody in the district knows who they are. Seventy is also the number of Gideon’s sons, the household of a man who lived like a king, and of the brothers Abimelech killed on one stone (9:5). The book does not press the point. It simply keeps counting.

In the hill country of the Amalekites. The writer sets down the last phrase of the chapter without comment. Pirathon is in Ephraim, the heartland, Joshua’s own tribe, as far from the frontier as it is possible to get, and a district in those hills is called after the Amalekites. Amalek was the people who attacked Israel first, at Rephidim, before Sinai, picking off the stragglers at the back (Exodus 17:8; Deuteronomy 25:17–19). God swore to blot out their memory from under heaven (Exodus 17:14). Generations later there is countryside in the middle of Israel that carries their name, a judge of Israel is buried in it, and nobody in the chapter thinks it worth a comment.

How a compromise ends. Not with a decision, but with a place name that nobody notices any more. The thing you failed to remove stops being an enemy and becomes an address.

So the chapter closes. Twenty-five years, three judges, no oppression named, no deliverance recorded, a hundred sons and grandsons, seventy donkeys, sixty marriages, and a stretch of Amalekite hill country in the middle of the promised land. Israel has leaders, and no one is leading it anywhere. It needs a shepherd-king who will lead his people somewhere, and give them the rest no judge could (Hebrews 4:8–10).

Uncertain wording. No one knows why part of Ephraim’s hill country bore the Amalekites’ name: Amalekites may once have lived or raided there, or the name may survive from an older episode. The text records it and leaves it unexplained.

keyVerse.quote: they said to him, “Then say Shibboleth,” and he said, “Sibboleth,” for he could not pronounce it right. Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan.
keyVerse.note: The fords that once trapped Israel’s enemies now trap Israel’s own sons, and a man dies for an accent. The verse shows how far the people have fallen when a judge who is right about God turns his strength on his brothers. It sets off the welcome of Christ, who asks no password at the river: everyone who calls on his name will be saved.

12.reflection:
Jephthah’s reply to Ephraim was true in every detail (vv. 2–3), yet it led to war, while Gideon’s softer answer to the same complaint brought peace (8:1–3). When have you been right but not wise? How does being justified by grace free us from needing to win?

The fords of the Jordan, once used against Israel’s enemies, are turned against fellow Israelites (vv. 5–6). What are the “shibboleths” Christians sometimes use to shut out other believers, and how can we tell a real gospel boundary from a test of accent?

For the first time a great deliverer’s story ends with no rest recorded, and the judges who follow are remembered for sons, marriages and donkeys (vv. 7–15). What does this teach about leaders who serve themselves, and about the rest that only Christ gives?

A judge is buried “in the hill country of the Amalekites” and no one remarks on it (v. 15). What compromises in your life or church have become so familiar that nobody notices them any more?

13.title: Samson's Birth
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.<sup>2</sup>There was a certain man of Zorah, of the tribe of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. And his wife was barren and had no children.<sup>3</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, "Behold, you are barren and have not borne children, but you shall conceive and bear a son.<sup>4</sup>Therefore be careful and drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean,<sup>5</sup>for behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines."<sup>6</sup>Then the woman came and told her husband, "A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name,<sup>7</sup>but he said to me, 'Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. So then drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.'"<sup>8</sup>Then Manoah prayed to the LORD and said, "O Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come again to us and teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born."<sup>9</sup>And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman as she sat in the field. But Manoah her husband was not with her.<sup>10</sup>So the woman ran quickly and told her husband, "Behold, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me."<sup>11</sup>And Manoah arose and went after his wife and came to the man and said to him, "Are you the man who spoke to this woman?" And he said, "I am."<sup>12</sup>And Manoah said, "Now when your words come true, what is to be the child's manner of life, and what is his mission?"<sup>13</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "Of all that I said to the woman let her be careful.<sup>14</sup>She may not eat of anything that comes from the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, or eat any unclean thing. All that I commanded her let her observe."<sup>15</sup>Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please let us detain you and prepare a young goat for you."<sup>16</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "If you detain me, I will not eat of your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, then offer it to the LORD." (For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the LORD.)<sup>17</sup>And Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that, when your words come true, we may honor you?"<sup>18</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?"<sup>19</sup>So Manoah took the young goat with the grain offering, and offered it on the rock to the LORD, to the one who works wonders, and Manoah and his wife were watching.<sup>20</sup>And when the flame went up toward heaven from the altar, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. Now Manoah and his wife were watching, and they fell on their faces to the ground.<sup>21</sup>The angel of the LORD appeared no more to Manoah and to his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>And Manoah said to his wife, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God."<sup>23</sup>But his wife said to him, "If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things, or now announced to us such things as these."<sup>24</sup>And the woman bore a son and called his name Samson. And the young man grew, and the LORD blessed him.<sup>25</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
13.overview:
Where we are. After Jephthah and three judges remembered for their families (chapters 11–12), the book’s cycle turns for the sixth and last time. Israel again does evil, and the Philistines rule over them for forty years, the longest oppression in the book.

The message. God begins to rescue a people who have stopped asking. To a barren woman with no name, on the losing edge of a losing tribe, he promises a son set apart to him from the womb who will begin to save Israel. And he shows himself as the one whose name is wonderful, who accepts a sacrifice and goes up in its flame, so that a frightened couple learn that a God who has accepted their offering does not mean to destroy them.

Why it was said. Israel had settled into life under the Philistines and no longer cried out (compare 15:11), and Dan was failing to hold its land (1:34; see the introduction). The chapter shows that God’s rescue does not wait for his people to want it.

How the chapter makes its case. The cycle runs with no cry (v. 1). The angel of the LORD promises Manoah’s wife a son, lays the Nazirite vow first on her, and limits the boy’s commission: he will begin to save Israel (vv. 2–7). Manoah prays to be taught, and his question about the boy’s mission is answered only with the vow (vv. 8–14). His meal becomes a burnt offering, the visitor’s name is “wonderful”, and he goes up in the altar flame (vv. 15–21). Manoah fears death, his wife reasons from what God has done, and Samson is born and stirred by the Spirit (vv. 22–25).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the character of God revealed. The barren mothers of Scripture lead on to Elizabeth and then to Mary, who conceived as a virgin. The angel of the LORD, whose name is wonderful, is best read as the Son before his incarnation, and Isaiah gives the child to come the name “Wonderful Counselor” (Isaiah 9:6). The one who receives the offering goes up in it, a mystery solved when Christ “appeared once for all … to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26). And where Samson would only begin to save, Jesus “will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

For us. God’s grace comes to people who have not asked for it, and that includes us. Parents can hold their children as God’s before they are ours, doing what is given us and leaving the outcome to him. And when fear says God is against us, reason as Manoah’s wife did: he has accepted the offering, his Son, and he has not done that in order to destroy us.
13.theology:
Grace to people who did not send for it. Forty years without one recorded prayer, and God raises up a deliverer anyway. Through all four Samson chapters the initiative is entirely God's, towards a nation too comfortable in its captivity to want rescuing.

A vow broken one part at a time. Samson is a Nazirite for life, bound by the three restrictions of Numbers 6. He will break all three, and the razor comes last, when the other two are long gone.

Begin, not finish. No other judge is given a limited task. Samson is announced as a start before he is conceived, and someone else will finish the work. That is a hard word for anyone who wants a completed work to show, and a true one.

The one called Wonderful. The visitor speaks as God, accepts a burnt offering made to the LORD, keeps his name beyond reach, and goes up in the altar flame. The chapter points beyond itself to the Son, in whom the one who receives the offering becomes the offering.

Reasoning from grace already given. Manoah's doctrine is right and his conclusion is wrong. His wife reasons from what God has already done to what he must therefore intend, and that is the logic of Christian assurance.
13.examples:
Then: A childless couple in a frontier village were told they would have a son who would only begin the work, were refused any account of his mission, and were given instead a set of instructions for the next nine months. Then the messenger went up in the fire of their own sacrifice, and the husband concluded they were about to die and the wife proved they were not.

Now: Manoah asked what the child was for and where it was all going, and was given only today's duty, with the future left in God's hands. Many of us ask the same of an illness, a job or a child, and are given the same answer. The Spirit who stirred Samson now lives in believers to make that daily obedience possible (Gal. 5:16). And when the fear comes that God has shown you kindness in order to destroy you afterwards, use his wife's method rather than his: list what God has already done. He accepted the offering. He has shown you these things. He has told you what is coming. Nobody pays a price like Calvary and then changes his mind.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 1 — The Cycle With No Cry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cycle turns a sixth time, and the cry is missing. Israel again does evil in the LORD’s sight, and he gives them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years, twice as long as any earlier oppression (v. 1). Every earlier cycle in the book has followed the oppression with Israel crying out to the LORD, but here the sentence stops. The people have made their peace with their masters. What follows is therefore pure grace: God sends a deliverer to a people who did not ask for one, and the rest of the chapter shows him doing it, unbidden, in a frontier village.
verseByVerse.theology: Five times the next clause has been a cry to the LORD. This time nobody cries.
verseByVerse.examples: They are not groaning under the Philistines. They have learned to live with them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel sins again and falls under the Philistines for forty years, and this time nobody cries out, so God’s rescue that follows is grace no one asked for.

No cry this time. Read the verse and see what is not in it. Five times this book has followed the oppression with the same clause: Israel cried out to the LORD (3:9, 15; 4:3; 6:6; 10:10). Here, nothing.

For forty years. It is the longest oppression in the book. Cushan had eight years, Eglon eighteen, Jabin twenty, Midian seven, Ammon eighteen. This one runs twice as long as the longest of them and produces not a single recorded groan.

Why nobody cries. Two chapters on, Judah explains it. Samson is hiding in a rock, and three thousand men of Judah come out, not to fight the Philistines but to hand him over: “Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us?” (15:11). That is the language of a people who have decided the arrangement is survivable and are annoyed with the man disturbing it.

Grace unasked for. Israel is not oppressed enough to pray, and God sends a deliverer anyway. Nobody asked for him, which is what grace has always looked like: “while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6). Not for people who sent for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–7 — To a Woman Who Is Never Named
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God comes first to a barren woman who is never named, and lays on her both a promise and a vow. In Zorah, a frontier village of Dan, Manoah’s wife has no children (v. 2). The angel of the LORD tells her she will bear a son, and that she must drink no wine and eat nothing unclean, for the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb, his hair never cut; and he will begin to save Israel from the Philistines (vv. 3–5). She tells her husband exactly what she saw and heard, owning what she does not know, adding that the vow lasts to the day of his death, and leaving out the mission (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The angel comes to her, not to him, and the book never tells us what she was called. Manoah is named again and again in this chapter. His wife is the woman throughout, and she is the one who sees, listens, reports accurately and works out what it means.
verseByVerse.examples: Scripture has walked this road before: a barren woman, an announced son. The deliverer is God's gift, not something his parents achieved.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a certain man of Zorah, of the tribe of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. And his wife was barren and had no children. And the angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, "Behold, you are barren and have not borne children, but you shall conceive and bear a son. Therefore be careful and drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To a barren woman in a failing frontier tribe, God promises a son who will belong to him from the womb under a Nazirite vow, and who will begin, not finish, Israel’s rescue from the Philistines.

A certain man of Zorah. Zorah sits on the western edge of the hill country, right on the frontier where Israel’s land runs down into the Philistine plain. Dan is the tribe that failed to take its allotted territory (1:34) and will shortly abandon it altogether (chapter 18). This is a family on the losing edge of a losing tribe.

His wife was barren. Scripture has taught us to read barrenness as the beginning of something: Sarah and Isaac, Rebekah and Jacob, Rachel and Joseph, Hannah and Samuel, Elizabeth and John. Each time God opens a closed womb, the child belongs to God in a way no ordinary child does, and the parents know they did not produce him.

For those longing for a child. If you are childless and longing, these stories are not a promise that every closed womb will open, and they are not a verdict on you. They are the places God chose to bring his deliverers into the world. And the same God sought out a woman with no name in a village on the edge of things, spoke to her first, and named her sorrow before anything else. He has not overlooked yours.

The Nazirite vow. The vow arrives before the child does, and it is laid on the mother first: “be careful”. Numbers 6 sets out the vow in three parts. Nothing from the vine: no wine, no strong drink, no grapes, not even the skins or the seeds. No razor on the head, the hair left uncut as the visible sign. And no contact with a dead body, not even a parent’s (Numbers 6:3–7). It was normally something a person chose, for a set period, ended with a sacrifice.

From the womb. Nothing about Samson’s vow is normal. He does not choose it, it is not temporary, and it starts before he is conceived: “a Nazirite to God from the womb”. His mother keeps the food restrictions for the pregnancy, so that the boy is under the vow from the very beginning.

Watch the three parts. Fix them in your mind, because this is the last time in the story that all three are intact. Samson will hold a seven-day feast at his wedding, and the Hebrew word for it is built on the verb to drink (14:10). He will scoop honey out of a lion’s carcass, eat it and give some to his parents (14:8–9). And the razor will come at last in Delilah’s lap (16:19).

He shall begin to save Israel. Begin, not finish. God tells this couple, before the child is conceived, that their son’s life work will be incomplete. No other judge is given a limited task; the others are simply raised up to save. Samson is announced as a start. The Philistine war he begins runs on through the days of Samuel and Saul, and is not decisively won until David breaks the Philistines at Baal-perazim and in the Valley of Rephaim and subdues them (2 Samuel 5:17–25; 8:1). Samson is the first crack in a wall somebody else pulls down.
verseByVerse.note: Zorah lay in the Shephelah, the lowlands between Judah’s hills and Philistia.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the woman came and told her husband, "A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name, but he said to me, 'Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. So then drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manoah’s wife reports the visit with careful honesty, owning what she does not know, grasping that the vow is for life, and saying nothing about the mission.

A man of God came to me. She is exact about what she does not know. A man of God is the term for a prophet, the safe, sober description of what she can be sure of. His appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, and she does not push the comparison further. And she volunteers the two gaps in her information: she did not ask where he came from, and he did not say who he was.

Very awesome. She has met something overwhelming and is not exaggerating about it. It is her one phrase for the impression, and it is a word for holy fear, not for admiration.

From the womb to the day of his death. The angel had said “from the womb”, and she adds “to the day of his death”. She may have been told more than verse 5 records, or she may have understood correctly what a lifelong vow means and said so. Either way it is not carelessness: she has grasped that there is no end date and no releasing sacrifice at the finish.

What she leaves out. The angel had said the boy would begin to save Israel from the Philistines, and she does not repeat it. The text does not say why, and it would be easy to make too much of it. But she has held on to every word about the vow, the part that is her responsibility, starting today, and said nothing about the national mission, which is God’s business and years away. That is a good instinct in someone just handed something enormous: given a promise and a duty, she goes home talking about the duty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Teach Us What We Are to Do
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manoah prays to be taught, and God answers by sending the messenger back to the woman. Manoah asks that the man of God come again to teach them how to raise the child; God listens, and the angel comes again, but to the wife alone in the field (vv. 8–9). She runs for her husband, who asks the visitor whether he is the one who spoke to her (vv. 10–11). Manoah then asks about the boy’s manner of life and mission, and the angel answers only with the vow: let her keep all that I commanded her (vv. 12–14). Their part is faithfulness, not the plan.
verseByVerse.theology: It is a prayer for instruction rather than rescue, and God listens to it. He simply does not answer in the way Manoah expected.
verseByVerse.examples: The instruction that comes back is not about the boy's career but about the mother's diet.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Manoah prayed to the LORD and said, "O Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come again to us and teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born." And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman as she sat in the field. But Manoah her husband was not with her. So the woman ran quickly and told her husband, "Behold, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me." And Manoah arose and went after his wife and came to the man and said to him, "Are you the man who spoke to this woman?" And he said, "I am."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manoah believes the message and prays humbly to be taught how to raise the child, and God answers by sending the messenger back to his wife, who has believed from the start.

Manoah prayed to the LORD. This is the best prayer prayed by a man in the book of Judges. He does not ask for a sign to test the message, as Gideon did twice with the fleece. He does not bargain, as Jephthah did. He does not ask for the Philistines to be dealt with, which is nearly the only thing anyone in this book asks for.

Teach us what we are to do. He has been told he is to be father to someone set apart for God, and his first reaction is that he does not know how to do this and needs instructing. He does not ask whether the message is true; he asks to be taught how to carry it out. And he prays for both of them: teach us.

God listened to the voice of Manoah. God listened, and then arranged the meeting exactly as before. It is nearly comic and entirely deliberate. Manoah prays that the man of God would come again to us; the messenger comes back, but to the woman, sitting alone in a field, with her husband somewhere else. Heaven has now twice chosen to speak to the wife and twice arranged for the husband not to be there. God answers Manoah’s prayer in a way that says quietly whose word is to be trusted in that house.

The woman ran quickly. She runs, because she knows what this is, and he goes after his wife to be shown. His first words are a check: “Are you the man who spoke to this woman?” There is nothing wrong with the question. But she never asked one. She has believed the message since verse 3, and has spent this whole scene as the person who knows.

verseByVerse.quote: And Manoah said, "Now when your words come true, what is to be the child's manner of life, and what is his mission?" And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "Of all that I said to the woman let her be careful. She may not eat of anything that comes from the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, or eat any unclean thing. All that I commanded her let her observe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manoah asks how the boy is to live and what he will do, and the angel answers only with the vow: their part is to keep it faithfully and leave the rest to God.

What is his mission? The first question is fair enough: how is the boy to be raised? That is what Manoah prayed for. The second is the one every parent secretly wants answered: what is he going to do? What is this boy for?

Of all that I said to the woman. The angel answers the first question and passes over the second entirely: nothing about the Philistines, nothing about what the boy will grow up to do. He simply repeats the instructions already given, and twice presents them as given to her: “Of all that I said to the woman”; “All that I commanded her”. He even expands the detail: not merely no wine, but “anything that comes from the vine”, the full restriction of Numbers 6. He is making sure she has it exactly.

Your job is the vow. So the answer to “What is he for?” is: keep the vow, and wait. That is how God often deals with people who want the plan. It is not a refusal to answer. It is the answer: your part is the vow, not the mission. And there is an irony coming that neither parent can see. The one thing they were told to guard is the one thing that will finally matter. Samson’s whole story turns not on strategy or armies but on whether the hair is cut. The parents were told to watch the very thing the son eventually threw away.

The child as a project. “What is his mission?” is the question many modern parents ask without saying it aloud. Children were once received as a gift; now they are often treated, very lovingly, as a project to be completed: the right school, the right activities, the right record by eighteen. The child’s success becomes the parents’ report card, and so, quietly, their justification. That is a heavy thing to lay on a small person. A child who must vindicate his parents cannot afford to fail, and parents whose worth rides on a child cannot afford to let him be anyone in particular. The angel declines to feed that hunger. Manoah is told what is his to do and nothing about results, because the boy is “a Nazirite to God” (v. 7), God’s before he is theirs. Samson’s story will show how little any parent controls the outcome.

Another Son finished the work. The gospel frees parents from needing to control it. Your standing before God does not rest on how your children turn out; it rests on another Son, who finished the work his Father gave him (John 17:4). Parents who know that can hold their children with open hands, and love them for who they are rather than for what they might become.

Uncertain wording. The two Hebrew words behind “manner of life” and “mission” are general ones, roughly “the rule for the boy” and “his work”. They may both refer to how he is to be raised, in which case the angel’s answer covers both; the ESV’s “mission” takes the second as his life’s work, which the angel then leaves unanswered. Either way, the angel’s reply is all about the vow.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manoah’s hospitality is turned into worship, and the visitor reveals himself without giving his name. Manoah offers to prepare a young goat, but the angel will not eat; if Manoah prepares a burnt offering, let him offer it to the LORD, for Manoah still does not know who he is (vv. 15–16). Asked his name, the visitor answers that it is wonderful (vv. 17–18). Manoah offers the goat on a rock to the LORD, the one who works wonders, and as the flame goes up the angel goes up in it, while the couple fall on their faces (vv. 19–20). Then Manoah knows that this was the angel of the LORD (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Manoah still takes his visitor for a prophet. The reader is being shown, step by step, that he is far more than that.
verseByVerse.examples: Manoah asked for a name to honor (v. 17), and was given a fire instead.

verseByVerse.quote: Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please let us detain you and prepare a young goat for you." And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "If you detain me, I will not eat of your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, then offer it to the LORD." (For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the LORD.) And Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that, when your words come true, we may honor you?" And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The visitor will not eat Manoah’s meal but directs him to offer a burnt offering to the LORD, and will not give his name, for it is wonderful, beyond human grasp.

Let us detain you. Feeding a visitor is what a decent man does. Abraham did exactly this at Mamre: he ran to the herd, took a calf, and stood by while three strangers ate under the tree (Genesis 18:7–8). Manoah is offering ordinary hospitality to someone he still takes to be a prophet.

I will not eat of your food. The visitor turns the offer from a meal to an altar. If Manoah wants to bring that goat, he must bring it as a burnt offering, and bring it to the LORD.
