He will not receive as a guest what should be given as worship, and the narrator steps in with a parenthesis to make sure we see what Manoah is missing: he did not know who he was talking to. The visitor standing in front of him has just told him to sacrifice to the LORD, and in a moment will go up in that sacrifice’s flame.

What is your name? Manoah’s request has a good motive, and it cannot be granted. He wants to know whom to thank: when the baby is born and the promise is proved, he means to honour the man who brought the news. Jacob asked the same question at the Jabbok and got the same non-answer (Genesis 32:29). Moses asked it at the bush and was given “I AM WHO I AM”, a name that gives no one a hold over him (Exodus 3:14).

Seeing it is wonderful. The word is not wonderful in the weak modern sense. It is the word for what only God can do, a miracle. Verse 19 will call the LORD “the one who works wonders”, from the same root, in the very next breath. The KJV renders it “secret”; the sense is a name beyond human grasp, too wonderful to be handled. It is also the word Isaiah reaches for when he names the child who is to be born: “his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6).

Gather the evidence. See what is standing on this hillside: a person who appears in the form of a man, speaks as God and is called the angel of the LORD, refuses food but directs a burnt offering to the LORD, keeps his name beyond asking, and in a moment will ascend to heaven in fire.

The name given at last. Manoah wanted a name so that he might honour him when the words came true. He was not given one. It would be about eleven hundred years before the name was given, and then to another couple, in another small town, by another angel: “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Not begin to save. Save.

Where Christians differ: who is the angel of the LORD? He speaks as God himself and is called “the LORD”. Some take him as a created angel speaking with God’s full authority. This commentary’s view: the best reading, held by many in the Reformed tradition and before it, is that he is the LORD appearing in person, most likely the Son before his incarnation.

verseByVerse.quote: So Manoah took the young goat with the grain offering, and offered it on the rock to the LORD, to the one who works wonders, and Manoah and his wife were watching. And when the flame went up toward heaven from the altar, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. Now Manoah and his wife were watching, and they fell on their faces to the ground. The angel of the LORD appeared no more to Manoah and to his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manoah offers the goat to the LORD, the one who works wonders, and the visitor goes up in the flame of the offering; only then does Manoah understand whom he has met.

Offered it on the rock to the LORD. He does as he was told, on a rock, with no priest and no tabernacle. This is not the homemade worship that chapter 17 condemns: the law allowed an altar “in every place where I cause my name to be remembered” (Exodus 20:24), and here the LORD himself has appeared and told Manoah what to offer (v. 16), as he did with Gideon at Ophrah (6:20–21). The visitor said his name was wonderful; Manoah offers to the God who works wonders. The writer joins the two before Manoah has worked it out.

Went up in the flame of the altar. Stand in that field for a moment. The goat is on the rock, the flame climbs, and the man who has been talking to them steps into the column of fire and rises with it. They are, the text says twice, watching, and then their faces are in the dirt. The one who receives the offering is carried up inside the offering. He is not standing beside the altar taking delivery; he is in the flame, going up with the smoke, as though the sacrifice and the one it is made to were going home together.

He turned out to be the offering. There is a mystery here that the Old Testament keeps circling and cannot resolve, and it is resolved at Calvary. The one to whom the offering is made turned out to be the offering: “he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26).

Then Manoah knew. Manoah worked it out at the last possible moment, one moment too late to ask anything. The narrator has been telling us since verse 3. Manoah has been through two conversations, asked the name and been refused, been told to offer a sacrifice, and understood none of it until the fire carried the visitor away. That is description, not criticism. God is often recognised only afterwards. The two on the Emmaus road knew who had been walking with them at the very moment he vanished from their sight (Luke 24:31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–25 — She Reasons Better Than He Fears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The husband fears death, the wife reasons from grace, and the promised son is born. Manoah says they will surely die, for they have seen God (v. 22). His wife answers with three pieces of evidence: the LORD has accepted their offering, shown them these things and promised them a future, so he does not mean to kill them (v. 23). She bears a son and names him Samson; the LORD blesses him as he grows, and the Spirit of the LORD begins to stir him at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol (vv. 24–25), the place where his story will end.
verseByVerse.theology: The husband knows the right doctrine; the wife reads the evidence. The accepted sacrifice is the proof that God does not intend their death.
verseByVerse.examples: The place named in v. 25 is where he will be buried (16:31).

verseByVerse.quote: And Manoah said to his wife, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God." But his wife said to him, "If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things, or now announced to us such things as these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manoah reasons from a true principle to despair, but his wife reasons from what God has done to hope: a God who has accepted their offering and made them promises does not mean to kill them.

We shall surely die, for we have seen God. His theology is correct and his conclusion is wrong. He is quoting the settled understanding of Israel: “man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20). Gideon said much the same when he realised who had been sitting under his terebinth (6:22). But Manoah has reasoned from a true principle straight to despair.

But his wife said to him. The woman with no name reasons better than anyone else in Judges. She does not deny his premise. She tests his fear against the evidence and produces three pieces. First, “he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands”: God took the sacrifice and went up in its flame, and a God who intends to destroy you does not first accept your offering. Second, he would not have “shown us all these things”: twice to her, once in the fire to both of them. Third, he would not have “now announced to us such things as these”: you do not tell a dead couple about the future of their child.

Reasoning forward from grace. She reasons from grace received to grace to come, which is exactly the logic of Christian assurance: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The argument is the same, and the sacrifice infinitely greater. If God has already accepted an offering on your behalf (and he has, and it was his Son), then whatever else is coming, it is not your condemnation. That question was settled at the cross. You may be as much in the dark about the future as Manoah was, but God did not accept that offering in order to destroy you afterwards.

The same fire. Manoah looked at the fire and saw his death in it. His wife looked at the same fire and saw that their offering had been received. She was right.

verseByVerse.quote: And the woman bore a son and called his name Samson. And the young man grew, and the LORD blessed him. And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promised son is born, blessed by the LORD and first stirred by his Spirit in the very place where his story will end.

Called his name Samson. Samson’s name is usually connected with the Hebrew word for the sun, an odd, bright, hopeful name for a boy born on the Philistine frontier. There is something poignant in it, because Beth-shemesh, the house of the sun, was just down the valley.

The LORD blessed him. Whatever comes later, that is the sentence over his childhood.

The Spirit of the LORD began to stir him. The verb is a strong one: to thrust or impel, to push at something until it moves. So the chapter ends with a young man made restless by the Spirit of God. He is not yet sent anywhere or doing anything, but something in him will not settle, and it is God who is doing the unsettling. The great strength has not yet appeared. The first thing the Spirit produces in him is discontent.

Between Zorah and Eshtaol. Hold on to those two village names. Three chapters from now, when the temple has come down at Gaza and his brothers have carried the body up out of Philistine country, the last verse of his story reads: “and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father” (16:31). He is buried where the Spirit first stirred him. Everything in between (the riddle, the foxes, the jawbone, the prostitute at Gaza, Delilah’s lap, the mill, the shaven head) happens away from those two villages, and in the end he is carried back to them. Whatever we make of the next twenty years, that is where he starts: an answered prayer, a kept promise, and the Spirit of God stirring a boy on the edge of enemy territory.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of the name Samson is not certain. It is very likely formed from the word for sun, perhaps “little sun” or “sunny one”, but the Bible does not explain it, and whether it carried any echo of the sun-worship of the nearby town is unknown.

keyVerse.quote: for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines.
keyVerse.note: This verse sets the terms for Samson’s whole story: he belongs to God from before his birth, and his work will be a beginning, not an ending. His life turns on that vow, and its limits leave the reader waiting for another deliverer. The child Isaiah named Wonderful and the angel named Jesus would not begin to save, but save completely.

13.reflection:
Israel was oppressed for forty years and never cried out (v. 1), yet God sent a deliverer anyway. Where have you seen God’s grace come before anyone asked for it, and are there ways we, like Judah in 15:11, grow used to living under what we should resist?

Manoah asked “what is his mission?” and was told only to keep the vow (vv. 12–14). What does that teach about the parts of life that are ours to do and the parts that are God’s? How might it free parents from treating children as projects?

The visitor refused a meal, directed a sacrifice to the LORD, called his name wonderful and went up in the flame (vv. 15–20). What do these details suggest about who he was, and how do they point to Jesus, who is both the one we worship and the offering made for us?

Manoah’s wife reasoned that a God who had accepted their offering did not mean to kill them (v. 23). How does Romans 8:32 make the same argument, and how could it help you when you fear that God is against you?

14.title: Samson's Marriage
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Samson went down to Timnah, and at Timnah he saw one of the daughters of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>Then he came up and told his father and mother, "I saw one of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife."<sup>3</sup>But his father and mother said to him, "Is there not a woman among the daughters of your relatives, or among all our people, that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes."<sup>4</sup>His father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.<sup>5</sup>Then Samson went down with his father and mother to Timnah, and they came to the vineyards of Timnah. And behold, a young lion came toward him roaring.<sup>6</sup>Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and although he had nothing in his hand, he tore the lion in pieces as one tears a young goat. But he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.<sup>7</sup>Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she was right in Samson's eyes.<sup>8</sup>After some days he returned to take her. And he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey.<sup>9</sup>He scraped it out into his hands and went on, eating as he went. And he came to his father and mother and gave some to them, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey from the carcass of the lion.<sup>10</sup>His father went down to the woman, and Samson prepared a feast there, for so the young men used to do.<sup>11</sup>As soon as the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.<sup>12</sup>And Samson said to them, "Let me now put a riddle to you. If you can tell me what it is, within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes,<sup>13</sup>but if you cannot tell me what it is, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes." And they said to him, "Put your riddle, that we may hear it."<sup>14</sup>And he said to them, "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." And in three days they could not solve the riddle.<sup>15</sup>On the fourth day they said to Samson's wife, "Entice your husband to tell us what the riddle is, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire. Have you invited us here to impoverish us?"<sup>16</sup>And Samson's wife wept over him and said, "You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is." And he said to her, "Behold, I have not told my father nor my mother, and shall I tell you?"<sup>17</sup>She wept before him the seven days that their feast lasted, and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him hard. Then she told the riddle to her people.<sup>18</sup>And the men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" And he said to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle."<sup>19</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men of the town and took their spoil and gave the garments to those who had told the riddle. In hot anger he went back to his father's house.<sup>20</sup>And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.
14.overview:
Where we are. The Philistines have ruled Israel for forty years and nobody has cried out (13:1). God has given a barren couple a son, a Nazirite from the womb who will “begin to save Israel” (13:5). This chapter is his first recorded act.

The message. God keeps his purpose for his people even through a deliverer who lives by his own eyes. Samson chooses a Philistine wife because “she is right in my eyes” (v. 3), quietly breaks his vow, and turns his wedding into a wager, a betrayal and a killing; yet “it was from the LORD” (v. 4), who was using the whole tangled episode to begin striking the oppressor. God’s purposes are not blocked by our sin, and they never excuse it.

Why it was said. Israel had settled down under the Philistines and stopped asking God for anything (see the introduction). The book’s closing verdict, “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (21:25), is here spoken by the deliverer himself, and the first hearers are shown that the rot reached even the man God sent to rescue them.

How the chapter makes its case. Samson sees a Philistine woman and orders his parents to get her, overriding their objection from God’s law, while God, unseen, is at work (vv. 1–4). He tears a lion apart in the Spirit’s strength, later eats honey from its carcass, and keeps both secrets (vv. 5–9). At the wedding feast he poses an unsolvable riddle, and his bride, threatened with fire, wears the answer out of him (vv. 10–18). The Spirit rushes on him again; he kills thirty men in Ashkelon to pay the bet, goes home in hot anger, and his wife is given to his best man (vv. 19–20).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the pattern of God’s sovereign working and by the need it exposes. As God worked through Samson’s wilfulness to begin his rescue, so he worked through the lawless hands that crucified his Son, “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23). And Samson’s riddle names more than he knew: out of the strong came something sweet, food out of death. Israel needed a deliverer who would not live by his own eyes but say, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42), and whose death would itself become the food of the world (John 6:51).

For us. Our own eyes are poor guides to marriage, pleasure or anything else, and what we have to hide is usually what we already know is wrong. God may bring good out of our wilfulness, but that is his mercy, not our permission. Bring the secrets to the God who forgives what is confessed rather than covered.
14.theology:
Right in my eyes. Yashar b'einay, “right in my eyes” (v. 3), is the phrase the book uses for the lawlessness of the whole period. Samson is not merely living in that age; he is the clearest picture of it. The Deliverer Israel needed would say the opposite, in a garden, with far more at stake: not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42), and by that one man's obedience the many who trust him are made righteous (Rom. 5:19).

God rules a sin he does not author. Verse 4 says the marriage was from the LORD, and not one word of the parents' objection is withdrawn. God works his purpose through human wrongdoing while the wrongdoer remains answerable for all of it.

The strength was never in the hair. It was the Spirit's. The uncut hair is the sign of the vow, not its source.

Gifts are not certificates. The same Spirit who gave strength against the lion gives it at Ashkelon, where Samson kills thirty strangers over a bet. What God does through a person is no verdict on that person's heart.

He was shown the method and did not learn it. The tears, the pressing and the betrayed secret at his wedding all come back, in almost the same words, in Delilah's house.
14.examples:
Then: A man raised up to deliver Israel married into the enemy because she looked good to him, broke his vow at a carcass and hid it, cheated thirty villagers with an unanswerable riddle, and murdered thirty strangers in another city to cover the loss, and God used the whole squalid business to begin breaking the Philistine grip on a nation that had never asked him to.

Now: The chapter leaves two questions. Is there something you are keeping quiet about, as Samson hid where the honey came from (v. 9)? Then bring it into the light; God forgives what is confessed. And if God has used you, in a word that helped someone or a work that prospered, do not take it as proof that all is well between you and him (v. 19). He struck the first blow for Israel through a man settling a gambling debt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samson’s first recorded act is to demand a wife his parents rightly object to, and God is at work behind it. He goes down to Philistine Timnah, sees a woman, and orders his father and mother to get her for him (vv. 1–2). They appeal, gently and correctly, to the covenant: why marry among the uncircumcised? He gives no answer to the argument, only his reason: “she is right in my eyes” (v. 3), the very phrase the book will use for the whole age. Then the narrator adds what nobody in the scene knew: it was from the LORD, who was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines, Israel’s rulers (v. 4). God’s purpose stands without making Samson’s choice any less wrong.
verseByVerse.theology: Samson's appetite overrides his parents' plea from Scripture, and God is at work behind it all.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 does not excuse a word of it. God governs the sin he never authors, and the sinner is answerable for every bit of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Samson went down to Timnah, and at Timnah he saw one of the daughters of the Philistines. Then he came up and told his father and mother, "I saw one of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife." But his father and mother said to him, "Is there not a woman among the daughters of your relatives, or among all our people, that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes." His father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samson demands a Philistine wife because she pleases him, brushing aside his parents’ right appeal to God’s law; yet behind his wilful choice God is quietly at work against Israel’s oppressors.

Samson went down to Timnah. Two verbs hold the whole man: he went down, and he saw. Zorah sits in the hills; Timnah lies four miles away in the valley, on the Philistine side of the line. The writer uses went down again and again in these chapters, and the geography is accurate every time, but it is doing other work too: every step down takes Samson further from where he belongs. The Spirit had begun to stir him at Mahaneh-dan (13:25), and the first recorded result is that he walked into enemy territory and looked at a girl.

Get her for me as my wife. He does not ask. There is no “please”, no case made, only an order to the two people who had waited years for him and kept a vow through a pregnancy on his behalf.

The uncircumcised Philistines. His parents are entirely right, and they say so gently: they put it as a question, offer an alternative, and appeal to circumcision, the sign of God’s covenant. The law was explicit: “You shall not intermarry with them… for they would turn away your sons from following me” (Deuteronomy 7:3–4). The reason is not racial but spiritual: the danger is to Israel’s worship. They are not being snobs; they are being Israelites.

She is right in my eyes. He does not answer the argument. He repeats the order and gives his reason, and it is the most important sentence in the chapter. In Hebrew it is yashar b’einay, the phrase the book will use as its whole diagnosis of the period: “Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (17:6; 21:25). Here the man God raised up to deliver the age speaks its verdict about himself. He does not claim that God led him, or that she fears the LORD, or that he might win her. He looked at her, and she suited him. That is the entire justification, offered to godly parents quoting Scripture, and it wins.

It was from the LORD. The narrator’s aside is the verse that troubles readers most. Behind Samson’s appetite, unknown to his parents and to Samson himself, God was working: “he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines,” a reason to strike them, and this marriage would provide it. The last clause explains why: “At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel,” and nobody in Israel had asked him to do anything about it.

God’s purpose and human guilt. Be careful with what this does and does not say. It does not say God gave Samson the lust, approved the marriage, or suspended Deuteronomy 7. Every criticism his parents made stands, and God’s use of the episode removes not one ounce of Samson’s guilt. What it does say is that God is not blocked by human sin and does not wait for it to finish before he acts. Joseph’s brothers meant evil and God meant good (Genesis 50:20). Above all, Christ was delivered up “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” and crucified “by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23): the worst sin ever committed became the means of salvation, and the men who did it were still guilty.

Does this apply to Christians? The law forbade marrying the Canaanites because they would turn Israel to their gods (Deuteronomy 7:3–4). The New Testament carries the principle forward: a believer is to marry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39; 2 Corinthians 6:14). If you are already married to someone who does not share your faith, Paul’s word to you is different and kind: do not leave; your marriage is not unclean, and your spouse may yet be won (1 Corinthians 7:12–16; 1 Peter 3:1–2).
verseByVerse.note: Timnah lay in Philistine territory. The Philistines had probably come from the Aegean world (Scripture says from Caphtor, Amos 9:7) and controlled the coastal plain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — The Lion and the Honey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The strength of the Spirit and the carelessness of the man appear side by side. On the way to Timnah, among the vineyards a Nazirite should have avoided, a young lion attacks, and the Spirit of the LORD rushes on Samson so that he tears it apart bare-handed (vv. 5–6). He tells no one. He talks with the woman and she still pleases him (v. 7). Returning later for the wedding, he turns aside to the carcass, scoops honey out of it, eats it on the road and gives some to his parents without telling them where it came from (vv. 8–9). Two parts of his vow are already compromised, and his silence shows he knows it.
verseByVerse.theology: The strength comes from the Spirit; the secrets come from Samson.
verseByVerse.examples: Each secret is worse than the one before.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samson went down with his father and mother to Timnah, and they came to the vineyards of Timnah. And behold, a young lion came toward him roaring. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and although he had nothing in his hand, he tore the lion in pieces as one tears a young goat. But he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of the LORD gives Samson strength to tear a lion apart bare-handed, but the man who receives the power is already walking where his vow should have kept him away, and he keeps the deed to himself.

The vineyards of Timnah. Notice where he is before the lion arrives. Samson is a Nazirite, and the first restriction in Numbers 6 is not merely no wine but nothing from the vine at all: no grapes, fresh or dried, not even the seeds or skins (Numbers 6:3–4). Here he is, walking through the vineyards on the road to his Philistine wedding. The writer does not comment; he simply tells us where the man was standing.

The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him. The first display of the strength, and its source must be stated precisely. It is not in his muscles and not in his hair. The verb is violent, a sudden seizing, and the narrator adds that he had “nothing in his hand” so that no one can suppose a weapon did it. A man tears a lion the way another might tear a kid goat for the pot. When we reach chapter 16, the hair will not be a battery. It is a sign, the visible token of the vow that marked him as God’s. The power was always the Spirit’s.

He did not tell his father or his mother. This is the first of the chapter’s three secrets. He tells nobody, not even the parents who would have understood better than anyone alive. The habit runs right through him: he hides the lion (v. 6) and the honey (v. 9), and boasts to his wife that he has not told his parents the riddle (v. 16). Samson holds things back, and in the end the one secret he cannot keep is the only one that mattered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she was right in Samson's eyes. After some days he returned to take her. And he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey. He scraped it out into his hands and went on, eating as he went. And he came to his father and mother and gave some to them, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey from the carcass of the lion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samson goes out of his way to a carcass, eats unclean honey from it in breach of his vow, and feeds it to his unknowing parents: his silence shows he knows what he has done.

She was right in Samson’s eyes. This time the narrator says the phrase himself. In verse 3 it was Samson’s excuse; here it is the writer’s flat description of the courtship. He went down, he talked with her, and she suited him.

He turned aside to see the carcass. It was a deliberate detour on the road to his wedding, and a Nazirite is forbidden to go near a dead body at all. The rule is severe: he may not make himself unclean even for his father, mother, brother or sister when they die (Numbers 6:6–7). Samson is not caught out by a corpse on the path. He walks over to it.

He scraped it out into his hands. We know the story too well to feel the shock. He scoops honey out of the body of a dead lion with his palms and walks on, licking his fingers. Under the law he is unclean from the moment he touches it, and Numbers 6:9–12 sets out what a defiled Nazirite must do: shave his head, bring offerings, start the count again. He does none of it. He eats and keeps walking.

He gave some to them, and they ate. The second secret is worse than the first. Keeping quiet about the lion was pride or reticence; this is deception with a consequence. Two people who had ordered their lives around this vow are handed food from a carcass by their son, and eat, and are defiled, and do not know. His silence is what shows he knew. A man unaware of having done wrong would have told them where the honey came from; it is a marvellous story. He says nothing, because he knows exactly what he has done.

The same test for us. What you have to keep quiet is usually what you already know is wrong. The way out is the one Samson never took: say it to God, who promises to forgive what is confessed rather than covered (Psalm 32:5; 1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — A Riddle Nobody Could Answer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samson’s wedding becomes a contest he means to win and a betrayal he provokes. He holds a seven-day feast, and the town supplies thirty companions who look like a guard (vv. 10–11). He stakes sixty garments on a riddle no one could solve, because its answer is his secret lion (vv. 12–14). When the thirty threaten to burn his bride and her family, she weeps at him for the rest of the feast until he tells her, and she tells them (vv. 15–17). They answer just before sunset, and he accuses them of plowing with his heifer (v. 18). Here, in week one, is the method that will finally undo him in chapter 16.
verseByVerse.theology: The wedding becomes a contest Samson has rigged, and then a threat on his bride's life.
verseByVerse.examples: He survives the pressure here. He will not survive it in Delilah's house.

verseByVerse.quote: His father went down to the woman, and Samson prepared a feast there, for so the young men used to do. As soon as the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him. And Samson said to them, "Let me now put a riddle to you. If you can tell me what it is, within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes, but if you cannot tell me what it is, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes." And they said to him, "Put your riddle, that we may hear it." And he said to them, "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." And in three days they could not solve the riddle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At a seven-day wedding feast Samson stakes a fortune on a riddle no one could solve, because its answer is his own secret; without knowing it, he names the shape of the gospel, sweetness out of the strong.

Samson prepared a feast there. The Hebrew word, mishteh, is built on the verb “to drink”. A wedding feast customarily lasted seven days (compare Laban’s “complete the week of this one”, Genesis 29:27), hence the riddle’s deadline. The text does not say that Samson drank, and it is fair to say so. It says a Nazirite hosted a seven-day drinking feast in Philistine Timnah. Line his vow up against it: he has broken the rule about corpses outright and walked through the vineyards to host the drinking. Only the razor is still intact. Two of the three parts of the vow are compromised long before Delilah appears, and nobody has noticed, including him.

They brought thirty companions. These may be more than groomsmen. The phrasing is careful: “as soon as the people saw him,” they brought them. A Philistine town looks at a very large Israelite and decides he needs an escort. They look very like a guard, arranged on the spot.

Thirty linen garments. The stake is sixty garments, two for each man, far beyond what ordinary villagers could raise. Fine linen and changes of clothing were serious property, the sort of thing given as a reward or taken as spoil. He is proposing a wager thirty men cannot cover, at his own wedding, with his bride’s people.

Let me now put a riddle to you. It is a good line and a dishonest game. A riddle hides an answer in an image that a clever hearer can work out. This one cannot be worked out by anybody, because the answer is not an image at all but a private memory of a dead lion that only Samson has seen inside.

Out of the strong came something sweet. There is something in the riddle he cannot see and we can. He has made a joke out of sweetness coming from a killer, life coming out of a carcass. It is the one moment in his life when he says something larger than himself, and he uses it to win clothes off villagers. It is not a prophecy, and the lion is not a symbol. But Christians have long heard more in it than Samson meant, because the shape it names, food out of death and sweetness out of the strong, is the shape of the gospel: life for the world comes out of the death of the strongest one of all (John 6:51; 12:24).

A life lived for the thrill. Notice how seldom Samson is bored: a lion, a secret, a riddle, a wager nobody can cover. Søren Kierkegaard described a way of living he called the aesthetic, the life of someone who lives for the interesting moment and dreads above all to be bored. Such a person can be brilliant and magnetic, and Kierkegaard saw that underneath he is in despair, because he never gives himself to anything that could hold him once the excitement fades. Our culture has turned that life into an economy: the next trip, the next screen, the next relationship. Samson shows where it goes. A man who lives for the thrill cannot keep a vow, because a vow is the same tomorrow as today, and nothing is duller to him than that. The gospel does not answer him with a smaller, greyer life. It offers a joy deep enough to make faithfulness possible. Christ, “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2), kept his word all the way to death, and the joy he gives does not need the next novelty to stay alive.

verseByVerse.quote: On the fourth day they said to Samson's wife, "Entice your husband to tell us what the riddle is, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire. Have you invited us here to impoverish us?" And Samson's wife wept over him and said, "You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is." And he said to her, "Behold, I have not told my father nor my mother, and shall I tell you?" She wept before him the seven days that their feast lasted, and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him hard. Then she told the riddle to her people. And the men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" And he said to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Threatened with fire, Samson’s bride wears the secret out of him with tears, and when he loses the wager he lashes out at her: here, at his own wedding, is the very method that will later destroy him.

On the fourth day. By day four the wedding has turned into a hostage situation. “Have you invited us here to impoverish us?” is the complaint of men who know what sixty garments would cost them and suspect the bride’s family of setting them up. So they threaten to burn her alive, with her father’s household, unless she gets the answer. She is a girl caught between a husband she has known for days and a town that has promised to kill her. Whatever she does next, remember where she is standing.

You only hate me. Her weapon is tears and an accusation about love; his defence is a boast about secrecy. He does not say the riddle is not hers to have, only that he has not even told his parents, so why should she rank above them? It is the chapter’s third secret, produced as a trophy. He is proud of what he withholds.

On the seventh day he told her. He gives way, and the scene will happen again. Years later Delilah will say, “How can you say, ‘I love you,’ when your heart is not with me?” and the narrator will write, “when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death” (16:15–16). The same method in nearly the same words, on the same man. Nothing Delilah does will be new to him. He is shown the whole method in week one, at a cost of thirty lives, and walks into it again.

If you had not plowed with my heifer. They give the answer as two questions, a taunt in his own rhythm, minutes before the deadline. His reply is coarse, and it blames her: she is his heifer, and they plowed with her, as if she were their accomplice. It is an ugly thing to say of a woman in public at what was meant to be her wedding, and it is not even the right target. She was not in league with them. Thirty men threatened to burn her alive and she believed them, and the only reason she had anything to tell was that Samson told her. He has lost a wager he designed to be unloseable, and his instinct is that somebody else cheated.

Textual note. The standard Hebrew text of verse 15 reads “on the seventh day”. Some ancient translations read “the fourth day”, which the ESV follows because it fits the three days of verse 14 and the weeping through the rest of the feast in verse 17. Nothing in the story’s meaning turns on it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit’s power and Samson’s grudge meet in one verse, and the chapter ends in loss. The Spirit of the LORD rushes on him again, and he goes to Ashkelon, kills thirty men, and pays his debt with their clothes (v. 19). It is the first blow against the Philistines that 13:5 promised, struck in the middle of a private quarrel. He goes back to his father’s house in hot anger without his bride, and she is given to his best man (v. 20). Everyone has done what was right in his own eyes, and the cost falls on a woman the book never names.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the deliverance beginning, and it looks like a tantrum.
verseByVerse.examples: The wife he demanded is the one who pays.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men of the town and took their spoil and gave the garments to those who had told the riddle. In hot anger he went back to his father's house. And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of the LORD empowers Samson to strike the first blow against Israel’s oppressors, yet he strikes it in a private rage over a lost bet: God’s gifts prove God’s power, not the soundness of the man who carries them.

He went down to Ashkelon. Do not soften either half of the verse. “The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him,” the same phrase as with the lion. And what he does with it is walk more than twenty miles to a city on the coast, kill thirty men who had never heard his riddle and owed him nothing, strip their bodies, and carry the clothes back to settle a bet. The writer states both without embarrassment. The Spirit’s coming upon a man is not God’s endorsement of the man; it is God equipping him for a purpose that belongs to God. Ashkelon is the first blow of the deliverance announced in 13:5, and it is struck by a furious young man in the middle of a private grudge.

Gifts prove only God’s power. Do not build a doctrine of your own soundness on what God has done through you. Some will list mighty works done in his name on the last day and hear “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:22–23). Gifts prove God’s power. They prove nothing else.

In hot anger. The bleak comedy of it: the man who told his parents “Get her for me” and overrode them with “she is right in my eyes” is back in their house within days, in a temper, without the bride, having killed thirty strangers to pay for a joke.

Samson’s wife was given to his companion. She has been threatened with fire, used as a lever, publicly called a heifer, abandoned at her own wedding feast, and married off to one of the thirty. She is never named. Within a chapter she will be burned alive with her father, just as the thirty threatened, because of something else Samson did (15:6). Everyone in this chapter does what is right in his own eyes, and the woman nobody names pays for it. That is what the phrase costs when it is finally totalled up, and why the book keeps repeating it.

keyVerse.quote: His father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
keyVerse.note: This aside unlocks the whole Samson story. Nothing in the chapter is approved, yet nothing escapes God’s purpose: he works through a wilful man to begin rescuing a people who had stopped asking. It prepares us for the cross, where human wickedness and God’s saving plan meet in the same event.

14.reflection:
Samson’s reason for his choice is “she is right in my eyes” (v. 3), the phrase the book uses for the whole age (21:25). Where are you most tempted to let what pleases your own eyes overrule what God has said, especially in relationships?

Verse 4 says God was at work through a choice that was still wrong. How does that comfort you about past mistakes, and why must it never become an excuse for future ones?

Samson kept quiet about the lion and the honey because he knew what he had done (vv. 6, 9). What do you tend to keep hidden, and what would it look like to bring it into the light before God and a trusted friend?

Samson’s riddle speaks of sweetness coming out of the strong and food out of death (v. 14). How does that shape point us to Jesus, and how has his death become “food” for you?

15.title: Samson's Vengeance
15.text: <sup>1</sup>After some days, at the time of wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife with a young goat. And he said, "I will go in to my wife in the chamber." But her father would not allow him to go in.<sup>2</sup>And her father said, "I really thought that you utterly hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead."<sup>3</sup>And Samson said to them, "This time I shall be innocent in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm."<sup>4</sup>So Samson went and caught 300 foxes and took torches. And he turned them tail to tail and put a torch between each pair of tails.<sup>5</sup>And when he had set fire to the torches, he let the foxes go into the standing grain of the Philistines and set fire to the stacked grain and the standing grain, as well as the olive orchards.<sup>6</sup>Then the Philistines said, "Who has done this?" And they said, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife and given her to his companion." And the Philistines came up and burned her and her father with fire.<sup>7</sup>And Samson said to them, "If this is what you do, I swear I will be avenged on you, and after that I will quit."<sup>8</sup>And he struck them hip and thigh with a great blow, and he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.<sup>9</sup>Then the Philistines came up and encamped in Judah and made a raid on Lehi.<sup>10</sup>And the men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" They said, "We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us."<sup>11</sup>Then 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam, and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?" And he said to them, "As they did to me, so have I done to them."<sup>12</sup>And they said to him, "We have come down to bind you, that we may give you into the hands of the Philistines." And Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves."<sup>13</sup>They said to him, "No; we will only bind you and give you into their hands. We will surely not kill you." So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.<sup>14</sup>When he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire, and his bonds melted off his hands.<sup>15</sup>And he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and put out his hand and took it, and with it he struck 1,000 men.<sup>16</sup>And Samson said, "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey have I struck down a thousand men."<sup>17</sup>As soon as he had finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone out of his hand. And that place was called Ramath-lehi.<sup>18</sup>And he was very thirsty, and he called upon the LORD and said, "You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"<sup>19</sup>And God split open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water came out from it. And when he drank, his spirit returned, and he revived. Therefore the name of it was called En-hakkore; it is at Lehi to this day.<sup>20</sup>And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.
15.overview:
Where we are. Samson has walked out of his own wedding in a rage after killing thirty men in Ashkelon, and his bride has been given to his best man (14:19–20).

The message. Revenge has no stopping place, and a people at peace with its oppressor will hand over its deliverer; yet God still saves, and he hears the first humble cry of a man who has always relied on himself. Samson’s private feud escalates into burned fields, a burned woman and a slaughter, and Judah binds him for the Philistines. But the Spirit breaks the ropes, and when the victor is about to die of thirst, the LORD answers his prayer with water from the ground.

Why it was said. The first hearers needed to see how far Israel had sunk (see the introduction). Judah, the tribe of the promised sceptre, says, “Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us?” (v. 11). That one question explains why no one cried out: they had learned to live with it.

How the chapter makes its case. Samson returns to find his wife given away, and declares himself innocent in advance of any harm he does (vv. 1–3). He burns the Philistine harvest with foxes and torches; they burn his wife and her father; he strikes them down and hides in the rock of Etam (vv. 4–8). The Philistines invade Judah, and three thousand men of Judah bind Samson and hand him over (vv. 9–13). At Lehi the Spirit melts the ropes, and with a donkey’s jawbone he kills a thousand men and sings about himself (vv. 14–17). Then, desperately thirsty, he prays for the first time, God splits open the ground, and he revives; he judges Israel twenty years (vv. 18–20).

Where it leads. To Christ, by contrast and by pattern. The men of Judah bound their deliverer and gave him to the occupying power to keep the peace, as Jerusalem would cry, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15); but Samson broke the ropes, and Jesus let them hold, and died for those who handed him over. And Samson’s thirst points beyond itself: at Lehi God split the ground to save his servant, but at Calvary the Son said, “I thirst,” received no spring, and was pierced so that “blood and water” came out (John 19:28, 34), for all who come to him and drink (John 7:37).

For us. Do not appoint yourself judge in your own cause; leave vengeance to God. Ask where you have made peace with what Christ came to destroy. And when your strength runs out, call on the LORD: he gives water to people who have done nothing to deserve it.
15.theology:
Marking your own paper. A wronged person who decides alone that his revenge is justified is grading his own work. Scripture takes the pen away, because we are not the judge. The Judge has already dealt with our own wrongs at the cross, and his Spirit makes it possible to leave the rest with him.

The chain that killed her. An unwinnable riddle, a threat of fire, a betrayal made to escape it, an insult, an abandonment, a burnt harvest, and at last the fire itself. Every link is someone doing what was right in his own eyes, and the person who dies is the one with the fewest choices. Sin is never as private as the sinner supposes.

Judah's quiet sin. Samson's failures are loud, and you can see each one coming. Judah's is sensible, collective and unremarkable: three thousand reasonable men who had made their peace with the thing God sent a deliverer to destroy. It is the easier sin to miss, and the more common.

Power without holiness. The strength keeps coming while the vow lies in tatters, because it was always the Spirit's and never the man's. That is mercy, and it is also a trap: a man who goes on succeeding while disobeying concludes that the disobedience does not matter. Chapter 16 is where he finds out that it does.

The spring of him who called. God gives water to a man who has earned none, without a word of rebuke. Many Christians have set this thirst beside another: the thirst Christ endured on the cross (John 19:28-34), which is why the thirsty may now come to him and drink.
15.examples:
Then: A deliverer burned a nation's harvest to settle a private score and got a woman killed by it; his own tribe mustered three thousand men to arrest him rather than fight the occupier; he killed a thousand of the enemy with a dead donkey's jawbone and sang about himself; and then he got thirsty, prayed for the first time the book records, and God gave him water without one word of reproach.

Now: Watch for the two sins in this chapter, because they are opposites and most of us lean towards one of them. Samson's is the private verdict: deciding alone that what you are about to do is justified because of what was done to you. Judah's is the settled arrangement: making your peace with the thing God means to destroy, and coming to resent whoever disturbs it. Then take En-hakkore with you. When you come to pray after a day you are not proud of, the spring is not named for the deserving. It is named for the man who called.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samson’s grievance turns into a self-issued licence for revenge. After some days, at wheat harvest, he comes back with a young goat, expecting to resume the marriage he had walked out on (v. 1). Her father bars the door: he thought Samson hated her and gave her to the best man, and he anxiously offers the younger sister instead (v. 2). Samson’s answer is a verdict passed on himself before he acts: “This time I shall be innocent in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm” (v. 3). He has made himself accuser, judge and executioner in his own cause, and nobody, least of all God, has been consulted.
verseByVerse.theology: Samson builds a legal case for a revenge he has already decided on.
verseByVerse.examples: The grievance is real: his wife has been given to another man. But it became possible because he walked out of his own wedding feast in a temper (14:19-20).

verseByVerse.quote: After some days, at the time of wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife with a young goat. And he said, "I will go in to my wife in the chamber." But her father would not allow him to go in. And her father said, "I really thought that you utterly hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead." And Samson said to them, "This time I shall be innocent in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finding his wife given to another man, Samson declares himself innocent of whatever harm he is about to do: he has made himself judge in his own case.

Samson went to visit his wife. He arrives with a young goat as a present and an assumption. He has sent no apology or message since he walked out in a rage. He comes to her father’s house, probably because this was a form of marriage in which the wife went on living with her family and the husband visited her, which is why her father still decides who may go in to her. Samson’s temper has cooled, and he expects the door to open.

I really thought that you utterly hated her. The father is frightened, and not unreasonable. His daughter’s bridegroom lost a wager at his own wedding, called her a heifer in front of the town, disappeared, and was next heard of killing thirty men in Ashkelon. Anybody would have thought so. So he did what a father in that position did: he gave her to the best man rather than leave her abandoned. Now, faced with the man himself at the door, he offers the younger daughter, which shows how badly he wants this settled without violence.

This time I shall be innocent. Samson pronounces himself not guilty before he has done anything, and that shows how his conscience works. This is not blind fury but reasoning in advance, with a formula. The words “this time” imply he knows Ashkelon was another matter, and they tell him that what follows is permitted. He has drawn up the charge, heard the case, delivered the verdict and licensed the sentence, filling every role himself.

Leave it to the wrath of God. The habit is not confined to strong men with a grudge. The most dangerous thing we can do with a wrong done to us is to establish, quietly and alone, that our response is now justified. The reasoning is always convincing, because the one judging it is the one who made it. Scripture takes the pen out of our hand: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19). Revenge is forbidden not because wrongs should go unpunished, but because we are not the judge. God is, and at the cross he has shown that he deals with wrongs justly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — Foxes, Fire, and a Woman Burned
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every act of revenge demands another, and the innocent pay. Samson patiently catches three hundred foxes, ties torches between their tails, and sends them through the Philistines’ harvest and olive orchards (vv. 4–5). The Philistines ask who did it, hear the reason, and burn his wife and her father alive, the very fate she had betrayed his riddle to avoid (v. 6). Samson swears one more act of vengeance “and after that I will quit” (v. 7), strikes them “hip and thigh”, and goes to hide in the cleft of the rock of Etam (v. 8). The feud is now open war, and its first victim was the woman with the fewest choices.
verseByVerse.theology: Revenge answers revenge, and the fire threatened at the wedding comes at last.
verseByVerse.examples: The victims are farmers and a frightened young woman, not soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: So Samson went and caught 300 foxes and took torches. And he turned them tail to tail and put a torch between each pair of tails. And when he had set fire to the torches, he let the foxes go into the standing grain of the Philistines and set fire to the stacked grain and the standing grain, as well as the olive orchards. Then the Philistines said, "Who has done this?" And they said, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife and given her to his companion." And the Philistines came up and burned her and her father with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samson’s calculated revenge destroys the Philistine farmers’ harvest, and they answer by burning his wife and her father alive: the chain of vengeance ends on the one person with the fewest choices.

Samson went and caught 300 foxes. Three hundred animals caught alive, one at a time: this is not a flash of rage but long, patient trapping, carried out cold. Verse 1 told us the season, wheat harvest, when the fields stand dry and ready.

The stacked grain and the standing grain. Three things burn, and each loss reaches further. The stacked grain is what is already cut, this year’s food. The standing grain is the rest of the same year’s crop. The olive orchards are not one year’s loss at all: an olive tree takes years to come into bearing and goes on bearing for generations, so burning the orchards takes food from children not yet born. And those who lose are the farmers of the Philistine plain, not the lords of the five cities or the men at his wedding.

They burned her and her father with fire. Turn back to 14:15. The threat to burn her and her father’s house is why she wept at him for seven days and gave away the riddle; it is the reason for everything Samson took as treachery. She was trying not to be burned alive, and now she is, by the Philistines, exactly as the thirty had promised. What finally brought it on her was not her betrayal but Samson’s revenge for losing her.

Follow the chain. The writer means us to. Samson designs an unwinnable riddle; they threaten her with fire; she gives them the answer; he calls her a heifer and abandons her; her father marries her to someone else; he burns their harvest for it; they burn her for that. Every link is a man doing what was right in his own eyes, and the one who dies is the person who had the fewest choices of anybody in the story. She has no name in this book. She is “Samson’s wife”, then “the Timnite’s” daughter, and then ash.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samson said to them, "If this is what you do, I swear I will be avenged on you, and after that I will quit." And he struck them hip and thigh with a great blow, and he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samson promises that one more act of vengeance will end it, strikes the Philistines hard, and then hides in a cleft of rock: a feud has no natural stopping place.

After that I will quit. It is the oldest sentence in the history of grudges, and it has never once been true. A feud does not end when one side is satisfied, because the other side is now owed as well. His purpose has also quietly changed. In verse 3 the harm was to be his compensation; now it is his answer to their answer. He is no longer setting a price; he is taking a turn.

Hip and thigh. The phrase means that he struck them comprehensively, a crushing blow.

The cleft of the rock of Etam. Then the judge of Israel, at the height of his strength, hides in a crevice in the hills of Judah, and the next people to come looking for him are his own countrymen.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says literally that he struck them “leg upon thigh”. It is plainly an idiom for a thorough, devastating attack, and English “hip and thigh” has come from it, but its origin is not known: suggestions include a wrestling hold or bodies heaped on one another. The general sense is certain; the picture behind it is not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — Judah Comes Out Three Thousand Strong
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah has made peace with its oppressor, and so it treats its deliverer as the problem. The Philistines camp in Judah and raid Lehi, and the men of Judah ask politely why; they are told the army has come for Samson (vv. 9–10). Three thousand men of Judah march, not against the Philistines, but to the rock of Etam, where they complain, “Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us?” (v. 11). Samson replies with his private reckoning and asks only that they will not kill him themselves. They bind him with two new ropes and bring him up from the rock to be handed over (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Here at last is the explanation of the missing cry at 13:1.
verseByVerse.examples: The tribe of the coming king acts as the occupier's police.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Philistines came up and encamped in Judah and made a raid on Lehi. And the men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" They said, "We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us." Then 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam, and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?" And he said to them, "As they did to me, so have I done to them." And they said to him, "We have come down to bind you, that we may give you into the hands of the Philistines." And Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves." They said to him, "No; we will only bind you and give you into their hands. We will surely not kill you." So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rather than fight the Philistine army camped in their land, three thousand men of Judah arrest their own deliverer and hand him over bound, because they have made their peace with being ruled.

Why have you come up against us? An occupying army camps inside Judah, and Judah’s response is not to muster or to cry to the LORD, as their fathers had done, but to ask a polite question. Told the trouble, they organise the arrest.

Then 3,000 men of Judah went down. Judah can put three thousand men into the field within days. Gideon beat Midian with three hundred; Shamgar killed six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad (3:31). Three thousand armed men of Judah went out in force and marched in the wrong direction. Consider who they are: the tribe God named when Israel asked who should go up first against the Canaanites (1:1–2), the tribe Judah that Jacob called a lion and promised the sceptre (Genesis 49:9–10), the tribe of David and, at last, of Christ. That tribe is out here as the occupier’s police force.

Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? Here is why forty years produced no cry. Judah is not in anguish. It has looked at the occupation, judged it liveable, and is angry with the one man who will not leave it alone: “What then is this that you have done to us?” It is as if the trouble in the land were Samson. Their sin is quiet and sensible, shared by three thousand men who all thought they were being reasonable. They had made their peace with what God had sent a man to destroy.

As they did to me. Samson’s defence is the same private reckoning as in verse 3. He surrenders and asks only that they will not kill him themselves. That is all he expects from his own people, and they give him exactly that and nothing more: bound with two new ropes, he is to be given “into the hands of the Philistines”. The man God raised up to begin saving Israel from the Philistines is delivered to them by his countrymen, who fear what the rulers will do if they refuse. Centuries later, at another handing over, the words would be, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). A people surrendering its deliverer to the occupying power to keep the peace is older than Pilate.

The occupation we have learned to live with. C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, pictured this world as enemy-occupied territory, and Christianity as the news that the rightful king has landed in disguise and is calling his people to resist. The men of Judah show why that news is not always welcome. Occupations stop feeling like chains once you are used to them, and the modern ones are mostly comfortable: a career that owns our evenings, a phone that owns our attention, an appetite we have stopped fighting, an anxiety we have learned to call normal. We have adjusted. And when anyone threatens the arrangement, God included, our first instinct is Judah’s: “What then is this that you have done to us?” That is often why Jesus offends people who have nothing against religion in general: he will not leave the arrangement alone. But see what each deliverer did when his own people bound him and handed him over. Samson broke the ropes. Jesus let them hold, and went to the cross for the very people who surrendered him, so that the powers they had made peace with could be broken for them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — Heaps upon Heaps, and Then a Drink
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God saves by his Spirit, and then teaches the strong man to pray. At Lehi the Philistines shout in triumph, the Spirit rushes on Samson, and the ropes melt like burning flax (v. 14). With a fresh jawbone of a donkey he kills a thousand men and sings a punning two-line song in which God does not appear (vv. 15–17). Then he is desperately thirsty, and for the first time he calls upon the LORD, crediting God with “this great salvation” (v. 18). God splits open the hollow place at Lehi, water flows, and his spirit revives; the spring is named for his cry (v. 19). He judges Israel twenty years, but still “in the days of the Philistines” (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The song and the prayer are two verses apart and say opposite things. Thirst taught him in an afternoon what a thousand dead men had not.
verseByVerse.examples: God's answer to a flawed prayer is water, not a lecture.

verseByVerse.quote: When he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire, and his bonds melted off his hands. And he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and put out his hand and took it, and with it he struck 1,000 men. And Samson said, "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey have I struck down a thousand men." As soon as he had finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone out of his hand. And that place was called Ramath-lehi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of the LORD melts Samson’s bonds and gives him victory over a thousand men, but his victory song celebrates only himself and his weapon.

As flax that has caught fire. The Philistines came shouting, sure it was over. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him, and the writer’s image is exact: two new ropes, strong enough to satisfy three thousand men, go the way dry flax goes when a spark touches it. They are not snapped but “melted off his hands”.

A fresh jawbone of a donkey. “Fresh” means recently dead; an old sun-dried bone would have shattered. So it is newly part of a carcass, and from a donkey, an unclean animal, and Samson picks it up without hesitation.

The vow broken, the strength still given. He is a Nazirite, forbidden to go near a dead body (Numbers 6:6–7). He has now handled a corpse to get honey and a corpse to get a weapon, and hosted a seven-day drinking feast in between, and the strength keeps coming. The power never depended on Samson’s faithfulness: it was the Spirit of the LORD, rushing on a man in no condition to deserve it. That is a mercy, and also a trap, because a man who keeps succeeding while disobeying concludes that the disobedience does not matter. Chapter 16 is where he finds out that it does.

Heaps upon heaps. His victory song is a pun, and it has no God in it. The Hebrew word for donkey and the word for heap sound almost identical, so the line runs something like “with the jaw of an ass I have assed them in heaps”. It is clever, and it is two lines long, and its subject is a jawbone and the man swinging it. Set it beside the other victory song in this book. Deborah and Barak sang for thirty-one verses, calling Israel to “bless the LORD!” (5:2), and their song is about him from end to end: his marching from Seir, the stars fighting from heaven, his people offering themselves willingly (5:2–5, 20). Samson sings two lines about his weapon.

Ramath-lehi. The place is named after the bone, “the height of the jawbone”. The map now carries the memory of the weapon; the next verses will put another name on the same ground, and that one will remember something else entirely.

Uncertain wording. The middle words of verse 16 are a pun whose exact sense is uncertain. The ESV takes the repeated word as “heap”, giving “heaps upon heaps”; others link it with the word for donkey and translate along the lines of “I have made donkeys of them”. Either way it is wordplay on the donkey’s jawbone, and the boast is the same.
verseByVerse.note: “Ramath-lehi” means “the hill of the jawbone” (ESV note). A pun: the Hebrew words for “donkey” and “heap” are spelled alike, hamor.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was very thirsty, and he called upon the LORD and said, "You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?" And God split open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water came out from it. And when he drank, his spirit returned, and he revived. Therefore the name of it was called En-hakkore; it is at Lehi to this day. And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of his strength, Samson prays for the first time, owning that the victory was God’s salvation, and God answers his thirsty, imperfect prayer with water from the ground.

He was very thirsty. A thousand men lie dead, and Samson is beaten by thirst. The man who tore a lion cannot get through the afternoon. It is the first thing in his life he has not been able to do for himself, and it is what finally brings him to prayer.

You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant. This is Samson’s first recorded prayer. Everything until now has been demand, riddle, insult, threat and song, and this is better theology than anything else he has said. Not “I have struck down a thousand men”, as he sang two verses ago: now the victory is God’s gift. And “your servant” is the first humble word out of his mouth in three chapters.

Shall I now die of thirst? Be honest about the rest of it. The second half is a complaint with an edge: there is concern for his own dignity in it, and a hint that it would reflect badly on God to let his servant end like this. It is not a model prayer. It is a real one, from a man who has just discovered he is not self-sufficient and is not sure he likes it.

God split open the hollow place. God does not lecture him; he splits open the ground. There is no rebuke, no interrogation about the vineyards, the carcasses or the song. He asked for water and water came, at once, from the ground where he stood. “His spirit returned, and he revived”: the phrase is used of someone brought back from the point of collapse.

En-hakkore. The place gets a second name, after the cry rather than the weapon: “the spring of him who called”. It is not the spring of the faithful Nazirite but the spring of the man who called, and he had that same day broken his vow on a corpse, killed a thousand men in a private feud, and sung a song without God in it. He called, and God gave him water.

The split rock and another thirst. Israel had drunk from a split rock before, in the wilderness, and Paul says “the Rock was Christ” (Exodus 17:6; 1 Corinthians 10:4). Many Christians have set one more thirst beside this one, as an echo rather than the meaning of Lehi. At Lehi a strong man cried out that he was dying of thirst, and God split open the ground and he revived. At Calvary another man said, “I thirst,” and no spring came; he was given sour wine on a sponge, and he died (John 19:28–30). Then a soldier pierced his side, “and at once there came out blood and water” (John 19:34). At Lehi God split open the ground to save his servant. At Golgotha God let his Son be pierced to save his enemies, and the water came out of him. He had said what he intended to do with it: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).

In the days of the Philistines. The phrase sums up his whole time as judge: after twenty years, these are still the Philistines’ days. Ehud gave the land eighty years of rest and Deborah forty; Samson’s twenty end with the enemy where they were when he started. That is what the angel said: he would “begin to save Israel” (13:5). God announced the limit before the man was conceived, and the limit held. The full deliverance would need another.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 19 says God split open “the hollow place that is in Lehi”, and since Lehi means “jaw”, it can also be read “the hollow place that is in the jaw”. Older translations took it that way, as if the water came from the jawbone itself. Modern translations, including the ESV, take Lehi as the place name, which fits the naming of a spring that is “at Lehi to this day”.
verseByVerse.note: “En-hakkore” means “the spring of him who called” (ESV note).

keyVerse.quote: And he was very thirsty, and he called upon the LORD and said, “You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?”
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the chapter and Samson’s first recorded prayer. The man who sang about himself now calls the victory God’s salvation and himself God’s servant, and God answers a thirsty, imperfect cry at once. It shows the grace that runs beneath the whole Samson story.

15.reflection:
Samson declares himself innocent before he takes his revenge (v. 3). Where are you tempted to settle in your own mind that your response to a wrong is justified? How does Romans 12:19 change that?

Follow the chain of revenge in verses 1–8. Who pays the highest price, and what does that teach about where doing “what was right in his own eyes” leads?

The men of Judah had made their peace with Philistine rule and treated Samson as the problem (v. 11). What “occupations” have Christians today learned to live with, and how might Jesus be disturbing an arrangement in your life?

Samson’s first prayer came only when his strength ran out, and God answered with water (vv. 18–19). How does Jesus’ thirst on the cross and his invitation in John 7:37 speak to you when you are at the end of yourself?

16.title: Samson and Delilah
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute, and he went in to her.<sup>2</sup>The Gazites were told, "Samson has come here." And they surrounded the place and set an ambush for him all night at the gate of the city. They kept quiet all night, saying, "Let us wait till the light of the morning; then we will kill him."<sup>3</sup>But Samson lay till midnight, and at midnight he arose and took hold of the doors of the gate of the city and the two posts, and pulled them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that is in front of Hebron.<sup>4</sup>After this he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.<sup>5</sup>And the lords of the Philistines came up to her and said to her, "Seduce him, and see where his great strength lies, and by what means we may overpower him, that we may bind him to humble him. And we will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver."<sup>6</sup>So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me where your great strength lies, and how you might be bound, that one could subdue you."<sup>7</sup>Samson said to her, "If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>8</sup>Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them.<sup>9</sup>Now she had men lying in ambush in an inner chamber. And she said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings, as a thread of flax snaps when it touches the fire. So the secret of his strength was not known.<sup>10</sup>Then Delilah said to Samson, "Behold, you have mocked me and told me lies. Please tell me how you might be bound."<sup>11</sup>And he said to her, "If they bind me with new ropes that have not been used, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>12</sup>So Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And the men lying in ambush were in an inner chamber. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like a thread.<sup>13</sup>Then Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten it tight with the pin, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>14</sup>So while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web. And she made them tight with the pin and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he awoke from his sleep and pulled away the pin, the loom, and the web.<sup>15</sup>And she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and you have not told me where your great strength lies."<sup>16</sup>And when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death.<sup>17</sup>And he told her all his heart, and said to her, "A razor has never come upon my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If my head is shaved, then my strength will leave me, and I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>18</sup>When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called the lords of the Philistines, saying, "Come up again, for he has told me all his heart." Then the lords of the Philistines came up to her and brought the money in their hands.<sup>19</sup>She made him sleep on her knees. And she called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to torment him, and his strength left him.<sup>20</sup>And she said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And he awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as at other times and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him.<sup>21</sup>And the Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes and brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles. And he ground at the mill in the prison.<sup>22</sup>But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.<sup>23</sup>Now the lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to rejoice, and they said, "Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand."<sup>24</sup>And when the people saw him, they praised their god. For they said, "Our god has given our enemy into our hand, the ravager of our country, who has killed many of us."<sup>25</sup>And when their hearts were merry, they said, "Call Samson, that he may entertain us."
