So they called Samson out of the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.<sup>26</sup>And Samson said to the young man who held him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean against them."<sup>27</sup>Now the house was full of men and women. All the lords of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about 3,000 men and women, who looked on while Samson entertained.<sup>28</sup>Then Samson called to the LORD and said, "O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes."<sup>29</sup>And Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the house rested, and he leaned his weight against them, his right hand on the one and his left hand on the other.<sup>30</sup>And Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he bowed with all his strength, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it. So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.<sup>31</sup>Then his brothers and all his family came down and took him and brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.
16.overview:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of the last judge in the book’s great cycle. Samson has judged Israel twenty years “in the days of the Philistines” (15:20), his vow broken in all but one point, his strength apparently untouchable.

The message. Sin destroys slowly and then suddenly, and the strongest people are the ones most sure they can stop whenever they like; yet God does not abandon his glory or his servant. Samson gives away the last of his vow and does not even notice that the LORD has left him. But in the darkness of the mill his hair begins to grow, and when the Philistines credit Dagon with victory over the God of Israel, a blind man asks to be remembered, and is heard.

Why it was said. Israel’s deliverers had grown steadily worse, and the people with them (see the introduction). The first hearers are shown where doing what is right in your own eyes ends: in blindness, slavery and a mill. They are also shown that God will defend his own name, even when his people and his judge have disgraced it.

How the chapter makes its case. Samson visits a prostitute in Gaza and carries off the city gate, with no mention of the Spirit (vv. 1–3). Delilah, bribed by the Philistine lords, asks openly for his secret; three times he lies, three times she tries to have him taken, and he stays (vv. 4–14). Worn down, he tells her all his heart; she has him shaved, and he wakes not knowing that the LORD has left him. Blinded, he grinds at the mill in Gaza, but his hair begins to grow (vv. 15–22). Brought out for sport at Dagon’s festival, he prays to be remembered, brings down the house, and is buried in his father’s tomb (vv. 23–31).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by sharp contrast. Like Samson, Jesus was betrayed for silver, seized, mocked as entertainment, blindfolded and struck, and achieved more by his death than by his life. But Samson prayed, “Let me die with the Philistines,” and brought judgment down on his enemies; Jesus prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), and took judgment on himself for his enemies. Samson’s “Remember me” is echoed by a dying thief, to whom Jesus promised paradise (Luke 23:42–43).

For us. Do not measure your standing with God by whether your gifts still work, and do not play with what you think you can put down at will. If you are already at the mill, take heart: God is not finished with people who are finished with themselves. Call on him to remember you, and trust the Saviour who was forsaken so that you will not be.
16.theology:
He did not know. This is the heart of the whole Samson cycle. The strength was never in the hair, which was only the sign of a vow; every display of strength is credited to the Spirit (14:6, 14:19, 15:14). What Samson lost was the LORD, and he lost him without noticing, because he had gone on succeeding for years while the vow came apart.

He was not deceived. Delilah states her purpose to his face and carries it out in front of him before he gives anything away. This is not a trap sprung on an innocent but a man who no longer believes in consequences, and whose lies drift steadily towards the truth.

Why the last scene happens. Not because Samson has earned anything, but because God will not let Dagon have his glory. The hair growing back is a sign restored where nobody is watching, on a man who can ask for nothing, and that is the sort of place God begins again.

Heard, though the prayer is mixed. Samson's last prayer is about his own eyes, and God answers it. That is why Hebrews lists him among those made strong out of weakness (Heb. 11:32-34).

Where the parallel breaks. Samson's death is a flawed and partial pattern of the deliverer who conquers by dying, and it is clearest where it fails: he pulled the house down on his enemies, and Christ let the judgment fall on himself.
16.examples:
Then: A man who had watched a woman try three times to hand him to his enemies went back a fourth, handed over the vow that had marked him for God since before he was born, woke expecting to be strong as usual, and found that the LORD had left him, and he had not known it. He lost the eyes that had led him everywhere, ground grain in the dark, and prayed twice that we are told of, once for water and once for strength, and was heard both times.

Now: The warning is v. 20, and it is not mainly about lust. Ask whether anything in your life is running on momentum: the gift working, the reputation holding, the ministry going on, while faithfulness quietly comes apart in private. Where the vow has come apart, Christ kept faith perfectly in our place, and his faithfulness is counted to all who come back to him (Rom. 5:19). The comfort is v. 22, and it is for people who have already fallen: the hair grew back where nobody could see it, on a man who could not have asked for it, and God was not finished with him. If you can still say remember me, you are not past the point Samson prayed from.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samson’s last free act is magnificent, pointless and godless. He goes deep into Philistine country to Gaza, sees a prostitute and goes in to her (v. 1). The city locks the gate and waits for daylight to kill him (v. 2). At midnight he rises, tears up the doors of the gate with its posts and bar, and carries them on his shoulders to the hill in front of Hebron, in Judah (v. 3). Here, as with the foxes and the slaughter that followed (15:4–8), the narrator does not mention the Spirit of the LORD. The strength is still there, but Samson is now using it for his own amusement, and his eyes are leading him just as they did at Timnah.
verseByVerse.theology: Samson leaves the enemy capital standing open, as a joke on his way home from a brothel.
verseByVerse.examples: It is a magnificent feat, and God's name is nowhere near it.

verseByVerse.quote: Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute, and he went in to her. The Gazites were told, "Samson has come here." And they surrounded the place and set an ambush for him all night at the gate of the city. They kept quiet all night, saying, "Let us wait till the light of the morning; then we will kill him." But Samson lay till midnight, and at midnight he arose and took hold of the doors of the gate of the city and the two posts, and pulled them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that is in front of Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samson walks into the enemy’s chief city for a prostitute and then carries off its gate in contempt, a feat of strength with no mention of the Spirit and no purpose but his own.

Samson went to Gaza. Gaza was the greatest of the five Philistine cities, and the judge of Israel goes there alone, deep into enemy country, for this. The verb is the one that has run through his whole story: he “saw”. He saw the woman at Timnah; he sees this one. Twenty years of judging have not touched the eyes. The text offers nothing to excuse it: no Spirit rushing, no word that God was seeking an opportunity. Just a man, a city and a purchase.

Let us wait till the light of the morning. The whole city knows quickly, and they are sensible about it. They do not attack him in the dark; they lock the only way out and wait for daylight, when they can see what they are fighting. It is good planning against a man they have every reason to fear.

The doors of the gate of the city. He does not break out; he takes the door with him. A city gate was the strongest thing a town possessed: massive doors hung on posts set into the wall, barred at night. It was also where the elders sat and cases were heard, as when Boaz went to the gate to settle a legal matter (Ruth 4:1). The gate was the city’s strength and authority in one structure, and Gaza wakes to find a hole in its front wall.

No Spirit this time. Notice what the writer leaves out. Every other feat has the clause attached: the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him at the lion (14:6), at Ashkelon (14:19), at Lehi (15:14). Here, nothing. Samson is doing this on his own account, for his own amusement, and the narrator declines to put God’s name anywhere near it.

The hill that is in front of Hebron. He puts in the destination instead. Hebron is in Judah, the tribe that had just come down three thousand strong to tie Samson up and hand him to the Philistines (15:11–13). So the gates of the enemy city are dumped on the doorstep of the men who would not fight. It is a magnificent, pointless, contemptuous act, and it is the last free thing he does.

Uncertain wording. “In front of Hebron” could mean on a hill near Hebron itself, nearly forty miles away and a long climb from the coastal plain into the hill country, or on a hill nearer Gaza that faces towards Hebron. The Hebrew allows both. Most take the first; the insult to Judah stands either way.
verseByVerse.note: Gaza to Hebron is about 40 miles, uphill.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–14 — A Game He Thought He Could Win
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samson plays with the one thing that can destroy him, sure he can stop whenever he chooses. He loves Delilah, and the five Philistine lords offer her a fortune to find the secret of his strength so they can bind and humble him (vv. 4–5). She asks him outright (v. 6). Three times he lies: fresh bowstrings, new ropes, his seven locks woven into a loom. Three times she does exactly what he says, with men waiting in an inner room, and cries, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” Each time he breaks free (vv. 7–14). He has watched her try to betray him, and he stays. Each escape teaches him the wrong lesson, and the third answer is already about his hair.
verseByVerse.theology: Samson plays a game he is sure he cannot lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Sin that is managed rather than killed keeps moving closer.

verseByVerse.quote: After this he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah. And the lords of the Philistines came up to her and said to her, "Seduce him, and see where his great strength lies, and by what means we may overpower him, that we may bind him to humble him. And we will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samson loves Delilah, and the rulers of all five Philistine cities pay her a fortune to find the secret of his strength so they can bind and humble him.

After this he loved a woman. This is the first time the book says Samson loved anyone; of the girl at Timnah it said only that she was right in his eyes.

Whose name was Delilah. Delilah is also the only woman in Samson’s story who is named. His mother is “the woman”. His wife is “Samson’s wife”, then “the Timnite’s” daughter. The woman in Gaza is “a prostitute”. The one who is named is the one who destroys him.

The Valley of Sorek. It runs down from the hills to the plain, past Zorah where he was born. He has not gone far: he is in the borderland he grew up in, and so is she.

The lords of the Philistines. The Philistines had five cities, Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath, and all five lords make the journey to a woman’s house in a border valley because one Israelite is more than their army can handle.

We will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver. Eleven hundred pieces each from five lords is some five and a half thousand shekels of silver, a fortune several times over, offered to a woman who evidently did not need long to decide. Money has bought betrayal before and since. Judas took thirty pieces of silver for the Son of God, a fraction of this, and the smallness of that sum is part of its horror (Matthew 26:15). What Delilah’s price shows is that the Philistines had learned, over twenty years, that Samson could not be beaten by force, but could be beaten through a woman.

That we may bind him to humble him. Read their instructions carefully, because she follows them to the letter and he watches her do it: find where the strength lies, find how to overpower him, bind him “to humble him”. They do not say kill him. They want him brought low, and in the end they get exactly that: blind, shackled, grinding grain, and brought out to be laughed at.
verseByVerse.note: Eleven hundred shekels from each lord was a huge sum: over 25 pounds of silver each.

verseByVerse.quote: So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me where your great strength lies, and how you might be bound, that one could subdue you." Samson said to her, "If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, then I shall become weak and be like any other man." Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them. Now she had men lying in ambush in an inner chamber. And she said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings, as a thread of flax snaps when it touches the fire. So the secret of his strength was not known. Then Delilah said to Samson, "Behold, you have mocked me and told me lies. Please tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If they bind me with new ropes that have not been used, then I shall become weak and be like any other man." So Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And the men lying in ambush were in an inner chamber. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like a thread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Delilah asks openly how Samson can be subdued and twice tries to hand him to the Philistines, and he knows it, lies, and stays: he believes he can play with danger and walk away whenever he likes.

Please tell me where your great strength lies. She does not disguise it at all: no pretext, no clever indirection. It is the lords’ instruction repeated to his face almost word for word. And he knows what she is asking. Note who appears in his answer: “If they bind me.” Nobody has told him there is a “they”. He has worked it out, says so, and plays on.

The Philistines are upon you, Samson! So now he has seen it done. She got the bowstrings from somewhere, so she is in contact with them. She tied him up while he lay there and let her. There were armed men in the inner room. And she shouted the alarm that was meant to be the last thing he heard.

You have mocked me and told me lies. He snapped the strings and stayed. Her complaint is breathtaking: she has just tried to hand him to his enemies, and her grievance is his dishonesty. She reproaches him for not cooperating in his own destruction, and he accepts the reproach as reasonable.

New ropes that have not been used. His second answer is what Judah used on him at the rock of Etam (15:13), and those ropes came off at Lehi like burning flax. He is naming a method that has already failed on him. He is not even trying to be plausible; he is enjoying it.

He is not tricked. The chapter is often told as though Samson were charmed into giving his secret away without realising. He is not tricked. He has been told her purpose, watched her carry it out twice, heard the alarm with men waiting in the next room, and he goes back for a third round. He believes he can hold something lethal and put it down whenever he chooses. He has survived so much for so long that he has stopped believing in consequences, and every escape has taught him the wrong lesson. That is how sin destroys strong people: it waits while they prove to themselves, over and over, that they can handle it, and the proof is the trap. “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12).

Why do we think we can stop whenever we like? Because we have been taught that freedom means keeping our options open: I am in charge, and I can always choose differently tomorrow. Samson believed exactly that, and so does nearly everyone at the start of an addiction, an affair or a habit of small dishonesty. Augustine knew better from the inside. In his Confessions he described how a twisted desire, indulged, became a habit, and how a habit not resisted became a necessity, until his own will had been forged into a chain he could not break. Each link was a choice; together they were a prison. That is why the gospel does not simply tell strong people to try harder. Samson’s strength was never his safety; it was what made him careless. The freedom the Bible offers comes from outside us: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36). The first step out of Delilah’s house is the admission Samson never made until the mill: that we cannot put this down by ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten it tight with the pin, then I shall become weak and be like any other man." So while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web. And she made them tight with the pin and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he awoke from his sleep and pulled away the pin, the loom, and the web.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samson’s third lie brings his hair into the game: he has moved from things unconnected with his vow to the one thing that is, and he shows Delilah where to look.

The seven locks of my head. Bowstrings and ropes had nothing to do with him. The seven locks of his head are still a lie, but a lie built out of the truth, and she now knows the hair is somewhere in this.

While he slept. The strongest man alive lies asleep while a woman who has twice tried to have him taken weaves his hair, the sign that he is set apart for God, into her loom. This is the shape of every gradual fall. He is not being dragged; he is drifting inward one concession at a time, and each feels small because it is only slightly worse than the one before. Nobody gives away what matters most all at once. He gives away lesser things first, finds he has survived, and goes a step further.

Textual note. The standard Hebrew text of verses 13–14 is shorter and seems to have lost a line, probably because a copyist’s eye jumped between two similar phrases. The ESV restores the missing words (from “and fasten it tight” in verse 13 to “wove them into the web” in verse 14) from an early translation. The story is the same either way.

Uncertain wording. Exactly how the loom was set up, and what the “web” and the “pin” were, is not certain: the pin was probably the wooden peg or beater used to fix the woven threads tight. The picture is clear enough: his hair is woven into the cloth on the loom, and he wakes and tears the whole thing away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The vow is given away, the LORD departs unnoticed, and in the darkness God begins again. Delilah presses him day after day until he tells her all his heart: he is a Nazirite to God from the womb (vv. 15–17). She sends for the lords and their silver, lulls him to sleep on her knees, and has his head shaved (vv. 18–19). He wakes expecting to shake himself free “as at other times”, but he did not know that the LORD had left him (v. 20). The Philistines gouge out his eyes and set him grinding at the mill in Gaza (v. 21). Then one word turns the story: “But the hair of his head began to grow again” (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The razor only finished what twenty years of small surrenders had begun.
verseByVerse.examples: Samson tells the truth at last, and it costs him everything.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and you have not told me where your great strength lies." And when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death. And he told her all his heart, and said to her, "A razor has never come upon my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If my head is shaved, then my strength will leave me, and I shall become weak and be like any other man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worn down by Delilah’s daily pressure, Samson tells her all his heart, and what he hands over is not a fact about hair but his vow to God, the last thing in his life that belonged to God.

How can you say, ‘I love you’? Go back to 14:16: “You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is.” That was his bride at Timnah, years before: the same accusation about love, the same complaint about a secret withheld, the same aim. He has heard this speech before, from a woman put up to it by the same people, and thirty men in Ashkelon died the last time he gave in to it.

His soul was vexed to death. Day after day: this is not a moment of weakness but a siege. The Hebrew says his soul was “shortened” to death, the idiom for endurance that has run out, a man worn down until he will pay anything to make it stop. The same idiom appears once before in this book, of God: when Israel put away their foreign gods, “his soul was shortened” over Israel’s misery, and he could bear it no longer (10:16). The same phrase, with opposite results. God’s patience runs out in pity, and what comes of it is mercy for people who deserved nothing. Samson’s runs out under the pressure of a woman paid to wear him down, and what comes of it is a shaved head and a millstone.

He told her all his heart. The narrator says it twice. Weigh what the secret is. Not a fact about hair, but a vow: “I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb.” The one thing in Samson’s life that had been about God, kept since before he was conceived and guarded by a mother who went without wine to carry him, he hands to a woman on the Philistine payroll to buy an hour’s peace. He has been giving the vow away in pieces for twenty years. The razor was all that was left, and he gives it away in words: not overpowered, not drugged, not deceived. He told her.

verseByVerse.quote: When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called the lords of the Philistines, saying, "Come up again, for he has told me all his heart." Then the lords of the Philistines came up to her and brought the money in their hands. She made him sleep on her knees. And she called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to torment him, and his strength left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Delilah knows the truth when she hears it, collects her silver, and has Samson shaved as he sleeps trustingly on her knees, and his strength leaves him.

He has told me all his heart. She knew at once that this time it was true, because the first three answers were about equipment and this one was about God. A man does not invent a childhood vow and a mother’s abstinence to get a woman off his back. The lords come up “and brought the money in their hands”: a man asleep inside, and outside the door his price being counted.

She made him sleep on her knees. The sentence contains no violence, and none in the chapter is more terrible. The posture is trust: his head in her lap, asleep, the deepest trust a strong man can show, and from that position she calls in the barber. The shaving is done by a man she summons, carefully, while Samson lies still. Twenty years of Philistine warfare are ended by a razor and a steady hand.

She began to torment him. The verb is the one the lords used in verse 5: “to humble him”. She is testing him before she raises the alarm, and this time nothing snaps. Their commission is being fulfilled.

His strength left him. This is the clause the chapter has been moving towards. Not “the hair was gone, therefore he was weak”. Something left him, and the next verse will say who.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And he awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as at other times and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him. And the Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes and brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles. And he ground at the mill in the prison. But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samson wakes expecting his strength as always, not knowing that the LORD has left him, and is blinded and enslaved; yet in the darkness God quietly begins to restore the sign of his calling.

As at other times. The fourth time she shouts it, he expects it to go like the first three. That phrase is a man’s whole life in four words: it has always worked before; it will work now. He stands up out of her lap, shakes himself, and reaches for what has never once failed him.

He did not know that the LORD had left him. Few sentences in the Old Testament are sadder. First: it is “the LORD” who has left, not merely his hair or his strength. The strength was always the Spirit of the LORD rushing upon him; the hair was the visible token of a vow; the power was a Person, and the Person has gone. Second: he had lost God and could not tell. He had been performing for years while the vow came apart in pieces, the carcass, the feast, the jawbone, and nothing had ever visibly changed. So the departure was not sudden. What was sudden was the discovery.

Gift without presence. This reaches people who will never go near a Delilah. A man can lose the presence of God and go on preaching, leading family prayers, running the meeting, admired for his gift, because the gift is not the presence, and the gift can outlive it for a long time. The Spirit gave Samson victories on a day when he was breaking his vow on a corpse. God is generous like that, and his generosity is no sign that he approves of how we live. So you cannot measure your standing with God by whether things are still working. Samson’s were working right up to the morning they were not.

They seized him and gouged out his eyes. They “seized” him, who had never been held. They “gouged out his eyes”, and consider which organ they took. It was seeing that ruined him: he saw a woman at Timnah and a prostitute in Gaza, and everything was right in his own eyes. The punishment is a picture of the sin. Blinding was a common way of dealing with dangerous captives in the ancient world, leaving a prisoner harmless but fit for labour (compare King Zedekiah, 2 Kings 25:7).

He ground at the mill in the prison. They brought him down to Gaza, back to the scene of his last free act, in chains. Turning a millstone was the work of slaves, women and animals. The strongest man in Israel walks in a circle in the dark, on the same round until he dies. That is what sin offers everyone in the end: it shows you what you want, takes what you see with, brings you back where you started, and puts you to work going round in circles.

But the hair of his head began to grow again. One word turns the chapter: “but”. This is not saying the power was in the hair after all and is recharging like a battery; God is not bound by hair, and the writer has never said the strength was in it. What is growing back is the sign, the mark of a man set apart to God from his mother’s womb, returning on a head that is blind, shaved, shackled and grinding. Nobody in Gaza watches a prisoner’s hair. It happens where only God can see, on a man who has nothing and can do nothing. God is not finished with people who are finished with themselves, and the proof here is a quiet fact noticed by no one and written down for ever.

Can a believer lose the Spirit? In the Old Testament the Spirit came on judges and kings to empower them for their office, and that empowering could be withdrawn (1 Samuel 16:14). In the new covenant the Spirit dwells in every believer for ever (John 14:16) as the seal of salvation (Ephesians 1:13–14). Samson lost his strength, not necessarily his salvation; Hebrews counts him among those who had faith (Hebrews 11:32). If you are a Christian afraid that you have lost God without knowing it, your fear is not Samson’s condition: he did not know and did not care. A troubled conscience over sin is a sign of the Spirit’s presence, not his absence. David prayed, “take not your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11), and he was heard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — Let Me Die with the Philistines
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God defends his own name through a blind man’s last prayer. The Philistine lords gather to sacrifice to Dagon, crediting their god with victory over Samson, and the crowd joins in (vv. 23–24). They bring Samson out to entertain them, and he asks the boy leading him to let him feel the pillars (vv. 25–26). The house is full, with all the lords inside and three thousand on the roof (v. 27). Samson prays, “please remember me”, and asks for strength once more (v. 28). He pushes the two middle pillars and the house falls; he kills more at his death than in his life (vv. 29–30). His family bury him beside his father (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: From verse 23 the question is no longer what Samson deserves but whose glory is at stake.
verseByVerse.examples: A ruined man calls on God, and is heard.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to rejoice, and they said, "Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand." And when the people saw him, they praised their god. For they said, "Our god has given our enemy into our hand, the ravager of our country, who has killed many of us." And when their hearts were merry, they said, "Call Samson, that he may entertain us." So they called Samson out of the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Philistines publicly credit their god Dagon with victory over the God of Israel, and that, more than Samson’s fate, is why the story does not end at the mill.

Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand. With this song the matter changes, because it is no longer about Samson. They do not say “we caught him”. Dagon is being publicly credited with a victory over the God of Israel, at a great sacrifice, by the assembled rulers of a nation. Nothing in the Old Testament is more serious. When Israel is beaten, the nations conclude not that Israel was unfaithful but that Israel’s God is weak. Moses argued with God on exactly that ground (Numbers 14:13–16), and God says he acts “for the sake of my holy name”, so that the nations will know that he is the LORD (Ezekiel 36:22–23). So the last scene happens not because Samson has earned another chance, but because a temple full of people is giving God’s glory to Dagon, and God will not have it.

The ravager of our country. It is a fair description from where they stand. He burned their harvest and their olive groves, killed thirty men in Ashkelon over a bet and a thousand at Lehi. To a Philistine farmer Samson was a terror, and the relief in this room is genuine.

Call Samson, that he may entertain us. They send for him as the after-dinner amusement, whatever a blind, shaved strongman could be prodded into doing to make a hall laugh. The man who tore a lion is led out by the hand to be laughed at. This is what the lords paid for at the beginning: “bind him to humble him” (v. 5). They have got everything they paid for.
verseByVerse.note: Dagon was the chief god of the Philistines.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samson said to the young man who held him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean against them." Now the house was full of men and women. All the lords of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about 3,000 men and women, who looked on while Samson entertained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blind and led by a boy, Samson asks only to lean on the pillars, and the narrator counts the crowded house: the rulers and people of Philistia are all resting on what a blind man now touches.

The young man who held him by the hand. One picture shows how far he has fallen. The strongest man in the world holds a boy’s hand because he cannot cross a room alone, and asks permission to lean on something. It is the request of a tired old man. The boy agrees; there is no reason not to. The prisoner has been harmless for a long time.

The house was full of men and women. The narrator counts the house before anything happens. All five lords are inside, the whole ruling class of Philistia in one building. The floor is full, and on the flat roof three thousand more press to the edges, looking down at the show. Their weight rests on the roof, the roof rests on the pillars, and the pillars are what a blind man has just been allowed to touch.

Could two pillars hold such a building? Excavated Philistine temples, such as one at Tell Qasile in modern Tel Aviv, had their roofs carried on two central wooden pillars set on stone bases close together in the middle of the hall. The narrator describes a building of the kind archaeologists have found.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samson called to the LORD and said, "O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes." And Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the house rested, and he leaned his weight against them, his right hand on the one and his left hand on the other. And Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he bowed with all his strength, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it. So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blind and ruined, Samson cries to God to remember and strengthen him once more, and God hears a mixed, self-interested but real prayer and uses his death to strike Israel’s oppressors.

O Lord GOD, please remember me. In his second and last recorded prayer he uses three names for God in one breath, like someone reaching for every handle he can find. It is the prayer of a man who has every reason to think he has been forgotten and would deserve it, and it is very like the dying thief’s prayer centuries later: “Jesus, remember me” (Luke 23:42). He does not ask for restoration or a career: “only this once”.

For my two eyes. Be honest about the last clause, because the chapter is. Not a word about Israel, or about the God whose name is being handed to Dagon in that very room. To the end, the account he is settling is his own. And God answers him. Hold both together without tidying either: the prayer is self-interested, and the prayer is real; the motive is mixed, and the man is genuinely calling on the LORD; and the God who had left him in verse 20 does not say no in verse 28. Samson prays as what he is, a ruined, blinded man with no illusions left about his record, and heaven does not require him to pray better before it listens.

What it means for God to remember. “Remember me” can sound as if God might lose track of someone. But in the Bible, when God remembers, he acts. “God remembered Noah,” and a wind began to dry the earth (Genesis 8:1). “God remembered his covenant,” and the rescue from Egypt began (Exodus 2:24). To be remembered by God is to have him turn towards you and move on your behalf. Our real fear, like Samson’s, is not that God has forgotten the facts but that, knowing them, he has stopped being for us. With Samson’s record that fear was reasonable. The thief on the cross had a worse record and asked the same thing, and Jesus answered at once: “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). He could promise it because he was being forsaken in the thief’s place, so that no one he remembers is ever forgotten. So when you feel set aside, pray those three words, and expect him to act, though not always in the way you would choose.

Made strong out of weakness. This is why Hebrews can name Samson in the roll of faith (Hebrews 11:32), among those who “were made strong out of weakness” (Hebrews 11:34): an exact description of a blind prisoner asking the God of Israel for strength one last time and staking his life on the answer.

Let me die with the Philistines. This is not despair; it is a soldier choosing to die in destroying the enemy. He stands between the two pillars with three thousand on the roof, and there is no version of this in which he walks out. The narrator’s verdict, that “the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life”, is sad and true. Twenty years of judging, and the greatest blow struck for Israel was struck by a blind man in a pagan temple in the last moments he had.

Beside another death. Set that sentence, carefully, beside another death. Scripture never calls Samson a picture of Christ, and he was too wilful to be a clean one. But the deliverer who conquers by dying is a shape the whole Bible moves towards, and here it appears in flawed, partial form, which makes the place where it breaks all the clearer. Another deliverer was betrayed for silver, seized, mocked, blindfolded, struck and told to prophesy, and accomplished more by dying than by living. So far the two match. But Samson prayed, “Let me die with the Philistines,” and pulled the house down on his enemies. Jesus prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34), and let the judgment fall on himself. Samson killed more in his death than in his life; Christ saved more in his death than in his life, and every one he saved had been his enemy, like the crowd on that roof.

Was Samson’s death suicide? It is not held up as a model for taking one’s own life. Samson prayed for strength to bring judgment on God’s enemies, God answered, and he died in the act, like a soldier in battle; those in the house were the Philistine rulers and people gathered to celebrate Dagon over the LORD (vv. 23–27). It was a unique moment of judgment. It gives no warrant for suicide, or for killing others for a cause; life is God’s to give and take. If you have lost someone to suicide, this chapter is no verdict on them or on you; bring that grief to the Lord who was himself a man of sorrows. If you are thinking of ending your own life, please tell someone today: a pastor, a friend, a doctor, or an emergency line if you are in danger now. Your life is precious to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his brothers and all his family came down and took him and brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samson’s family carry him home to be buried where his story began: the deliverer who only began to save leaves the Philistines still in the land, and Israel still waiting for a greater deliverer.

His brothers and all his family came down. His family come for the body. Nobody else does: no national mourning, no song like Deborah’s. His brothers and his father’s household walk down to Gaza, take him from the rubble of a Philistine temple, and carry him home.

Between Zorah and Eshtaol. Turn back three chapters: “And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol” (13:25). Where the Spirit first made a young man restless, they put him in the earth. Everything in between, the girl at Timnah, the lion, the riddle, the foxes, the jawbone, the gates of Gaza, the lap, the razor, the mill and the pillars, happened away from those two villages, and in the end he was carried back.

The tomb of Manoah his father. He is buried with the man who prayed, “teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born” (13:8), and was told to keep the vow and wait.

He had judged Israel twenty years. And the Philistines are still there. Chapter 13 said he would only begin, and he only began; the war he opened is not finished until David (2 Samuel 5:17–25; 8:1).

The last word on Samson. The last word on Samson is not a triumph, and the book is not embarrassed about it. He is the deliverer who did what was right in his own eyes and destroyed himself doing it; who was given more raw power than perhaps anyone else in Scripture and used most of it on private quarrels; who lost God and did not notice; and who at the very end, blind, shaved and mocked, called on the LORD and was heard. He asked to be remembered, and he was. The God who left him in verse 20 answered him in verse 28, not because the man had improved, but because a temple full of people was crediting Dagon with a victory over the living God, and the living God had one servant left in the building. Israel would need a better Deliverer: one whose strength never left him, who kept every vow, and who finished what he began.

keyVerse.quote: Then Samson called to the LORD and said, “O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes.”
keyVerse.note: Everything in Samson’s life has led to this blind, ruined man calling on the LORD, and God hears a prayer as mixed as the man who prays it. It shows both how far Samson fell and how far God’s grace reaches, and it points ahead to the thief who asked Jesus, “remember me”, and was promised paradise.

16.reflection:
Samson stayed with Delilah after watching her try three times to betray him (vv. 6–14). Why do we keep returning to what we know is dangerous, and what helps a Christian break such a pattern rather than merely promise to stop?

“He did not know that the LORD had left him” (v. 20). Why is it dangerous to judge our standing with God by whether our gifts and plans still seem to work? What better marks of walking with God should we look for?

“But the hair of his head began to grow again” (v. 22). Where have you seen God begin to restore someone at their lowest point, and how does that encourage you to pray for people who seem beyond hope?

Compare Samson’s dying prayer (vv. 28–30) with Jesus’ prayers on the cross (Luke 23:34, 43). What does the contrast show you about the kind of Deliverer Jesus is?

17.title: Micah's Idol
17.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah.<sup>2</sup>And he said to his mother, "The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my ears, behold, the silver is with me; I took it." And his mother said, "Blessed be my son by the LORD."<sup>3</sup>And he restored the 1,100 pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, "I dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image. Now therefore I will restore it to you."<sup>4</sup>So when he restored the money to his mother, his mother took 200 pieces of silver and gave it to the silversmith, who made it into a carved image and a metal image. And it was in the house of Micah.<sup>5</sup>And the man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household gods, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest.<sup>6</sup>In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.<sup>7</sup>Now there was a young man of Bethlehem in Judah, of the family of Judah, who was a Levite, and he sojourned there.<sup>8</sup>And the man departed from the town of Bethlehem in Judah to sojourn where he could find a place. And as he journeyed, he came to the hill country of Ephraim to the house of Micah.<sup>9</sup>And Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to sojourn where I may find a place."<sup>10</sup>And Micah said to him, "Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year and a suit of clothes and your living." And the Levite went in.<sup>11</sup>And the Levite was content to dwell with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his sons.<sup>12</sup>And Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of Micah.<sup>13</sup>Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest."
17.overview:
Where we are. Samson is dead and buried between Zorah and Eshtaol (16:31), and the cycle of judges is over. Chapters 17 to 21 form the book’s close: two stories, probably from early in the period (18:30), placed last to show what the whole age was like. The first begins in a house in the hill country of Ephraim.

The message. God’s people can lose him while keeping his name constantly on their lips. Micah and his mother never abandon the LORD: they dedicate silver to him, build him a shrine and hire him a Levite, and every piece of it breaks his word. Religion built to our own design, by our own judgment of what is right, is not faith but a machine for securing blessing, and the God it claims to serve is not in it.

Why it was said. The first hearers lived under the kings (see the introduction). The refrain “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (v. 6) showed them what Israel became when every man was his own authority, and warned a later Israel, which would set up its own shrines at Dan and Bethel (1 Kings 12:28–30), where that road began.

How the chapter makes its case. A theft is confessed under a curse, a blessing cancels the curse, and the silver is dedicated to the LORD for an idol (vv. 1–4). Micah furnishes a private shrine and ordains his own son, and the narrator gives his verdict on the age (vv. 5–6). A wandering Levite from Bethlehem is hired as “a father and a priest” for ten pieces of silver a year, and Micah concludes, “Now I know that the LORD will prosper me” (vv. 7–13).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes. Israel needed a king to rule it rightly and a priest who could not be bought, and the chapter shows the cost of having neither. Christ is both: the priest God himself appointed, who “holds his priesthood permanently” (Hebrews 7:24), and the King under whom no one need be his own final judge of what is right. Through him we come to God not by a correctly built arrangement but by grace.

For us. We can worship the true God in ways of our own devising and feel entirely sincere. Ask why you pray, read and give: because God is God, or because these things are the lever by which you expect life to go well? The gospel frees us from the machine. God’s favour comes freely through the priest he appointed, and our practices are his gifts to people already welcomed.
17.theology:
Not apostasy but devotion done wrong. Nobody in this house has abandoned the LORD. They use his name constantly and mean the images as piety. That is what makes it more dangerous than open idolatry: a family worshipping the true God in a manner he forbade, and feeling generous about the cost.

Words used as mechanisms. A curse, a confession to escape it, a blessing to cancel it: nothing in the exchange is addressed to God, and his name is in every line of it.

Right in his own eyes. These are not people knowingly doing evil but people who have each become the final authority on what is good, and every one of them is satisfied.

You cannot hire a father. Once a salary is attached, the man whose task is to tell you the truth is the man whose keep depends on you. Micah wants a priest's authority and a servant's compliance.

Religion as a machine. Micah's confidence in verse 13 is superstition spoken in entirely correct religious words. Each thing he names is true and good; the relationship is upside down, with God's blessing treated as the product of a correctly built arrangement. Chapter 18 shows what becomes of such a system.

The priest nobody hires. Against Micah's hired Levite stands Christ, the priest God himself appointed, who holds his office for ever, cannot be bought and cannot be carried away.
17.examples:
Then: A man returned stolen money to escape a curse, his mother dedicated it to the LORD to have an idol cast, he built a chapel in his front room and ordained his own son, and then hired a wandering Levite on a small annual salary and concluded that his prospects were now secure.

Now: Micah's vocabulary was faultless, so the chapter's question is not whether you believe the right things but whether you are using them to secure a result. The difference shows on the day the things you relied on are taken away. And the mother's arithmetic is worth checking against our own: what we pledge out loud and what we actually give are not always the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Eleven Hundred Pieces of Silver
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Religion that has kept God’s name and lost God. Micah confesses that he stole his mother’s 1,100 pieces of silver, not from sorrow but because he heard her curse the thief (vv. 1–2). She answers with a blessing in the LORD’s name to cancel the curse, and then dedicates the silver to the LORD to have a carved image and a metal image made, breaking the second commandment in the very act of honouring him (v. 3). She gives two hundred pieces to a silversmith, and the idol stands in Micah’s house (v. 4). Every line uses the LORD’s name, and nothing in it is addressed to him.
verseByVerse.theology: Confession, blessing and dedication all happen here, and none of them is what it seems.
verseByVerse.examples: The narrator reports the figures and lets the reader notice the gap.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah. And he said to his mother, "The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my ears, behold, the silver is with me; I took it." And his mother said, "Blessed be my son by the LORD." And he restored the 1,100 pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, "I dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image. Now therefore I will restore it to you." So when he restored the money to his mother, his mother took 200 pieces of silver and gave it to the silversmith, who made it into a carved image and a metal image. And it was in the house of Micah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micah confesses his theft only to escape his mother’s curse, and she turns the recovered silver into an idol dedicated to the LORD: God’s name in every line, and his command broken in the middle of it.

The 1,100 pieces of silver. It is the sum each Philistine lord offered Delilah (16:5): a distinctive figure, twice in adjoining chapters, both times buying something that should never have been for sale.

Also spoke it in my ears. Micah confesses not because he has been caught, nor because he is sorry, but because he was standing there when his mother cursed the thief, and he has lived under the curse ever since. A public curse on an unknown thief was the recognised way to bring a theft to light (compare Lev. 5:1), and here it has worked.

Blessed be my son by the LORD. Her reply is not forgiveness but a countermeasure: a blessing in the LORD’s name, spoken to cancel the curse. Mother and son handle words like charms: something said might damage him, so something must be said to undo it. Nothing here is addressed to God, and both of them speak of him constantly.

A carved image and a metal image. Verse 3 holds the whole chapter: the covenant name of the God of Israel and a direct breach of his second commandment in one breath, with no sense of any difficulty. The commandment could hardly be plainer: You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath (Ex. 20:4). She is not turning to Baal; she means it as piety, in the LORD’s honour, on behalf of her son. Nobody in this house has decided to abandon God. They have decided to worship him in a way he forbade, and to feel good about the expense.

His mother took 200 pieces of silver. She declared all eleven hundred dedicated to the LORD from my hand, and took less than a fifth of it to the silversmith. Perhaps the rest went on the shrine and the ephod; the text does not say she kept it. But the narrator lets the gap stand in plain sight. There is a kind of religion that is generous in its language and careful with its money, and it is worth asking whether anyone has ever seen the gap between what we pledged out loud and what actually went.

Uncertain wording. Her words Now therefore I will restore it to you (v. 3) are puzzling, since Micah has just given the silver back to her. Most take her to mean that she will return it to him in another form, as the images for his house. Some scholars think the sentences of verses 2 to 4 were once arranged differently. Either way, the sense of the passage is clear.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Micah completes a religion of his own making, and the narrator names the disease of the age. Micah has a shrine, an ephod for seeking guidance, household gods, and one of his sons ordained as priest, though he is no Levite and nothing in the room was given by God (v. 5). Then comes the sentence on which the last five chapters are built: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (v. 6). These are not people knowingly doing evil but people sure they are doing right, and that is exactly the trouble.
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing in Micah's religion was given or commanded by God; all of it came from inside his own household.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer's verdict is not that Israel chose wrong, but that everyone chose for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household gods, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest. In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micah furnishes a complete religion in his own house, none of it given by God, and the narrator names the condition of the whole age: no king, and everyone his own judge of what is right.

The man Micah had a shrine. Everything in verse 5 is homemade. The building is his own house of gods, not the tabernacle. The ephod is the priestly garment used for seeking God’s guidance, the very thing Gideon made out of the Midianite gold, which became a snare to him and his household (8:27). The household gods are teraphim, family figurines like those Rachel stole from Laban (Gen. 31:19). And the priest is his own son, ordained by his own father, from the tribe of Ephraim, not Levi.

Ordained one of his sons. The Hebrew, literally filled the hand of, is the technical term for installing a priest. Micah uses the right word for something he has no right whatever to do. Not one item was given by God; the whole collection stands in his own front room, where he can get at it.

No king in Israel. Verse 6 is the writer’s verdict on everything from here to the last verse; it returns in shorter form at 18:1 and 19:1, and in full at 21:25. Take its two halves separately. There was no king in Israel: no central authority, no one to enforce the covenant, no one over the tribes. These five chapters show what happens without one.

Everyone did what was right in his own eyes. The second half is the deeper diagnosis, because a king alone would not have cured it. Not what was wrong in his own eyes, but what was right. This is not a nation of people knowingly doing evil but of people each of whom has become his own final authority on what is good, and every one of them is satisfied. Micah is the case in point. He has restored stolen money, honoured his mother, built a place of worship, provided for the LORD’s service and installed a priest. Ask him, and he would sincerely tell you he was a religious man doing his best.

A phrase met before. Three chapters ago Samson said of the Philistine woman, she is right in my eyes (14:3). The writer has taken that private sentence from the deliverer’s mouth and laid it over the whole nation. Samson was not the exception in his generation but a typical example of it.

Everyone right, and nobody agreeing. To modern ears verse 6 can sound like a description of a healthy society: who else should decide what is right for me? But the narrator saw a country full of sincere people, each sure he was right, and no way left to settle anything between them. The philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre argued in After Virtue that this is largely our condition too: once a society loses any shared account of what human beings are for, moral argument cannot come to an end, because each side is finally announcing its preferences more loudly than the other, and what is left is pressure and power. Judges shows where that goes in its last three chapters.

Not a stricter list but a King. Yet the Bible does not offer the moralist’s cure, a stricter list kept by better people; Micah is a very religious man. The rebel and the religious man are doing the same thing, deciding for themselves what will make them right. What Judges waits for is a king (see the note on 21:25), and the King who came does not only tell us what is right. He makes us right with God, at his own cost.
verseByVerse.note: “Ordained” is literally “filled the hand of” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — A Priest for Ten Pieces a Year
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Micah upgrades his shrine with a real Levite and is sure that God must now bless him. A young Levite has left Bethlehem, which was not a Levitical town, and is wandering in search of a place to live (vv. 7–9). Micah offers him a post as “a father and a priest” for ten pieces of silver a year, clothes and keep; the Levite is content, and Micah ordains him (vv. 10–12). Micah’s conclusion lays the whole system bare: “Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest” (v. 13). Chapter 18 will show how secure it was.
verseByVerse.theology: A Levite with no post meets a householder who wants a priest, and each gets what he wants.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 13 gives away what the whole apparatus is for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a young man of Bethlehem in Judah, of the family of Judah, who was a Levite, and he sojourned there. And the man departed from the town of Bethlehem in Judah to sojourn where he could find a place. And as he journeyed, he came to the hill country of Ephraim to the house of Micah. And Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to sojourn where I may find a place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A young Levite, already away from the place God gave his tribe, drifts north looking for somewhere to settle, and arrives at the door of a man who needs a priest.

A young man of Bethlehem in Judah. A Levite living in Bethlehem is the first thing wrong. The tribe of Levi had no territory of its own. That was deliberate: the LORD himself was to be their inheritance, and in place of land they were given forty-eight cities scattered through the other tribes, so that the whole nation would have men among them who knew the law and could teach it (Num. 18:20; Josh. 21). Bethlehem was not one of the forty-eight. Of the family of Judah means he was a Levite by descent who lived among Judah’s clans.

To sojourn where he could find a place. So he is away from his post before the story starts, and all he wants is somewhere to settle. Walking north with no destination, he arrives at Micah’s door because that is the door he happens to reach. Asked who he is, he says first that he is a Levite and, in the same sentence, that he is looking for a place. Micah, whose priest at present is one of his own sons, is listening very carefully.

verseByVerse.quote: And Micah said to him, "Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year and a suit of clothes and your living." And the Levite went in. And the Levite was content to dwell with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his sons. And Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of Micah. Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micah hires the Levite as “a father and a priest” on a small salary and concludes that God’s blessing is now guaranteed: religion has become a machine, and the machine stands in his house.

Be to me a father and a priest. The two halves of the offer do not belong in the same sentence. Father is a title of respect for a spiritual guide, someone whose counsel you submit to. Then come the terms of employment: ten pieces of silver a year, one suit of clothes, and board. A father cannot be hired. Once a salary is attached, the man who is supposed to tell you the truth is the man whose keep depends on you, and everyone in the arrangement knows it. Micah wants the authority of a priest and the compliance of a servant, and thinks the two can be bought together.

Ten pieces of silver a year. Two hundred pieces of silver went into the images; the priest gets ten a year. Micah’s spending shows which he values more.

The Levite was content. It is the writer’s word, and the most damning thing said about him. He does not argue about the images, or ask whose shrine this is, or point out that a carved image in a private house in Ephraim is not what Levites were scattered through Israel to maintain. He belongs to the tribe set apart to teach the law of Moses, and he settles down.

Micah ordained the Levite. Micah filled his hand, the ordination phrase again, and the Levite lets him. An Ephraimite householder has installed a priest on his own authority, a right that belonged to God alone, and the priest had every reason to know it and said nothing.

Now I know that the LORD will prosper me. Verse 13 shows what it was all for. Now I know is certainty, at last. That the LORD will prosper me is the desired outcome. Because I have a Levite as priest is the lever, the thing that makes the outcome follow. Micah has assembled a machine: shrine, ephod, images, and now a genuine Levite to work the controls. God’s blessing has become what a correctly built arrangement must produce, and the arrangement stands in his house where he can maintain it.

God’s answer. The next chapter is God’s answer to Micah’s sentence. Six hundred armed men will walk into his house, take the images, the ephod, the household gods and the Levite, and leave him standing in the road with nothing. A mechanism you can build is a mechanism somebody else can carry away.

The priest nobody hires. Set beside Micah’s Levite the priest nobody hires. No one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God: Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest; his Father appointed him (Heb. 5:4–5). He holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues for ever, and therefore he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:24–25). He cannot be bought for ten pieces of silver a year, and he cannot be taken from you by six hundred men.

In everyday life. Everything in Micah’s sentence is true and good in itself; he has the words right and the whole relationship upside down. The question is not whether we believe the right things but whether we are using them. Do I read, pray, attend, give and serve because God is God, or because these practices are the mechanism by which I expect life to come out well? The second feels like faith and behaves like machinery, and the word that gives it away is because: now I know it will go well for me, because I have the arrangement right. But God’s favour was never a result to be secured. He gives it freely, through the priest he himself appointed, and the practices are his gifts to those already welcomed.

keyVerse.quote: In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
keyVerse.note: The verdict that governs the book’s closing chapters is spoken first over a man building a shrine to the LORD. Micah is not a rebel but a sincere worshipper who has made himself the judge of what pleases God, and that is the disease of the whole age. The refrain leaves the reader longing for the King who would rule his people rightly, fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

17.reflection:
Micah’s mother blessed her son in the LORD’s name and dedicated silver to the LORD to make an idol (vv. 2–3). In what ways can we use God’s name sincerely while ignoring what he has actually said about how he is to be worshipped?

“Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (v. 6). Why can it be more dangerous to be sincerely wrong than knowingly wrong? Where does our culture, or your own heart, make the self the final judge of what is good?

Micah hired a Levite to be “a father and a priest” for ten pieces of silver a year (v. 10). What happens when people choose teachers whose living depends on pleasing them? How can a church protect its ministers’ freedom to tell the truth?

“Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest” (v. 13). Do you ever treat prayer, Bible reading or church-going as a way to make life go well? How does knowing Christ as the priest God appointed change why we do these things?

18.title: The Danites Steal the Idol
18.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the people of Dan was seeking for itself an inheritance to dwell in, for until then no inheritance among the tribes of Israel had fallen to them.<sup>2</sup>So the people of Dan sent five able men from the whole number of their tribe, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land and to explore it. And they said to them, "Go and explore the land." And they came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.<sup>3</sup>When they were by the house of Micah, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. And they turned aside and said to him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What is your business here?"<sup>4</sup>And he said to them, "This is how Micah dealt with me: he has hired me, and I have become his priest."<sup>5</sup>And they said to him, "Inquire of God, please, that we may know whether the journey on which we are setting out will succeed."<sup>6</sup>And the priest said to them, "Go in peace. The journey on which you go is under the eye of the LORD."<sup>7</sup>Then the five men departed and came to Laish and saw the people who were there, how they lived in security, after the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting, lacking nothing that is in the earth and possessing wealth, and how they were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.<sup>8</sup>And when they came to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers said to them, "What do you report?"<sup>9</sup>They said, "Arise, and let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. And will you do nothing? Do not be slow to go, to enter in and possess the land.<sup>10</sup>As soon as you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people. The land is spacious, for God has given it into your hands, a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the earth."<sup>11</sup>So 600 men of the tribe of Dan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol,<sup>12</sup>and went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. On this account that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day; behold, it is west of Kiriath-jearim.<sup>13</sup>And they passed on from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah.<sup>14</sup>Then the five men who had gone to scout out the country of Laish said to their brothers, "Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household gods, a carved image, and a metal image? Now therefore consider what you will do."<sup>15</sup>And they turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite, at the home of Micah, and asked him about his welfare.<sup>16</sup>Now the 600 men of the Danites, armed with their weapons of war, stood by the entrance of the gate.<sup>17</sup>And the five men who had gone to scout out the land went up and entered and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, while the priest stood by the entrance of the gate with the 600 men armed with weapons of war.<sup>18</sup>And when these went into Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, the priest said to them, "What are you doing?"<sup>19</sup>And they said to him, "Keep quiet; put your hand on your mouth and come with us and be to us a father and a priest. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?"<sup>20</sup>And the priest's heart was glad. He took the ephod and the household gods and the carved image and went along with the people.<sup>21</sup>So they turned and departed, putting the little ones and the livestock and the goods in front of them.<sup>22</sup>When they had gone a distance from the home of Micah, the men who were in the houses near Micah's house were called out, and they overtook the people of Dan.<sup>23</sup>And they shouted to the people of Dan, who turned around and said to Micah, "What is the matter with you, that you come with such a company?"<sup>24</sup>And he said, "You take my gods that I made and the priest, and go away, and what have I left? How then do you ask me, 'What is the matter with you?'"<sup>25</sup>And the people of Dan said to him, "Do not let your voice be heard among us, lest angry fellows fall upon you, and you lose your life with the lives of your household."<sup>26</sup>Then the people of Dan went their way. And when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his home.<sup>27</sup>But the people of Dan took what Micah had made, and the priest who belonged to him, and they came to Laish, to a people quiet and unsuspecting, and struck them with the edge of the sword and burned the city with fire.<sup>28</sup>And there was no deliverer because it was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone. It was in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. Then they rebuilt the city and lived in it.<sup>29</sup>And they named the city Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor, who was born to Israel; but the name of the city was Laish at the first.<sup>30</sup>And the people of Dan set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan the son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land.<sup>31</sup>So they set up Micah's carved image that he made, as long as the house of God was at Shiloh.
18.overview:
Where we are. Micah has his shrine, his images and his hired Levite, and is sure the LORD will prosper him (17:13). Now the tribe of Dan, which never took the land allotted to it (1:34), comes north looking for somewhere easier.

The message. Religion you build yourself can be carried off by someone stronger, and religion you hire will tell you what you want to hear. The Danites get an instant blessing from a priest who consults nothing, call a defenceless town God’s gift, steal Micah’s gods and buy his priest with a bigger post. Micah is left with the truest question in the story: “what have I left?” And all the while the house of God stood at Shiloh, near, free and ignored.

Why it was said. For readers under the kings the shrine at Dan was no ancient curiosity: Jeroboam set a golden calf there (1 Kings 12:29), and false worship continued there until the land went into captivity (v. 30; see the introduction). The chapter shows where it came from.

How the chapter makes its case. Dan sends five scouts, who lodge at Micah’s house and get a ready blessing from his Levite (vv. 1–6). They find Laish, quiet and unsuspecting, call it God’s gift, and six hundred armed men march (vv. 7–13). The Danites strip Micah’s shrine and offer the Levite a bigger post, and his heart is glad (vv. 14–20). Micah pursues, protests, “You take my gods that I made”, and goes home empty-handed (vv. 21–26). Laish is destroyed and renamed Dan, the image is set up, its priest turns out to be Moses’ grandson, and the house of God was at Shiloh all along (vv. 27–31).

Where it leads. To Christ, by contrast and by the need it exposes. Over the hireling who changes masters for a better post stands the good shepherd, who is no hired hand and lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11–13). Over gods that must be carried stands the God who carries his people (Isaiah 46:1–4), who in Christ came to dwell among us and cannot be owned, hired or stolen. And Laish, which had “no deliverer”, shows the world’s need of the Deliverer who came for the defenceless.

For us. Ask of anything you rely on: if it were taken, what would you have left? Beware of reading an easy opportunity as God’s will, and of teachers whose only word is “Go in peace”. The true God is not a possession to be guarded but a Lord to be trusted, and in Christ he is near, and free, and will never be carried away.
18.theology:
A failure rewritten as a shortage. What Dan refused to fight for becomes, in their telling, what was never offered, and the rewritten history licenses the raid.

The hired oracle. The Levite fetches no ephod (used to seek God’s guidance), waits for nothing and asks no one, and gives an answer that is soothing and cannot be tested. A man whose keep depends on his hearers will find over time that the word of the LORD agrees with them, and he will never experience it as dishonesty. That the journey then succeeds proves nothing about him.

Providence read backwards. The Danites call an easy target God's gift, and the reason for their confidence is that the victims will not see them coming. Ease is not the same as God's will, and the test is whether we would still call a thing God's will if it were hard or costly.

Gods that can be carried. A god you can make is a god stronger men can take from you. Micah's loss shows what he had really been trusting, and the prophets make the same point with something close to laughter.

The hired hand and the good shepherd. Content when he found a post and glad when a bigger one came, the Levite carries the stolen images out himself. Jesus drew the contrast: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). The Levite took a better living; the Shepherd gave his life.

Three generations from Sinai. The priest is Moses' own grandson, and the shrine he serves outlasts everyone in the chapter. Faithfulness is not inherited; it can be lost in a single lifetime, even in the best family in Israel.

And the house of God was at Shiloh. The real tabernacle stood in the same hill country the entire time, and nobody went, because the real thing was near, free, and impossible to manage. The New Testament carries this to its end. God's dwelling is now his Son, the temple raised on the third day (John 2:19-21), and the Father is worshipped neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem but in spirit and truth (John 4:21-24). He is nearer than Shiloh ever was, freely given, and no more ours to control than the ark was.
18.examples:
Then: A tribe that would not fight for the land God gave it marched north instead, chose a town for the sole reason that it could not defend itself, called that God's gift, robbed a private chapel on the way, bought the chaplain with a bigger job, and founded a shrine that lasted until the exile, all in the same hill country as the tabernacle.

Now: The chapter puts three questions to us. Am I calling something God's will because it is right, or because it is easy? If what I rely on were taken from me by force, what would I have left? And is there a substitute I prefer to the real thing, not because it is closer but because I can manage it? The genuine thing is nearer than Shiloh ever was: God has come to us in his Son, freely given to people who could never earn him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Tribe Looking for Somewhere Easier
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dan, unwilling to fight for its own land, goes looking for somewhere easier, and finds a priest who will bless the search. The refrain “no king” returns, and Dan’s complaint that no inheritance had fallen to it hides the fact that it never took the land it was given (v. 1; 1:34). Five scouts set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, Samson’s country, and lodge at Micah’s house (v. 2). They recognise the young Levite and ask what he is doing there; he tells them he has been hired (vv. 3–4). Asked to inquire of God, he consults nothing and answers at once: “Go in peace” (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: Dan did have an inheritance (Josh. 19:40-48). The grievance in v. 1 is worded as though God had left them out.
verseByVerse.examples: The priest consults nothing, and puts the LORD's name on the answer his questioners came for.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the people of Dan was seeking for itself an inheritance to dwell in, for until then no inheritance among the tribes of Israel had fallen to them. So the people of Dan sent five able men from the whole number of their tribe, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land and to explore it. And they said to them, "Go and explore the land." And they came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dan sets out to find an easier inheritance, describing its failure to take the land God gave it as though it had simply been given nothing.

In those days there was no king in Israel. The refrain returns, followed by a claim that is not quite true. Read on its own, verse 1 sounds as though Dan had been overlooked when the land was divided.

What Joshua 19 says. Dan was allotted a territory, named town by town: Zorah, Eshtaol, Aijalon, Timnah, Ekron and more, out to the border over against Joppa, some of the best country on the coastal plain (Josh. 19:40–46). It fell to them exactly as the other lots did. What happened next is recorded in the first chapter of this book: The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the plain (1:34). They had the deed and never took possession.

A careful edit. So the grievance in verse 1 is careful editing: not we would not fight for what God gave us but nothing had fallen to us. The failure has been rewritten as a shortage, and the shortage justifies what they are about to do. People do the same with their own histories, and it is worth asking where we have done it.

From Zorah and from Eshtaol. These are Samson’s two villages.
