He was born at Zorah, the Spirit first stirred him between them, and his brothers buried him between them two chapters ago (13:2, 25; 16:31). The scouting party sets out from the ground where God’s deliverer for this tribe lies in his father’s tomb, and it goes the other way. Samson went down to the Philistine plain to begin taking what Dan had abandoned; his tribe now sends five men north, to look for somewhere easier.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were by the house of Micah, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. And they turned aside and said to him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What is your business here?" And he said to them, "This is how Micah dealt with me: he has hired me, and I have become his priest." And they said to him, "Inquire of God, please, that we may know whether the journey on which we are setting out will succeed." And the priest said to them, "Go in peace. The journey on which you go is under the eye of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scouts find a Levite who freely admits he is for hire, and without consulting God he gives them exactly the blessing they wanted.

They recognized the voice of the young Levite. Perhaps they placed him by his accent the moment he spoke: a southern voice from Bethlehem in Judah, a long way north, in a private house in Ephraim. This book has already shown what an accent could do at a river crossing (12:6); here it simply makes a stranger recognisable.

Who brought you here? Their three questions are the right ones. A Levite belongs in one of the forty-eight cities given to his tribe, teaching the law. He is a long way from any of them, and everyone can see it.

He has hired me. He answers with the terms of his employment and hears nothing wrong in it. That is his whole account of his calling.

Inquire of God, please. Having established that he is for hire, they ask him for a word from God. The request is polite and the theology behind it is old and good: before a campaign, ask God. Israel asked at the start of this very book and was answered (1:1–2); Joshua’s mistake with Gibeon came from not asking (Josh. 9:14).

Go in peace. He answers at once, and he consults nothing. There is an ephod in the house, the very instrument used for enquiring of God, and he does not fetch it, or pray, or ask for time. What he gives them is a blessing with no content: soothing, untestable, and precisely what five armed men looking for a soft target wanted to hear. This is why the arrangement in chapter 17 was rotten from the first day: a man whose keep depends on the goodwill of his hearers will never find himself with anything uncomfortable to say.

Itching ears. Paul saw the same market and named it: the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Tim. 4:3). The hearers want such teachers first; the teachers always turn up.

The journey succeeds. The journey will succeed, and that is the most sobering thing here: a false prophet’s word coming true proves nothing at all. Moses had already said so: even if the sign comes to pass, if he leads you after other gods, do not listen (Deut. 13:1–3).

A god who only ever says go in peace. In the nineteenth century Ludwig Feuerbach argued that God is a projection: human beings take their own wishes, magnify them and bow down to the result. The odd thing is how much of it the Bible agrees with. Micah’s Levite is exactly what Feuerbach described, a god on hand to tell the customer what he already wanted to hear, and much modern spirituality is the same: a higher power whose only known opinions are that I should be true to myself and that my plans are blessed. But wish-fulfilment would never have invented the God of Israel, who sends prophets to say no, judges his own people first, and keeps telling them what they least want to hear; still less a Messiah who is crucified. The gospel begins with a verdict we would never have chosen, and only then gives a peace no hired priest could promise: peace with God, made through the blood of the cross (Col. 1:20).

Uncertain wording. Under the eye of the LORD (v. 6) is literally before the LORD, and it can mean either that the LORD approves the journey or simply that he sees it. Like many oracles it can be heard both ways. The Danites hear approval; the rest of the chapter shows that God was certainly watching.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The scouts find a soft target and call it God’s gift. Laish, in the far north, lives quiet and unsuspecting, wealthy, far from help and without allies (v. 7). Every detail of the report measures how easy the town would be to take; nothing asks whether God gave the land or whether its people deserved judgment. Back home the five borrow the language of the conquest, “God has given it into your hands” (vv. 8–10). Six hundred armed men set out, camp at the place afterwards called Mahaneh-dan, and come to Micah’s house (vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The scouts choose by weakness, then use the language of faith.
verseByVerse.examples: Easy is not the same as right.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the five men departed and came to Laish and saw the people who were there, how they lived in security, after the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting, lacking nothing that is in the earth and possessing wealth, and how they were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone. And when they came to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers said to them, "What do you report?" They said, "Arise, and let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. And will you do nothing? Do not be slow to go, to enter in and possess the land. As soon as you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people. The land is spacious, for God has given it into your hands, a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scouts find a peaceful, isolated town that cannot defend itself, and treat its weakness as proof that God has given it to them.

They lived in security. Every detail of the report measures how easy the town would be to take. Security: no defences worth the name. Quiet and unsuspecting: no watch and no expectation of attack. Lacking nothing… possessing wealth: worth taking. Far from the Sidonians: their kin are too far off to come; no dealings with anyone: no allies, and nobody who owes them anything. Laish lay at the far north of the land, by a spring of the Jordan below Mount Hermon; after the manner of the Sidonians means it lived like the prosperous Phoenician trading cities of the coast.

What is missing. Not one word about whether the land was promised to Israel, and not one about the people’s wickedness, which is the reason God gave for driving out the Canaanites (Gen. 15:16; Deut. 9:4–5). A prosperous, peaceable, isolated town that cannot defend itself: that is the entire case.

Arise, and let us go up against them. The stirring speech is borrowed from Caleb and Joshua at Kadesh, urging a frightened nation into the country God had sworn to their fathers (Num. 13:30; 14:7–9). It is the language of faith, used to recruit a raiding party.

God has given it into your hands. This is the phrase of the conquest, what the LORD said to Joshua about Jericho and Ai: God has determined the outcome, and Israel is to act on his word. Here it is used of a town nobody asked God about. And notice the order. You will come to an unsuspecting people comes first, and for God has given it into your hands a few words later. The real reason for confidence is stated first, and it is not God: the victims will not see them coming.

Reading opportunity as God’s will. They reason back from an opportunity to God’s will: the thing is easy, therefore God must intend it. The test is simple: would you still call it God’s will if it were hard, or costly, or if the people concerned could defend themselves?

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 7 is difficult in places. The words rendered possessing wealth are obscure, and older versions took them differently: the King James Version has there was no magistrate in the land, that might put them to shame in any thing, that is, no ruler oppressing them. Either way the picture is the same: a town at ease, prosperous and unprotected.

verseByVerse.quote: So 600 men of the tribe of Dan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, and went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. On this account that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day; behold, it is west of Kiriath-jearim. And they passed on from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six hundred armed men of Dan march north, camping on the way near the place where God had first stirred Samson to save Israel.

600 men of the tribe of Dan. The writer counts them here and twice more (vv. 16, 17), because the number is the argument. Everything that happens from now on happens because six hundred men with weapons want it to.

Mahaneh-dan. The name means camp of Dan, and it is where the Spirit of the LORD began to stir Samson (13:25). The two uses could hardly be further apart: there, God moving one man to begin saving Israel; here, six hundred of that man’s own tribe camped on the road north, leaving the fight behind them. They stop at Micah’s house, which the five had told them about.
verseByVerse.note: “Mahaneh-dan” means “camp of Dan” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — Is It Better to Serve One House or a Tribe?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Danites take the gods, and the priest goes gladly with them. The scouts tell their brothers what is in Micah’s house and leave the hint hanging: “consider what you will do” (v. 14). While six hundred armed men stand at the gate and the Levite is asked after his welfare, the five carry out the images, the ephod and the household gods (vv. 15–18). When the priest objects, he is told to keep quiet and offered a bigger post, priest to a tribe instead of one man’s house. “The priest’s heart was glad”, and he carries the stolen gods himself (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: A promotion offer works instantly on a man who was hired in the first place.
verseByVerse.examples: The words Micah used to hire him (17:10) are used to buy him away.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the five men who had gone to scout out the country of Laish said to their brothers, "Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household gods, a carved image, and a metal image? Now therefore consider what you will do." And they turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite, at the home of Micah, and asked him about his welfare. Now the 600 men of the Danites, armed with their weapons of war, stood by the entrance of the gate. And the five men who had gone to scout out the land went up and entered and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, while the priest stood by the entrance of the gate with the 600 men armed with weapons of war. And when these went into Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, the priest said to them, "What are you doing?" And they said to him, "Keep quiet; put your hand on your mouth and come with us and be to us a father and a priest. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?" And the priest's heart was glad. He took the ephod and the household gods and the carved image and went along with the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Danites strip Micah’s shrine, and his priest, offered a larger congregation, gladly carries the stolen gods out himself.

Consider what you will do. This is as close as anyone comes to saying it out loud. They do not propose a theft; they mention an inventory and leave a pause, and everyone understands. What they want is not the silver, the livestock or the house but the religious equipment: a tribe on its way to take a city by surprise would like some gods to travel with.

Household gods. Teraphim were household images used for divination (seeking guidance by forbidden means) and as tokens of family inheritance (Gen. 31:19; 1 Sam. 19:13). They were always on the wrong side of the law.

Asked him about his welfare. They ask after the Levite’s health while the army fills the doorway: a friendly conversation at the front, six hundred armed men at the gate, and the five scouts walking past both into the shrine.

What are you doing? The priest is not overpowered. He stands at the gate with the soldiers while his sanctuary is emptied behind him, and when he speaks it is a question rather than a refusal.

Put your hand on your mouth. The answer is a threat and a promotion: be quiet, and then, in the same breath, the offer in Micah’s exact words, be to us a father and a priest. Micah had said be to me a father and a priest (17:10). The men stealing him know precisely what he was bought with.

The priest’s heart was glad. The argument is put as a career question: is it better to be priest to one man’s house or to a whole tribe? Not whether it is right, or whose gods these are, only which is the bigger position. No hesitation is recorded. His heart is glad, and he picks up the stolen gods with his own hands, so that the theft is completed by the clergyman. He came looking for a place (17:8), was content when he found one (17:11), and is glad when a better offer arrives. Every word the narrator gives him is about his own comfort, and not one is about God.

The hired hand. A man who takes a post for the living will leave it for a better living, and he will no more regard the second move as a betrayal than he regarded the first as a compromise. The Lord drew the line exactly here: the hired hand is not the shepherd, and when he sees the wolf coming he leaves the sheep and flees, because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. The good shepherd does the opposite: he lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11–13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–26 — My Gods That I Made
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Micah pursues his gods and learns what they were worth. The Danites put their little ones and their goods in front and march on (v. 21). Micah and his neighbours catch up, and are asked mildly what the fuss is about (vv. 22–23). His answer is the truest sentence in the story: “You take my gods that I made and the priest, and go away, and what have I left?” (v. 24). The Danites warn him that angry men may kill him and his household (v. 25), and seeing that they are too strong for him, Micah turns and goes home with nothing (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: Micah pleads for his gods and is threatened into silence.
verseByVerse.examples: His confidence of chapter 17 ends in a bare shelf.

verseByVerse.quote: So they turned and departed, putting the little ones and the livestock and the goods in front of them. When they had gone a distance from the home of Micah, the men who were in the houses near Micah's house were called out, and they overtook the people of Dan. And they shouted to the people of Dan, who turned around and said to Micah, "What is the matter with you, that you come with such a company?" And he said, "You take my gods that I made and the priest, and go away, and what have I left? How then do you ask me, 'What is the matter with you?'" And the people of Dan said to him, "Do not let your voice be heard among us, lest angry fellows fall upon you, and you lose your life with the lives of your household." Then the people of Dan went their way. And when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Micah chases the men who took his gods, and in protesting he states the whole case against idolatry: gods he made could be taken, and without them he has nothing left.

Putting the little ones… in front of them. The Danites put the vulnerable at the front, which is sound tactics: the pursuit will come from behind.

What is the matter with you? Micah and a few Ephraimite farmers have caught up with a war party, which asks him mildly, with six hundred men behind the question, what the fuss is about.

My gods that I made. He says it in his own defence, in front of witnesses, and hears nothing wrong with it. My gods are possessions, listed like furniture. That I made is the manufacturer’s claim, produced as proof of ownership. He has given the complete case against idolatry in five words, and uses it as an argument.

The prophets’ laughter. The prophets meet this with something close to laughter. Isaiah watches Babylon’s great gods loaded onto beasts of burden: Bel bows down; Nebo stoops… these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts… they cannot save the burden (Isa. 46:1–2). The god has to be loaded onto an animal, and the animal is tired. Isaiah goes straight on to the contrast: the LORD has carried his people from the womb and will carry them to old age (Isa. 46:3–4). And the psalm says what idols are: silver and gold, the work of human hands, with mouths that do not speak and eyes that do not see; those who make them become like them (Psalm 115:4–8).

What an idol is. A god you can make is a god that men stronger than you can take away. That is not a flaw in Micah’s particular idols; it is what an idol is.

And what have I left? The rest of his sentence is the truest thing anybody says in these two chapters. Nothing. He had assembled the entire apparatus and concluded, now I know that the LORD will prosper me (17:13). The system was complete, and it walked up the road with somebody else.

Ask the question yourself. Ask it of anything you are relying on: if six hundred men came and took it, what would be left? The thing whose loss would leave you with nothing is your real god. Micah’s could be carried off; the God who carries his people cannot.

Lest angry fellows fall upon you. The threat is put with a kind of courtesy, which makes it worse: not we will kill you but there are men in this column with tempers, and you have a family.

He turned and went back to his home. Nothing more is said of Micah. He does not pray, or repent, or go to Shiloh, or do anything at all. He looks at the size of the column, works out that he cannot win, and walks back to a house with a bare shelf in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–31 — Laish, and a Shrine That Lasted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with a peaceful town destroyed and a counterfeit shrine that lasted for centuries, while the true house of God stood ignored at Shiloh. The Danites fall on Laish, “a people quiet and unsuspecting”, put it to the sword and burn it, and there was no deliverer (vv. 27–28). They rebuild it and name it Dan (v. 29). They set up Micah’s image, and its priest is named at last: Jonathan, grandson of Moses, whose sons serve there until the captivity of the land (v. 30). And all this time the house of God was at Shiloh (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The word in v. 28 for what Laish did not have is the book's own word for its deliverers (3:9, 15).
verseByVerse.examples: The last verse is the sharpest: the real thing was available, and nobody went near it.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of Dan took what Micah had made, and the priest who belonged to him, and they came to Laish, to a people quiet and unsuspecting, and struck them with the edge of the sword and burned the city with fire. And there was no deliverer because it was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone. It was in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. Then they rebuilt the city and lived in it. And they named the city Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor, who was born to Israel; but the name of the city was Laish at the first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dan destroys a peaceful town that had no one to save it and puts its own name on it: a conquest God never commanded, recorded in a book about deliverers.

A people quiet and unsuspecting. The narrator repeats the scouts’ phrase, and the repetition is the judgment. In verse 7 it was a strategic assessment, the reason the town was chosen. Here it stands immediately beside struck them with the edge of the sword and burned the city with fire, so that we see what it meant.

There was no deliverer. A deliverer, a saviour, is what this whole book has been about. God raised up deliverers for Israel when they cried out: Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah; Samson was announced before his birth as the one who would begin to deliver. Here, in the story of Samson’s own tribe, the word turns up for the people that tribe put to the sword. Laish had nobody. In a book about deliverance, the last conquest recorded is Israelites destroying a town that had no deliverer.

They named the city Dan. They put their own name on it, and the name lasted. From Dan to Beersheba became the standard phrase for the whole length of Israel for the rest of the Old Testament (for example 1 Sam. 3:20), and its northern end is this town, taken from a peaceable people by a tribe that would not fight for the land God actually gave it.

A Deliverer for those who have none. The book ends still waiting for a deliverer who would not fail. When he came, he came precisely for people with no one to save them: while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly (Rom. 5:6).

Was this the conquest God commanded? No. That war was against peoples whose wickedness had come to its full measure (Gen. 15:16), in the territory God allotted. Laish lay far outside Dan’s allotment and was chosen for its weakness, and it is told as a sign of how far the age had fallen. Scripture records it without approving it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Dan set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan the son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land. So they set up Micah's carved image that he made, as long as the house of God was at Shiloh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The stolen image becomes the tribe’s shrine for centuries, its priest turns out to be Moses’ own grandson, and all the while the true house of God stood at Shiloh, unvisited.

Jonathan the son of Gershom, son of Moses. The Levite gets a name at last, and it is the last name anyone expected. Gershom was Moses’ firstborn, so named because Moses had been a sojourner in a foreign land (Ex. 2:22), and the grandson has spent this whole story sojourning wherever he could find a place. Sinai to a shrine in Dan in three generations: that is how fast it can go, and it went that fast in the best family in Israel.

When this happened. The name also dates the story. If the line is complete, a grandson of Moses was a young man early in the time of the judges, so these closing chapters are probably not the last events in the book but come from its first generations, placed at the end to show what the whole age was like.

Until the day of the captivity of the land. The shrine was no passing episode. Most likely it lasted for centuries, until the Assyrian deportation of the north (2 Kings 15:29), though some take the captivity as the loss of the ark in Eli’s day (1 Sam. 4), which would fit the mention of Shiloh in the next verse (see the introduction). When the kingdom divided, Jeroboam put one of his two golden calves at Dan and told Israel, Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt (1 Kings 12:28–30), on ground given to false worship long before. A carved image made from a mother’s dedicated silver, in a private house in Ephraim, ended as the northern shrine of a whole kingdom that turned from God.

As long as the house of God was at Shiloh. With the last line the writer quietly condemns everybody in the chapter. The tabernacle, with the ark and the mercy seat and the appointed priesthood, stood at Shiloh the entire time, in the same hill country of Ephraim as Micah’s house. Nobody in two chapters, not the mother, not Micah, not the Danites, not Moses’ grandson, made the journey to the place where God had said he would meet with his people.

Not ignorance. Shiloh was where the nation assembled; everyone knew what was there. They preferred a shrine they could carry, a priest they could pay, and an oracle that agreed with them. The real thing was near, and free, and could not be controlled, and that is why they left it alone. Two chapters of religion, expensive, busy and full of the LORD’s name, were conducted in the same hills as the place where God actually was.

The God who cannot be carried off. The God who met his people at Shiloh came nearer still: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and in him the hour came when true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:23). He is not a shrine to be set up or a priest to be hired, and no war party can take him away.

Textual note. Ancient Hebrew scribes raised one letter above the line in Moses’ name so that it could be read as Manasseh, probably to spare the lawgiver’s name (see the note below). The ESV prints Moses; the KJV and NKJV follow the scribes’ mark and print Manasseh. Men who loved the Scriptures found this sentence hard enough to want to soften it, and yet they kept the true letters on the page.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “Manasseh”: Hebrew scribes raised one letter above the line so the name could be read that way, probably to protect Moses’ name.

keyVerse.quote: You take my gods that I made and the priest, and go away, and what have I left?
keyVerse.note: Micah’s protest states the whole case against idolatry in one sentence: a god you have made can be taken by someone stronger, and then you have nothing left. It is a question worth asking of anything we rely on. The living God is not made by us and cannot be carried off; he carries his people (Isaiah 46:3–4).

18.reflection:
Dan described its failure to take the land as though no inheritance “had fallen to them” (v. 1; compare 1:34). Where are we tempted to rewrite our own failures as things that simply happened to us, and what do we then feel entitled to do?

The Levite told the Danites what they wanted to hear without consulting God (vv. 5–6), and the scouts read an easy opportunity as God’s will (v. 10). How can we tell God’s guidance from our own wishes dressed in religious words?

The priest’s heart was glad at the offer of a bigger post (vv. 19–20). How does Jesus, the good shepherd who is no hired hand (John 10:11–13), challenge the way we serve in the church and choose where to belong?

“You take my gods that I made… and what have I left?” (v. 24). If the things you rely on most were taken away, what would you have left? What difference does it make that the true God cannot be carried off?

19.title: The Levite's Concubine
19.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days, when there was no king in Israel, a certain Levite was sojourning in the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim, who took to himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.<sup>2</sup>And his concubine was unfaithful to him, and she went away from him to her father's house at Bethlehem in Judah, and was there some four months.<sup>3</sup>Then her husband arose and went after her, to speak kindly to her and bring her back. He had with him his servant and a couple of donkeys. And she brought him into her father's house. And when the girl's father saw him, he came with joy to meet him.<sup>4</sup>And his father-in-law, the girl's father, made him stay, and he remained with him three days. So they ate and drank and spent the night there.<sup>5</sup>And on the fourth day they arose early in the morning, and he prepared to go, but the girl's father said to his son-in-law, "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread, and after that you may go."<sup>6</sup>So the two of them sat and ate and drank together. And the girl's father said to the man, "Be pleased to spend the night, and let your heart be merry."<sup>7</sup>And when the man rose up to go, his father-in-law pressed him, till he spent the night there again.<sup>8</sup>And on the fifth day he arose early in the morning to depart. And the girl's father said, "Strengthen your heart and wait until the day declines." So they ate, both of them.<sup>9</sup>And when the man and his concubine and his servant rose up to depart, his father-in-law, the girl's father, said to him, "Behold, now the day has waned toward evening. Please, spend the night. Behold, the day draws to its close. Lodge here and let your heart be merry, and tomorrow you shall arise early in the morning for your journey, and go home."<sup>10</sup>But the man would not spend the night. He rose up and departed and arrived opposite Jebus (that is, Jerusalem). He had with him a couple of saddled donkeys, and his concubine was with him.<sup>11</sup>When they were near Jebus, the day was nearly over, and the servant said to his master, "Come now, let us turn aside to this city of the Jebusites and spend the night in it."<sup>12</sup>And his master said to him, "We will not turn aside into the city of foreigners, who do not belong to the people of Israel, but we will pass on to Gibeah."<sup>13</sup>And he said to his young man, "Come and let us draw near to one of these places and spend the night at Gibeah or at Ramah."<sup>14</sup>So they passed on and went their way. And the sun went down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin,<sup>15</sup>and they turned aside there, to go in and spend the night at Gibeah. And he went in and sat down in the open square of the city, for no one took them into his house to spend the night.<sup>16</sup>And behold, an old man was coming from his work in the field at evening. The man was from the hill country of Ephraim, and he was sojourning in Gibeah. The men of the place were Benjaminites.<sup>17</sup>And he lifted up his eyes and saw the traveler in the open square of the city. And the old man said, "Where are you going? And where do you come from?"<sup>18</sup>And he said to him, "We are passing from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim, from which I come. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to the house of the LORD, but no one has taken me into his house.<sup>19</sup>We have straw and feed for our donkeys, with bread and wine for me and your female servant and the young man with your servants. There is no lack of anything."<sup>20</sup>And the old man said, "Peace be to you; I will care for all your wants. Only, do not spend the night in the square."<sup>21</sup>So he brought him into his house and gave the donkeys feed. And they washed their feet, and ate and drank.<sup>22</sup>As they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, worthless fellows, surrounded the house, beating on the door. And they said to the old man, the master of the house, "Bring out the man who came into your house, that we may know him."<sup>23</sup>And the man, the master of the house, went out to them and said to them, "No, my brothers, do not act so wickedly; since this man has come into my house, do not do this vile thing.<sup>24</sup>Behold, here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. Let me bring them out now. Violate them and do with them what seems good to you, but against this man do not do this outrageous thing."<sup>25</sup>But the men would not listen to him. So the man seized his concubine and made her go out to them. And they knew her and abused her all night until the morning. And as the dawn began to break, they let her go.<sup>26</sup>And as morning appeared, the woman came and fell down at the door of the man's house where her master was, until it was light.<sup>27</sup>And her master rose up in the morning, and when he opened the doors of the house and went out to go on his way, behold, there was his concubine lying at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold.<sup>28</sup>He said to her, "Get up, let us be going." But there was no answer. Then he put her on the donkey, and the man rose up and went away to his home.<sup>29</sup>And when he entered his house, he took a knife, and taking hold of his concubine he divided her, limb by limb, into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout all the territory of Israel.<sup>30</sup>And all who saw it said, "Such a thing has never happened or been seen from the day that the people of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt until this day; consider it, take counsel, and speak."
19.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 17 and 18 showed religion made to order; chapters 19 to 21 show a society coming apart. Once again there is a Levite, once again the hill country of Ephraim and Bethlehem in Judah, and once again there is “no king in Israel” (v. 1).

The message. When everyone does what is right in his own eyes, the weakest pay, and God’s own people become Sodom. The chapter retells Genesis 19 in an Israelite town, with no angel at the door: a Levite hands his concubine to a mob to save himself, and she dies on the threshold. Scripture tells it plainly, excuses no one, and lays a command on every reader: “consider it, take counsel, and speak” (v. 30).

Why it was said. The first hearers lived under the kings (see the introduction), when Gibeah was known as Saul’s town and Bethlehem as David’s (1 Samuel 10:26; 16:1). The chapter showed them what Israel had been before God gave it a king, and how far a people with the covenant could sink. Centuries later Hosea could still speak of “the days of Gibeah” (Hosea 9:9).

How the chapter makes its case. A Levite goes to Bethlehem to win back his concubine, and her father’s pressing hospitality keeps them five days (vv. 1–9). Late in the day the Levite refuses to lodge in Jebusite Jerusalem and presses on to Israelite Gibeah, where no one takes them in (vv. 10–15). Only an old man from Ephraim offers a bed (vv. 16–21). The men of the town surround the house as Sodom did; the host offers the women, and the Levite pushes his concubine out to them (vv. 22–26). In the morning he finds her at the door, cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them through Israel (vv. 27–30).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by contrast. The chapter cries out for a king who protects the weak and a husband who will not save himself at his bride’s expense, and Christ is both. The Levite came to speak to his wife’s heart and then handed her over. Christ came to a people who had left him, and when the armed crowd came, he gave himself up and said, “let these men go” (John 18:8).

For us. God sees the people the world discards, and so must his people. Abuse must never be excused, hidden or explained away, and those who suffer it should seek safety and help at once. Do not assume that a religious name makes any community safe. And look to the one who stood between his people and the mob.
19.theology:
Gibeah has become Sodom. The parallel with Genesis 19 is exact and deliberate: Israel has become the city God destroyed, and this time there is no rescue.

The label is not the safeguard. Membership of God's people has never in itself made a community safe. The Levite trusted the name "Israelite" and was wrong about his own side.

Where "right in his own eyes" ends. Every person in the chapter had a reason, and not one of them thought he was the villain. The book's refrain, followed all the way down, ends not in a homemade shrine but in a body on a doorstep.

She is unnamed here, but not with God. Scripture does not explain this away and does not leave it out. Nothing done to her in the dark was dark to him (Ps. 139:11-12).

The sentence that was never kept, and the one that was. The Levite came to speak to her heart and handed her over to save himself. Christ came to a people who had left him and, when the mob was at the door, gave himself up so that his own would go free.
19.examples:
Then: A woman was refused shelter by a whole Israelite town, offered to a mob by the man who had taken her in, pushed through the door by the man who had come to win her back, abused until dawn, and found dead on the threshold by a husband whose first words were an instruction to hurry.

Now: The chapter ends with a command rather than a moral, consider it, take counsel, and speak, and the command still stands. Reasonable men, each doing what looked right to him, produced this between them; and God put it in his book, so that she would not be forgotten. That is part of the answer to anyone who has wondered whether he was watching. If you have suffered sexual violence, hear this plainly: what was done to her was evil, it was not her fault, and God’s own law counts a woman forced in this way innocent and her attacker as a murderer (Deuteronomy 22:25–27). Abuse is never to be tolerated or hidden. If you are in danger, seek safety at once, tell someone you trust and the police, and let your church’s elders help you. The God who wrote her down has not forgotten you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A broken marriage seems to be mending, and generous hospitality unknowingly sets the trap. A Levite living in the remote hill country of Ephraim takes a concubine from Bethlehem; she leaves him and goes home to her father for four months (vv. 1–2). He follows her to speak kindly to her and bring her back, and her father comes to meet him with joy (v. 3). Day after day the father presses him to eat and stay: three days, then a fourth, then most of a fifth (vv. 4–9). The scene feels safe, but every delay pushes the journey home later into the day, and the woman at its centre never says a word.
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator slows the story almost to a stop, and every delay matters.
verseByVerse.examples: Bethlehem's warmth will be set against Gibeah's coldness.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days, when there was no king in Israel, a certain Levite was sojourning in the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim, who took to himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah. And his concubine was unfaithful to him, and she went away from him to her father's house at Bethlehem in Judah, and was there some four months. Then her husband arose and went after her, to speak kindly to her and bring her back. He had with him his servant and a couple of donkeys. And she brought him into her father's house. And when the girl's father saw him, he came with joy to meet him. And his father-in-law, the girl's father, made him stay, and he remained with him three days. So they ate and drank and spent the night there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Levite goes to Bethlehem to win back the concubine who has left him, and for a moment the story promises reconciliation.

A certain Levite was sojourning. Here is another Levite, and again the hill country of Ephraim and Bethlehem in Judah, the same two places as chapter 17, and again the word sojourning: a man of the priestly tribe living wherever he happens to have settled.

A concubine. A concubine was a wife of the second rank: joined to a man and bound to him, with a wife’s duties and very little of a wife’s standing or protection. She is his, and she has almost no claim on him.

To speak kindly to her. He went, literally, to speak to her heart, the phrase used of a man wooing, of comfort spoken to the grieving, and of God himself promising to bring Israel into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her (Hos. 2:14). It is the best sentence anybody says about this man.

She brought him into her father’s house. Hold on to it, because before this chapter ends he will push her through a door into the hands of a mob. Whatever the trouble was, she is the one who opens the door to him. Her father comes with joy to meet him, and the narrator deliberately lets the scene feel safe.

What we do not know. We are not told what went wrong between them, and the narrator is not interested in grading her. She will not speak a single word in this chapter. Everything that happens to her is done by men, every judgment passed on her is passed by men, and the writer declines to add his own.

Does Scripture approve of concubines? It records the custom, as it records polygamy, without commending it, and the stories in which it appears are nearly all stories of grief. God’s pattern from the beginning is one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6).

Textual note. The Hebrew of verse 2 says she was unfaithful to him. The ancient Greek translation, probably made from a Hebrew text older than our oldest complete manuscripts, says she was angry with him and left (the ESV gives became angry with him in its footnote). The behaviour recorded fits the second reading better: a woman who had committed adultery could expect no shelter in her father’s house, and this father receives his son-in-law with open delight, which is not how a man greets the husband of a daughter who has disgraced him. Beyond that we do not know.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the fourth day they arose early in the morning, and he prepared to go, but the girl's father said to his son-in-law, "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread, and after that you may go." So the two of them sat and ate and drank together. And the girl's father said to the man, "Be pleased to spend the night, and let your heart be merry." And when the man rose up to go, his father-in-law pressed him, till he spent the night there again. And on the fifth day he arose early in the morning to depart. And the girl's father said, "Strengthen your heart and wait until the day declines." So they ate, both of them. And when the man and his concubine and his servant rose up to depart, his father-in-law, the girl's father, said to him, "Behold, now the day has waned toward evening. Please, spend the night. Behold, the day draws to its close. Lodge here and let your heart be merry, and tomorrow you shall arise early in the morning for your journey, and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her father’s warm hospitality keeps the Levite day after day, and so, without meaning to, sends them onto the road too late.

Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread. The delays pile up. On the fourth day the father presses a morsel of bread on him, and the bread becomes a meal and the meal another night. On the fifth day he does it a third time, and then a fourth (v. 9), which is nearly a plea: the old man is running out of arguments and points to the lengthening shadows. Look how late it is; one more night, and go at dawn.

Why so many verses? The writer never wastes words (he tells the whole story of the judge Shamgar in one verse, 3:31), yet here he gives us four rounds of a man being persuaded to stay for another meal. There are two reasons. First, this hospitality is what puts them on the road at the wrong hour. They leave on the afternoon of the fifth day, with nowhere near enough light to reach home, and everything that follows happens because they are looking for a bed after dark. The kindest man in the story sets the trap without meaning to.

Bethlehem and Gibeah. The second reason is contrast. Bethlehem, in Judah, cannot stop feeding a stranger; Gibeah, in Benjamin, will not take him in at all. The writer wants five verses of open-handed generosity in our minds when the Levite sits down in an empty square with nobody looking at him. For readers who lived under the kings the two names said more still: Bethlehem was David’s town and Gibeah was Saul’s (1 Sam. 10:26; 16:1), and many think the contrast is deliberate.

Her silence. Count the speakers in this passage: the father, the father, the father, the father. She has been the reason for the whole journey and has not said a word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — We Will Not Turn Aside Into the City of Foreigners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levite avoids a pagan town for safety and walks his household into an Israelite town that will not take them in. Leaving late, they reach Jebus, still a Jebusite city, as the day is nearly over (vv. 10–11). The servant urges them to stop there, but the Levite will not turn aside into “the city of foreigners” and presses on to Gibeah of Benjamin (vv. 12–14). The sun sets as they arrive. They sit down in the open square, and no one takes them into his house (v. 15). The covenant name has not produced covenant behaviour, and the town has shown what it is before the horror begins.
verseByVerse.theology: The decision that leads to her death is made for the sake of safety.
verseByVerse.examples: Gibeah has told us what it is before the horror begins.

verseByVerse.quote: But the man would not spend the night. He rose up and departed and arrived opposite Jebus (that is, Jerusalem). He had with him a couple of saddled donkeys, and his concubine was with him. When they were near Jebus, the day was nearly over, and the servant said to his master, "Come now, let us turn aside to this city of the Jebusites and spend the night in it." And his master said to him, "We will not turn aside into the city of foreigners, who do not belong to the people of Israel, but we will pass on to Gibeah." And he said to his young man, "Come and let us draw near to one of these places and spend the night at Gibeah or at Ramah." So they passed on and went their way. And the sun went down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin, and they turned aside there, to go in and spend the night at Gibeah. And he went in and sat down in the open square of the city, for no one took them into his house to spend the night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refusing to stay in a pagan town, the Levite presses on to an Israelite one, and in Gibeah of Benjamin nobody opens a door.

He rose up and departed. They get about six miles before the light starts to go.

Jebus (that is, Jerusalem). Jebus is Jerusalem, and it is not yet Israelite. Benjamin had been given it and had not driven out the Jebusites (1:21); it will not belong to Israel until David takes it, generations later (2 Sam. 5:6–9). Tonight it is a Canaanite town on the road north.

We will not turn aside into the city of foreigners. The servant, who has no standing in this story, gives the only good advice anybody offers. The Levite’s refusal is the decision that leads to her death, and there is nothing stupid in it. He will not put his household in a pagan city overnight: these people are not God’s covenant people and do not fear the God of Israel, and who knows what a Canaanite town does to travellers after dark? Better to press on a few more miles to Gibeah, where the men are Benjaminites, sons of Jacob, circumcised, under the law of Moses.

Sensible and wrong. Nothing in the chapter is more sensible. It is spoken by a Levite, a man trained to know the difference between the holy and the common. And it is wrong in every particular, because the Israelite town is the one where they meet the mob. Belonging outwardly to God’s covenant people has never in itself made a community safe; a town can be full of the circumcised and be Sodom by nightfall. The Levite assumed that the label secured the behaviour, and he assumed it about his own side.

The sun went down on them near Gibeah. The sunset falls on the story like a sentence of judgment. Then nobody opens a door. Hospitality to a traveller was not a nicety but close to a sacred duty, and a stranger sitting in the open square at nightfall was a standing accusation against the whole town. Abraham ran to meet three strangers and pressed food on them (Gen. 18:2–8). This man is a Levite, plainly no threat, travelling with a woman, a servant and two donkeys, and Gibeah looks at him and goes indoors. The horror has not begun yet, and the town has already told us what it is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — The Only Man Who Offers a Bed Is Not From There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a town of Israelites, the only man who welcomes the stranger is himself a stranger. An old man from Ephraim, living in Gibeah, comes in from the fields at evening (v. 16). He sees the travellers in the square and asks where they are going; the Levite explains that no one has taken them in, though they need nothing but a roof (vv. 17–19). The old man takes them home, urging them above all not to spend the night in the square, and does every duty of a host: feed for the donkeys, water for their feet, food and drink (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: A stranger in the town does what the town would not.
verseByVerse.examples: He knows what his neighbours are, and the rest of the chapter shows that knowing was not enough.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, an old man was coming from his work in the field at evening. The man was from the hill country of Ephraim, and he was sojourning in Gibeah. The men of the place were Benjaminites. And he lifted up his eyes and saw the traveler in the open square of the city. And the old man said, "Where are you going? And where do you come from?" And he said to him, "We are passing from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim, from which I come. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to the house of the LORD, but no one has taken me into his house. We have straw and feed for our donkeys, with bread and wine for me and your female servant and the young man with your servants. There is no lack of anything." And the old man said, "Peace be to you; I will care for all your wants. Only, do not spend the night in the square." So he brought him into his house and gave the donkeys feed. And they washed their feet, and ate and drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The only man in Gibeah who welcomes the stranger is himself a stranger there, and he does for the travellers every duty the town has refused.

An old man was coming from his work. The narrator sets two sentences side by side on purpose: the old man was from Ephraim, and the men of the place were Benjaminites. The only person in the town who behaves like an Israelite is not from the town. He is an outsider, coming in tired from a day’s work in the fields, and he notices the stranger in the square when every householder in Gibeah has managed not to.

No one has taken me into his house. The Levite mentions the house of the LORD, identifying himself as a man in God’s service, and it does him no good. Then he ends with the complaint that matters. He is not begging: they have straw and feed, bread and wine, enough for all of them, and need only a roof. He states the fact and lets it stand.

Only, do not spend the night in the square. The old man’s last clause matters most. He does not say the travellers would be more comfortable indoors; he says, whatever happens, do not sleep out there. He has lived in Gibeah long enough to know exactly what is on those streets after dark, and he gets three travellers off them as fast as he can. He is right about the danger and wrong about the safety of his house, and by morning both will be clear.

They washed their feet, and ate and drank. Feed for the animals, water for their feet, food and wine: every duty of a host, done properly, by an outsider, in a town that would not do any of it.

Textual note. Where the Hebrew has the house of the LORD (v. 18), the ancient Greek translation reads my house, which may be the original. The sense of the passage is the same either way: the Levite is on his way home, and no one in Gibeah will give him a bed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gibeah becomes Sodom, and there is no angel at the door. While the guests are eating, worthless men of the town surround the house and demand the Levite, in almost the words of the men of Sodom (v. 22; Genesis 19:5). The old man pleads with them, and then offers his own virgin daughter and the Levite’s concubine instead (vv. 23–24). When they will not listen, the Levite seizes his concubine and pushes her out to them. They abuse her all night, and at dawn she falls at the door of the house where her master is (vv. 25–26). Scripture records the horror without softening it or excusing anyone.
verseByVerse.theology: Every element of the scene matches Sodom (Gen. 19:4-8), except the rescue.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 25 must be read exactly as it stands: it says who opened the door.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, worthless fellows, surrounded the house, beating on the door. And they said to the old man, the master of the house, "Bring out the man who came into your house, that we may know him." And the man, the master of the house, went out to them and said to them, "No, my brothers, do not act so wickedly; since this man has come into my house, do not do this vile thing. Behold, here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. Let me bring them out now. Violate them and do with them what seems good to you, but against this man do not do this outrageous thing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men of Gibeah demand the Levite as the men of Sodom did, and the old host, who rightly calls it wickedness, offers them two women instead.

As they were making their hearts merry. It is the same phrase as at Bethlehem (vv. 6, 9), and this time it is the last quiet moment.

Worthless fellows. Literally sons of Belial, sons of worthlessness. The English is the same as for the gang Abimelech hired and the men who gathered around Jephthah in Tob (9:4; 11:3), though the Hebrew here is harsher. And chapter 20 will show that the city stood behind them.

That we may know him. We have read this demand before, almost word for word. Two visitors come to Lot in Sodom, and before they lie down the men of the city surround the house and call out, Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them (Gen. 19:4–5). The writer lays one scene on top of the other, and every element matches: the mob at the door, the demand for the guest, the host going out to them, the address my brothers, the plea not to do this wicked thing, and the daughters offered in the guest’s place. The demand is sexual, as verse 25 shows: the gang rape of a guest, violent and humiliating evil, and the sign of how far Israel had become like Canaan.

No angel in this house. One thing in Genesis is missing. In Sodom the angels reached out, pulled Lot back inside, and struck the men at the door with blindness (Gen. 19:10–11). There is no angel in this house.

No, my brothers. The old man goes out to them, which takes courage, and his argument is right as far as it goes: this man is under my roof, and what you propose is wickedness and outrage. He knows right from wrong, and he names the thing correctly.

Here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. Then he says the unspeakable thing. He offers a mob his own daughter and his guest’s wife, tells them to violate them and do with them what seems good to you, and does it in the same breath in which he defends the honour of his household. Hear his phrase: in Hebrew what is good in your eyes, a near echo of the sentence stamped across these chapters, “Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (17:6; 21:25), spoken to a mob about two women by a decent man, as the best solution he can think of.

Reported, not commended. Lot did this too (Gen. 19:8), and it was monstrous there as well. Scripture reports it; it does not commend it. Some readings treat the host as a hero because he meant to protect a guest, and that will not do. Two women are being offered to a rape gang by the man responsible for them, and no calculation about ancient hospitality makes that anything other than what it plainly is.

Is this scene about same-sex relations? What Gibeah demanded was violent rape. Scripture’s teaching on same-sex relations rests on wider texts (Lev. 18:22; Rom. 1:26–27), not on this scene alone.
verseByVerse.note: The scene deliberately echoes Sodom: Israel has become like Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: But the men would not listen to him. So the man seized his concubine and made her go out to them. And they knew her and abused her all night until the morning. And as the dawn began to break, they let her go. And as morning appeared, the woman came and fell down at the door of the man's house where her master was, until it was light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To save himself, the Levite forces his own concubine out to the mob; they abuse her all night, and at dawn she falls at the door of the house where he lies safe.

The man seized his concubine. The man here is not the old host, whose offer the mob refused. What follows is done by the Levite, and every word of it is against him. Seized: she did not go willingly. His concubine: his own, the woman he had travelled all that way to bring home, to speak to her heart. Made her go out: he put her through the door, and it was shut behind her. He did it to save himself; there is no other reading, for the mob had asked for him. When the tribes assemble and he tells the story, he will describe the night at length and leave this detail out (20:5).

All night until the morning. It went on all night: not a moment of violence but hours of it, by a crowd, until the sky began to lighten. Then they let her go, as one might release something no longer of use. Inside the house a man slept.

She fell down at the door. The most terrible detail in the chapter is that she got back. However far they had taken her, and in whatever state they left her, she crossed Gibeah in the half-dark, reached the house, and fell at the door. The narrator calls the man inside her master, not her husband. She could not open it, or nobody heard her, or nobody came, and she lay there until it was light.

No explanation. Nothing in Scripture asks us to explain this away, and there is no explanation. What Scripture does is refuse to leave it out. This account is in the word of God because God would not have it forgotten, and the men who did it and the man who opened the door have not been allowed the last word on that night. Israel did not forget: centuries later Hosea summed up the corruption of his own generation by saying, They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah (Hos. 9:9).

Her name with God. She has no name in the book. She has one with God, who keeps count of his people’s tossings, puts their tears in his bottle and writes them in his book (Psalm 56:8), and who has never yet mislaid a single person the world discarded.

If this is close to your own story. God sees, and Scripture calls this evil by its name. Nothing done to you was your fault, and none of it measures your worth. Abuse must never be hidden or excused, whoever the abuser is and whatever his religious standing. If you are in danger, get to safety and call the emergency services the same day; tell someone you trust, report it, and seek help from a wise pastor or biblical counsellor. If it happened long ago and still weighs on you, that is not a failure of faith: the harm is real and lasting, and a biblical counsellor experienced in helping survivors of abuse, together with your doctor, can walk with you.

Why is a story like this in the Bible at all? Many readers meet this chapter and conclude that the Bible is on the side of men like the Levite. The scholar Phyllis Trible, writing as a feminist, called this and similar passages texts of terror, and terrible they are. But look at how the story is told. Much ancient literature sang of the strong, with women and slaves as the scenery. This narrator makes a woman who never speaks the moral centre of the chapter. He records every evasion of the man who put her out, and in the next chapter lets him tell his own version so that we can see what he leaves out (20:5). He calls the mob worthless fellows, lays Gibeah over Sodom, and ends by handing the reader a duty: consider it, take counsel, speak. That is not a text approving violence against women but an indictment so exact that it still convicts. The modern reader’s outrage at this chapter is real and right, and this book shares it and gives it deep roots: it says every human being is made in God’s image (Gen. 1:27), and it gives us a Saviour who stood with the despised woman every time he met one (Luke 7:36–50).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–30 — Consider It, Take Counsel, and Speak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The morning shows what kind of man the Levite is, and the chapter ends by handing the reader a duty. He opens the door to go on his way and finds her lying there with her hands on the threshold; he tells her to get up, and there is no answer (vv. 27–28). At home he cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them through all the territory of Israel (v. 29). Everyone who sees it says nothing like it has happened since the exodus: “consider it, take counsel, and speak” (v. 30). The next two chapters show what Israel does with that command.
verseByVerse.theology: The morning brings no grief from the Levite, only haste.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends by handing the reader an assignment rather than a conclusion.

verseByVerse.quote: And her master rose up in the morning, and when he opened the doors of the house and went out to go on his way, behold, there was his concubine lying at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold. He said to her, "Get up, let us be going." But there was no answer. Then he put her on the donkey, and the man rose up and went away to his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the morning the Levite opens the door to leave, finds her with her hands on the threshold, tells her to get up, and when there is no answer loads her on his donkey and goes home.

Her master rose up in the morning. Three ordinary clauses, and every one is an accusation. He slept. He got up in the morning. And he was leaving: the sentence tells us his intention before it tells us what he found, which means he had not been out to look for her.

With her hands on the threshold. She had reached the door of the house where he was and put her hands on the step, and that is where she stopped. The last thing she did was try to get in.

Get up, let us be going. These are the worst words in the chapter. No cry, no kneeling beside her, no question about who did this, no rage, no grief, not one syllable of tenderness from the man who had come to speak to her heart. He looks at what is lying across his doorstep and tells it to get up because he wants to leave.

But there was no answer. Not a lament, not a plain statement, only a silence where a reply should have been: that is how the chapter tells us she is gone. She never spoke in this chapter, and we notice it at the moment she cannot.

He put her on the donkey. Then he loads her onto the donkey like the rest of the baggage and goes home. The verse gives her the same treatment the animals get.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew never actually says that she was dead, only that there was no answer. Most readers take the silence to mean that she had died at the door, but some think the text leaves open the dreadful possibility that she was still alive when he took the knife (v. 29). Either way, he never stopped to find out.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he entered his house, he took a knife, and taking hold of his concubine he divided her, limb by limb, into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout all the territory of Israel. And all who saw it said, "Such a thing has never happened or been seen from the day that the people of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt until this day; consider it, take counsel, and speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levite cuts up her body to summon the tribes, and the chapter ends by commanding Israel, and every reader, to consider what has been done and to speak.

He took a knife. He butchers her in his own house. The language is the language of the altar: taking hold of the body and dividing it limb by limb, as with a sacrificial animal. He does it to a woman on his floor, and there is no sign that it occurred to him to bury her.

Into twelve pieces. Twelve pieces, for twelve tribes. It is not madness but a calculated summons, and it works. Later Saul, a Benjaminite from this same Gibeah, will send a yoke of oxen cut in pieces through Israel to muster the nation against the Ammonites (1 Sam. 11:7), and the echo of this night is probably part of the message.

One more thing done to her. Yet look at what he has done to get the tribes to act over a woman’s death: he has mutilated her body. His response to what was done to her is one more thing done to her. And when he explains it all in chapter 20, he will not mention that he was the one who put her out of the door (20:5).

Consider it, take counsel, and speak. Three commands: set your heart on this thing; talk it over; say something. The narrator will not tell us what to think. He puts the pieces on the table and hands us the assignment, and that is the most uncomfortable thing he could have done.

So consider it. Every person in this chapter had a reason. The father-in-law was being generous. The Levite was avoiding a pagan town for the sake of safety, and later saving his own life. The old man was protecting a guest under his roof, a sacred obligation. The men of Gibeah were doing what seemed good to them. Not one of them thought of himself as the villain, and between them they left a woman dead on a doorstep with her hands on the step. That is what everyone did what was right in his own eyes comes to when it is followed all the way down. It does not stop at a private shrine and a hired priest. It ends here.

A man came from a far country. Now consider one thing more, because the chapter has one good sentence in it, a promise the Levite did not keep. A man came from a far country to a woman who had left him, to speak to her heart and bring her home. It is a beautiful sentence, and he betrayed it before the week was out: when the mob was at the door, he handed her over and saved himself.

Another came from further. Another came from further, to a people who had left him, to speak to their hearts and bring them home. And when the mob was at the door, he did not put anybody through it. If you seek me, let these men go: he said it in the garden, with the torches on his face, and John notes that he said it to fulfil his own word, Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one (John 18:8–9). The Levite went out of the door in the morning and found her on the step. Christ went out in the night to meet the armed crowd himself, and stood between it and his own.

Never cast out. No one who comes to that door and lays a hand on the threshold will ever be told to get up and be going. Whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

keyVerse.quote: Such a thing has never happened or been seen from the day that the people of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt until this day; consider it, take counsel, and speak.
keyVerse.note: The chapter ends not with the narrator’s verdict but with a command. Scripture will not let this evil be forgotten, excused or passed over in silence; it calls God’s people to look at it, think it through and speak. The command still stands wherever the weak are abused and others look away.

19.reflection:
The Levite would not stay among “foreigners” and trusted an Israelite town, where no one took them in (vv. 12–15). Why is it dangerous to assume that a religious name guarantees safe or godly behaviour, in a church as well as a town?

The only man who welcomed the travellers was himself an outsider (vv. 16–21). What does this chapter teach about hospitality, and who are the people left sitting in the square in your own town?

Every person in the chapter had a reason for what he did, yet between them they left a woman dead at the door (vv. 22–28). How do “reasonable” choices add up to great evil, and how should a church respond when abuse comes to light?

The Levite saved himself at his concubine’s expense; Jesus said, “If you seek me, let these men go” (John 18:8). How does Christ’s self-giving love reshape the way we treat people weaker than ourselves?

20.title: Civil War Against Benjamin
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then all the people of Israel came out, from Dan to Beersheba, including the land of Gilead, and the congregation assembled as one man to the LORD at Mizpah.<sup>2</sup>And the chiefs of all the people, of all the tribes of Israel, presented themselves in the assembly of the people of God, 400,000 men on foot that drew the sword.<sup>3</sup>(Now the people of Benjamin heard that the people of Israel had gone up to Mizpah.) And the people of Israel said, "Tell us, how did this evil happen?"<sup>4</sup>And the Levite, the husband of the woman who was murdered, answered and said, "I came to Gibeah that belongs to Benjamin, I and my concubine, to spend the night.<sup>5</sup>And the leaders of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house against me by night. They meant to kill me, and they violated my concubine, and she is dead.<sup>6</sup>So I took hold of my concubine and cut her in pieces and sent her throughout all the country of the inheritance of Israel, for they have committed abomination and outrage in Israel.<sup>7</sup>Behold, you people of Israel, all of you, give your advice and counsel here."<sup>8</sup>And all the people arose as one man, saying, "None of us will go to his tent, and none of us will return to his house.<sup>9</sup>But now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot,<sup>10</sup>and we will take ten men of a hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred of a thousand, and a thousand of ten thousand, to bring provisions for the people, that when they come they may repay Gibeah of Benjamin for all the outrage that they have committed in Israel."<sup>11</sup>So all the men of Israel gathered against the city, united as one man.<sup>12</sup>And the tribes of Israel sent men through all the tribe of Benjamin, saying, "What evil is this that has taken place among you?<sup>13</sup>Now therefore give up the men, the worthless fellows in Gibeah, that we may put them to death and purge evil from Israel." But the Benjaminites would not listen to the voice of their brothers, the people of Israel.<sup>14</sup>Then the people of Benjamin came together out of the cities to Gibeah to go out to battle against the people of Israel.<sup>15</sup>And the people of Benjamin mustered out of their cities on that day 26,000 men who drew the sword, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, who mustered 700 chosen men.<sup>16</sup>Among all these were 700 chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.<sup>17</sup>And the men of Israel, apart from Benjamin, mustered 400,000 men who drew the sword; all these were men of war.<sup>18</sup>The people of Israel arose and went up to Bethel and inquired of God, "Who shall go up first for us to fight against the people of Benjamin?" And the LORD said, "Judah shall go up first."<sup>19</sup>Then the people of Israel rose in the morning and encamped against Gibeah.<sup>20</sup>And the men of Israel went out to fight against Benjamin, and the men of Israel drew up the battle line against them at Gibeah.<sup>21</sup>The people of Benjamin came out of Gibeah and destroyed on that day 22,000 men of the Israelites.<sup>22</sup>But the people, the men of Israel, took courage, and again formed the battle line in the same place where they had formed it on the first day.<sup>23</sup>And the people of Israel went up and wept before the LORD until the evening. And they inquired of the LORD, "Shall we again draw near to fight against our brothers, the people of Benjamin?" And the LORD said, "Go up against them."<sup>24</sup>So the people of Israel came near against the people of Benjamin the second day.<sup>25</sup>And Benjamin went against them out of Gibeah the second day, and destroyed 18,000 men of the people of Israel. All these were men who drew the sword.<sup>26</sup>Then all the people of Israel, the whole army, went up and came to Bethel and wept. They sat there before the LORD and fasted that day until evening, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.<sup>27</sup>And the people of Israel inquired of the LORD (for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days,<sup>28</sup>and Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, ministered before it in those days), saying, "Shall we go out once more to battle against our brothers, the people of Benjamin, or shall we cease?" And the LORD said, "Go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand."<sup>29</sup>So Israel set men in ambush around Gibeah.<sup>30</sup>And the people of Israel went up against the people of Benjamin on the third day and set themselves in array against Gibeah, as at other times.<sup>31</sup>And the people of Benjamin went out against the people and were drawn away from the city. And as at other times they began to strike and kill some of the people in the highways, one of which goes up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, and in the open country, about thirty men of Israel.<sup>32</sup>And the people of Benjamin said, "They are routed before us, as at the first." But the people of Israel said, "Let us flee and draw them away from the city to the highways."<sup>33</sup>And all the men of Israel rose up out of their place and set themselves in array at Baal-tamar, and the men of Israel who were in ambush rushed out of their place from Maareh-geba.<sup>34</sup>And there came against Gibeah 10,000 chosen men out of all Israel, and the battle was hard, but the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was close upon them.<sup>35</sup>And the LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel, and the people of Israel destroyed 25,100 men of Benjamin that day. All these were men who drew the sword.<sup>36</sup>So the people of Benjamin saw that they were defeated. The men of Israel gave ground to Benjamin, because they trusted the men in ambush whom they had set against Gibeah.<sup>37</sup>Then the men in ambush hurried and rushed against Gibeah; the men in ambush moved out and struck all the city with the edge of the sword.<sup>38</sup>Now the appointed signal between the men of Israel and the men in the main ambush was that when they made a great cloud of smoke rise up out of the city<sup>39</sup>the men of Israel should turn in battle. Now Benjamin had begun to strike and kill about thirty men of Israel. They said, "Surely they are defeated before us, as in the first battle."<sup>40</sup>But when the signal began to rise out of the city in a column of smoke, the Benjaminites looked behind them, and behold, the whole of the city went up in smoke to heaven.<sup>41</sup>Then the men of Israel turned, and the men of Benjamin were dismayed, for they saw that disaster was close upon them.<sup>42</sup>Therefore they turned their backs before the men of Israel in the direction of the wilderness, but the battle overtook them. And those who came out of the cities were destroying them in their midst.<sup>43</sup>Surrounding the Benjaminites, they pursued them and trod them down from Nohah as far as opposite Gibeah on the east.<sup>44</sup>Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all of them men of valor.<sup>45</sup>And they turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. Five thousand men of them were cut down in the highways. And they were pursued hard to Gidom, and 2,000 men of them were struck down.<sup>46</sup>So all who fell that day of Benjamin were 25,000 men who drew the sword, all of them men of valor.<sup>47</sup>But 600 men turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon and remained at the rock of Rimmon four months.<sup>48</sup>And the men of Israel turned back against the people of Benjamin and struck them with the edge of the sword, the city, men and beasts and all that they found. And all the towns that they found they set on fire.
20.overview:
Where we are. A Levite’s concubine has been raped to death at Gibeah in Benjamin, and her husband has sent her dismembered body through all Israel (chapter 19). Now the nation gathers to act.

The message. A people can be right about the wrong done, right about the law, even right in God’s eyes, and still bring disaster on itself, because a just cause does not make us just. Benjamin is destroyed for standing behind guilty men. Israel loses forty thousand men before it asks God whether to fight at all, and only when it offers him the word “cease” does he answer with a promise. Then, with God’s victory in its hands, it burns every town in Benjamin.

Why it was said. This story comes from early in the period (Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, is still priest, v. 28), but the writer sets it near the end of the book to show what the whole age was like when “there was no king in Israel” (see the introduction). The first hearers see that tribal loyalty, self-serving testimony and unchecked zeal can tear God’s people apart as surely as any foreign enemy.

How the chapter makes its case. All Israel musters “as one man” at Mizpah, hears the Levite and demands the guilty men; Benjamin refuses (vv. 1–13). Israel asks God only who should go first, and is beaten twice (vv. 14–25). The third time the nation weeps, fasts and sacrifices, and asks “or shall we cease?”; God promises victory, and an ambush wins it, as “the LORD defeated Benjamin” (vv. 26–36). The battle is retold: Gibeah burns, six hundred Benjaminites escape, and Israel destroys every town in Benjamin (vv. 37–48).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by contrast. The book opened by asking, “Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites?” (1:1); here the same question is asked about Israel’s own brothers (v. 18). Judges longs for a king who will do justice without excess. And Benjamin, which put itself between guilty men and their punishment and died with them, is the dark opposite of Jesus, who stood between the guilty and justice to bear their punishment: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). Benjamin died with the guilty; Christ died instead of them.

For us. Do not shield your own group, family or church from the truth about wrong done within it; people justified by grace can afford to say, “give up the men.” Tell your failures honestly. When you are most sure you are right, keep asking God, and keep weighing every further step. The cross is where our sin is neither excused nor avenged by us, but borne.
20.theology:
Benjamin's choice (v. 13). Loyalty to one's own, right or wrong, binds a whole community to the worst thing done inside it. Benjamin is destroyed not for the crime at Gibeah but for standing behind it.

The three enquiries. "Who goes first?" (v. 18) assumed the war and asked about the marching order. "Shall we go again against our brothers?" (v. 23) at least named them as kin. Only the third, or shall we cease? (v. 28), puts the whole thing back in God's hands with a refusal genuinely possible, and that is the one he answers with tomorrow I will give them into your hand. Such prayer is not doubt about God, who has already bound himself to his people; it is trust that he may know better than we do.

Right, and terrible (v. 48). The crime was real, the demand lawful, and the LORD himself gave the victory; and by nightfall a tribe was destroyed. When we are certain we are right, we stop weighing what we do.

With, or instead. Benjamin put itself between guilty men and the justice they had earned and was destroyed in their place, and deserved it, because it was covering sin, not bearing it. One other stood in that position, not to hide sin but to carry its punishment: he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Pet. 2:24). Benjamin perished with the guilty because it took their side; Christ perished instead of them because he took their place, and only one of those leaves anybody alive.
20.examples:
