Then: A nation that would not raise an army against any of its enemies raised four hundred thousand men against one of its own tribes, was right about everything, lost forty thousand men before it asked God whether to fight at all, and then burned every town in Benjamin.

Now: Two things. First, watch how you tell the story of something that went wrong with your help. The Levite got every fact right and left himself out of the one sentence that mattered, and four hundred thousand men acted on it. We can afford to put ourselves back in the story, because the God who laid our sins on Christ forgives what is confessed (1 John 1:9). Second, and harder: when you are certain you are in the right, notice whether you have stopped asking. Israel's prayers improved as its army shrank, and the only prayer God answered with a promise was the one that offered him the word cease. A cause that cannot be halted by God is not being held before him; it is being announced to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is united at last, but against itself, and the trouble starts with how the story is told and who will face the truth. The whole nation, from Dan to Beersheba and Gilead too, gathers “as one man” at Mizpah, four hundred thousand swordsmen (vv. 1–2). The Levite tells what happened at Gibeah, accurately but leaving out his own part (vv. 3–7). The assembly vows not to go home, organises supplies, and sends to Benjamin with a demand that is exactly right: hand over the worthless men of Gibeah to be put to death, and so “purge evil from Israel” (vv. 8–13). Benjamin will not listen to its brothers.
verseByVerse.theology: Unity is not the same as being right. The first thing the whole nation ever does together is go to war with itself.
verseByVerse.examples: Before acting on someone's account of a wrong, ask what part the teller played. Israel asked the Levite how it happened (v. 3) and asked nothing further.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people of Israel came out, from Dan to Beersheba, including the land of Gilead, and the congregation assembled as one man to the LORD at Mizpah. And the chiefs of all the people, of all the tribes of Israel, presented themselves in the assembly of the people of God, 400,000 men on foot that drew the sword. (Now the people of Benjamin heard that the people of Israel had gone up to Mizpah.) And the people of Israel said, "Tell us, how did this evil happen?" And the Levite, the husband of the woman who was murdered, answered and said, "I came to Gibeah that belongs to Benjamin, I and my concubine, to spend the night. And the leaders of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house against me by night. They meant to kill me, and they violated my concubine, and she is dead. So I took hold of my concubine and cut her in pieces and sent her throughout all the country of the inheritance of Israel, for they have committed abomination and outrage in Israel. Behold, you people of Israel, all of you, give your advice and counsel here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All Israel unites, at last, to deal with the crime at Gibeah, and it acts on the Levite’s account: true in every fact he gives, but silent about his own part.

Assembled as one man. No other muster in the book manages this: Dan to Beersheba, Gilead too, every tribe as one man. Barak could not get Reuben, Dan or Asher to leave their sheepfolds and their ships (5:16–17). Gideon was left with three hundred. Jephthah faced Ammon with Gilead alone. Judah turned out three thousand men, to arrest Samson (15:11). Four hundred thousand men could be raised in this country; they had simply never been raised against an enemy.

The Levite answered and said. The Levite’s statement is true in every fact, and it is not honest. He says the leaders of Gibeah, where chapter 19 said worthless fellows of the city. They meant to kill me is a reasonable inference from what they demanded, not what they said. They violated my concubine, and she is dead is exactly what happened.

What he leaves out. He leaves out the door: that the mob asked for him, that the old man offered two women in his place, and that he himself seized his concubine and put her outside (19:25). He is perfectly willing to describe how he took hold of her and cut her in pieces; only the earlier taking hold is missing. Four hundred thousand men are about to go to war on an account whose one missing detail is the speaker’s part.

Worse than a lie. It is worse for not being a lie: a true account arranged so that the speaker is absent from the part he would have to answer for, which is what any of us produces when we tell the story of a disaster we helped cause. The gospel gives us a reason to put ourselves back into the story, because the God who laid our sins on Christ forgives what is confessed (1 John 1:9).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for thousand (’eleph) can also mean a clan or a military unit, and some careful conservative scholars think the figures in these chapters count units rather than individual men, which would make the armies much smaller. Others take them at face value. Either way the writer’s point is the contrast: this is the largest army in the book.
verseByVerse.note: “From Dan to Beersheba” means the whole land, north to south.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people arose as one man, saying, "None of us will go to his tent, and none of us will return to his house. But now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot, and we will take ten men of a hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred of a thousand, and a thousand of ten thousand, to bring provisions for the people, that when they come they may repay Gibeah of Benjamin for all the outrage that they have committed in Israel." So all the men of Israel gathered against the city, united as one man. And the tribes of Israel sent men through all the tribe of Benjamin, saying, "What evil is this that has taken place among you? Now therefore give up the men, the worthless fellows in Gibeah, that we may put them to death and purge evil from Israel." But the Benjaminites would not listen to the voice of their brothers, the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel makes exactly the right demand, that the guilty men of Gibeah be handed over for justice, and Benjamin refuses, choosing loyalty to its own over the law of God.

None of us will go to his tent. Their oath not to go home is the first of three in these two chapters that will cost them dearly (compare 21:1, 5). They organise properly, a tenth of the men bringing food for the rest, and the response is still aimed at one town: this is what we will do to Gibeah.

Give up the men. The demand is entirely right. They do not attack first. They send messengers, state the charge and ask for the guilty men: not the tribe, not the town, the men. Purge evil from Israel echoes the formula Deuteronomy attaches to the gravest offences, purge the evil from your midst (Deut. 13:5; 17:7; 19:19; 22:21). Here Israel is doing exactly what God required of it.

Benjamin would not listen. Everything turns on that refusal, and there is no defending it. Benjamin was asked to give up no land and no independence, only a gang of rapists and murderers, by its own brothers, under its own law. It chose the tribe over the law: whatever the men of Gibeah had done, they were Benjaminites.

Ours, right or wrong. It is the oldest and most respectable form of corruption, always defended in the language of loyalty: we do not hand our own over to outsiders. What it produces, every time, is a whole community bound to the worst thing done inside it, because to condemn the man is now to betray the family. Benjamin is about to be almost wiped out, not for the crime at Gibeah, the act of a mob, but for the decision to stand behind it.

The tribe over the truth. George Orwell, in his essay “Notes on Nationalism”, observed that partisans do not merely excuse atrocities committed by their own side; they have a remarkable capacity for never hearing about them at all. Benjamin is the oldest example; the newest is the party, the movement, the firm, the family and, to its shame, the church that will not give up its own. When my identity rests on belonging to the good side, admitting that my side has done evil feels like losing myself, so I explain it away, call it a smear and turn on the accuser. The gospel breaks the spell at the root. A Christian’s standing does not depend on his group’s innocence; the church is a community people enter by confessing that they are guilty (1 John 1:8–9). People justified by grace can afford to hear the worst about their own side and to say, before anyone has to drag it out of them, “give up the men.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A right cause, pursued without asking God the right question, ends in defeat. Benjamin brings twenty-six thousand swordsmen and seven hundred left-handed slingers who never miss (vv. 14–17). At Bethel Israel asks only who should go up first, and is told, “Judah” (v. 18). On the first day Benjamin kills twenty-two thousand Israelites (vv. 19–21). Israel weeps before the LORD, asks whether to fight “our brothers” again, and is told, “Go up,” with no promise of victory; on the second day eighteen thousand more fall (vv. 22–25). The lawful demand, the numbers and a word from God have not made the war safe.
verseByVerse.theology: Victory is not a verdict. Israel loses twice in a just cause, so the outcome of a battle cannot tell anyone who is in the right.
verseByVerse.examples: Most of us know the first two prayers well: asking God's help with a decision already made. The answer is not to pray less but to bring him the decision itself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Benjamin came together out of the cities to Gibeah to go out to battle against the people of Israel. And the people of Benjamin mustered out of their cities on that day 26,000 men who drew the sword, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, who mustered 700 chosen men. Among all these were 700 chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss. And the men of Israel, apart from Benjamin, mustered 400,000 men who drew the sword; all these were men of war. The people of Israel arose and went up to Bethel and inquired of God, "Who shall go up first for us to fight against the people of Benjamin?" And the LORD said, "Judah shall go up first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin musters to defend Gibeah, and Israel asks God only who should lead the attack, not whether to fight at all.

26,000 men who drew the sword. Outnumbered fifteen to one, Benjamin comes anyway, without hesitating. Whatever else is true of this tribe, it is not cowardly, and the writer pauses to tell us its speciality.

700 chosen men who were left-handed. Seven hundred left-handed slingers, each able to hit a hair. The name Benjamin means “son of the right hand” (Gen. 35:18), and its elite troops are all left-handed. Ehud was a left-handed Benjaminite too, which let him carry a blade where nobody thought to look (3:15–16). The sling will be famous again when a shepherd boy from Judah brings down a Philistine with one (1 Sam. 17:49).

Who shall go up first? Israel’s question at Bethel, and God’s answer, are almost word for word the first two verses of the book (1:1–2). The book has come full circle; the difference is who stands on the other side of the valley. In chapter 1 it was the Canaanites; here it is Benjamin. Between them lies the story of a nation that would not fight its enemies and ended able to fight nobody but itself.

What they did not ask. They asked about the order of march. They did not ask whether God wanted this war fought at all, whether four hundred thousand men should march against twenty-six thousand of their own countrymen, or what he thought of the case. The campaign was decided at Mizpah before anyone came to Bethel, and God was consulted only about the arrangements.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Israel rose in the morning and encamped against Gibeah. And the men of Israel went out to fight against Benjamin, and the men of Israel drew up the battle line against them at Gibeah. The people of Benjamin came out of Gibeah and destroyed on that day 22,000 men of the Israelites. But the people, the men of Israel, took courage, and again formed the battle line in the same place where they had formed it on the first day. And the people of Israel went up and wept before the LORD until the evening. And they inquired of the LORD, "Shall we again draw near to fight against our brothers, the people of Benjamin?" And the LORD said, "Go up against them." So the people of Israel came near against the people of Benjamin the second day. And Benjamin went against them out of Gibeah the second day, and destroyed 18,000 men of the people of Israel. All these were men who drew the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel has the just cause, the numbers and a word from God, and still loses forty thousand men in two days, because it has assumed God’s backing rather than sought it.

22,000 men of the Israelites. This is the chapter’s stubborn difficulty. Everything they had done was correct, and they lost more men in one day than Gideon ever took into battle.

Our brothers. The second question is better than the first, and the phrase that makes it better is our brothers. They weep and name Benjamin as kin; the arrest of criminals is now seen for what it is, a war between brothers. But the question is still “shall we again draw near to fight”, and the answer is Go up against them, with no promise attached.

The assumption underneath. What was wrong was not the cause but the assumption beneath it: that God’s agreement could be taken for granted because their case was good, and only the arrangements were left to settle with him. Forty thousand men die before anybody asks a question that leaves God free to say no. This is not a warning against being right. It is exactly when our cause is good that we stop asking God and start telling him, because when a thing is obviously just, asking whether to do it feels like weakness.

Why did they lose? God did not deceive them; he told them the truth both times. He simply promised them nothing, and they did not notice. Many commentators add a second answer, and it is fair to the book. The whole nation, not Benjamin alone, had been tolerating idols (the shrine at Dan was still standing, 18:30–31), and the defeats humbled all Israel before the victory came. God was punishing Gibeah’s crime and, at the same time, humbling the tribes he used to punish it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel finally humbles itself and leaves God free to say no, he gives victory. The whole army goes to Bethel, weeps, fasts until evening, and offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, with Phinehas ministering before the ark (vv. 26–28). This time they ask, “or shall we cease?”, and the LORD answers, “Go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand” (v. 28). On the third day Israel sets an ambush, feigns retreat as before, and draws Benjamin away from Gibeah (vv. 29–32). The hidden force breaks out, and the narrator gives the credit plainly: “the LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel” (vv. 33–36).
verseByVerse.theology: Repentance comes before the promise: weeping, fasting and offerings, and then a question that leaves God free to say no.
verseByVerse.examples: When a cause you were sure of goes badly wrong, the third day is the pattern: stop, grieve, come to God, and let him decide whether you go on.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people of Israel, the whole army, went up and came to Bethel and wept. They sat there before the LORD and fasted that day until evening, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. And the people of Israel inquired of the LORD (for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days, and Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, ministered before it in those days), saying, "Shall we go out once more to battle against our brothers, the people of Benjamin, or shall we cease?" And the LORD said, "Go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Humbled at last, Israel weeps, fasts, sacrifices and asks whether it should stop, and to that question God answers with a promise of victory.

All the people of Israel went up and wept. They had wept once before (v. 23); the fasting, the burnt offerings and the peace offerings are new. The war council has become a nation in mourning.

Or shall we cease? It took forty thousand deaths to reach the question. For the first time Israel offers God the possibility of stopping. Twice he had said go up and nothing more. Now: Go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand. Nothing about their case has changed; what has changed is that they are asking rather than assuming, prepared to be told no. Prayer genuinely willing to receive a refusal is different from prayer that has already decided, and God treats the two differently.

The ark at Bethel. The ark is at Bethel here, though the tabernacle was at Shiloh (18:31). It had probably been brought to Bethel, about ten miles south, for the war, as it was later carried into battle (1 Sam. 4:4). The KJV translates the place as the house of God in these chapters (20:18, 26; 21:2), which is what Bethel means; modern versions take it as the town.

Phinehas the son of Eleazar. The name dates these chapters. Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, stopped the plague at Peor with a spear in Moses’ own lifetime (Num. 25:7–11). If he is still ministering, this is very near the beginning of the time of the judges, within a generation or two of Joshua. These last five chapters are not the final collapse after Samson. The writer has gathered the worst of the age and placed it at the end as a summary, and the point is not “look what Israel came to” but “look what Israel was, from the start”: the private shrine, the priest for hire, the migration, Gibeah, all within living memory of the conquest.
verseByVerse.note: Burnt offerings were given wholly to God; peace offerings were shared in a meal, a sign of fellowship restored.

verseByVerse.quote: So Israel set men in ambush around Gibeah. And the people of Israel went up against the people of Benjamin on the third day and set themselves in array against Gibeah, as at other times. And the people of Benjamin went out against the people and were drawn away from the city. And as at other times they began to strike and kill some of the people in the highways, one of which goes up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, and in the open country, about thirty men of Israel. And the people of Benjamin said, "They are routed before us, as at the first." But the people of Israel said, "Let us flee and draw them away from the city to the highways."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel sets an ambush, and Benjamin, trusting that the third day will go like the first two, is drawn away from Gibeah into the trap.

Israel set men in ambush around Gibeah. The plan is Joshua’s plan at Ai, and it works the same way (Josh. 8:3–22): hide a force behind the city, offer the main army as bait, run when the garrison comes out, and let the ambush take the town from behind.

As at other times. This phrase is the trap. The third morning looks exactly like the first two: about thirty Israelites down, the line giving way. Because the same opening has twice ended in victory, Benjamin follows it a third time without looking, and its own experience kills it.

Let us flee. Twice the army had really run on this ground (vv. 21, 25); now it runs on purpose, and Benjamin cannot tell the difference. The flight draws the defenders out along the two highways that lead away from the town, one of them to Bethel, where the army had just been weeping before the LORD (v. 26), and every step of the chase takes them further from the gate they should be guarding.

Uncertain wording. The ESV has the other highway going “to Gibeah”, but the battle is at Gibeah and the roads lead away from it. Most likely the road went to Gibeon, a few miles to the north-west; the two names look much alike in Hebrew and are easily confused.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the men of Israel rose up out of their place and set themselves in array at Baal-tamar, and the men of Israel who were in ambush rushed out of their place from Maareh-geba. And there came against Gibeah 10,000 chosen men out of all Israel, and the battle was hard, but the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was close upon them. And the LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel, and the people of Israel destroyed 25,100 men of Benjamin that day. All these were men who drew the sword. So the people of Benjamin saw that they were defeated. The men of Israel gave ground to Benjamin, because they trusted the men in ambush whom they had set against Gibeah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ambush breaks out while Benjamin thinks it is winning, and the narrator gives the victory to the LORD, keeping the promise he had made.

Did not know that disaster was close upon them. The reader sees what Benjamin cannot: they think they are winning, and ruin is already behind them. It is the blindness of Samson, who “did not know that the LORD had left him” (16:20): confidence built on past success is most dangerous at the moment it feels surest.

The LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel. The narrator will not let the ambush have the credit. The plan was good and the ten thousand fought hard, yet the sentence that explains the day names God. He had said tomorrow I will give them into your hand, and this is that word being kept.

So the people of Benjamin saw. Verse 36 sums up the end of the day, and then the writer goes back over the same battle in closer detail, from the side of the ambush (vv. 36–46). Hebrew narrative often tells a story twice in this way, first the outcome and then how it came about, which is why the thirty fallen men, Benjamin’s boast and the death toll all appear twice.

The numbers. Verse 35 counts 25,100 Benjaminites killed; verses 44–46 give the round total, 25,000. Benjamin had mustered 26,700 (v. 15) and 600 escaped (v. 47), so about a thousand are not accounted for; some Greek manuscripts give a lower figure at verse 15, and others suppose some Benjaminites fell in the first two days.

Uncertain wording. Neither Baal-tamar nor Maareh-geba can now be identified with certainty. Baal-tamar means “lord of the palm tree”, and Maareh-geba probably means an open place near Geba, a little east of Gibeah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–48 — What a Just War Became
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A just war ends in a slaughter that goes far beyond justice. The writer retells the battle from the ambush’s side: the city is struck, the smoke signal rises, and Benjamin, looking back, sees Gibeah burning and knows that disaster has come (vv. 37–41). They flee toward the wilderness, and twenty-five thousand brave men fall (vv. 42–46). Six hundred reach the rock of Rimmon and hold out there four months (v. 47). Then Israel turns back through Benjamin, strikes down people and animals alike, and sets every town on fire (v. 48). The demand was for the guilty men of one town; the result is a tribe almost wiped out.
verseByVerse.theology: What was demanded at v. 13 was the surrender of the guilty men of one town. What is done at v. 48 is the destruction of a tribe, its women, children, animals and towns, in language borrowed from the conquest of Canaan.
verseByVerse.examples: Anger that begins as justice for a victim can end by making many new victims. Notice how far v. 48 has travelled from v. 13.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men in ambush hurried and rushed against Gibeah; the men in ambush moved out and struck all the city with the edge of the sword. Now the appointed signal between the men of Israel and the men in the main ambush was that when they made a great cloud of smoke rise up out of the city the men of Israel should turn in battle. Now Benjamin had begun to strike and kill about thirty men of Israel. They said, "Surely they are defeated before us, as in the first battle." But when the signal began to rise out of the city in a column of smoke, the Benjaminites looked behind them, and behold, the whole of the city went up in smoke to heaven. Then the men of Israel turned, and the men of Benjamin were dismayed, for they saw that disaster was close upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer retells the decisive moment from closer up: the ambush takes Gibeah, the smoke goes up, and Benjamin, turning round, sees that all is lost.

The appointed signal. Verses 37–39 explain what verse 33 left out: the ambush was to take the city and send up a great cloud of smoke, the main army’s cue to stop running and turn. Benjamin’s boast is heard again, Surely they are defeated before us, as in the first battle (compare v. 32), because the writer is retelling the same moment (see the note on vv. 33–36).

The city went up in smoke to heaven. The men of Benjamin turn round in the middle of a battle they think they are winning and see their town burning, and when the fleeing army turns to fight, they understand everything at once.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they turned their backs before the men of Israel in the direction of the wilderness, but the battle overtook them. And those who came out of the cities were destroying them in their midst. Surrounding the Benjaminites, they pursued them and trod them down from Nohah as far as opposite Gibeah on the east. Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all of them men of valor. And they turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. Five thousand men of them were cut down in the highways. And they were pursued hard to Gidom, and 2,000 men of them were struck down. So all who fell that day of Benjamin were 25,000 men who drew the sword, all of them men of valor. But 600 men turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon and remained at the rock of Rimmon four months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin’s army is caught between two forces and destroyed, and of twenty-six thousand brave men only six hundred escape to the rock of Rimmon.

The battle overtook them. They run east toward the wilderness, but the army is in front of them and the force from the burning town (those who came out of the cities) closes from behind. The figures in verses 44–46, eighteen thousand, then five thousand and two thousand more, make up the round twenty-five thousand of verse 46 (on the numbers, see the note on vv. 33–36).

The rock of Rimmon. Probably the limestone crag by the modern village of Rammun, a few miles east of Bethel, a place of caves where a small band could hold out.

All of them men of valor. The writer says it twice, over their bodies: these were brave men, and their bravery was spent defending the indefensible. Six hundred are left, and the whole tribe of Benjamin is now this: men with no wives, no towns and no children, sitting on a crag in the desert for four months, waiting to see whether anyone is still hunting them. The tribe survives, but it stays small: when Saul is chosen as Israel’s first king, he can call it the least of the tribes of Israel (1 Sam. 9:21).

Uncertain wording. In verse 43 the ESV reads a place name, Nohah, but the Hebrew word can also be read as “resting place” or “with ease”, which is why older versions say Israel trod Benjamin down “with ease”. Gidom (v. 45) is otherwise unknown. Either way the picture is a pursuit that gave Benjamin no rest.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Israel turned back against the people of Benjamin and struck them with the edge of the sword, the city, men and beasts and all that they found. And all the towns that they found they set on fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the victory God gave, Israel goes far beyond justice: the demand had been for the guilty men of one town, and the end is a whole tribe’s towns burned and its people killed.

The whole territory. The last verse undoes everything the chapter began with. In verse 13 Israel demanded the men, the worthless fellows in Gibeah: one town, the guilty, under the law. Now it kills everything it finds in Benjamin, women and children who never went near Gibeah included, and burns every town, in the language of the conquest of Canaan, now turned on a tribe of Israel. The next chapter opens with the whole nation at Bethel weeping over what it has done.

Hold the two facts together. Separating them is how this chapter gets misread. Israel was right: the crime at Gibeah was real and monstrous, the demand lawful, Benjamin’s refusal indefensible. Israel wept, fasted, sacrificed and asked whether to stop, and God himself gave the victory. By nightfall they had destroyed a tribe.

Perished instead of the guilty. Benjamin died for sheltering guilty men, covering their sin rather than bearing it. One other stood between guilty men and the justice they had earned and was destroyed in their place, not to hide their sin but to pay for it: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Pet. 2:24). Benjamin perished with the guilty because it took their side; Christ perished instead of the guilty because he took their place. Only one of the two leaves anybody alive.

The danger of a just cause. Being in the wrong makes a person cautious. Being demonstrably in the right takes the brake off, because every further step is carried by the certainty that justified the first. Israel never asked whether burning the villages was warranted; it had settled who was righteous days earlier, and after that there was nothing left to weigh.

Did God command this? No. He promised the defeat of Benjamin’s army (v. 28); nowhere did he order the killing of its women and children or the burning of its towns. The narrator records it, as he records everything in these chapters, without approving it.

Uncertain wording. In the city, men and beasts, the Hebrew word read as “men” can, with different vowels, mean “entire”, giving “the entire city”. Either way the sense is the same: everything living in the towns was struck down.

keyVerse.quote: “Shall we go out once more to battle against our brothers, the people of Benjamin, or shall we cease?” And the LORD said, “Go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand.”
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the chapter. After forty thousand deaths Israel at last asks a question that leaves God free to say no, and only then does he answer with a promise. It shows the difference between telling God our plans and truly asking him.

20.reflection:
The Levite’s account was true in every fact but left out his own part (vv. 4–7; compare 19:25). Why is it so tempting to tell our stories this way, and what does the gospel give us that makes honest confession possible?

Benjamin chose loyalty to its own over justice (v. 13). Where do families, churches or other groups we belong to face that same temptation, and what would it look like to “give up the men”?

Compare Israel’s three questions to God (vv. 18, 23, 28). What is the difference between asking God to bless a decision we have already made and genuinely seeking his will?

Israel was in the right, yet ended by burning every town in Benjamin (v. 48). How can being sure we are right make us careless, and how does Christ, who bore sin rather than covering or avenging it, show us a better way?

21.title: Benjamin's Survival and the Final Verdict
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah, "No one of us shall give his daughter in marriage to Benjamin."<sup>2</sup>And the people came to Bethel and sat there till evening before God, and they lifted up their voices and wept bitterly.<sup>3</sup>And they said, "O LORD, the God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that today there should be one tribe lacking in Israel?"<sup>4</sup>And the next day the people rose early and built there an altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.<sup>5</sup>And the people of Israel said, "Which of all the tribes of Israel did not come up in the assembly to the LORD?" For they had taken a great oath concerning him who did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah, saying, "He shall surely be put to death."<sup>6</sup>And the people of Israel had compassion for Benjamin their brother and said, "One tribe is cut off from Israel this day.<sup>7</sup>What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since we have sworn by the LORD that we will not give them any of our daughters for wives?"<sup>8</sup>And they said, "What one is there of the tribes of Israel that did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah?" And behold, no one had come to the camp from Jabesh-gilead, to the assembly.<sup>9</sup>For when the people were mustered, behold, not one of the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead was there.<sup>10</sup>So the congregation sent 12,000 of their bravest men there and commanded them, "Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword; also the women and the little ones.<sup>11</sup>This is what you shall do: every male and every woman that has lain with a male you shall devote to destruction."<sup>12</sup>And they found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead 400 young virgins who had not known a man by lying with him, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.<sup>13</sup>Then the whole congregation sent word to the people of Benjamin who were at the rock of Rimmon and proclaimed peace to them.<sup>14</sup>And Benjamin returned at that time. And they gave them the women whom they had saved alive of the women of Jabesh-gilead, but they were not enough for them.<sup>15</sup>And the people had compassion on Benjamin because the LORD had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.<sup>16</sup>Then the elders of the congregation said, "What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since the women are destroyed out of Benjamin?"<sup>17</sup>And they said, "There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, that a tribe not be blotted out from Israel.<sup>18</sup>Yet we cannot give them wives from our daughters." For the people of Israel had sworn, "Cursed be he who gives a wife to Benjamin."<sup>19</sup>So they said, "Behold, there is the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh, which is north of Bethel, on the east of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah."<sup>20</sup>And they commanded the people of Benjamin, saying, "Go and lie in ambush in the vineyards<sup>21</sup>and watch. If the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out of the vineyards and snatch each man his wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.<sup>22</sup>And when their fathers or their brothers come to complain to us, we will say to them, 'Grant them graciously to us, because we did not take for each man of them his wife in battle, neither did you give them to them, else you would now be guilty.'"<sup>23</sup>And the people of Benjamin did so and took their wives, according to their number, from the dancers whom they carried off. Then they went and returned to their inheritance and rebuilt the towns and lived in them.<sup>24</sup>And the people of Israel departed from there at that time, every man to his tribe and family, and they went out from there every man to his inheritance.<sup>25</sup>In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
21.overview:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of Judges. Israel has defeated Benjamin and then burned its towns and killed its people, until only six hundred men are left on the rock of Rimmon (20:47–48). Now the victors have to live with what they have done.

The message. Grief without repentance, and rules without God, only make things worse. Israel weeps over the missing tribe but never says “we did this”. Bound by rash oaths it will not bring to God, it saves Benjamin by destroying a town and abducting girls at a feast of the LORD, keeping the letter of its vows while trampling everything they were for. The book ends with its diagnosis: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (v. 25).

Why it was said. The writer is looking back from the time of the kings (see the introduction). These last scenes, from early in the period, show the first hearers what Israel was when God’s people had no king and every man was his own judge: sincere, religious, emotional, and utterly lost.

How the chapter makes its case. At Bethel Israel weeps over Benjamin, asks God why it has happened, and builds an altar, but does not reconsider its oath to give Benjamin no wives (vv. 1–7). A second oath, death to any town that missed the muster, is turned on Jabesh-gilead: the town is destroyed and four hundred young women are taken for Benjamin, not enough (vv. 8–15). The elders send the remaining Benjaminites to seize girls dancing at the yearly feast at Shiloh, and prepare an answer for their fathers (vv. 16–22). Benjamin rebuilds, everyone goes home, and the book ends with no king (vv. 23–25).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by promise. The book ends asking for a king, and the next book in our Bibles, Ruth, “in the days when the judges ruled” (Ruth 1:1), ends with David, born at Bethlehem. But David too failed, and Micah promised another ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2). Jesus is that King: he does what is right in his Father’s eyes, gives his people new hearts, and reigns for ever, “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Revelation 19:16).

For us. Sorrow over the damage we have caused is not the same as confessing that we caused it; the gospel makes it safe to say “I did this”. Do not keep the letter of a promise or rule while defeating its purpose and harming others. And refuse the age’s creed, that each of us decides what is right: we have a King, and life under him is freedom.
21.theology:
Grief is not repentance (v. 3). The tears are real, but the wording leaves out who did it: why has this happened, not “what have we done”.

Jephthah's error, held nationally (v. 7). Since we have sworn is Jephthah's conviction again (11:35), now held by a whole people, with the same refusal to look at what the law provided for a rash oath.

Providence made to carry it (vv. 3, 15). Twice the destruction of Benjamin is laid at God's door. He gave the victory; he never told them to burn the towns, swear the oath, or destroy Jabesh-gilead.

Verse 22 is the whole book in one piece of legal advice. You did not give them to them, else you would now be guilty. Every word of the oath survives and its entire purpose is defeated. This is not lawlessness but rule-keeping to the letter that throws away what the rule was for, the instinct the Lord named in his own day (Mark 7:11-13; Matt. 23:24).

The ending is a need, not an answer. No judge, no enemy defeated, no repentance, no rebuke, no word from God, and no the land had rest. Ruth follows in English Bibles, in the days when the judges ruled, beginning at Bethlehem and ending with the line of David (Ruth 1:1; 4:21-22). And David was not the last word either. The book is finally answered by the other man from Bethlehem (Mic. 5:2), whose rest does not end after forty years, and whose name is written King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16).
21.examples:
Then: A nation wept all day over a tribe it had destroyed, asked God why he had let it happen, and then, rather than reconsider two oaths it had never asked him about, wiped out an Israelite town for its virgins and staged an abduction at a festival of the LORD, so that no man present would technically be guilty.

Now: Two questions and a hope. First, listen to how you grieve over damage you have done: why has this happened and what have I done are not the same prayer, and only the second can be answered with forgiveness: the God who has already provided the sacrifice forgives what is owned before him (Psalm 32:5). Second, look for verse 22 in your own reasoning: the arrangement that keeps every rule intact while defeating everything the rule was for, and costs somebody who is not in the room. And then the hope, which is why the book ends where it does. It leaves you in a country with no king and does not pretend to fix it. Ruth begins on the next page in Bethlehem and ends with David, and David was not enough either. In those days there was no king in Israel. There is one now. And to anyone who has been taken, forced or abused as the women of Jabesh-gilead and Shiloh were: Scripture records it here and condemns it elsewhere, for God’s law made kidnapping a capital crime (Exodus 21:16; Deuteronomy 24:7) and declared the forced woman innocent (Deuteronomy 22:25–27). It was never your fault. If you are in danger, seek safety at once and tell someone who can help; the King who reigns now never asks anyone to stay in harm’s way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel grieves over Benjamin but will not own what it has done or undo its rash oath. At Mizpah the men had sworn not to give their daughters to Benjamin (v. 1). Now they sit at Bethel until evening, weep bitterly, and ask God, “why has this happened in Israel, that today there should be one tribe lacking in Israel?” (vv. 2–3), as if nobody had done it. They build an altar and sacrifice (v. 4). Then they remember a second oath, death to any town that stayed away from Mizpah (v. 5), and with real compassion for “Benjamin their brother” face the problem: six hundred men, no wives, and a vow in the way (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: An oath sworn in anger and never brought to God becomes the master of everything that follows. They asked him nothing before swearing it, and they ask him nothing about keeping it.
verseByVerse.examples: Their compassion for Benjamin (v. 6) is not play-acting. It is the second half of the sentence that dooms everybody: they will not reconsider the vow.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah, "No one of us shall give his daughter in marriage to Benjamin." And the people came to Bethel and sat there till evening before God, and they lifted up their voices and wept bitterly. And they said, "O LORD, the God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that today there should be one tribe lacking in Israel?" And the next day the people rose early and built there an altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel weeps bitterly before God over the loss of a tribe, but its grief never becomes repentance: nobody says “we did this”.

The men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah. The narrator reaches back to an oath we had not heard of, sworn in the first heat of the outrage, and it made sense at the time: a tribe that would shelter the men of Gibeah was not a tribe you married your daughters into. But the whole business of these chapters has been men resolving first and enquiring afterwards, and this vow was never brought to God at all.

They wept bitterly. The weeping is real. They do not celebrate the victory or count the spoil; the whole army sits before God until dark and cries aloud. They have destroyed their own brother and they know it.

Why has this happened in Israel? Then they ask God why, and everything that follows grows out of the question. As though it had simply happened, with nobody doing it; as though a tribe had gone missing overnight. They had marched on Benjamin, burned every town and killed everything they found (20:48). There is no mystery about why one tribe is lacking.

Built there an altar. They build an altar and sacrifice. The instinct is right and it goes nowhere, because in a moment they will turn from the altar to the problem and solve it entirely by themselves. God is worshipped in this chapter and never consulted. They weep at him, sacrifice to him, and then hold a committee.

Sorrow and repentance. Sorrow and repentance are not the same thing, and this scene shows the difference. Everything here looks like the real thing; what is missing is one sentence beginning we. A person can be genuinely broken-hearted about a situation he created and never once own it, grieving over the result and asking God why, but never saying “I did this”.

The passive voice of the heart. Public life has a whole grammar for this: things went wrong, lessons will be learned, mistakes were made. Nobody is lying; the subject of the sentence has simply disappeared. We do it in private too, and the reason is deeper than pride. Most of us carry an unspoken sense that our worth depends on being basically good, and to say “I did this” about something terrible would take away the ground we stand on. The religious do it as easily as anyone: Israel is weeping in front of an altar. The gospel makes the first person safe to use. If God has already seen the worst of us and dealt with it at the cross, confession is not the end of our standing but the way into it. David could say, “I have sinned against the LORD,” and hear in the same breath, “The LORD also has put away your sin” (2 Sam. 12:13). Only a forgiven people can afford the word we.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel said, "Which of all the tribes of Israel did not come up in the assembly to the LORD?" For they had taken a great oath concerning him who did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah, saying, "He shall surely be put to death." And the people of Israel had compassion for Benjamin their brother and said, "One tribe is cut off from Israel this day. What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since we have sworn by the LORD that we will not give them any of our daughters for wives?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s compassion for Benjamin is real, but it treats two rash oaths as unbreakable and asks only how to get round them, never whether they were right.

A second oath. At Mizpah they swore two things: no daughter to Benjamin, and death to any town that stayed away. Neither was commanded; neither was brought to God. Between them, over the next twenty verses, they will produce a massacre and a mass abduction.

Compassion for Benjamin their brother. The word is warm and meant; the enemy of the battle is their brother again, and their hearts are pointing the right way.

Since we have sworn. The second half of the sentence is where it goes wrong. The oath is treated as the one fixed object in the room. Compassion may move, the tribe may be saved, the plan may be anything at all, but the vow does not come up for discussion. So the question is not “was that oath righteous?” but “how do we get round it?” A nation that has decided it must keep the letter of a bad promise will find a way, and the way will cost somebody who is not in the room.

Jephthah again. The book has shown us this before. Jephthah said, I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow (11:35), and his daughter died for it, though the law he appealed to had made provision to redeem her. The same conviction is at work here, held by a whole nation: a word given to God is unbreakable, so whatever it costs must be paid. And as with Jephthah, nobody goes and looks. Leviticus 5:4–6 provides for exactly this case: a man who swears rashly with his lips, when he realises it, is guilty, brings a sin offering and is forgiven. There was an altar standing in front of them, and they had just been sacrificing on it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To get round one rash oath, Israel carries out another, and a whole town dies. Jabesh-gilead, east of the Jordan, had sent no one to the assembly (vv. 8–9). The congregation sends twelve thousand men to destroy it, women and children included, sparing only the virgins (vv. 10–11). Four hundred young women are brought to the camp at Shiloh (v. 12). Peace is proclaimed to the six hundred on the rock of Rimmon, and they return and are given the women, but there are not enough (vv. 13–14). The people feel for Benjamin, “because the LORD had made a breach in the tribes of Israel” (v. 15), laying at God’s door what they had done themselves.
verseByVerse.theology: This is a massacre carried out to repair the damage of a massacre, and the arithmetic is the whole reason for it: they needed wives, and the only lawful-seeming source was a town already under a death sentence by their own oath.
verseByVerse.examples: Remember Jabesh-gilead. Generations later a Benjaminite king will ride to its rescue in his first act as king (1 Sam. 11:1-11), and its men will risk their lives to recover his body from a Philistine wall (1 Sam. 31:11-13). The bond between that town and that tribe starts here, in blood.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said, "What one is there of the tribes of Israel that did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah?" And behold, no one had come to the camp from Jabesh-gilead, to the assembly. For when the people were mustered, behold, not one of the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead was there. So the congregation sent 12,000 of their bravest men there and commanded them, "Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword; also the women and the little ones. This is what you shall do: every male and every woman that has lain with a male you shall devote to destruction." And they found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead 400 young virgins who had not known a man by lying with him, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To keep one oath without breaking another, Israel destroys a whole Israelite town and takes its young women as brides for Benjamin.

Did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah. They go looking for a town under sentence, and find one. Follow the logic, because it is careful and it is monstrous. We may not give our daughters to Benjamin. But we swore that any town which missed the muster should die. If such a town exists, its people are already condemned, and its unmarried girls are not given by anyone; they are taken as spoil. The oath is untouched. Jabesh-gilead, east of the Jordan, had not come.

Also the women and the little ones. The order is explicit, and it is given not by a mob but by the assembly of Israel, just after it wept before God and built an altar, in a formal resolution, with twelve thousand picked men to carry it out.

Devote to destruction. This is the herem, the ban, by which a city was given wholly over to God in destruction: the word used of Jericho (Josh. 6:17). God had commanded that against the Canaanites, for their wickedness, after four centuries of patience. Israel now pronounces it on an Israelite town, on its own authority, to solve a shortage of brides.

400 young virgins. Four hundred girls are marched to Shiloh over the bodies of their families, and the writer records it flatly, as he does throughout these chapters. A woman was violated at Gibeah, and the nation went to war over it. In two chapters that war has produced the near extermination of a tribe and the abduction of hundreds of girls, and every step was taken by men who believed they were putting things right.

Jabesh-gilead later. The town is not finished in Scripture. When the Ammonites besiege Jabesh-gilead, it is Saul, a Benjaminite, who rescues it, and when Saul dies, its men risk their lives to recover his body (1 Sam. 11:1–11; 31:11–13). Many have suggested that the women taken here explain that bond between Jabesh and the tribe of Benjamin.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the whole congregation sent word to the people of Benjamin who were at the rock of Rimmon and proclaimed peace to them. And Benjamin returned at that time. And they gave them the women whom they had saved alive of the women of Jabesh-gilead, but they were not enough for them. And the people had compassion on Benjamin because the LORD had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace is made with Benjamin, but the women are not enough, and Israel speaks as if the LORD alone had made the breach it had made itself.

Proclaimed peace to them. After four months on the rock (20:47), the last men of Benjamin walk back into a nation that destroyed them.

But they were not enough. Six hundred men, four hundred women. The whole of Jabesh-gilead has been put to the sword and the sum still does not work, and the narrator states the shortfall as flatly as a storekeeper counting stock.

The LORD had made a breach. A breach is a gap where a tribe should be. Twice now the destruction of Benjamin has been spoken of as something that simply befell the nation (compare v. 3). There is a sense in which it is true: God did give Israel the victory, and said he would (20:28). But he never told them to burn the towns, kill the women and children, swear the oath or destroy Jabesh-gilead.

Blaming providence. Providence, God’s rule over everything that happens, gets the blame for the results of decisions God was never asked about. It is one of the commonest things people do with that truth, and this chapter shows how it works: you take the part he did, and quietly stretch it to cover the part you did.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book ends with the letter of an oath kept by a crime, and with its verdict on the whole age. The elders still need wives for two hundred men, but will not break their curse on anyone who gives a daughter to Benjamin (vv. 16–18). So they send the Benjaminites to hide in the vineyards at the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh and snatch girls as they dance, and they prepare what to tell the fathers: you did not give them, so you are not guilty (vv. 19–22). It works. Benjamin rebuilds, everyone goes home (vv. 23–24), and the book closes: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The scheme protects the men from guilt and does nothing at all for the girls. Rules kept for their own sake end by caring only for the people who keep them.
verseByVerse.examples: When you find yourself working out how to keep the wording of a promise while defeating its purpose, stop and ask who is paying for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the elders of the congregation said, "What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since the women are destroyed out of Benjamin?" And they said, "There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, that a tribe not be blotted out from Israel. Yet we cannot give them wives from our daughters." For the people of Israel had sworn, "Cursed be he who gives a wife to Benjamin." So they said, "Behold, there is the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh, which is north of Bethel, on the east of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah." And they commanded the people of Benjamin, saying, "Go and lie in ambush in the vineyards and watch. If the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out of the vineyards and snatch each man his wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin. And when their fathers or their brothers come to complain to us, we will say to them, 'Grant them graciously to us, because we did not take for each man of them his wife in battle, neither did you give them to them, else you would now be guilty.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders arrange the abduction of girls at a feast of the LORD so that no man breaks the letter of his oath: the rule is kept and everything it was for is trampled.

What shall we do for wives? The elders take over, and the problem is now purely technical: two hundred short. They hold two things with equal firmness: a tribe must not be blotted out, and we cannot give them our daughters. The oath has hardened since verse 1: it is no longer only we will not give but Cursed be he who gives a wife to Benjamin.

The yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh. Notice where the plan is set. Shiloh is where the house of God was, the place everyone in chapters 17 and 18 ignored (18:31), and this is the yearly feast of the LORD, with the young women out dancing as they did every year in safety. With dancing in the vineyards it was probably the autumn Feast of Booths, kept when the grapes were gathered in (Deut. 16:13–15). The careful directions in verse 19 suggest that the book’s first readers no longer knew the place: Shiloh was later destroyed, probably by the Philistines in Eli’s day (1 Sam. 4; Jer. 7:12).

Lie in ambush in the vineyards. The elders of Israel station armed men around a worship festival and tell them to seize the girls as they come out. The word is snatch.

Else you would now be guilty. Verse 22 holds the whole book. Neither did you give them to them: so the oath is intact, because giving was the forbidden act and no father gave anything. Else you would now be guilty: and there is the only thing they actually care about. Not the girls, not the fathers: only that no man should be technically in breach of a vow he should never have sworn. Every word of the oath survives; its whole purpose is defeated, since two hundred daughters of Israel end up in Benjamin exactly as if they had been handed over.

Religion with only rules. This is what religion becomes when nothing is left in it but rules. It is not lawlessness but its opposite, scrupulous and worked out with care by the elders at a feast of the LORD, and it produces an outcome so plainly wicked that no argument is needed; you only have to picture the vineyards.

Gnats and camels. The Lord Jesus met this instinct in his own day and named it. Men would not help a parent, having declared the money given to God, and he told them they had made void the word of God by their tradition, straining out gnats and swallowing camels (Mark 7:11–13; Matt. 23:24). Israel here strains out a gnat, and the camel goes down whole.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 22 is compressed and hard to construe, and translations differ in detail. The general sense is clear: the elders will ask the fathers to let the matter stand, because the war did not provide Benjamin with wives, and because the fathers, not having given their daughters, are not guilty of breaking the oath.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Benjamin did so and took their wives, according to their number, from the dancers whom they carried off. Then they went and returned to their inheritance and rebuilt the towns and lived in them. And the people of Israel departed from there at that time, every man to his tribe and family, and they went out from there every man to his inheritance. In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin is restored and everyone goes home, and the book ends not with rest or a deliverer but with a diagnosis: Israel had no king, and everyone was his own judge of what was right.

The people of Benjamin did so. It works. Benjamin goes home, rebuilds the burnt towns and settles in them, and no tribe is blotted out of Israel. Two hundred girls from Shiloh and four hundred from Jabesh-gilead never saw it coming, and nobody asked them anything at any point.

Every man to his inheritance. Everybody goes home, and that is the whole conclusion. No judge is raised up, no enemy is defeated, nobody repents or is rebuked, and God says nothing at all. The writer does not say that the land had rest, because it did not.

No king in Israel. There the book stops. The no king line has appeared four times in these five chapters, and this time nothing follows it: no closing prayer, no promise. The last sentence of Judges is a diagnosis.

Downhill all the way. Look back down the whole book. Othniel, and the land had rest forty years. Ehud, and eighty. Deborah, and forty. Gideon, and forty, and then an ephod that became a snare and seventy sons murdered on one stone. Jephthah, and no rest recorded at all. Samson, who only began to save Israel (13:5). Then a private shrine, a priest for hire, a woman dead on a doorstep, a war that destroyed a brother, and an ambush at a festival of the LORD. The writer’s explanation never changes: no king, and every man his own authority on what was good.

What Israel needed. The judges could not supply it. Every one was temporary, local and flawed. Israel needed not another deliverer for another crisis but a king: someone permanently over them, whose word settled what was right, so that a man’s own eyes were no longer the final court.

Turn the page. In English Bibles, which follow the order of the Greek Old Testament, the next words are: In the days when the judges ruled there was a famine in the land, and a man of Bethlehem in Judah went to sojourn in the country of Moab (Ruth 1:1). (The Hebrew Bible places Ruth later, among the Writings.) It is the same period, and a story that begins in Bethlehem, the town these closing chapters keep returning to (17:7; 19:1), and ends with a genealogy: Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David (Ruth 4:21–22). Ruth is the answer to Judges 21:25.

David was not the last word. Israel’s best king had a man killed to cover his adultery. The book that ends Everyone did what was right in his own eyes is not finally satisfied by a man from Bethlehem with a crown and a harp.

The other one from Bethlehem. But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel (Mic. 5:2). He came, born in Bethlehem, buried in a borrowed grave and raised on the third day, and no verse anywhere says that his rest came to an end after forty years. Where everyone did what was right in his own eyes, he did what was right in his Father’s, and gives that righteousness to all who trust him.

King of kings. Judges shows well-meaning people producing catastrophe because there is nobody over them, as in any life or age with no one on the throne. On leadership and order as God’s gift in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21. The last book of the Bible answers the last verse of Judges directly: on the robe and thigh of the rider on the white horse is written King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16). In those days there was no king in Israel. There is one now.

Is this an argument for monarchy? Samuel later treats the people’s demand for a king as a rejection of God (1 Sam. 8:7), and Gideon refused a crown because the LORD should rule (8:23). Both are true. Israel needed a king, but the right king in the right way: God had planned one (Deut. 17:14–20), and he chose David, whose Son is the King Israel finally needed.
verseByVerse.note: The book’s last words explain its chaos and point forward to the need for a godly king.

keyVerse.quote: In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
keyVerse.note: The last words of Judges explain the whole book, and especially its final five chapters. Without God’s rule through a faithful king, every man became his own judge, and sincere, religious people produced disaster. The verse leaves the reader longing for the King whom God would provide, fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

21.reflection:
Israel wept bitterly and asked God, “Why has this happened?” but never said “we did this” (vv. 2–3). What is the difference between sorrow and repentance, and why does the gospel make it safe to say “I did this”?

The people felt bound by rash oaths and asked only how to get round them (vv. 7, 18). Are there promises, rules or habits in your life or church that you keep to the letter while defeating their purpose? What would it look like to bring them honestly to God?

Verse 15 says “the LORD had made a breach”, yet the people had done the damage. How do we sometimes use God’s sovereignty to avoid taking responsibility?

Judges ends, “Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (v. 25). Where do you see that creed in our culture and in your own heart, and what difference does it make that Jesus is King?
